Either (a) state that additional hosts/scheduling were applied and quantify the new capacity, or (b) keep prefix caching as a partial mitigation and show that it alone cannot close an 18.6× gap. Do not claim that a 13% prefill reduction explains a 2.4 s → <2 s recovery under 18.6× oversubscription.
issue.acceptance_test: Recompute the post-mitigation prefill demand and capacity in the mini-case. The stated cause of the p95 TTFT recovery must be quantitatively sufficient to move the system from 2.4 s to below the SLO. If prefix caching is credited, the arithmetic must show that the remaining oversubscription is compatible with the observed latency.

issue.quoted_clause: The architecture is memory- and compute-sane at the 10 rps design point but was never sized for the lunch peak.
issue.observed: The mini-case diagnoses ~18.6× prefill oversubscription at 40 rps using a host capacity of ~2.77 PFLOP/s. At 10 rps, the same arithmetic gives 10 × 1.29 ≈ 12.9 PFLOP/s, which is ~4.66× the stated host capacity. A single host is therefore not compute-sane at 10 rps either.
issue.evidence: 10 rps × 1.29 PFLOP/request = 12.9 PFLOP/s. 12.9 / 2.77 ≈ 4.66. The text's own capacity figure makes the 10 rps design point oversubscribed if only one host is assumed. If multiple hosts are assumed, the 18.6× figure at 40 rps no longer follows from the stated host capacity.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case does not specify the host count consistently. The 18.6× figure assumes one host; the 'sane at 10 rps' claim assumes enough hosts to serve 10 rps. Both cannot be true with the same host count.
issue.correction: Specify the deployed host count in the mini-case. Then recompute both the 10 rps design-point utilization and the 40 rps peak oversubscription against that host count. If the architecture has N hosts, state N and use N × 2.77 PFLOP/s as capacity throughout.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case must contain an explicit host count and a capacity calculation that is consistent at both 10 rps and 40 rps. The 18.6× oversubscription figure must be reproducible from the stated host count and per-host capacity.

issue.observed: The text says percentiles are read by linear interpolation on the sorted sample. With N = 10,000 and exactly 100 stragglers at 5.0 s, the p99 rank is approximately 1 + (N−1)×0.99 = 9900.01. Linear interpolation between rank 9900 (1.33 s) and rank 9901 (5.0 s) gives approximately 1.37 s, not 1.33 s.
issue.evidence: 1.33 + 0.01 × (5.0 − 1.33) = 1.3667 s. The printed p99 ≈ 1.33 s is the nearest-rank or floor value, not the linear-interpolation value.
issue.root_cause: The percentile convention stated in the text does not match the percentile value printed.
issue.correction: Either change the p99 value to ≈1.37 s under linear interpolation, or state that the p99 is computed by nearest-rank/floor convention. Do not say 'linear interpolation' and then print the floor value.
issue.acceptance_test: Recompute p99 from the stated sample and percentile convention. The printed value must match the stated convention within rounding tolerance.

issue.quoted_clause: ≈ 1.5 PFLOP full-square total
issue.observed: The text computes linear prefill FLOPs as ≈1.29 PFLOP, then says the quadratic attention term adds ≈0.2 PFLOP for a ≈1.5 PFLOP full-square total. But the required rate and Table 6-1 use 1.29 PFLOP ÷ 1.08 s ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS, not 1.5 PFLOP ÷ 1.08 s ≈ 1.39 PFLOPS.
issue.evidence: 1.5 / 1.08 ≈ 1.39 PFLOPS. The text and table use 1.19 PFLOPS while also presenting 1.5 PFLOP as the full-square total.
issue.root_cause: The chapter mixes linear-only and full-square prefill FLOPs without consistently labeling which one is used in the rate calculation.
issue.correction: Choose one convention and use it consistently. Either use linear-only 1.29 PFLOP throughout and remove the full-square total from the rate discussion, or use the full-square 1.5 PFLOP and update the required rate to ≈1.39 PFLOPS and Table 6-1 accordingly.
issue.acceptance_test: Every prefill FLOP total, required PFLOPS value, and Table 6-1 entry must use the same stated convention. Recompute 1.29/1.08 and 1.5/1.08 and verify that the printed values match the chosen convention.

issue.quoted_clause: high HBM util, low FLOP util
issue.observed: The decode row's resource tell says 'high HBM util', but the same row states '~21–25% achieved HBM util at the canonical point'. 21–25% is not high HBM utilization.
issue.evidence: The table's own number contradicts its resource-tell label. The text also says a decode kernel pinned at ~95% HBM bandwidth is the illustrative bandwidth-bound signature, which is far above 21–25%.
issue.root_cause: The resource-tell column describes a generic bandwidth-bound signature, while the verdict column describes the canonical operating point where HBM utilization is only ~21–25% because the TPOT budget includes other costs.
issue.correction: Either change the resource tell to 'moderate HBM util, low FLOP util' for the canonical point, or explicitly distinguish the generic signature (~95% HBM) from the canonical operating point (~21–25% HBM). Do not label 21–25% as 'high'.
issue.acceptance_test: The resource-tell text for the decode row must be consistent with the utilization number printed in the same row. If the table keeps 'high HBM util', the number must be high; if the number stays 21–25%, the label must be changed or qualified.

issue.quoted_clause: high FLOP / MFU util, mid bandwidth
issue.observed: The prefill row's resource tell says 'high FLOP / MFU util', but the text says the canonical 8×H100 host has aggregate peak ~7.9 PFLOPS and 'comfortably satisfies' the ~1.19 PFLOPS prefill rate. That is ~15% MFU, not high FLOP/MFU utilization.
issue.evidence: 1.19 / 7.9 ≈ 0.15. The table's H100 capacity column is single-device (~0.989 PFLOPS), but the canonical host is 8×H100. The resource tell conflates a single-device roofline illustration with the canonical host's actual utilization.
issue.root_cause: The table mixes single-device capacity comparisons with canonical-host utilization language without distinguishing the two scopes.
issue.correction: Qualify the prefill resource tell as a single-device roofline illustration, or change it to 'compute-regime (intensity above ridge), not necessarily high MFU on the 8-GPU host'. If the table is about the canonical host, use the aggregate 7.9 PFLOPS capacity and state the actual MFU.
issue.acceptance_test: The prefill resource-tell text must be consistent with the capacity basis used in the same row. If the row uses single-device capacity, say so; if it uses the canonical 8×H100 host, the MFU number must match 1.19/7.9 ≈ 15%.

issue.quoted_clause: zeroing goodput
issue.observed: The common-mistakes bullet says bigger batches can 'zero goodput'. The earlier goodput example says the extra tokens can leave goodput 'effectively unchanged' in Scenario A, and Scenario B shows goodput rising from 48 to 65.8. Neither is zero.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own worked example does not support 'zeroing goodput'. A p95 breach can reduce or fail to improve goodput, but it does not necessarily zero it.
issue.root_cause: Overstated claim strength in a summary bullet.
issue.correction: Replace 'zeroing goodput' with 'reducing goodput or preventing it from improving' or similar qualified language.
issue.acceptance_test: The common-mistakes bullet must be consistent with the goodput scenarios in §3. No claim of zero goodput should appear unless a scenario actually computes zero.

issue.quoted_clause: ~20 ms/token
issue.observed: The scope note says the 50→70 tok/s figures are low-batch decode operating points with '~20 ms/token'. 50 tok/s corresponds to 20 ms/token, but 70 tok/s corresponds to ~14.3 ms/token.
issue.evidence: 1 / 50 = 0.020 s = 20 ms. 1 / 70 ≈ 0.0143 s = 14.3 ms. The single '~20 ms/token' label does not apply to both rates.
issue.root_cause: The per-token latency label is attached to a range of throughput values without recomputing per-token latency for the upper value.
issue.correction: State the per-token latency for each rate, or say '~14–20 ms/token' for the 50–70 tok/s range.
issue.acceptance_test: The per-token latency range must be consistent with the stated tokens/s range: 50 tok/s ↔ 20 ms/token, 70 tok/s ↔ ~14.3 ms/token.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 6, §3 Reading Telemetry Into a Decision
issue.quoted_clause: byte-identical shared prefix
issue.observed: Prefix caching operates on token sequences, not raw bytes. 'Byte-identical' is imprecise and can mislead readers into thinking the cache matches raw text bytes rather than tokenized prefixes.
issue.evidence: The chapter elsewhere correctly describes prefix caching as reusing a shared prompt prefix and discusses token counts (1,200-token prompt). The mechanism is token-level KV reuse.
issue.root_cause: Terminology drift between byte-level and token-level descriptions of caching.
issue.correction: Replace 'byte-identical shared prefix' with 'token-identical shared prefix' or 'exact token prefix'.
issue.acceptance_test: Search Chapter 6 for 'byte-identical' in the context of prefix caching. It should be replaced with token-level terminology unless the text is explicitly discussing byte-level storage.

issue.page_hint: Table 7-2 and its note; Fig 7.6 caption
issue.quoted_clause: fine-tuning (QLoRA, 4-bit base + LoRA) | quantized base + LoRA adapters + KV ... the ~24 GB KV that Fig 7.6 lists
issue.observed: The QLoRA fine-tuning row and note include a KV cache in the training memory floor. Fine-tuning does not use an autoregressive KV cache; it uses activations, gradients, optimizer state, and workspace. Including ~24 GB of inference KV overstates the QLoRA training floor and contradicts the chapter's own definition of the fine-tuning floor as weights + gradients + optimizer states.
issue.evidence: The chapter states earlier: 'In fine-tuning, the floor rises further to weights + gradients + optimizer states.' Table 7-2 then lists 'quantized base + LoRA adapters + KV' and the note says the QLoRA floor 'holds ... the ~24 GB KV that Fig 7.6 lists.' That is an inference-state component, not a training-state component.
issue.root_cause: Inference KV residency was carried into the fine-tuning comparison without re-inventorying state by lifetime.
issue.correction: Remove KV from all fine-tuning rows and from the QLoRA note. Replace it with an explicit activation/workspace term or state that activations are excluded from the floor and must be measured. If the book wants to discuss inference after fine-tuning, separate that from the training floor.
issue.acceptance_test: No fine-tuning row or note includes KV cache as a training memory component; the QLoRA floor is derived from 4-bit base + adapters + optimizer + explicitly labeled activation/workspace assumptions.

issue.quoted_clause: When evaluating a model where the hidden dimension or layer count differs from LLaMA-70B, recompute the constant factor
issue.observed: The text uses LLaMA-70B as if it followed the full-MHA formula and had ~2.62 MB/token at FP16. Earlier in the same chapter, LLaMA-2 70B is correctly described as GQA with 64 query heads and 8 KV heads, giving ~0.33 MB/token. The measurement formula is explicitly the full-MHA formula using d_hidden, so it cannot be applied to LLaMA-70B by changing only layer count and hidden dimension.
issue.evidence: The chapter's GQA sensitivity note says: 'LLaMA-2 70B, for instance, has 64 query heads but only 8 KV-heads, so per-token KV shrinks by the head ratio to ... ≈0.33 MB/token.' Measurement point 1 then says 'For a 70B model at FP16 the answer is 2×80×8192×2 B = 2,621,440 B ≈ 2.62 MB/token' and refers to 'LLaMA-70B' as the baseline.
issue.root_cause: The canonical full-MHA teaching geometry and the named LLaMA-70B GQA model were conflated.
issue.correction: Replace 'LLaMA-70B' in measurement point 1 with 'the canonical full-MHA 70B teaching geometry.' State that for any real model the formula is 2 × layers × n_KV-heads × head_dim × bytes, and that LLaMA-2 70B must use 8 KV heads, not hidden_dim.
issue.acceptance_test: No passage implies LLaMA-70B has 2.62 MB/token at FP16; every per-model KV calculation uses n_KV-heads and head_dim, and the canonical full-MHA geometry is labeled as constructed.

issue.quoted_clause: The residency floor is therefore set by weights + KV (+ activations, in fine-tuning)
issue.observed: This sentence omits gradients and optimizer states from the fine-tuning floor, even though the next paragraph correctly says fine-tuning requires weights + gradients + optimizer states. The parenthetical '( + activations, in fine-tuning)' is incomplete and can mislead a reader into thinking activations are the only additional training term.
issue.evidence: The immediately following paragraph: 'In fine-tuning, the floor rises further to weights + gradients + optimizer states, because every parameter update requires its own momentum and velocity vectors (Adam) or per-parameter scaling (LAMB/RMSProp).'
issue.root_cause: Compressed summary sentence dropped the dominant training-state terms.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'The residency floor is weights + KV for inference; for fine-tuning it is weights + gradients + optimizer states + activations/workspace.'
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in the chapter states or implies that fine-tuning residency is only weights + KV + activations.

issue.quoted_clause: at 17.5 concurrent requests a rank reaches ~99.7% of its 80 GB capacity (17.5 + 8 + 54.25 = 79.75 GB) ... Per-rank budget: 17.5 + 54.5 + 8 = 80 GB ≤ 80 GB
issue.observed: The note mixes two KV-per-rank quantities without labeling them: 54.25 GB is 17.5 × the rounded 3.1 GB/request per rank, while 54.5 GB is the full 436/8 KV budget. The 99.7% figure is computed from the rounded 3.1 GB/request; using the chapter's own 24.90368 GB/request gives 17.5 × 3.11296 = 54.4768 GB and 79.9768 GB, i.e. ~99.97%, not ~99.7%. The difference is small but the arithmetic is presented as a hard-ceiling check.
issue.evidence: The chapter gives per-request KV per rank as '24.9 ÷ 8 = ~3.1 GB' and later uses 54.25 = 17.5 × 3.1. It also gives '436 ÷ 8 = ~54.5 GB' as the full KV budget per rank. The two are different quantities and should not be interchanged in a capacity check.
issue.root_cause: Rounding 3.11296 GB to 3.1 GB and then using the rounded value in a percentage-of-capacity calculation.
issue.correction: Either use exact values (24.90368/8 = 3.11296 GB; 17.5 × 3.11296 = 54.4768 GB; total 79.9768 GB ≈ 99.97%) or explicitly label 54.25 GB as 'using rounded 3.1 GB/request' and 54.5 GB as 'full KV budget per rank.' Do not present both as if they were the same per-rank KV quantity.
issue.acceptance_test: The per-rank capacity check uses one clearly labeled KV-per-rank value and the percentage follows from that value; no unlabeled 54.25 vs 54.5 swap remains.

issue.quoted_clause: its size depends on the model's layer count, hidden dimension, and the precision chosen for key and value storage
issue.observed: This early sentence names layer count and hidden dimension but omits KV-head count and head dimension. For GQA/MQA models, KV size depends on n_KV-heads × head_dim, not hidden_dim. The chapter later corrects this, but the first definition is incomplete and can seed the exact misconception the chapter later tries to prevent.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own GQA note says per-token KV is 2 × layers × n_KV-heads × head_dim × bytes, and LLaMA-2 70B is ~8× smaller than the full-MHA hidden-dim formula.
issue.root_cause: The opening definition was written for the full-MHA special case and not generalized.
issue.correction: Change to: 'its size depends on layer count, KV-head count, head dimension, and KV precision (equivalently, the KV width per layer).'
issue.acceptance_test: The first definition of KV size includes KV-head count/head dimension or explicitly says it is stating the full-MHA special case.

issue.page_hint: §1 Concept, quantization paragraph; §5 Common Mistakes, KV-quant bullet
issue.quoted_clause: realized savings land between these 2× and 4× reduction factors ... realized savings land between, once block/scale metadata is counted
issue.observed: The phrase 'land between' has no clear referents and is repeated in the Common Mistakes bullet. For 4-bit KV, the raw bound is 4×; metadata reduces the realized reduction below 4×, but the text does not justify 2× as a lower bound. A reader can reasonably ask 'between what and what?' and may infer a guaranteed 2×–4× range that the arithmetic does not establish.
issue.evidence: The sentence contrasts FP8 2× and 4-bit raw 4×, then says realized savings land 'between these 2× and 4× reduction factors.' But the realized 4-bit reduction could be below 2× if metadata/block overhead is large, and the text gives no lower-bound derivation.
issue.root_cause: Compressed prose replaced an explicit inequality with an ambiguous 'between.'
issue.correction: State the bound explicitly: 'For 4-bit KV the raw payload bound is 4×; scale/zero metadata and block layout reduce the realized reduction below 4×. Do not assume a specific realized multiplier without the actual layout.' If a 2× lower bound is intended, derive it or label it as a typical planning assumption.
issue.acceptance_test: The text no longer says 'between' without naming both endpoints and the condition under which the lower bound holds.

issue.quoted_clause: any block-layout/scale-offset metadata overhead is NOT vendor-measured
issue.observed: The intended meaning is that metadata overhead is not included in the 1.31 MB/token figure. 'NOT vendor-measured' is the wrong phrase: the overhead is not measured by the vendor, but the real issue is that it is not included in the accounting. This is a small wording defect but it weakens the precision of the table note.
issue.evidence: The same row says 'raw tensor byte-halving' and the surrounding text says metadata is not included. The phrase 'NOT vendor-measured' does not say 'not included.'
issue.root_cause: Wording slip in a table note.
issue.correction: Replace with: 'block-layout/scale-offset metadata overhead is NOT included in this raw-tensor figure.'
issue.acceptance_test: The table note says the metadata is excluded from the quoted figure, not that it is 'not vendor-measured.'

issue.quoted_clause: the ~500 GB headroom (Ch. 4/7, single-request)
issue.observed: The ~500 GB figure is 640 − 140, i.e. headroom after weights only. For a single request at 9.5K, weights + KV ≈ 165 GB, so the actual single-request headroom is ~475 GB, not ~500 GB. The parenthetical 'single-request' makes the number ambiguous.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own numbers: 640 GB pool, 140 GB weights, 24.9 GB KV at 9.5K. 640 − 140 − 24.9 = 475.1 GB.
issue.root_cause: Headroom after weights was labeled as single-request headroom without subtracting the single-request KV.
issue.correction: Either call it '~500 GB after weights' or use '~475 GB after weights + one 9.5K request's KV.'
issue.acceptance_test: The headroom number is labeled with the exact subtraction it represents.

issue.page_hint: Ch 8 §3, 'The 1.08 s budget versus the 35% planning rate' paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: The canonical prefill takes about 1.08 s for 9.2K input tokens (Ch 4)
issue.observed: The sentence states as fact that canonical prefill 'takes about 1.08 s', but 1.08 s is the design *budget* (1.2 s TTFT minus ~120 ms retrieval), not a measured or derived prefill time. The very next sentence correctly calls it 'the end-to-end prefill budget'. At the chapter's own 35% MFU planning rate, prefill would take ~0.465 s, not 1.08 s.
issue.evidence: 1.288 PFLOP ÷ (8 × 346 TFLOPS) = 0.465 s at 35% MFU. The 1.08 s figure is 1.2 s − 0.12 s retrieval, i.e. a budget allocation, not a measured duration. The text itself says '1.08 s is the end-to-end prefill budget inside the 1.2 s TTFT'.
issue.root_cause: Wording conflates a design budget with a measured/derived time, creating a false impression that the canonical prefill actually consumes the full 1.08 s.
issue.correction: Replace 'The canonical prefill takes about 1.08 s' with 'The canonical prefill budget is 1.08 s' or 'If prefill consumes the full 1.08 s budget, that implies ~15% MFU'. Keep the subsequent clarification.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence no longer asserts a measured prefill time; the 15% MFU is explicitly framed as the rate implied by consuming the full budget, not as the actual prefill rate.

issue.quoted_clause: **Attention / memory constrained (within prefill)** — the quadratic attention term, not the linear weights, grows with context
issue.observed: The label says 'Attention / memory constrained', but the explanation is entirely about the quadratic attention *compute* term (4·n_layers·L²·d FLOPs), not about memory bandwidth or capacity. The label conflates attention compute with memory pressure.
issue.evidence: The bullet's own text: 'the quadratic attention term... grows with context; at 128K+ contexts this term dominates prefill cost (at 32K it is already ~+60% — the 4·n_layers·L²·d term)'. This is a FLOP-count argument, not a memory argument.
issue.root_cause: Label drift: 'memory' is carried over from the general prefill/decode discussion but does not describe the actual constraint being diagnosed.
issue.correction: Rename the candidate to 'Attention-compute constrained (within prefill)' or 'Attention-term dominated'. If KV-cache write pressure during prefill is also intended, state it explicitly as a separate sub-case.
issue.acceptance_test: The label matches the explanation: a reader can tell from the label alone that the constraint is attention FLOPs, not memory bandwidth or capacity.

issue.page_hint: Ch 8 §8 mini-case, fourth candidate bullet, final clause
issue.quoted_clause: so the fix is to reduce the attention term (flash-attention, sparse/linear attention), not to batch harder
issue.observed: FlashAttention is listed as a fix for reducing the attention *term* (a FLOP count), but FlashAttention is an I/O-aware kernel that reduces HBM traffic, not attention FLOPs. If the attention term dominates the FLOP count, FlashAttention does not reduce it; sparse/linear attention does.
issue.evidence: FlashAttention reorganizes attention to tile through on-chip memory and cut HBM traffic while preserving the mathematical result (the book's own Ch 15 framing). It does not change the 4·n_layers·L²·d FLOP count. Sparse/linear attention changes the FLOP count.
issue.root_cause: Conflation of two distinct optimizations: reducing attention FLOPs (sparse/linear attention) vs. reducing attention memory traffic (FlashAttention).
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'the fix is to reduce the attention FLOP term (sparse/linear attention) or, if the attention kernel is memory-bound, to reduce its HBM traffic (FlashAttention)'. Distinguish the two mechanisms explicitly.
issue.acceptance_test: The text no longer implies FlashAttention reduces attention FLOPs; the two optimizations are assigned to their correct resource (FLOPs vs. bytes).

issue.page_hint: Ch 8 §6 Architecture Consequence, second bullet, final clause
issue.quoted_clause: while decode's bandwidth demand is served by wide-memory GPUs or even CPU offload
issue.observed: 'or even CPU offload' is a hand-wavy claim. CPU decode is dramatically slower and viable only for very low-throughput or latency-tolerant scenarios; presenting it as a peer option alongside wide-memory GPUs overstates its practicality.
issue.evidence: CPU decode throughput is typically orders of magnitude below GPU decode for 70B-class models; it is not a general-purpose alternative for the canonical 10–40 rps workload.
issue.root_cause: Compression of a nuanced trade-off into a two-word aside.
issue.correction: Either remove 'or even CPU offload' or qualify it: 'or, for latency-tolerant or very low-throughput workloads, CPU offload'. Do not present it as a peer option for the canonical scenario.
issue.acceptance_test: The CPU-offload mention is either removed or explicitly scoped to latency-tolerant/low-throughput workloads.

issue.page_hint: Ch 8 §3, paragraph beginning '19 / 21 / 22 — the full-utilization compute screens...'
issue.quoted_clause: 19 / 21 / 22 — the full-utilization compute screens for cases (i) / (iii) / (ii) — and their labeled 70% × 95% + N−1 policy totals, Ch 16/17: case (i) compute screen 19 → 29 and fleet 21 → 32, case (iii) 21 → 32, case (ii) 22 → 34, KV-only 21 → 32 (the ρ = 1 u-only screen reads 30 / 32 — ceil(N ÷ 0.7) for KV-only 21 and case (ii) 22)
issue.observed: This is a single ~90-word sentence packing six host-count pairs, two policy formulas, and a parenthetical sub-screen. The arithmetic checks out, but the sentence is very hard to parse on first reading.
issue.evidence: The sentence contains: three FLOP cases, three compute-screen values, three policy-total values, a KV-only case, a ρ=1 sub-screen, and a formula — all in one sentence.
issue.root_cause: Information density exceeds what a single sentence can carry without losing the reader.
issue.correction: Split into a short table or a bulleted list: one line per case (i)/(iii)/(ii)/KV-only, each showing compute screen → policy total. Keep the prose to a one-sentence summary ('the screens cluster at 19–22 full-utilization and 29–34 under policy').
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can extract the six host-count pairs without re-reading the sentence more than once; the values are presented in a scannable structure.

issue.page_hint: Ch 8 Table 8-1, 'prefill throughput per GPU' row
issue.quoted_clause: prefill throughput per GPU | ~2,471 tokens/s | 346 TFLOPS ÷ 140 GFLOP/token [DERIVED; **per-GPU scope**]
issue.observed: The throughput is derived from the linear-only 140 GFLOP/token, but the row does not say 'linear only'. A reader could mistake it for the full per-token cost including attention (~164 GFLOP/token at 9.2K), which would give ~2,110 tokens/s.
issue.evidence: The prefill FLOP rows above it are explicitly labeled 'linear only' / 'full-square' / 'causal-triangle', but the throughput row is not. The 140 GFLOP/token is the linear term; the full per-token cost at 9.2K is ~164 GFLOP/token.
issue.root_cause: Labeling inconsistency within the same table: the FLOP rows carry the case label, the throughput row does not.
issue.correction: Add 'linear-only case (i)' to the throughput row's derivation cell, or add a footnote: 'throughput uses the linear-only 140 GFLOP/token; including attention at 9.2K gives ~2,110 tokens/s'.
issue.acceptance_test: The throughput row's scope (linear-only vs. full per-token) is unambiguous from the table alone.

issue.quoted_clause: §1–§3 build the core arithmetic (FLOPs per token, prefill PFLOP counts, H100 sustained utilization) and the roofline that explains why prefill is compute-bound while decode is memory-bound
issue.observed: The roadmap says §1–§3 build 'the core arithmetic', but §2 is titled 'Mental Model' and is conceptual (the trip/ridge analogy, the resource-hierarchy figure), not arithmetic. The parenthetical does mention the roofline, but the framing '§1–§3 build the core arithmetic' is imprecise.
issue.evidence: Section headers: §1 Concept, §2 Mental Model, §3 Worked Example. §2 contains no arithmetic.
issue.root_cause: Roadmap written from memory of the section contents rather than from the section titles.
issue.correction: Reword to '§1–§3 establish the concept, mental model, and worked arithmetic (FLOPs per token, prefill PFLOP counts, H100 sustained utilization) and the roofline...'.
issue.acceptance_test: The roadmap's description of §1–§3 matches the actual section titles and contents.

issue.quoted_clause: In round r, rank i sends chunk (i−r) mod N in both phases, so rank r ends the reduce-scatter holding reduced chunk r.
issue.observed: The caption states that the same chunk-index formula applies in both reduce-scatter and all-gather, and that rank r ends reduce-scatter holding chunk r. In the standard balanced ring all-reduce, reduce-scatter and all-gather use different chunk indices. With 0-indexed rounds, rank r ends reduce-scatter holding chunk (r+1) mod N; all-gather then sends chunk (i−r+1) mod N at round r. With 1-indexed rounds, the reduce-scatter formula can be made to leave rank r holding chunk r, but the all-gather formula is still not the same as the reduce-scatter formula.
issue.evidence: Simulate N=4, rank 0. Reduce-scatter step 0 sends chunk 0 and receives chunk 3; step 1 sends chunk 3 and receives chunk 2; step 2 sends chunk 2 and receives chunk 1. Rank 0 ends holding reduced chunk 1, not chunk 0. All-gather step 0 must send chunk 1, not chunk 0. The caption's 'both phases' claim is therefore false under either indexing convention.
issue.root_cause: The caption collapses two different ring phases into one chunk-index formula and uses an ambiguous round index.
issue.correction: State the two phase-specific formulas explicitly, or re-index rounds and chunks so that the figure's arrows and the caption agree. For 0-indexed rounds: reduce-scatter sends chunk (i−r) mod N; all-gather sends chunk (i−r+1) mod N. For 1-indexed rounds: reduce-scatter sends chunk (i−r) mod N; all-gather sends chunk (i−r+1) mod N. Verify the figure arrows against a four-rank simulation.
issue.acceptance_test: A four-rank simulation of the caption's stated algorithm produces the same send/receive chunk indices as the figure and leaves each rank with the correct reduced chunk before all-gather.

issue.quoted_clause: When a GPU is idle waiting, we reach for DP (more work per GPU)
issue.observed: Data parallelism does not give an idle GPU more work. It adds independent replicas, each with its own model copy and its own request stream. If a single GPU is idle because arrivals are insufficient, DP does not raise that GPU's utilization; it adds another underutilized GPU. DP is a response to aggregate demand exceeding one replica's goodput, not to a single GPU being idle.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own definition says inference DP means 'independent model replicas each serve a disjoint set of requests; no gradient sync; throughput scales linearly until KV or memory binds.' That mechanism increases aggregate capacity by replication, not per-GPU work.
issue.root_cause: The resource-triangle heuristic conflates 'system has idle capacity' with 'a GPU is idle waiting for work.'
issue.correction: Replace with: 'When aggregate demand exceeds one replica's goodput, add DP replicas. When a single GPU is idle because the batch or arrival stream is too small, increase batching/admission or reduce over-provisioning; DP does not fill that GPU.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can explain why DP does not increase utilization of an already-idle GPU and can name the correct levers for low arrival rate versus insufficient aggregate capacity.

issue.quoted_clause: parallelism is splitting one of the three things a model occupies — its weights, its layers, or its data — across multiple devices.
issue.observed: The chapter immediately lists five strategies (TP, PP, DP, EP, CP) plus a sixth serving-only strategy (P/D disaggregation). Expert parallelism splits experts, which are weights; sequence/context parallelism splits the token sequence, which is neither 'weights,' 'layers,' nor 'data batch' in the sense used here. The 'three things' framing does not map cleanly onto the chapter's own taxonomy.
issue.evidence: The chapter's Table 10-1 has rows for Tensor, Pipeline, Data, Expert, and Sequence. The opening sentence names only three axes. The later 'resource triangle' names weights, activations, and data, which also does not include sequence/context as a separate axis.
issue.root_cause: A simplified three-axis framing was retained after the chapter expanded to five/six strategies.
issue.correction: Either (a) explicitly say 'three canonical axes plus specialist axes: expert and sequence/context parallelism,' or (b) replace the three-things sentence with a taxonomy that matches the five strategies in Table 10-1. Do not let the opening claim a three-way partition that the body contradicts.
issue.acceptance_test: Every strategy named in §10.1 maps to a named axis in the opening framing, and the opening framing does not imply that EP/CP are subcases of DP or PP without saying so.

issue.quoted_clause: If the budget can accommodate NVLink‑equipped hosts (GPUs connected on‑node), keeping the all-reduce on-node gives an ideal ring time about 1/11th the assumed InfiniBand case and about 1/180th the assumed RoCE case (§9.3)
issue.observed: The preceding sentence describes an eight-node data-parallel training job with one rank per node. An eight-node DP all-reduce cannot be 'kept on-node' by buying NVLink-equipped hosts; the collective is cross-host by construction. The later clarification says the ratios compare an eight-rank single-host collective with an eight-rank cross-host collective, but the earlier sentence reads as a deployment option for the same eight-node job.
issue.evidence: The paragraph itself later says: 'An eight-node data-parallel job uses NVLink/NVSwitch for intra-node exchanges and InfiniBand/RoCE for inter-node exchanges; compare InfiniBand vs Ethernet only for the inter-node portion. The 1/11 and 1/180 ratios compare an eight-rank single-host collective with an eight-rank cross-host collective ... not two fabrics for the same job.' That clarification contradicts the earlier 'keeping the all-reduce on-node' phrasing.
issue.root_cause: The text mixes a topology-change comparison (single host vs cross-host) with a fabric-choice comparison for the same job.
issue.correction: Rewrite the paragraph to say explicitly: 'The 1/11 and 1/180 ratios are not a fabric choice for the same eight-node job. They compare an eight-rank single-host collective with an eight-rank cross-host collective. For the eight-node job, NVLink/NVSwitch handles intra-node traffic and the inter-node fabric handles the DP all-reduce; compare InfiniBand vs Ethernet only for that inter-node portion.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader cannot infer that buying NVLink hosts eliminates the cross-host all-reduce in an eight-node DP job; the ratio's scope is stated before the ratio is used.

issue.quoted_clause: Candidate (c) does not advance as a finalist; it is carried only as a labeled sensitivity case
issue.observed: Earlier, §12.3 says candidate (c) is 'flagged for measurement against the quality gate, not dismissed by parameter counting' and 'its fate depends on the measured quality gate.' Section 12.8 says it 'stays in the gate evaluation (Ch 14) rather than being excluded pre-measurement.' Section 12.6 then says it 'does not advance as a finalist.' These are not the same status. A candidate cannot simultaneously be excluded from the finalist set before measurement and have its finalist fate determined by a later measurement.
issue.evidence: The contradiction is internal to Chapter 12: §12.3 calls (c) provisional and gate-dependent; §12.6 says it does not advance as a finalist; §12.8 says it remains in gate evaluation. Table 12-1 labels it 'gated, not a finalist.'
issue.root_cause: The manuscript uses 'finalist' in two senses: 'carried into Ch 14 evaluation' and 'survives the quality gate.' The text does not distinguish them.
issue.correction: Define a single status vocabulary. For example: 'Candidate (c) is a conditional candidate carried into the Ch 14 quality gate. If it passes, it becomes a finalist; if it fails, it is retained only as a labeled sensitivity case. It is not a finalist before that measurement.' Then make §12.6, §12.8, Table 12-1, and Fig 12.1 use that vocabulary consistently.
issue.acceptance_test: Every mention of candidate (c)'s status in Ch 12 uses the same term and the same decision rule; a reader can state exactly what measurement promotes or rejects it.

issue.quoted_clause: The canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload sits on the server tier as a fleet of ~21 server-class hosts at the 40 rps peak
issue.observed: Table 13-1 defines 'Server' as one host with 1–8 GPUs and 'Cluster' as multiple hosts (tens to hundreds of GPUs). A fleet of ~21 hosts is a cluster by that definition. The sentence tries to distinguish 'server-class model residency' from 'cluster-tier deployment,' but it uses 'server tier' for the deployment, which contradicts the table.
issue.evidence: The same paragraph later says 'the traffic scaling is a cluster of server-class hosts, not weight-splitting' and 'the server tier is the right model-residency archetype ... It does not mean one host serves the whole arrival rate.' The intended distinction is clear, but the first sentence's tier label is wrong.
issue.root_cause: The chapter uses 'tier' both for model-residency class and for deployment scale without disambiguating the two.
issue.correction: Rewrite the first sentence as: 'The canonical workload's model residency is server-class, but its deployment at the 40 rps peak is a cluster of ~21 server-class hosts.' Then use 'server-class residency' and 'cluster-tier deployment' consistently in §13.3 and §13.6.
issue.acceptance_test: The tier label in §13.3 matches Table 13-1's definition: one host = Server; multiple hosts = Cluster. A reader cannot conclude that a 21-host fleet is a single server-tier deployment.

issue.quoted_clause: each per-layer all-reduce is ~0.45 MB sent per rank — batch × hidden × bytes, sub-MB to a few MB
issue.observed: The parenthetical formula 'batch × hidden × bytes' gives the logical input tensor size, not the bytes sent per rank by a ring all-reduce. For a ring, each rank sends 2(N−1)/N times the logical tensor across reduce-scatter plus all-gather, or 1.75× for N=8. With batch 16, hidden 8,192, and BF16, the logical input is 256 KiB; the ring send per rank is 448 KiB. The quoted '~0.45 MB sent per rank' is consistent with the ring send, but the formula beside it is not.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own §10.3 calculation uses M = 16 × 8,192 × 2 = 256 KiB and then 1.75M = 448 KiB sent per rank. The mini-case's parenthetical omits the 1.75 factor.
issue.root_cause: The text mixes logical tensor size with physical ring send volume in one parenthetical.
issue.correction: Change to: 'each per-layer all-reduce has a logical input of batch × hidden × bytes; the ring send per rank is 1.75× that for an eight-rank ring, about 0.45 MB in this example.'
issue.acceptance_test: Recomputing from the quoted formula yields the quoted sent-per-rank number, including the ring normalization.

issue.quoted_clause: up to ~576 GB (140 + 436) at the canonical per-host KV budget
issue.observed: Section 12.3 defines the canonical per-host budget as 140 GB weights + 436 GB KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB. The §12.8 parenthetical gives 140 + 436 = 576 GB and calls it 'up to ~576 GB' without the ~64 GB runtime term. That is a partial sum, not the full host residency. A reader can misread 576 GB as the total residency and conclude there is 64 GB of headroom when the text elsewhere says zero headroom.
issue.evidence: Section 12.3: '140 GB weights + 436 GB KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB — exactly the pool, zero headroom.' Section 12.8: 'up to ~576 GB (140 + 436) at the canonical per-host KV budget.' The arithmetic is internally inconsistent in labeling.
issue.root_cause: The §12.8 summary drops the runtime term that §12.3 includes.
issue.correction: Write 'up to ~576 GB of weights+KV, plus ~64 GB runtime, for ~640 GB total at the canonical per-host KV budget' or simply 'up to ~640 GB total at the canonical per-host KV budget.'
issue.acceptance_test: The candidate (b) residency arithmetic in §12.8 sums to the same total and headroom as §12.3.

issue.quoted_clause: The analytical KV quotient C ≈ 17.5 FP16-KV request-equivalents (436 GB FP16 KV budget ÷ 24.9 GB per 9,500-token request; 9,500 × 2.62 MB ≈ 24.9 GB) gives at most 17 whole-context slots, not a deployable concurrency of 17.5.
issue.observed: The arithmetic is correct, but the text uses 9,500 tokens (9,200 input + 300 output) as the per-request KV footprint while the canonical workload is described as ~9,200 input tokens. The 9,500-token figure is a maximum sequence length, not the request's input length. This is defensible as a conservative whole-context slot calculation, but the prose does not state that the 9,500 includes the 300 output tokens and therefore may confuse readers who expect the KV quotient to be based on input tokens alone.
issue.evidence: 9,500 × 2.62 MB = 24,890 MB = 24.89 GB; 436 / 24.9 = 17.51. The calculation is internally consistent. The issue is explanatory: the text should explicitly say '9,500-token maximum sequence (9,200 input + 300 output)' so the reader does not think the canonical input is 9,500 tokens.
issue.root_cause: The canonical workload's input and output token counts are combined for KV sizing without a local reminder of the decomposition.
issue.correction: Rewrite the parenthetical as: '(436 GB FP16 KV budget ÷ 24.9 GB per 9,500-token maximum sequence; 9,500 = 9,200 input + 300 output; 9,500 × 2.62 MB ≈ 24.9 GB)'.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state why the KV quotient uses 9,500 tokens even though the canonical input is 9,200 tokens, and can reproduce 436 / 24.9 ≈ 17.5.

issue.quoted_clause: TPOT p50/p95 (≤ ~25 ms median).
issue.observed: The bullet says 'p50/p95' but then gives only a median bound. A p95 TPOT bound is not stated, so the reader cannot tell whether the p95 value is merely recorded or also constrained. This is a small but real ambiguity in a chapter about precise benchmark contracts.
issue.evidence: The canonical SLO elsewhere is 'TPOT ~25 ms/token' and the worksheet row says '~25 ms/token median'. The bullet's parenthetical should match that scope or state both bounds.
issue.root_cause: The bullet conflates the metric list (p50/p95) with the SLO bound (median only).
issue.correction: Change to: 'TPOT p50/p95 (SLO: p50 ≤ ~25 ms/token; record p95 for tail diagnosis).'
issue.acceptance_test: The benchmark protocol unambiguously states which TPOT percentiles are SLO-bound and which are diagnostic.

issue.quoted_clause: The "4 chars ≈ 1 token" estimate can be ~1.5–3× off for code/JSON/technical text (measure chars/token with the model's own tokenizer).
issue.observed: The 1.5–3× range is plausible but unsourced and unlabeled. In a chapter that insists on evidence labels and measured values, this empirical claim should carry a scope or be softened. It is not clear whether the range is measured, illustrative, or rule-of-thumb.
issue.evidence: The sentence gives no citation, no measurement context, and no evidence label. The chapter elsewhere is careful to label illustrative and derived claims.
issue.root_cause: A useful heuristic is stated with more quantitative precision than the surrounding evidence standard supports.
issue.correction: Either add a source/measurement note, or rewrite as: 'The 4-chars-per-token heuristic can be materially wrong for code/JSON/technical text; measure chars/token with the model's own tokenizer rather than assuming a fixed ratio.' If the 1.5–3× range is retained, label it [ILLUSTRATIVE] or cite a measurement.
issue.acceptance_test: The claim's evidence status is explicit, and a reader knows whether 1.5–3× is a measured range or an illustrative heuristic.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 14 §4 'Measure drafts, commitments and valid results separately'
issue.quoted_clause: Those are different events. A first-draft timestamp measures early visibility. A first-commit timestamp measures when a downstream consumer can safely act on text that will not be overwritten. Time to a validated answer includes any required schema checks, unit tests or task acceptance. Comparisons need the same boundary on both sides. [1P][FACT]; metric definitions [DERIVED]
issue.observed: The [1P][FACT] label is applied to a conceptual distinction, not a first-party measurement or specification. The distinction is sound, but labeling it [1P][FACT] overstates provenance. It is a derived metric-definition argument, not a first-party fact.
issue.evidence: The sentence defines draft/commit/validated-answer boundaries. No first-party source is cited. The adjacent clause already says 'metric definitions [DERIVED]', which conflicts with the [1P][FACT] label on the same span.
issue.root_cause: Evidence-label scope is too broad: the [1P][FACT] label binds the whole clause rather than only the uncontroversial observation that these are different events.
issue.correction: Change the label to '[DERIVED]' for the metric-definition span, or split the sentence: the observation that services can expose drafts and commits may be [1P][FACT] if a first-party source exists; the metric-boundary recommendation is [DERIVED].
issue.acceptance_test: The label matches the provenance of the claim: no first-party fact is asserted without a first-party source.

issue.quoted_clause: Two-stage benchmarking: the capability screen (which models qualify) feeds the deployment benchmark (which system meets our SLO), whose results pass the TCO + SLO gate to the deployed system, feeding selection and TCO.
issue.observed: The caption's causal order is muddled: deployment benchmark results 'pass the TCO + SLO gate to the deployed system, feeding selection and TCO.' Selection should precede deployment, and TCO should follow selection/deployment measurement. The phrase 'feeding selection and TCO' after 'deployed system' makes the diagram's reading order ambiguous.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own §6 bullet list gives the correct order: capability screen → deployment benchmark → chosen system → TCO and performance engineering. The caption should match that order.
issue.root_cause: The caption compresses the two-stage flow and the downstream TCO gate into one sentence, losing the sequence.
issue.correction: Rewrite the caption to: 'Two-stage benchmarking: the capability screen selects qualifying models; the deployment benchmark measures each survivor on the canonical workload; the resulting SLO-goodput and cost feed selection and TCO.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can infer the correct sequence from the caption alone: screen → benchmark → select → TCO.

issue.quoted_clause: Suppose candidate A (70B dense on 8×H100) passes the capability screen and achieves p95 TTFT 1.9 s at an illustrative offered load of 1.3 req/s, with the other request SLOs also satisfied.
issue.observed: The example says 'with the other request SLOs also satisfied' but the canonical SLO includes median TTFT ≤ 1.2 s, p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s, and TPOT ~25 ms. The text gives only p95 TTFT 1.9 s. It does not state the median TTFT or TPOT values, so 'other request SLOs also satisfied' is asserted rather than shown. This is acceptable for an illustrative example, but the chapter's standard is to make the acceptance boundary explicit.
issue.evidence: The example is labeled [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION][UNMEASURED], so it is not a factual claim. The issue is pedagogical: the reader cannot see which SLO rows are satisfied.
issue.root_cause: The illustrative result compresses several SLO checks into one phrase.
issue.correction: Add a short parenthetical: '(e.g., median TTFT 1.1 s, TPOT p50 24 ms; all within the stated SLOs)' or explicitly say 'the example assumes the unstated SLO rows are satisfied.'
issue.acceptance_test: The reader can distinguish which SLO values are illustrated and which are merely assumed.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 14 §4 'A video benchmark is a workload tuple'
issue.quoted_clause: HunyuanVideo-1.5 reports 5.5070 versus 2.9475 seconds per diffusion step for dense versus sparse attention at 720 × 1,280 pixels and 241 frames. Those measurements use eight H800 GPUs with context parallelism and a CFG-distilled model. Its separate 50-step table adds SageAttention, compilation, and feature caching, and reports 96.78 versus 58.39 seconds for the same shape.
issue.observed: The phrase 'for the same shape' is potentially misleading: the 50-step table adds SageAttention, compilation, and feature caching, so it is not the same experimental configuration as the per-step table. 'Same shape' appears to mean same pixel dimensions and frame count, not same recipe. The text should say 'same pixel/frame shape' to avoid implying identical settings.
issue.evidence: The preceding sentence explicitly says the 50-step table 'adds SageAttention, compilation, and feature caching.' That is a different configuration.
issue.root_cause: Shorthand 'same shape' conflates spatial/temporal shape with experimental recipe.
issue.correction: Change 'for the same shape' to 'for the same pixel/frame shape but with the added optimizations listed above.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader cannot mistake the 50-step table for a controlled comparison against the per-step table.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 14 §4 'Two fair comparisons answer different questions'
issue.quoted_clause: A p95 threshold is a configuration-level statistic; it is not itself a count of compliant work.
issue.observed: This is correct but potentially confusing in context. The paragraph is about request goodput and token goodput. Saying a p95 threshold is 'configuration-level' is true, but the reader may wonder how a p95 SLO is enforced per request. The text should clarify that a p95 SLO is evaluated over a population/window, while goodput counts requests that individually satisfy their SLOs.
issue.evidence: The surrounding text distinguishes request goodput from token goodput but does not explicitly connect percentile SLO evaluation to per-request compliance.
issue.root_cause: The sentence states a statistical fact without linking it to the goodput definition.
issue.correction: Add: 'A p95 SLO is evaluated over a defined population and window; goodput then counts the requests that individually meet their SLOs within that window.'
issue.acceptance_test: The reader can explain how a p95 SLO and request goodput coexist without contradiction.

issue.quoted_clause: Mean-only latency reporting. A 0.84 s mean hides a 5 s tail that breaches the p95 SLO (Ch6).
issue.observed: The 0.84 s mean and 5 s tail are presented without an evidence label or source. In a chapter that is otherwise careful about labeling illustrative numbers, this reads as a measured example. It may be canonical, but the local text does not say so.
issue.evidence: No citation or label appears. The number may be from Ch6, but the reader of Ch14 cannot tell.
issue.root_cause: A cross-chapter example is reused without a local label or reference.
issue.correction: Add '[CANONICAL]' or 'e.g., in the Ch6 example' so the number's status is clear.
issue.acceptance_test: The reader knows whether 0.84 s / 5 s is a measured, canonical, or illustrative pair.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 14 §4 'Acceptance test for a quantized deployment'
issue.quoted_clause: A bounded first screen can use at least 200 paired examples per critical task and three repetitions per load point, but these are illustrative starting budgets, not proof of rare-failure or p99 reliability.
issue.observed: The phrase 'at least 200 paired examples per critical task and three repetitions per load point' is labeled illustrative, which is good. However, 'three repetitions per load point' is very weak for tail-latency or p99 claims, and the text says so. The issue is that the sentence may still be read as a recommended minimum. It should explicitly say this is a smoke-screen, not a p99-valid experiment.
issue.evidence: The sentence already says 'not proof of rare-failure or p99 reliability.' The recommendation is therefore adequately qualified. This is a minor clarity issue, not a correctness issue.
issue.root_cause: The phrase 'at least' may imply a sufficient minimum rather than a lower bound for a first screen.
issue.correction: Change to: 'A bounded first screen might use 200 paired examples per critical task and three repetitions per load point as a smoke test; this is not sufficient for p99 or rare-failure claims.'
issue.acceptance_test: No reader interprets 200 examples / 3 repetitions as adequate for p99 reliability.

issue.quoted_clause: They are not competing on the same axis: the decode bottleneck is unaffected by caching.
issue.observed: The sentence says prefix caching does not affect the decode bottleneck. But §2 explicitly says prefix reuse removes KV capacity, and Table 15-1 treats KV capacity as a binding constraint at Light and Typical load. If prefix caching frees KV capacity, it can permit larger decode batches or more concurrent decode requests, which changes decode goodput. The statement is too absolute.
issue.evidence: §2: 'the shared prefix's KV need not be recomputed or re-allocated — removing prefill FLOPs and KV capacity'. Table 15-1: KV demand ÷ host KV budget is 0.97× at Light and 4.91× at Typical, so capacity is a first-order decode-side constraint. A mechanism that reduces KV residency can therefore affect decode, even if it does not reduce decode-time HBM traffic per active token.
issue.root_cause: The sentence conflates 'prefix caching does not reduce decode-time HBM traffic for an active request' with 'prefix caching has no effect on the decode bottleneck'. The former is true; the latter is false when KV capacity constrains concurrency.
issue.correction: Narrow the claim: 'Prefix caching does not reduce the decode-time HBM traffic of an already-resident request; its decode-side effect is indirect, through freed KV capacity that may permit larger batches or more concurrent requests.'
issue.acceptance_test: The text no longer says the decode bottleneck is unaffected by caching. It distinguishes direct decode-traffic effects from indirect capacity effects.

issue.quoted_clause: recording offered load alongside p95 TTFT and p95 TPOT/ITL separately (report p95 only at offered loads ≤ the host's admission capacity, ~2 rps per host: 17 slots ÷ 8.6 s)
issue.observed: The sentence says to report p95 only at offered loads at or below the host's admission capacity (~2 rps), but the benchmark is described as a 40 rps saturation run. It is unclear whether p95 is being recorded but not reported at 40 rps, or whether the 40 rps run is exempt from the reporting rule. The protocol is ambiguous.
issue.evidence: The same paragraph says the 40 rps run is 'a saturation run on one host ... whose queue is expected to grow'. A growing queue means the host is above admission capacity, so the parenthetical reporting rule would exclude the very run being described.
issue.root_cause: The sentence mixes two different benchmark goals: a saturation run to observe queue growth, and an SLO-reporting run at or below admission capacity. The reporting rule is stated without clarifying which run it applies to.
issue.correction: Separate the two runs explicitly: 'Run A: saturation at 40 rps to observe queue growth; do not report p95 SLO numbers from this run. Run B: step through offered loads up to the host's admission capacity (~2 rps) and report p95 TTFT/TPOT only for Run B.'
issue.acceptance_test: The benchmark protocol clearly states which runs produce reportable p95 values and which are saturation-only.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 15, §7 What We Still Don't Know, chunked-prefill bullet
issue.quoted_clause: real user traffic exhibits bursts (e.g. social-media events) that may require larger chunks or alternative back-pressure mechanisms
issue.observed: The bullet says bursty traffic 'may require larger chunks'. The chapter's own chunked-prefill mechanism says smaller chunks reduce decode stall, while larger chunks improve prefill throughput but increase decode interference. For bursty traffic, the appropriate response is not obviously 'larger chunks'; it could be smaller chunks, admission control, or back-pressure. The claim is under-argued and potentially misleading.
issue.evidence: §Two Mechanisms: 'a smaller chunk reduces the decode stall but adds scheduler overhead ... chunk size is an empirically-chosen middle'. The open question should not presuppose that bursts push toward larger chunks without stating the trade-off.
issue.root_cause: The bullet treats 'bursty arrivals' as if they have a known directional effect on optimal chunk size, but the chapter has not established that direction.
issue.correction: Reframe as a genuine open question: 'Bursty arrivals may change the optimal chunk size in either direction — larger chunks can drain a prefill backlog faster, while smaller chunks protect decode latency — so the chunk-size policy must be measured under the target arrival process rather than assumed.'
issue.acceptance_test: The open question does not assert a directional recommendation ('larger chunks') without acknowledging the opposing trade-off.

issue.quoted_clause: No fire drill, no user-visible regression, no manual heroics — the factory made the wrong vendor claim cost nothing to the business
issue.observed: The same mini-case reports 12 legal-subset failures among 3,600 canary requests. If the 5% canary is production traffic, those 12 are user-visible failures; the claim of zero user-visible regression and zero business cost contradicts the reported canary outcome.
issue.evidence: Canary served 3,600 requests; 12 legal-subset failures; legal subset ≈360 requests. A canary serving real traffic cannot have both 12 failures and no user-visible regression.
issue.root_cause: Conflates 'contained blast radius' with 'zero impact'.
issue.correction: Say the regression was contained to the canary (12 users affected) and production-wide impact was avoided; or explicitly define the canary as shadow/internal traffic if zero user impact is intended.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case either reports the 12 canary failures as user-visible but contained, or explicitly states the canary was shadow traffic; it does not claim zero user-visible impact while reporting failures.

issue.page_hint: Ch 22 §3, 'The loop on a second workload'
issue.quoted_clause: KV footprint per request is 2.62 MB × 400 ≈ 1.05 GB rather than ~24.1 GB
issue.observed: For the stated 400-input/900-output workload, the KV cache at end of turn is 2.62 MB × (400+900) ≈ 3.41 GB, not 1.05 GB. The canonical table uses 9.5K max for 9.2K input + 300 output, so the second workload uses an inconsistent prompt-only basis.
issue.evidence: 2.62 MB/token × 1,300 tokens = 3,406 MB ≈ 3.41 GB. Canonical row: 2.62 × 9,500 = 24.9 GB max.
issue.root_cause: Inconsistent KV basis: prompt-only in the second workload vs max context in the canonical table.
issue.correction: Use 2.62 MB × 1,300 ≈ 3.41 GB for max KV, or label 1.05 GB as prompt-only and compare it to 24.1 GB prompt-only.
issue.acceptance_test: Both workloads use the same KV basis; recomputation from 400+900 and 9,200+300 matches the printed values.

issue.quoted_clause: this 30× ratio pushes the design toward high prefill compute and KV-capacity pressure
issue.observed: KV capacity is driven by absolute context length and model architecture, not by the input/output ratio. A 9.2K/9.2K workload has ratio 1 but the same KV capacity as 9.2K/300 at the same total context.
issue.evidence: KV bytes = 2 × n_layers × n_kv_heads × head_dim × tokens × bytes; the input/output ratio does not appear. The canonical 9.2K input drives KV; the 30× ratio drives prefill-vs-decode balance.
issue.root_cause: Conflates ratio with absolute input length.
issue.correction: Attribute KV pressure to the 9.2K context length; use the 30× ratio only for prefill/decode balance.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence separates ratio effects from absolute-context effects; a counterexample with ratio 1 and the same context is not contradicted.

issue.quoted_clause: The shard-invariant reason decode is memory-limited is its low arithmetic intensity (~1.0 FLOP/byte)
issue.observed: ~1.0 FLOP/byte is the batch-1 per-sequence intensity. At the canonical 10 rps, 300 output tokens, and 25 ms TPOT, concurrency is ~75, so weight reuse raises intensity to ~75 FLOP/byte (still below H100 ridge ~295, so memory-bound). The text presents ~1.0 as the system-level reason without stating batch.
issue.evidence: Little's law: 10 rps × 300 tokens × 0.025 s = 75 concurrent sequences. Intensity ≈ batch × 1 FLOP/byte = 75 FLOP/byte. H100 ridge ≈ 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s ≈ 295 FLOP/byte.
issue.root_cause: Uses batch-1 arithmetic intensity without qualifying batch/concurrency.
issue.correction: State 'per-sequence at batch 1' or compute intensity at the canonical batch; explain batching raises intensity but remains below the ridge point.
issue.acceptance_test: Arithmetic intensity is qualified by batch/concurrency and the memory-bound conclusion is re-derived at the canonical operating point.

issue.quoted_clause: the 2 × params × tokens approximation may ignore activation reuse across batched requests
issue.observed: Independent requests in a batch do not share activations; batching improves hardware utilization, not FLOP count. The 2NL approximation is not invalidated by cross-request activation reuse.
issue.evidence: Each request has its own hidden states; no cross-request activation reuse occurs in standard batched inference. FLOPs remain 2N per token for dense models.
issue.root_cause: Misconception about batching and activation reuse.
issue.correction: Remove 'activation reuse across batched requests'; if discussing corrections, refer to kernel overhead, padding, or activation memory, not cross-request reuse.
issue.acceptance_test: No claim of cross-request activation reuse; batching is described as utilization/efficiency, not FLOP reduction.

issue.quoted_clause: moves the 2NL prefill term and the ~140 GB weight read in the same direction but not the KV-cache term, which depends on context length and layer count rather than parameter count
issue.observed: A smaller dense model may have fewer layers or KV heads, so the KV-cache term can also shrink. Saying it does not move is misleading; it depends on layer count, KV-head count, head dimension, precision, and context length.
issue.evidence: KV bytes = 2 × n_layers × n_kv_heads × head_dim × tokens × bytes. Layer count often scales with model size, so replacing the model can change KV.
issue.root_cause: Overstates independence of KV from model size.
issue.correction: Say the KV term depends on layer/KV-head geometry and context length and may or may not shrink with a smaller model; it is not tied to parameter count alone.
issue.acceptance_test: The text acknowledges possible KV change when the model is replaced and lists the governing architecture variables.

issue.quoted_clause: If prefill needs FLOPS and decode needs bandwidth, a single homogeneous GPU pool is suboptimal.
issue.observed: The text later says P/D disaggregation depends on utilization, duplicated residency, KV-transfer cost, topology, workload shape, and burstiness. The unqualified 'is suboptimal' contradicts those caveats and overstates the case.
issue.evidence: Same section: 'Whether it needs fewer GPUs ... depends on ... those effects must be measured before the GPU-count conclusion is drawn.'
issue.root_cause: Universal claim where a conditional claim is supported.
issue.correction: Change to 'can be suboptimal' or 'may leave performance on the table'; keep the later measurement caveats.
issue.acceptance_test: The claim is qualified and consistent with the subsequent list of dependencies.

issue.quoted_clause: Gate pass rate / false-promotion rate — how often a gated change later regresses in production; a rising value means the evaluation suite is losing fidelity.
issue.observed: Gate pass rate and false-promotion rate are distinct. A rising gate pass rate can mean candidates are better or thresholds are looser; only a rising false-promotion rate directly indicates lost gate fidelity.
issue.evidence: Pass rate = passed candidates / candidates; false-promotion rate = passed candidates that later regress / passed candidates. They have different denominators and causal meanings.
issue.root_cause: Conflates two metrics under one definition.
issue.correction: Define them separately: gate pass rate measures candidate throughput; false-promotion rate measures gate fidelity. Only the latter's rise implies lost fidelity.
issue.acceptance_test: The two metrics have separate definitions and the causal claim is attached only to false-promotion rate.

issue.page_hint: Ch 21 §3, 'Cost of a bad ungated release'
issue.quoted_clause: the serving cost of the 216,000 requests exposed is ... (volume × unit rate — incurred whether or not the regression occurred)
issue.observed: If the serving cost is incurred whether or not the regression occurred, it is baseline serving cost, not the incremental cost of the bad release. The heading 'Cost of a bad ungated release' then overstates what the $5,394/$3,032 figures represent.
issue.evidence: The parenthetical explicitly says the cost is incurred regardless; the business cost of the regression is described separately as trust erosion and fire drill.
issue.root_cause: Labels baseline cost as release cost.
issue.correction: Rename the calculation 'baseline serving cost of the exposed requests' and separately state the incremental business cost is unquantified; or compute only incremental cost.
issue.acceptance_test: The text distinguishes baseline serving cost from incremental bad-release cost; the heading matches the quantity computed.

issue.page_hint: Ch 24 §3.3, peak KV residency check and Outcome paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: Candidate B's 8 hosts hold 140 — B fails peak KV as decisively as A
issue.observed: The same paragraph states the whole-slot convention is floor(436 ÷ 24.9) = 17 slots/host. 8 hosts × 17 slots/host = 136 slots, not 140. The later Outcome paragraph repeats '8 hosts hold 140 of the 344 in-flight'.
issue.evidence: 436/24.9 = 17.51; floor = 17. 8 × 17 = 136. If 140 were intended, it implies 17.5 slots/host, contradicting the stated floor convention.
issue.root_cause: Mixing fractional slot capacity (17.5) with the whole-slot floor convention (17) in the same calculation.
issue.correction: Change both occurrences of '140' to '136' (or explicitly state and justify a fractional-slot convention, which would conflict with the stated floor). Recompute the comparison: 136 of 344 in-flight, still below the 344 needed, so B still fails peak KV.
issue.acceptance_test: Search Ch 24 for '140' and 'hold 140'; verify 8 × floor(436/24.9) = 136 and that both occurrences are corrected or the convention is made explicit and consistent.

issue.quoted_clause: this null-model per-retrieval expectation (0.0052 ≈ 0.52%) already exceeds the §4.1 target of <0.3%
issue.observed: 0.0052 is the expected number of poisoned chunks per retrieval (k·p), not the probability that a retrieval returns at least one poisoned chunk. The target is a fraction of retrievals. The text later computes the correct probability 1−(1−p)^k ≈ 0.005197, but the note labels the expectation as a percentage and compares it directly to a probability target.
issue.evidence: E[poisoned chunks per retrieval] = 5 × 50/48000 ≈ 0.005208. P(≥1 poisoned chunk) = 1 − (1 − 50/48000)^5 ≈ 0.005197. They are numerically close here, but they are different quantities.
issue.root_cause: Conflating an expected count with a probability because the small-p approximation makes them numerically similar.
issue.correction: Rephrase: 'the expected number of poisoned chunks per retrieval is ≈0.0052; the probability that a retrieval returns at least one poisoned chunk is ≈0.52%, which already exceeds the §4.1 target of <0.3% under this null model.'
issue.acceptance_test: The text explicitly distinguishes E[count] from P(≥1) and does not call 0.0052 a percentage without qualification.

issue.page_hint: Ch 23 mini-case, 'The burst buffer, spelled out'
issue.quoted_clause: total time from burst start = 4 s (1 s burst + 3 s drain)
issue.observed: The last-arriving request at t=1 s waits 3 s in queue and then requires its own service time. At r=50 rps, service time is ≈20 ms, so completion is ≈4.02 s from burst start, not exactly 4 s. The text earlier says 'completes at 3 s plus its own service time', so the 4 s total omits that service time.
issue.evidence: D=1 s, arrival rate 200 rps, drain rate 50 rps. Queue at t=1 is 150. Drain time = 150/50 = 3 s. Last request starts at t=4 s; service time = 1/50 = 0.02 s; completion ≈4.02 s.
issue.root_cause: Reporting queue-drain time as total completion time without adding the final request's service time.
issue.correction: Change to 'total time from burst start to last completion ≈ 4 s + one service time (≈4.02 s at 50 rps)' or state that the 4 s is the drain/start time, not completion.
issue.acceptance_test: The burst-buffer arithmetic explicitly accounts for the final request's service time in the completion time.

issue.quoted_clause: all of it is decided by six numbers we can extract from a customer conversation
issue.observed: The sixth item in the list is 'operational reality — data privacy, geography, available staff, time-to-value', which is a constraint set, not a number. The preceding sentence says 'explicit number or constraint', so the later 'six numbers' is imprecise.
issue.evidence: List items 1–5 are numeric/quantifiable; item 6 is qualitative/operational. The chapter later calls them 'six bounds' and 'six numbers' interchangeably.
issue.root_cause: Terminology drift between 'numbers' and 'bounds/constraints'.
issue.correction: Use 'six bounds' or 'six numbers or constraints' consistently, especially in the Concept and Measurement sections.
issue.acceptance_test: Search Ch 23 for 'six numbers'; verify each occurrence is either changed to 'six bounds' or explicitly includes non-numeric constraints.

issue.quoted_clause: 6.24M requests/mo (business-hours basis: 10 rps average × 8 h × 260 workdays, Ch 16 arithmetic — so the monthly denominator averages ~2.4 rps
issue.observed: 10 rps × 8 h × 260 workdays = 74.88M requests/year, not 6.24M/month. 6.24M/month is 74.88M/year ÷ 12; the text omits the annual-to-monthly conversion.
issue.root_cause: Basis note mixes annual business-hours volume with monthly denominator without showing ÷12.
issue.correction: Add 'per year, ÷12' or write '10 rps × 8 h × (260/12) workdays per month = 6.24M/mo'.
issue.acceptance_test: The printed arithmetic closes explicitly from 10 rps business-hours to 6.24M/mo and ~2.4 rps.

issue.page_hint: Ch 25 Fig 25.1 caption; Table 25-1; ADR 0015 Falsification path
issue.quoted_clause: it is *kept, not edited*; 'update the ADR status'; 'ADR 0015 stays on file unchanged'
issue.observed: The figure says ADRs are not edited, but Table 25-1 requires updating status to superseded, and ADR 0015 says a successor supersedes it while it stays unchanged. Status metadata must change.
issue.evidence: Internal contradiction across three locations.
issue.root_cause: Conflates immutable decision body with mutable status/link metadata.
issue.correction: State that the decision body is kept, not rewritten; status may be updated to superseded with a link to the successor.
issue.acceptance_test: Fig 25.1, Table 25-1, and ADR 0015 use the same rule for status updates and supersession.

issue.quoted_clause: those reasons are verifiable (with ADR 0016 'no exact-match difference ... [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]')
issue.observed: ADR 0016's quality comparison is explicitly assumed, not measured. The format properties (2 B/param, exponent range) are verifiable; the no-quality-difference result is not yet.
issue.evidence: ADR 0016 tags the exact-match result [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] and says 'to be confirmed by the deployment quality gate'.
issue.root_cause: Overstates the evidentiary status of the worked ADR's assumed quality outcome.
issue.correction: Say the reasons are recorded and can be made verifiable by the validation plan; distinguish format facts from the assumed quality result.
issue.acceptance_test: §25.6 does not claim the assumed quality result is already verifiable.

issue.quoted_clause: per-request KV at 9.2K = 24.1 GB (2 × 80 layers × 9.2K × 8,192 × 2 B): KV, already inside the ~436 GB KV budget at concurrency
issue.observed: The sentence has no main verb after the colon and conflates 9.2K input with 9.5K total sequence length. The reader must reconstruct why 24.1 GB becomes 24.9 GB at concurrency.
issue.evidence: 9.2K input + 300 output = 9.5K; 9.5K × 2.62 MB = 24.9 GB. The text does not state this transition cleanly.
issue.root_cause: Compressed prose in a key calculation.
issue.correction: Rewrite as two sentences: 'At 9.2K input tokens, per-request KV is 24.1 GB. At concurrency, use the 9.5K maximum (9.2K input + 300 output), giving 24.9 GB per request; 17 concurrent requests occupy ~423 GB of the ~436 GB budget.'
issue.acceptance_test: The 24.1→24.9 GB transition and the 17×24.9≈423 GB budget check are explicit and grammatical.

issue.quoted_clause: Chain: ASSUMPTION (box 1 holds assumed scenario inputs, not instrumented FACTs) → DERIVED → PATTERN → ASSUMPTION; ... only measured FACTs enter the decision.
issue.observed: The caption says only measured FACTs enter the decision, but the stated chain begins and ends with ASSUMPTION. The final ASSUMPTION is not reconciled with the claim that measured FACTs govern the decision.
issue.evidence: The figure caption's own chain and its decision rule are inconsistent. A reader cannot tell whether the final box is an assumption, a hypothesis, or a validated decision state.
issue.root_cause: The figure is trying to show both the pre-validation hypothesis loop and the post-validation decision rule in one chain without distinguishing the two stages.
issue.correction: Redraw or relabel the chain so the pre-validation loop is explicitly ASSUMPTION → DERIVED → PATTERN → HYPOTHESIS, and the decision gate is a separate VALIDATE step that admits only measured FACTs. If the final box is a hypothesis, label it HYPOTHESIS, not ASSUMPTION.
issue.acceptance_test: The figure caption and the rendered figure must use one consistent evidence status for each box; no box may be both an assumption and a measured FACT in the same chain.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A, opening sections and repeated references
issue.quoted_clause: DeepSeek-V4 (A.3) ... Kimi K3 (A.4) ... Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (A.5) ... GLM-5.3-Flash (A.6) ... First-hand Sources (A.10)
issue.observed: The appendix's actual sections are numbered 1 through 8: §1 DeepSeek-V4, §2 Kimi K3, §3 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, §4 GLM-5.3-Flash, §5 What This Means for the Handbook's Canonical Arithmetic, §6 Where 2026 Capability Actually Comes From, §7 The Frontier Question, §8 First-hand Sources. The A.3/A.4/A.5/A.6/A.7/A.8/A.10 references therefore do not resolve to the intended sections.
issue.evidence: Systematic cross-reference mismatch. For example, 'DeepSeek-V4 (A.3)' points to what is actually §1; 'First-hand Sources (A.10)' points to what is actually §8. The same error recurs in 'A.7', 'A.8', and 'A.10' references throughout the appendix.
issue.root_cause: The appendix was renumbered from an A.x scheme to a 1–8 scheme, but the in-text references were not updated.
issue.correction: Either restore A.1–A.8 numbering for the appendix sections or change every A.x reference to the corresponding §1–§8 reference. Audit all A.x references in Appendix A and its cross-references.
issue.acceptance_test: Every A.x reference in the built PDF resolves to the intended section; no reference points to a nonexistent A.10 or to the wrong model section.

issue.quoted_clause: ## 8. First-hand Sources (all [1P]) ... ## 7A. Alternative inference in detail (moved from Ch 3)
issue.observed: Section 7A appears after Section 8. The appendix's section order is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, then 7A.
issue.evidence: The heading '## 7A. Alternative inference in detail' follows '## 8. First-hand Sources' in the manuscript chunk. This breaks the appendix's numerical order and makes the table of contents and navigation inconsistent.
issue.root_cause: A moved section was inserted at the end of the appendix without renumbering or repositioning.

issue.quoted_clause: The architectural consequence is conditional, and it is the reason this section sits in the model-understanding chapter rather than in a serving chapter.
issue.observed: The section is in Appendix A, not in the model-understanding chapter. The heading says it was 'moved from Ch 3.'
issue.evidence: Direct contradiction between the sentence and the section's actual location. The sentence appears to be a leftover from the section's former placement in Chapter 3.
issue.root_cause: Text was moved from Chapter 3 to Appendix A without updating the self-location sentence.
issue.correction: Change to 'the reason this material belongs with model understanding rather than serving' or 'the reason this appendix section exists,' or restore the section to Chapter 3 if that is the intended location.
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in Appendix A claims that the section sits in Chapter 3 or in the model-understanding chapter.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A, §7A 'Deriving attention FLOPs for a whole-clip video workload'
issue.quoted_clause: This example applies the §1 principle (fewer sequential evaluations ≠ less total work)
issue.observed: In Appendix A, §1 is 'DeepSeek-V4 — Making Long Context Cheap by Re-Architecting Attention.' The principle being invoked is from Chapter 3 §1's alternative-inference scope note, not Appendix A §1.
issue.evidence: The cross-reference is ambiguous and, read literally against Appendix A's numbering, points to the wrong section.
issue.root_cause: The section was moved from Chapter 3, but the '§1' reference was not qualified with the chapter.
issue.correction: Change to 'the Ch 3 §1 principle' or 'the alternative-inference scope note's principle.'
issue.acceptance_test: The cross-reference resolves to Chapter 3 §1, not Appendix A §1.

issue.quoted_clause: Post-snapshot observation (recorded 2026-09-27; outside the 2026-08-30 compile-date envelope). Beyond the four families above, Ornith-1.5-397B (released 2026-08-19 ...)
issue.observed: The model is said to be released on 2026-08-19, which is before the 2026-08-30 evidence cutoff. Only the author's observation is dated 2026-09-27. Calling the item 'post-snapshot' and 'outside the 2026-08-30 compile-date envelope' conflates the release date with the observation date.
issue.evidence: Date logic inconsistency: a model released before the cutoff cannot be a post-snapshot release merely because the author's probe occurred after the cutoff.
issue.root_cause: The text uses 'post-snapshot' to mean 'recorded after the snapshot' while also implying the item itself is outside the evidence cutoff.
issue.correction: Rewrite as 'post-snapshot observation of a model released before the cutoff but not included in the four-family comparison' or otherwise separate the release date from the observation date.
issue.acceptance_test: The text clearly distinguishes the model release date (2026-08-19) from the observation date (2026-09-27) and does not claim the release is outside the 2026-08-30 cutoff.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A, post-snapshot technology notes, editorial note and Intel/video supplements
issue.quoted_clause: A note keeps its place in Appendix A only when it changes how that comparison or the canonical arithmetic is read ... A note that only catalogs versions, pipelines or vendor backends, with no chapter cross-reference, belongs in a companion addendum rather than here.
issue.observed: The post-snapshot section includes the 'Intel backend supplement,' which catalogs PyTorch/vLLM/SGLang/OpenVINO release identities, Intel GPU availability, and Gaudi/NPU paths; and the 'Video systems snapshot,' which catalogs video-model mechanisms and release dates.
