issue.correction: Move out-of-scope notes to the companion addendum, or add an explicit chapter cross-reference and a sentence explaining how each note changes the four-family comparison or canonical arithmetic.
issue.acceptance_test: Every post-snapshot note either (a) changes the four-family comparison or canonical arithmetic and says how, or (b) is moved out of Appendix A.

issue.quoted_clause: [^oct-mt-huginn]^,^[^oct-mt-ouro]
issue.observed: Stray '^,^' sequences appear between many footnote markers throughout Appendix A (e.g., '[^oct-mt-huginn]^,^[^oct-mt-ouro]', '[^oct-ix-21]^,^[^oct-ix-22]', '[^oct-vg-VACE]^,^[^oct-vg-S2V]').

issue.issue: The figure encodes the KV write one decode step too early and contains an off-by-one token label. It shows token1 (sampled by prefill) and token2 (sampled by the first decode) being appended in the same step they are sampled, and labels token n as 'nth decode' even though token2 is labeled 'first decode'. This contradicts the caption's 'one step after it is sampled' and the prose on p. 14 that a token's K/V enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not the step in which it is sampled.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'for a generated token, written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled; prompt-token K/V is written during prefill.' p. 14: 'A token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled.' Figure labels: 'token1 from prefill' -> append K/V; 'token2 first decode' -> append K/V; '... token n nth decode' -> append K/V.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel or annotate the figure so the append arrows are offset by one step: prompt tokens append during prefill; token1 (prefill output) appends at first decode; token2 (first decode output) appends at second decode; ... token n appends at nth decode. Remove the 'token n nth decode' label or renumber tokens so token2 is not both 'first decode' and appended at first decode. Verify the rendered figure matches the caption and p. 14 timing convention.

issue.issue: The top process-band label is misspelled 'PREPFILL' instead of 'PREFILL'.
issue.evidence: Rendered figure label reads 'PREPFILL'; the caption and surrounding prose use 'PREFILL'.
issue.acceptance_test: Change the figure label to 'PREFILL' and re-render; search the figure source for 'PREPFILL' to confirm no remaining occurrence.

issue.issue: Panel C omits the solid bracket under A B at the intermediate step, so the figure does not show that the first block has been finalized before advancing.
issue.evidence: Panel C's second step shows 'A B ? ?' with a dashed box around the last two cells but no solid bracket under 'A B'. The text says 'Refine the active block; finalize/cache its state before advancing,' and the caption says 'Solid brackets identify finalized prefix state.' Panel A brackets each accepted prefix at every step; panel C brackets only the final 'A B C D'.
issue.acceptance_test: Add a solid bracket under 'A B' in panel C's second step, or explicitly revise the convention/text if the bracket is intentionally deferred; verify the bracket convention matches panel A and the caption.

issue.issue: The figure's second workload dimension is labeled 'Traffic / concurrency', but the caption calls the same dimension 'Request rate & arrival pattern'.
issue.evidence: Figure left box: 'Traffic / concurrency'. Caption: 'Request rate & arrival pattern → concurrency & batching'. These are not the same label, and 'traffic' vs 'request rate & arrival pattern' is a meaningful precision difference in a six-dimension taxonomy.
issue.acceptance_test: Use one label consistently in figure and caption (e.g., 'Request rate & arrival pattern' in the figure, or change the caption to 'Traffic/concurrency'); check the prose definition of the dimension.

issue.issue: The caption calls all five 'selection surfaces' model-selection dimensions, but one surface, 'retrieve-vs-generate', is an architecture decision rather than a model-selection dimension.
issue.evidence: Figure's 'Five selection surfaces' box lists 'quality · latency · KV cache · $/tok · retrieve-vs-generate'. Caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions.' The diagram then splits into 'Retrieval leg' and 'Generation leg', which is a system-architecture decision.
issue.acceptance_test: Either remove 'retrieve-vs-generate' from the five model-selection surfaces and show it as a separate architecture decision, or reword the caption to distinguish four model-selection dimensions from the retrieve-vs-generate architecture choice.

issue.issue: The figure classifies 'queue depth' as a Resource metric, while the preceding page explicitly classifies it as a Serving metric (a scheduler state).
issue.evidence: Page 94 text: 'Serving metrics — ... Time-to-first-token (TTFT), time-per-output-token (TPOT), inter-token latency, queue depth (a scheduler state), and goodput...' Figure 6.1's 'Resource metrics' box lists 'HBM BW · MFU · KV occupancy · queue depth'. This is a direct contradiction in the book's three-layer metric taxonomy.
issue.acceptance_test: Move 'queue depth' to the Serving metrics box in Fig 6.1, or reclassify it consistently in the p94 text and explain why it is a resource metric; ensure the three-layer taxonomy matches.

issue.issue: The y-axis label 'Authored intensity (0-1)' is undefined and is not explained by the caption or visible prose; the reader cannot tell what is being scored or whether higher means more intense.
issue.evidence: Y-axis reads 'Authored intensity (0-1)'; caption only says 'Workload fingerprints on the six axes' and the note says 'per-axis 0-1 scale; compare within an axis, not across axes.' No definition of 'authored intensity' appears on the page.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel the axis to a self-explanatory term such as 'Relative intensity (author-assigned, 0-1)' and add one caption sentence defining the score, or remove the axis label if the scores are not meant to be interpreted quantitatively.

issue.issue: The arrow label 'validate vs 800 ms target' conflicts with the caption's validation criterion and visually places validation before pattern selection.
issue.evidence: The figure shows an arrow from box 2 'DERIVED' to box 3 'PATTERN' labeled 'validate vs 800 ms target'. The caption says the validate step compares measured TTFT p99 against the hypothesis criterion 'TTFT p99 < 300 ms' under the capstone's 'p99 ≤ 800 ms TTFT target'. The figure label omits the 300 ms hypothesis criterion and makes validation look like a transition from derived state to pattern selection.

issue.issue: The subtitle says the denominator is each model's own vendor-reported total, but the Qwen bar uses only the 125B backbone, excluding the 51B n-gram embedding and 4B MTP; this contradicts the stated denominator and can mislead cross-model comparison.

Under that convention, a 'first decode step' occurs after the first token and therefore cannot be part of time-to-first-token. Ch 2 also says retrieval leaves 1.08 s for prefill without the later qualification that 1.08 s is a two-term upper cap.
issue.evidence: Ch 2: 'prefill = processing the prompt + sampling token 1, and decode = the per-token loop that begins with token 1 as its first input and produces token 2 onward.' Ch 4: 'the 1.08 s is therefore a two-term-only upper reach, NOT a feasible deployed prefill target: it leaves zero allowance for admission/queue, tokenization/transfer and the first decode step.'
issue.root_cause: Inconsistent prefill/decode boundary and TTFT decomposition across chapters.
issue.correction: Align the phase boundary. If prefill includes first-token sampling, define TTFT_e2e = retrieval + admission/queue + tokenization/transfer + prefill, with no separate first decode step. If the book wants to separate the first-token computation, call it a 'first-token step' and adjust Ch 2 so prefill does not include it. Add the two-term upper-cap qualification to Ch 2's 1.08 s statement.
issue.acceptance_test: Ch 2 and Ch 4 use the same prefill/decode boundary, and the TTFT budget decomposes into non-overlapping terms that end at first-token availability.

issue.quoted_clause: It becomes bandwidth-saturating above ~5 concurrent sequences per GPU (~40 per host) and compute-bound above ~295 concurrent sequences per GPU.
issue.observed: The ~5 per GPU threshold appears to assume each concurrent sequence causes a full 17.5 GB weight read (5 × 5.2 ms ≈ 26 ms), but in batched decode the weight read is shared across the batch. Under the book's own batched weight-streaming model, 5 sequences do not saturate HBM; KV traffic also matters.
issue.evidence: Per-GPU weight shard = 17.5 GB; 17.5 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 5.2 ms. For B batched sequences, weight read remains ~17.5 GB per step, not B×17.5 GB. With 9.5K context and full-MHA FP16 sharded KV (~0.3275 MB/token/GPU), KV read is ~3.1 GB per sequence per step; HBM saturation at 25 ms would require ~83.75 GB total, near B≈21 per GPU if KV is included, not B≈5. The compute-bound threshold B≈295 follows from per-GPU intensity B FLOP/byte only if KV traffic is ignored.
issue.root_cause: Mixing non-batched per-sequence weight traffic with batched arithmetic-intensity thresholds.
issue.correction: Recompute thresholds from the stated batched model: state whether B is batched (shared weight read) or non-batched. For batched decode, give the HBM-saturation threshold including weight + KV read/write, and give the compute-bound threshold including KV traffic or explicitly say 'ignoring KV traffic'.
issue.acceptance_test: The printed thresholds are reproducible from the per-GPU weight shard, KV bytes/token, TPOT budget, and H100 HBM peak, and are consistent with the 17-slot KV screen.

issue.quoted_clause: meeting that latency target calls for multi-GPU scaling or bandwidth-increasing topologies (e.g. NVLink-connected nodes).
issue.observed: NVLink/NVSwitch increase inter-GPU interconnect bandwidth, not HBM bandwidth. The decode weight-read bottleneck discussed in the same paragraph is HBM bandwidth; multi-GPU sharding reduces per-GPU HBM traffic, while NVLink is relevant to tensor-parallel communication overhead.
issue.evidence: The paragraph compares 140 GB / 25 ms = 5.6 TB/s against H100 HBM3 3.35 TB/s. NVLink is not an HBM bandwidth source.
issue.root_cause: Loose use of 'bandwidth-increasing topologies' after an HBM-bandwidth argument.
issue.correction: Reword to: 'multi-GPU sharding (which reduces per-GPU HBM weight traffic) and, where tensor parallelism is used, sufficient NVLink/NVSwitch interconnect for the added communication.'
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence implies NVLink raises HBM bandwidth or directly solves the 5.6 TB/s HBM demand.

issue.quoted_clause: The token-counting habits of Ch 1 §1.4 apply unchanged
issue.observed: Chapter 1's measurement material is in section 4, not section 1.4. The reference as written does not resolve to the intended token-counting habits.
issue.evidence: Chunk shows Chapter 1 headings: '## 4. Measurement' and no '§1.4'.
issue.root_cause: Stale or mistyped cross-reference.
issue.correction: Change to 'Ch 1 §4' or 'Ch 1, Measurement'.
issue.acceptance_test: The cross-reference points to the section that lists actual token count, input/output split, and peak/average context.

issue.quoted_clause: The durable mental model: total parameters set the ceiling; active parameters per token set the floor.
issue.observed: This compression is ambiguous and can mislead on memory: total parameters set a lower bound on weight residency (all weights must be resident unless offloaded), not a ceiling for memory; active parameters set a lower bound on per-token compute and active weight-read traffic, not a floor for residency.
issue.evidence: Later in the same chapter: 'total parameters → weight residency' and 'active parameters/token → approximate compute per token'.
issue.root_cause: Over-compressed metaphor that collapses two different budgets (residency vs compute).
issue.correction: Reword as: 'total parameters bound the maximum active work and set the residency floor; active parameters per token set the compute floor (and active weight-read traffic).'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state that total parameters drive weight residency and active parameters drive per-token compute without inferring that total is a memory ceiling.

issue.page_hint: Ch 3, §6, 'The 2026 baseline shift' and 'One verified 2026 transfer'
issue.quoted_clause: Qwen3.8-27B ([1P][FACT], source: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B) is a dense 27.8B model
issue.observed: The book's canonical 'dense' is also 'full-MHA'. Calling a model with 48 Gated DeltaNet layers 'dense' without qualification can make readers conflate dense parameter activation with full attention, especially in a chapter that contrasts full-MHA KV with hybrid/constant-state KV.
issue.evidence: The same section says Qwen3.8-27B has 16 full-attention layers and 48 Gated DeltaNet layers, i.e. hybrid attention, not full-MHA.
issue.root_cause: Using 'dense' for non-MoE parameter regime while the reader may expect 'dense' to mean full attention.
issue.correction: Say 'dense in the total-vs-active sense (non-MoE), but hybrid attention' or 'non-MoE 27.8B model with hybrid attention'.
issue.acceptance_test: The text distinguishes parameter-density from attention architecture and does not imply Qwen3.8-27B is full-MHA.

issue.quoted_clause: without admission scheduling, prefills queue behind one another and TTFT under load pushes well above 2 s
issue.observed: 'pushes well above 2 s' is a strong performance prediction without stated load, queue length, chunking, or measurement. It can be true in some configurations but is not established by the canonical arithmetic in this chapter.
issue.evidence: The chapter provides offered load and per-host planning rates, but no queueing model or measured TTFT under unscheduled prefills.
issue.root_cause: Claim strength exceeds evidence.
issue.correction: Soften to 'can push TTFT above the 2 s p95 ceiling under sustained load' or add 'in a discrete-batching, non-chunked configuration'.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence is scoped as a possible outcome, not a universal measured result.

issue.page_hint: Ch 2, §3, Canonical host verdict; Ch 4, §6, Memory planning
issue.quoted_clause: KV 24.1 GB per request against the 640 GB pool (~228 GB total resident: 140 GB weights + ~64 GB runtime/workspace reserve + 24.1 GB KV
issue.observed: 24.1 GB is the input-only 9.2K KV figure. Ch 4 uses 24.9 GB per 9.5K-token resident request for slot counting. In Ch 4, 'At 10 concurrent full-context requests the MHA figure is ~241 GB' also uses the input-only basis while the same section later uses the resident basis. Calling 24.1 GB 'per request' in resident totals can understate resident KV.
issue.evidence: Ch 4 canonical box: '2.62 MB/token → ~24.1 GB @ 9.2K input-only; ~24.9 GB @ 9.5K input+output — the resident slot-counting basis.' 10 × 24.9 = 249 GB, not 241 GB.
issue.root_cause: Mixing input-only and resident KV bases without labeling.
issue.correction: Label 24.1 GB as input-only wherever used. For resident request totals, use 24.9 GB (or explicitly say the total is at prefill completion before output tokens are cached). Adjust the 10-request example to 249 GB if resident.
issue.acceptance_test: Every KV total states whether it is input-only or resident, and 10-request totals match the stated basis.

issue.quoted_clause: Per 1K req (wall-clock paid-occupancy cost ÷ active-hours volume)
issue.observed: The table includes an 'active-hours basis' row whose monthly cost is 6 × 173.3 h × $20, not wall-clock paid-occupancy cost. The column header therefore mislabels that row's numerator.
issue.evidence: Row: 'Cloud, 6 hosts — active-hours basis (6 × 173.3 h × $20) | $20,800 | ≈ $3.33'. $20,800 is active-hours cost, while wall-clock paid-occupancy for 6 hosts is $87,600.
issue.root_cause: One column header applied to rows with different cost bases.
issue.correction: Change header to 'Per 1K active-hours requests (Monthly cost ÷ 6.24M active-hours requests)' or add a separate 'cost basis' column.
issue.acceptance_test: Each row's per-1K value is computed from the row's own monthly cost basis, and the header does not assert wall-clock paid-occupancy for active-hours rows.

issue.quoted_clause: if the input token count could be reduced to 2 K (e.g. via better retrieval or query expansion), cost per request drops to ~$0.003
issue.observed: Query expansion normally increases prompt length by adding reformulations or context; it is not a standard method for reducing input tokens. The example may mislead.
issue.evidence: The sentence's goal is reducing input token count from 9.2K to 2K; 'better retrieval' can do that, but 'query expansion' usually does the opposite.
issue.root_cause: Imprecise example of an input-reduction lever.
issue.correction: Replace 'query expansion' with 'query compression', 'retrieval pruning', or 'context selection'.
issue.acceptance_test: The listed levers plausibly reduce input tokens.

issue.page_hint: Ch 4, §3, Canonical Workload box, 'Mean request service time (planning)'
issue.quoted_clause: retrieval ~120ms + prefill ~1.08s + decode ~7.5s rounded to a comfortable planning figure
issue.observed: The named components sum to ~8.7 s, not ~10 s. Calling ~10 s a 'rounding' of 8.7 s is a 15% upward round and may look inconsistent with the derived 8.6 s execution time.
issue.root_cause: Using a coarse planning round without showing the gap.
issue.correction: Either use '~9 s' as the planning round, or explicitly say '~10 s is a coarse planning ceiling, not the arithmetic sum of the named terms'.
issue.acceptance_test: The planning round is either arithmetically close to the component sum or explicitly labeled as a conservative ceiling.

issue.quoted_clause: DECODE (bottom) is the single-token autoregressive loop, measured by TPOT (time per output token; equivalently the mean ITL, inter-token latency)
issue.observed: TPOT and mean ITL are not strictly equivalent for finite sequences if TPOT is defined over all output tokens while ITL is defined over intervals between tokens, especially under the book's convention that the first token is produced by prefill.
issue.evidence: With 300 output tokens and first token from prefill, there are 299 inter-token intervals after the first token; mean ITL over those intervals is not identical to total output-token time divided by 300 unless defined carefully.
issue.root_cause: Using 'equivalently' without defining the denominator.
issue.correction: Say 'measured by TPOT (time per output token; in steady state this is the mean ITL between generated tokens)' or define TPOT as decode time divided by number of decode steps.
issue.acceptance_test: The text states the denominator for TPOT and does not claim strict equivalence for finite sequences.

issue.quoted_clause: continuous batching (e.g. vLLM) is nearly mandatory under this load to hold the 1.2 s TTFT budget
issue.observed: 'nearly mandatory' is a strong design claim. Continuous batching is a common and often necessary mechanism under concurrency, but whether it is mandatory to hold a specific TTFT budget depends on queueing, chunked prefill, priorities, and engine behavior.
issue.evidence: The chapter does not provide a queueing model showing that non-continuous batching cannot meet 1.2 s.
issue.root_cause: Claim strength slightly exceeds the analytical basis.
issue.correction: Soften to 'continuous batching is a primary mechanism for holding TTFT under this concurrency' or 'is typically required in production engines under this load'.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence is a scoped design expectation, not an absolute requirement.

issue.quoted_clause: Using the canonical per-host bound from Chapters 15–20
issue.observed: The sentence first attributes the per-host bound to Chapters 15–20, then cites Chapters 14/16/17 for the whole-slot convention. The range is inconsistent and may misdirect the reader.
issue.evidence: Both citations appear in the same parenthetical; the chunk does not show which chapters actually contain the 17-slot convention.
issue.root_cause: Stale or imprecise cross-reference range.
issue.correction: Use a single accurate range, e.g. 'Chapters 14, 16, and 17' if that is where the convention is defined, or 'Chapters 14–20' if the bound is developed across that range.
issue.acceptance_test: The cross-reference range matches the locations where the 17-slot convention and per-host bound are defined.

issue.quoted_clause: Factual accuracy >85% on enterprise Q&A; reasoning via retrieval; no tool use beyond search API
issue.observed: 'reasoning via retrieval' is not a standard quality attribute and may be read as a claim that retrieval performs reasoning. The intended meaning is probably that the task requires retrieval-grounded answers, not deep multi-step reasoning.
issue.evidence: The quality dimension is about fidelity/accuracy/capability; 'reasoning via retrieval' mixes capability and mechanism.
issue.root_cause: Compressed table cell with ambiguous phrasing.
issue.correction: Reword as 'retrieval-grounded factual answers; no multi-step reasoning or tool use beyond search API'.
issue.acceptance_test: The quality row states a measurable capability without implying retrieval is a reasoning engine.

issue.page_hint: Ch 1, §1, KV cache as a concept
issue.quoted_clause: the vLLM FP8-KV blog post's often-quoted '54%' — from its Llama-3.1-8B Table 3 (vLLM blog, post dated 2026-04-22; retrieved 2026-11-15) [S6] — is, on this book's reading, a decode inter-token-latency (ITL) slope, not a memory ratio or footprint coefficient.
issue.observed: This is a strong interpretive claim about an external source. The chunk does not show the table or the calculation that makes the 54% an ITL slope. If the source actually reports a memory reduction or throughput improvement, the book's reinterpretation would be misleading.
issue.evidence: No primary table excerpt or derivation is included; the claim is labeled as 'on this book's reading'.
issue.root_cause: External-source interpretation without visible evidence at first use.
issue.correction: Either include the relevant table values and the slope calculation, or soften to 'the 54% figure is commonly cited, but its basis in the source is an ITL slope rather than a raw memory ratio; see source [S6]' with a footnote.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can verify from the cited source that 54% is an ITL slope, not a memory footprint coefficient.

issue.page_hint: Ch 2, Table 2-1, row 'Prefill: FLOPs (2 × params × tokens)'
issue.quoted_clause: Prefill: FLOPs (2 × params × tokens) | 1.29 PFLOP
issue.observed: The table row can be read as the total prefill FLOPs, but the surrounding text explicitly says 2NL is a parameterized-linear FLOP floor excluding attention-score/value aggregation and other non-matmul overhead.
issue.evidence: Ch 2: 'Call this what it is: the parameterized-linear FLOP floor, 2NL, excluding explicit attention-score/value aggregation and other non-matmul overhead. The full-attention component is not captured by 2NL.'
issue.root_cause: Table label omits the 'floor/lower bound' qualifier present in prose.
issue.correction: Change row to 'Prefill: parameterized-linear FLOP floor (2 × params × tokens)' or add 'excluding attention overhead'.
issue.acceptance_test: The table does not imply 1.29 PFLOP is the complete prefill FLOP count.

issue.quoted_clause: the total weights dominate the memory ceiling, ~125 × 10^9 params × 2 bytes/param ≈ 250 GB
issue.observed: Total weights set a lower bound on resident memory (what must be held), not a ceiling. The same sentence later says the ~250 GB total 'is what must be resident'.
issue.evidence: 250 GB is the minimum FP16 weight residency if all total weights are resident; it is not an upper limit on memory.
issue.root_cause: Misuse of 'ceiling' for a residency floor.
issue.correction: Change to 'the total weights dominate the residency floor' or 'set the minimum resident weight footprint'.
issue.acceptance_test: The text uses ceiling/floor consistently: total parameters set a residency lower bound, not an upper bound.

issue.page_hint: Ch 6 §3, Detecting the Regime, decode paragraph, final parenthetical
issue.quoted_clause: (This is an operating-point property, not an identity: at high batch decode climbs the intensity slope and can become compute-bound.)
issue.observed: Ch 8 later shows that including the canonical 9.2K KV re-read, decode intensity saturates at ~6.8 FLOP/byte and remains bandwidth-bound at every batch size; the weight-only 'can become compute-bound' is only valid when KV traffic is small or quantized.
issue.evidence: Ch 8 §3: 'Including it, the decode intensity is (164·b)/(140 + 24·b) ... saturates at ~6.8 FLOP/byte ... So with the KV term, decode stays bandwidth-bound at every batch size; the batch ≈ 295 figure is the weight-only first-order estimate (valid when the KV re-read is small relative to the weight stream, e.g. short contexts or KV quantization).'
issue.root_cause: Missing KV-term caveat in Ch 6, creating a cross-chapter inconsistency for the canonical long-context workload.
issue.correction: Add 'in the weight-only model, or when KV traffic is small/quantized; with the canonical 9.2K KV term, decode remains bandwidth-bound at all batch sizes (Ch 8)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Ch 6 statement no longer implies canonical long-context decode can become compute-bound at high batch without the KV caveat.

issue.page_hint: Ch 7 §3, Fig 7.7 technical note, first sentence
issue.quoted_clause: at 17.5 concurrent requests a rank reaches ~99.7% of its 80 GB capacity (17.5 + 8 + 54.25 = 79.75 GB)
issue.observed: The same note lists KV budget per rank as 436 ÷ 8 = ~54.5 GB and per-rank budget 17.5 + 54.5 + 8 = 80 GB; 54.25 is inconsistent with the stated 436 GB aggregate KV budget.
issue.evidence: 436/8 = 54.5; 17.5+8+54.5=80.0. If using 17.5 requests and per-request KV 24.9/8=3.1125, KV per rank = 54.47, not 54.25.
issue.root_cause: Arithmetic typo or stale value from a different reserve/weight split.
issue.correction: Change 54.25 to 54.5 and 79.75 to 80.0, or recompute with byte-accurate values and state the exact percentage.
issue.acceptance_test: The per-rank sum uses the same 436/8 value as the bullet list and equals 80 GB at the 17.5 ceiling.

issue.quoted_clause: Tokens per dollar (generation, runtime) | 9,000 tokens per dollar
issue.observed: The 50 tok/s input is an output-token rate; later text explicitly calls 9,000 an output-token metric. The table label can be read as total generation tokens per dollar.
issue.evidence: Ch 5 §3(b): 'The 9,000 tokens-per-dollar figure is an output-token metric (50 output tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20)'.
issue.root_cause: Missing output qualifier in table.
issue.correction: Change to 'Output tokens per dollar (generation, runtime)' or 'Output tokens per dollar at the 50 output tok/s low-batch point'.
issue.acceptance_test: Table row matches the later output-token scope and cannot be read as total input+output tokens per dollar.

issue.quoted_clause: and (on a multi-GPU host) tensor- or pipeline-parallel copies.
issue.observed: Tensor parallelism generally shards tensors and pipeline parallelism partitions layers; neither inherently requires 'copies' of the model. Some components may be replicated, but the term is too broad and can mislead the memory ledger.
issue.evidence: Ch 7 later treats TP=8 as sharding weights 140/8 and KV 24.9/8, not replication; Ch 8/9 parallelism discussions distinguish sharding from replication.
issue.root_cause: Imprecise wording in the runtime/workspace list.
issue.correction: Replace with 'tensor- or pipeline-parallel communication buffers and any replicated components (e.g., embeddings/LM head where applicable)' or remove 'copies'.
issue.acceptance_test: The practical host requirement list does not imply whole-model replication for TP/PP.

issue.quoted_clause: Because GQA caches only one K/V per group (8 K/V per token) instead of one per query head (64 K/V per token), the per-token KV falls ~8×
issue.observed: The counts 8 and 64 are per layer (KV heads vs query heads), not total K/V tensors per token across all 80 layers. As written, '8 K/V per token' can be misread as 8 total K/V entries for the whole model.
issue.evidence: The formula uses 2 × 80 × (8 × 128) × 2 B; the 8 is n_KV-heads per layer, and 64 is n_query-heads per layer.
issue.root_cause: Missing 'per layer' qualifier.
issue.correction: Say '8 KV heads per layer (64 query heads per layer)' or '8 K/V head pairs per token per layer'.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence cannot be read as 8 total K/V tensors per token for the full model.

issue.page_hint: Ch 8 §8 mini-case, paragraph after 'So a high TTFT is not evidence...'
issue.quoted_clause: Prefill's effective intensity is (2 × N × L) / (N × 2 bytes/param) = L = 9,200 FLOP/byte at the canonical 9.2K context
issue.observed: This is the weight-only upper bound; Ch 8 §5 says including the ~24 GB KV write gives ~7,850 FLOP/byte. Calling it 'effective intensity' without 'weight-only' may overstate the actual prefill intensity.
issue.evidence: Ch 8 §5: 'weight-only intensity ~9,200 FLOP/byte — an upper bound that omits the ~24 GB KV write; including it, ~7,850 FLOP/byte'.
issue.root_cause: Omitted scope qualifier in mini-case.
issue.correction: Say 'weight-only prefill intensity' or add 'including KV write, ~7,850 FLOP/byte; both are far above the ridge'.
issue.acceptance_test: Mini-case intensity statement matches the qualified value in Common Mistakes.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 10, §3 Worked Example, Data Parallelism: Replicating, Then Syncing Gradients
issue.quoted_clause: for N=8 the per-rank send volume is (N-1)/N × 280 ≈ 245 GB and the send-plus-receive total is 1.75 × 280 ≈ 490 GB ... At 25 GB/s (single 200Gb/s link) that is 245 / 25 ≈ 9.8 s per step ... At the H100 NVLink directional peak of 450 GB/s, the same ideal ring estimate is 245/450 ≈ 0.54 s
issue.observed: The 280 GB FP32 gradient case reuses the 140 GB FP16 gradient traffic numbers from Chapter 9. For a ring all-reduce with M=280 GB and N=8, the total per-rank send volume is 2*(N-1)/N*M = 490 GB, not 245 GB; the per-rank receive volume is also 490 GB, and send-plus-receive is 980 GB, not 490 GB.
issue.evidence: Reduce-scatter sends (N-1)/N*M = 245 GB per rank; all-gather sends another (N-1)/N*M = 245 GB per rank. Total send = 490 GB. 490/25 = 19.6 s; 490/450 ≈ 1.09 s. The printed 245/25 and 245/450 are the Chapter 9 140 GB values, not the 280 GB values.
issue.root_cause: The precision basis was changed from 140 GB FP16 to 280 GB FP32, but the downstream ring traffic and time calculations were not doubled.
issue.correction: Either state that 245 GB is the one-phase send volume and give the full two-phase send volume as 490 GB with times 19.6 s at 25 GB/s and ≈1.09 s at 450 GB/s, or explicitly keep the 140 GB FP16 example for the 9.8 s / 0.54 s numbers. Do not mix 280 GB logical size with 140 GB traffic arithmetic.
issue.acceptance_test: Recompute from M=280 GB, N=8: printed per-rank total send, total receive, send-plus-receive, and both bandwidth times must match 490 GB, 490 GB, 980 GB, 19.6 s, and ≈1.09 s respectively, or the text must clearly label 245 GB as one-phase only and use 490 GB for total send time.

issue.quoted_clause: If the architecture calls for data-parallel training of a 70B FP16 model across 8 nodes (an eight-rank DP group, e.g. one rank per node), the all-reduce bandwidth dictates whether the nodes are connected by InfiniBand, 200 GbE, or even 100 GbE. If the budget can accommodate NVLink-equipped hosts (GPUs connected on-node), keeping the all-reduce on-node gives an ideal ring time about 1/11th the assumed InfiniBand case and about 1/180th the assumed RoCE case
issue.observed: For the stated eight-node, one-rank-per-node DP group, the all-reduce is an inter-node collective. The 1/11 and 1/180 ratios compare an eight-rank group placed on one NVLink host with an eight-rank group placed across hosts; they do not apply to the same eight-node one-rank-per-node DP group.
issue.evidence: Chapter 9 §3 computes 0.54 s for an eight-rank NVLink ring and 6.1 s / 98 s for eight-rank cross-host rings. If the DP group has one rank per node across 8 nodes, the ranks are not on one NVLink domain; NVLink can only help intra-node subgroups or a different rank placement.
issue.root_cause: The paragraph conflates two different rank placements: an 8-rank on-node DP group and an 8-node one-rank-per-node DP group.
issue.correction: Reword to separate the cases: for the stated 8-node one-rank-per-node DP group, the all-reduce is inter-node; the 1/11 and 1/180 figures apply only if the 8-rank DP group is placed within one NVLink host, or to the intra-node portion of a hierarchical DP design.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader should not be able to infer that an 8-node one-rank-per-node DP all-reduce can be kept on NVLink; the text must explicitly state which rank placement the ratios describe.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 12, §8 Mini-Case, Candidate (b); also Table 12-1 row (b)
issue.quoted_clause: up to ~576 GB (140 + 436) at the canonical per-host KV budget (§12.3)
issue.observed: This is inconsistent with §12.3, which says the canonical per-host KV budget is 640 - 140 weights - ~64 runtime ≈ 436 GB, and that 140 + 436 + ~64 = 640 GB exactly. 576 GB is weights plus KV only; it excludes the ~64 GB runtime reserve.
issue.evidence: 140 + 436 = 576; 576 + 64 = 640. Table 12-1 also says "~576 GB at the full KV budget (140 + 436)", while §12.3 says the full pool is 640 GB including runtime.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case and table summarize the full KV budget as weights+KV only, while the main text includes runtime in the 640 GB pool total.
issue.correction: Make the quantity explicit: "weights+KV = 576 GB; including the ~64 GB runtime reserve, the host total is 640 GB" or change the total to 640 GB if the sentence is about whole-host residency.
issue.acceptance_test: Every statement of Candidate (b) full-KV residency must agree on whether 576 GB or 640 GB is being quoted, and 640 GB must include the ~64 GB runtime component.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 9, §5 Common Mistakes, "Ignoring contention from other traffic"
issue.quoted_clause: if other collectives (e.g., all-gather for optimizer state) are running simultaneously
issue.observed: FSDP-style training all-gathers parameter shards, not optimizer state. Optimizer state is sharded and updated locally; it is not the object normally all-gathered.
issue.evidence: Chapter 10 states FSDP "all-gathers parameter shards" in forward and "reduce-scatters gradients" in backward. The same chapter's FSDP example uses a 64 MiB unit all-gather, not optimizer-state all-gather.
issue.root_cause: Imprecise example of a concurrent collective.
issue.correction: Replace with "all-gather for parameter shards (FSDP)" or "reduce-scatter for gradients".
issue.acceptance_test: The example collective must correspond to a real FSDP/DP training communication pattern.

issue.quoted_clause: MoE models (if chosen per Ch3) push toward EP, because the full expert set must be resident (the active count sets compute per token, not residency) and EP shards the experts across GPUs.
issue.observed: "Must be resident" is too absolute. The same chapter later says the total expert residency must be sharded only "if the deployment keeps all experts resident in HBM", and that expert offloading or caching changes the capacity calculus.
issue.evidence: Chapter 10 §7: "the total expert residency that must be sharded if the deployment keeps all experts resident in HBM (expert offloading or caching otherwise changes the capacity calculus)".
issue.root_cause: The architecture-consequence bullet omits the residency assumption used later.
issue.correction: Add the condition: "when the deployment keeps the full expert set resident in HBM" or "for HBM-resident expert placements".
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence must not imply that offloaded or cached expert deployments necessarily require all experts to be resident in HBM.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 11, §6 Architecture Consequence, baseline bullet; also §5 Common Mistakes
issue.quoted_clause: PagedAttention packs the ~24.1 GB-per-request KV densely (fixed-size pages, minimal fragmentation) so more concurrent requests fit in the 640 GB node
issue.observed: PagedAttention reduces external fragmentation and over-reservation, but block-level internal fragmentation and metadata overhead remain. "Minimal fragmentation" and the related "removes the fragmentation tax" can be read as eliminating all fragmentation.
issue.evidence: Chapter 11 §2 says PagedAttention "reduces external fragmentation and over-reservation, improving effective KV capacity; block-level internal fragmentation and metadata overhead remain."
issue.root_cause: Shorthand conflates all fragmentation with external fragmentation.
issue.correction: Use "reduces external fragmentation; block-level internal fragmentation and metadata overhead remain" in both locations.
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence should state or imply that PagedAttention removes all KV fragmentation.

issue.quoted_clause: Latency/geography: SLO can't be met due to distance or contention → split prefill/decode (a within-tier move).
issue.observed: P/D disaggregation addresses phase contention and mismatched resource binding, not network distance or geography. Distance is a placement problem (edge/region/local), not a P/D problem.
issue.evidence: The same paragraph says "moving the serving edge closer (local) is a placement move to a lower rung, not a climb trigger".
issue.root_cause: Two different causes (distance and contention) are merged into one trigger with one remedy.
issue.correction: Split the trigger: "contention/phase interference → P/D disaggregation" and "distance/geography → placement to a lower or different tier, or regional replicas".
issue.acceptance_test: A reader should map distance to placement, not to P/D disaggregation.

issue.quoted_clause: because the architect climbed the ladder precisely one rung
issue.observed: The canonical 40 rps workload was already described as a fleet of ~21 server-class hosts, i.e. a cluster of server-class hosts. At 100 rps the deployment remains a cluster, just larger. "Climbed precisely one rung" can imply moving from a single server to a cluster, which may not match the prior canonical deployment.
issue.evidence: Chapter 13 §3: "the canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload sits on the server tier as a fleet of ~21 server-class hosts at the 40 rps peak ... the traffic scaling is a cluster of server-class hosts".
issue.root_cause: The mini-case does not state whether the prior on-prem service was a single server or the 21-host cluster.
issue.correction: Clarify the prior deployment size. If it was already a 21-host cluster, say the architect "scaled within the cluster tier"; if it was a single server, say so explicitly before using "one rung".
issue.acceptance_test: The rung language must match the stated prior and new tiers.

issue.quoted_clause: Total fleet cost $155.8K/mo (21 hosts) ÷ $15K = ~10.4× over the total budget
issue.observed: "10.4× over" is ambiguous or incorrect. The cost is 10.4 times the budget; the excess over the budget is 9.4 times the budget.
issue.evidence: 155.8 / 15 = 10.39. Later in the same paragraph the text correctly says "~10.4× the stakeholder's stated $15,000 total monthly budget".
issue.root_cause: Wording conflates "times the budget" with "times over the budget".
issue.correction: Use "10.4× the total budget" or "9.4× over the total budget".
issue.acceptance_test: The ratio wording must match the arithmetic: cost/budget = 10.4, not excess/budget = 10.4.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 13, §3 Worked Example, Escalating: When 10×Traffic Forces the Cluster Tier
issue.quoted_clause: the ~2.0 rps screen uses the unfloored 17.5-slot quotient and applies no utilization headroom, so 50 hosts could only deliver 50 × 17/8.6 ≈ 98.8 rps — below demand.
issue.observed: The sentence says the screen uses the unfloored 17.5-slot quotient, but the calculation uses the floored 17 slots. With 17.5 slots, 50 hosts deliver 50 × 17.5 / 8.6 ≈ 101.7 rps, not 98.8 rps.
issue.root_cause: The explanation mixes the unfloored and floored slot counts in the same sentence.
issue.correction: State both clearly: using the conservative floored 17 slots, 50 hosts deliver 98.8 rps; using 17.5 slots, they deliver ~101.7 rps but with no utilization headroom and based on a rounded 2.0 rps figure.
issue.acceptance_test: The slot count used in the arithmetic must match the slot count named in the sentence.

issue.quoted_clause: ✗ ~4 avg / ~15 peak hosts at the single-H100 rate (Table 12-2)
issue.observed: Candidate (c) is laid out as 1×H100 and Table 12-2 sizes it in "H100 cards", not 8-GPU hosts. Calling these "hosts" can be confused with the 8×H100 host unit used for Candidates (a) and (b).
issue.evidence: Table 12-2 says "~4 H100 cards" and "~15 H100 cards", and its units note says "(c) is sized in single H100 cards (one card per 7B instance)".
issue.root_cause: Terminology drift between host and card for single-GPU instances.
issue.correction: Change to "~4 avg / ~15 peak single-H100 cards" or "instances".
issue.acceptance_test: All Candidate (c) capacity units should be cards/instances, not 8-GPU hosts.

issue.quoted_clause: In round r, rank i sends chunk (i−r) mod N in both phases, so rank r ends the reduce-scatter holding reduced chunk r.
issue.observed: The stated send convention does not by itself imply the stated final ownership. A ring reduce-scatter's final chunk ownership depends on the receive direction and which local chunk is reduced; the caption omits that convention.
issue.evidence: For N=4, if rank i sends chunk i-r to i+1 and receives/reduces chunk i-r-1, the final ownership is offset from the simple "rank r holds chunk r" statement unless the round count and receive rule are specified. The caption's conclusion may be off by one under the usual convention.
issue.root_cause: The caption states a send formula and a final-ownership conclusion without the intermediate receive/reduce rule needed to make the conclusion follow.
issue.correction: Add the explicit convention, e.g. "rank i receives chunk i-r-1 from i-1 and reduces it with its local copy; after N-1 rounds rank i holds reduced chunk i+1" (or adjust the formula so the stated conclusion is true).
issue.acceptance_test: A 4-rank simulation using the caption's exact send/receive/reduce convention must produce the stated final chunk ownership.

issue.quoted_clause: When a GPU is idle waiting, we reach for DP (more work per GPU); CP addresses long-sequence/KV capacity, not idle-fill.
issue.observed: DP does not make an idle single GPU do more work; it adds independent replicas or increases total batch across devices. If a GPU is idle because arrivals are low, DP does not fill that GPU. If it is idle because the batch is small, the direct levers are batch size, microbatching, or continuous batching, not necessarily DP.
issue.evidence: Chapter 10 defines inference DP as "independent replicas each serve a disjoint set of requests" and training DP as "replicates all weights on every GPU, feeds each a different batch".
issue.root_cause: The resource-triangle heuristic conflates aggregate throughput scaling with per-GPU idle-fill.
issue.correction: Reword to: "When aggregate throughput is limited by batch size and the model fits, DP adds replicas/total batch; it is not a per-GPU idle-fill mechanism."
issue.acceptance_test: A reader should not infer that DP fills an underloaded single GPU.

issue.quoted_clause: The head-divisibility requirement for the Ulysses strategy is stated in Wan's official README at commit 9737cba9c1c3c4d04b33fcad41c111989865d315
issue.observed: The main text applies the divisibility requirement to Wan2.2's official multi-GPU path, but the cited source for the divisibility statement is a Wan2.1 README. The Wan2.2 citation supports the FSDP+Ulysses path, not necessarily the exact divisibility requirement for Wan2.2.
issue.evidence: The footnote cites Wan2.2 README for "Multi-GPU inference using FSDP + DeepSpeed Ulysses" and Wan2.1 README for "num_heads should be divisible by ulysses_size".
issue.root_cause: Source support mismatch between the version in the claim and the version of the cited requirement.
issue.correction: Cite a Wan2.2 source for the divisibility requirement, or qualify: "documented for Wan2.1/Ulysses; re-verify for the deployed Wan2.2 configuration."
issue.acceptance_test: The cited source for the divisibility requirement must match the model version in the claim, or the claim must be version-qualified.

issue.quoted_clause: de-escalate when 30-day p95 utilization < 40% AND SLO margin > 2× AND the smaller tier's failure domain is acceptable.
issue.observed: "SLO margin > 2×" is not computable without a denominator. It could mean 2× headroom in latency, 2× utilization margin, or something else.
issue.evidence: The caption gives no definition of the quantity being multiplied by 2.
issue.root_cause: Shorthand threshold left undefined.
issue.correction: Define the metric, e.g. "p95 latency ≤ 0.5× SLO" or "SLO headroom > 2× current p95 latency".
issue.acceptance_test: The threshold must be expressible as a measurable inequality.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 11, §6 Architecture Consequence, "Beyond a node" bullet
issue.quoted_clause: when prefill FLOPs and decode bandwidth fight on one pool, P/D disaggregation (Splitwise/DistServe/Mooncake) is the architecture of choice
issue.observed: "Architecture of choice" is too strong. P/D disaggregation is a candidate that pays off only when measured phase interference and KV-transfer cost justify it; other options (more hosts, chunked prefill, scheduling changes, prefix caching) may be better.
issue.evidence: Earlier in the same chapter: "it pays off when measured prefill/decode interference binds — evaluate it against measured phase conflict, not topology alone".
issue.root_cause: The conclusion is stated as a default rather than a conditional, measurement-dependent choice.
issue.correction: Reword to "a candidate architecture when measured phase interference and KV-transfer cost justify it".
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence should present P/D disaggregation as the automatic choice without the measurement condition.

issue.quoted_clause: This is the number that, multiplied by the number of devices in the candidate layout, must exceed the workload's tokens-per-second demand
issue.observed: Linear multiplication by device count is valid for independent data-parallel replicas, but not for TP/PP/EP layouts where communication, partitioning, and synchronization change the per-device contribution to host throughput.
issue.evidence: Chapter 10 explains TP/PP/EP communication costs; Chapter 12 itself uses per-host prefill rates for 8×H100 layouts rather than a simple per-GPU sum for model-parallel candidates.
issue.root_cause: Missing parallelism-mode qualifier in the throughput gate.
issue.correction: Specify: "for data-parallel replicas, multiply by replica count; for TP/PP/EP, use the measured per-host or per-layout goodput, not a simple per-device sum."
issue.acceptance_test: The statement must distinguish DP replication from model-parallel layouts.

issue.page_hint: Ch16 §3 Worked Example, Mode 2 cloud GPU instances, H_required equation
issue.quoted_clause: H_required = ∫_0^T N_required(t) dt + N_warm·T_warm + R_reserved; H_paid ≥ H_required ... N_required(t) is the number of hosts that must be running at time t
issue.observed: The equation adds warm-pool and reserved host-hours to the integral of N_required(t), but N_required(t) is defined as the number of hosts that must be running at time t. If N_required(t) already includes warm and reserved hosts, the separate terms double-count them. If N_required(t) is meant to exclude them, the definition is wrong. The following sentence 'H_required already includes the warm-pool and reservation terms' contradicts the displayed addition.
issue.evidence: Let N_required(t) be total required running hosts. Then ∫ N_required(t) dt already includes N_warm·T_warm and R_reserved for the times those hosts are running. Adding them again counts the same host-hours twice. Conversely, if the integral is meant to be burst-only, the definition 'number of hosts that must be running at time t' is too broad.
issue.root_cause: Ambiguous variable definition in the cloud occupancy model: total required hosts versus incremental burst hosts above warm/reserved capacity.
issue.correction: Either (a) define N_required(t) as total required running hosts and remove the separate N_warm·T_warm and R_reserved terms, or (b) define N_burst(t) as additional hosts above the warm/reserved baseline and write H_required = ∫ N_burst(t) dt + N_warm·T_warm + R_reserved. Make the prose match the equation.
issue.acceptance_test: The cloud host-hour equation counts each warm, reserved, and burst host-hour exactly once, and the definition of the integrated variable matches the terms added to it.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §1 Concept, canonical SLO sentence; compare Ch14 §3 and Ch14 §8
issue.quoted_clause: TPOT ≤ 40 ms (Ch 4/Ch 14)
issue.observed: Ch15 states the canonical SLO as 'TPOT ≤ 40 ms' and cites Ch4/Ch14. In this chunk, Ch14 repeatedly uses a 25 ms TPOT target: 'TPOT ~25 ms/token', 'TPOT p50/p95 (≤ ~25 ms median)', and 'median TPOT about 25 ms'. There is no visible 40 ms TPOT SLO in Ch14, and the percentile qualification is missing in Ch15.
issue.evidence: Ch14 §3: '~9,200 input tokens ... + ~300 output, TTFT budget (median ≤ 1.2 s, p95 ≤ 2 s), TPOT ~25 ms/token.' Ch14 §8: 'The SLO remains median TTFT ≤ 1.2 s, p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s and median TPOT about 25 ms.' Ch15 §1: 'TTFT median ≤ 1.2 s, p95 ≤ 2 s, TPOT ≤ 40 ms (Ch 4/Ch 14).'
issue.root_cause: Cross-chapter drift in the canonical TPOT SLO and missing percentile qualification (median vs p95).
issue.correction: Align the canonical TPOT SLO. If the intended SLO is median TPOT ≤ 25 ms and p95 TPOT ≤ 40 ms, state both explicitly in Ch14 and Ch15. If only one value is canonical, use that value in both chapters and remove the incorrect cross-reference.
issue.acceptance_test: Ch14 and Ch15 use the same percentile-qualified TPOT SLO, and any citation to Ch14 for a 40 ms TPOT bound is either supported by Ch14 text or removed.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 'Two Mechanisms, Read as Mechanisms', speculative decoding paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: the expensive part of decode is not the arithmetic per token but the serialization — each target-model step streams the weights from HBM
issue.observed: This presents decode as dominated by weight streaming/serialization rather than arithmetic without qualifying batch size or operating point. At low batch sizes this is often true, but at larger batches decode can become compute-bound or mixed. The book's own standard is to avoid making 'decode is bandwidth-bound' a universal law.
issue.evidence: The sentence uses 'the expensive part of decode' as a general mechanism explanation. Earlier in Ch15, the text correctly says whether a phase is compute- or bandwidth-bound is a property of model × workload × kernel × hardware operating point. The speculative-decoding paragraph does not carry that qualification.
issue.root_cause: A first-order low-batch decode model is stated as a general decode property.
issue.correction: Qualify the statement, e.g.: 'At low batch sizes, the dominant decode cost is often weight streaming rather than arithmetic; at higher batches, arithmetic can dominate. In the low-batch regime, if the draft can propose k tokens...' or add a cross-reference to the roofline/operating-point discussion.
issue.acceptance_test: The speculative-decoding explanation does not assert that decode's expensive part is universally serialization; it states the condition under which weight streaming dominates.

issue.quoted_clause: N_region = ⌈λ_region·W_KV/(C·u·ρ)⌉ + N_spare (Table 17-1 formula, applied per region; each region is sized for λ_peak = 40 rps — the failover load — not its share λ_region
issue.observed: The displayed formula uses λ_region, but the prose says each region is sized for λ_peak = 40 rps, not its traffic share λ_region. This is a variable mismatch: if the region must survive total failover, the formula should use the failover load, not the regional traffic share.
issue.evidence: Row 1 defines λ_region as the regional traffic share of λ_peak. Row 2 says the surviving region must carry 100% of λ_peak. Row 3 then writes N_region using λ_region while saying it is sized for λ_peak. Those are different quantities unless λ_region is redefined as failover load.
issue.root_cause: Ambiguous use of λ_region: traffic-share variable in the formula versus failover-load intent in the prose.
issue.correction: Use a distinct symbol for failover load, e.g. λ_failover, and write N_region = ⌈λ_failover·W_KV/(C·u·ρ)⌉ + N_spare. Alternatively, define λ_region in row 3 explicitly as the failover load assigned to that region, not the normal traffic share.
issue.acceptance_test: The multi-region worksheet formula and prose use the same load variable, and that variable is unambiguously the load each region must serve during failover.

issue.page_hint: Ch14 §3 Worked Example, Step 3 candidate A
issue.quoted_clause: Chapter 8's approximately 19,800 input tok/s idealized prefill ceiling
issue.observed: The 19,800 input tok/s figure is not the 100%-MFU idealized ceiling; it is the 35%-MFU planning screen. Ch15/Ch16 use 56,500 tok/s for 100% MFU and 19,780 tok/s for the 35% planning assumption. Calling 19,800 'idealized' without the 35% MFU qualifier can mislead readers into treating it as a peak-derived bound.
issue.evidence: 8×H100 FP16 dense peak = 8 × 989 TFLOPS = 7.91×10^15 FLOP/s. Linear-only 2N FLOP/token = 2×70×10^9 = 1.4×10^11 FLOP/token. 100% MFU ceiling = 7.91×10^15 / 1.4×10^11 ≈ 56,500 tok/s. 35% of that is ≈ 19,775 tok/s, rounded in the book to 19,780/19,800.
issue.root_cause: Missing efficiency assumption in the label 'idealized prefill ceiling'.
issue.correction: Change to 'Chapter 8's approximately 19,800 input tok/s 35%-MFU planning prefill screen' or '35%-MFU analytical prefill ceiling'. If 'idealized' is intended to mean non-measured, add the MFU assumption explicitly.
issue.acceptance_test: Every occurrence of ~19,800 input tok/s is explicitly tied to the 35% MFU planning assumption, not to 100% peak.

issue.quoted_clause: A minimal benchmark runs 40 rps — a saturation run on one host (6.5× the ~56,500 tok/s prefill ceiling at 100% MFU — theoretical peak), whose queue is expected to grow — with warm‑up, recording offered load alongside p95 TTFT and p95 TPOT/ITL separately (report p95 only at offered loads ≤ the host's admission capacity, ~2 rps per host: 17 slots ÷ 8.6 s)
issue.observed: The sentence can be read as contradictory: it says the minimal benchmark runs 40 rps on one host, then says report p95 only at offered loads ≤ ~2 rps per host. The intended meaning is likely that 40 rps is a saturation diagnostic while SLO p95 reporting is limited to feasible/admitted loads, but the current wording does not make that separation explicit.
issue.evidence: 40 rps on one host is far above the ~2 rps KV-slot admission ceiling (17/8.6 ≈ 1.98). Reporting p95 at 40 rps would measure a saturated queue, not an SLO-compliant operating point. The parenthetical 'report p95 only at offered loads ≤ ...' modifies the benchmark but is syntactically attached to the 40 rps run.
issue.root_cause: Ambiguous scope: saturation run versus SLO-reporting load range.
issue.correction: Rewrite to separate the two purposes, e.g.: 'A minimal benchmark includes a 40 rps single-host saturation run to observe queue growth, but SLO p95 values are reported only at offered loads ≤ the host's admission capacity (~2 rps per host: 17 slots ÷ 8.6 s).'
issue.acceptance_test: The reader can distinguish the 40 rps saturation diagnostic from the load range at which p95 SLO values are reported, with no apparent contradiction.

issue.quoted_clause: beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises (implying a knee near batch 4)
issue.observed: 'Typically rises' generalizes an illustrative scenario value into a common behavior. The surrounding text says the numbers are scenario values to be measured on the target stack, but 'typically' suggests a portable rule. A knee near batch 4 is workload-, model-, kernel-, and hardware-dependent.
issue.evidence: The sentence is introduced by 'The illustrative numbers below are scenario values to be measured on the target stack, not vendor or published figures'. The claim 'beyond batch-4 ... typically rises' is not supported by a measurement in this chunk and is not universally true across serving stacks.
issue.root_cause: Overgeneralization from an illustrative canonical scenario.
issue.correction: Change to 'in this illustrative scenario, p95 latency rises beyond batch 4 (suggesting a knee near batch 4 for this workload/stack)' or 'can rise beyond batch 4 when ...'. Keep the measurement requirement explicit.
issue.acceptance_test: The batch-4 knee is presented as scenario-specific or conditional, not as a typical portable fact.

issue.page_hint: Ch16 §3 Worked Example, after sizing table
issue.quoted_clause: Every host count in this table is an illustrative planning screen under its stated FLOP-counting case and the 35% MFU assumption — NOT measured SLO-goodput.
issue.observed: This sentence applies 'the 35% MFU assumption' to every host count in the table, including the KV-residency / service-time screen. The KV screen is derived from KV slots and assumed residency time, not from FLOP counting or MFU. Only the independent prefill compute screens depend on the 35% MFU assumption.
issue.evidence: The table's KV row uses ⌈λ·W/C⌉ with C=17 slots, no FLOP peak or MFU. The prefill rows use 19,780 tok/s/host, which is the 35%-MFU linear-only screen. Therefore 'every host count ... under ... the 35% MFU assumption' is too broad.
issue.root_cause: Imprecise scope of the MFU qualifier in a summary sentence.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'Every host count in this table is an illustrative planning screen, not measured SLO-goodput. The prefill compute screens are stated under their FLOP-counting case and the 35% MFU assumption; the KV-residency screen is stated under the assumed KV residency time and whole-slot floor.'
issue.acceptance_test: The 35% MFU assumption is not implied for the KV-residency host count, and the sentence accurately scopes which rows depend on MFU.

issue.quoted_clause: Step 2 — price each mode on N_hosts = 21 (FP16 KV screen / case (i) compute screen, provisioned for the 40 rps peak)
issue.observed: The 21-host count is the maximum of the FP16 KV screen (21) and the case (i) compute screen (19). The slash notation 'FP16 KV screen / case (i) compute screen' can be read as saying the 21-host figure is the case (i) compute screen, which is false. Earlier in the same chapter, case (i) peak prefill is explicitly 19 hosts.
issue.evidence: Sizing table: KV screen peak = ⌈40×8.6/17⌉ = 21; independent prefill case (i) peak = ⌈368,000/19,780⌉ = 19; N_hosts = max = 21. Thus 21 is not the case (i) compute screen alone.
issue.root_cause: Ambiguous shorthand for 'max of named screens'.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'Step 2 — price each mode on N_hosts = 21 (the peak maximum of the FP16 KV screen and the case (i) compute screen; the case (i) compute screen alone is 19), provisioned for the 40 rps peak.'
issue.acceptance_test: The text does not imply that the case (i) compute screen equals 21 hosts; it clearly identifies 21 as the max of the named screens.

issue.page_hint: Ch16 §8 End-of-Chapter Mini-Case, startup two-server memory geometry
issue.quoted_clause: 2 GPUs per replica → 8 replicas across the two hosts; ... 4 replicas × 140 GB weights = 560 GB of the 640 GB pool.
issue.observed: The text first says there are 8 replicas across the two hosts, then says 4 replicas × 140 GB = 560 GB of the 640 GB pool. Without 'per host', a reader may interpret 4 replicas as the total across both hosts, which would be inconsistent with 8 replicas total and with 560 GB of a 640 GB pool (the pool is per host).
issue.evidence: Two 8×H100 hosts have 16 GPUs. 2 GPUs per replica gives 8 replicas total, i.e. 4 replicas per host. Each host has 640 GB. 4 replicas per host × 140 GB = 560 GB per host. The arithmetic is correct only if '4 replicas' and '640 GB pool' are per-host quantities.
issue.root_cause: Missing per-host scope in the memory geometry sentence.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'Per host, 4 replicas × 140 GB weights = 560 GB of that host's 640 GB pool.' Or: 'Across the two hosts there are 8 replicas; on each host, 4 replicas consume 560 GB of the 640 GB pool.'
issue.acceptance_test: The reader can unambiguously see that 8 replicas is the two-host total and 4 replicas/560 GB/640 GB is the per-host calculation.

issue.page_hint: Ch16 §3 Worked Example, 32-host provisioning sensitivity bullet
issue.quoted_clause: + $10,000 staff ≈ ≈ $232.2K/month ($232,197.23 computed exactly, rounded only for display) → ≈ ≈ $37.21 per 1,000 requests
issue.observed: The text contains duplicated approximation symbols '≈ ≈' in two places in the same bullet.
issue.evidence: The quoted clause shows '≈ ≈' before $232.2K/month and before $37.21 per 1,000 requests.
issue.root_cause: Typographical duplication.
issue.correction: Remove one approximation symbol in each instance: '+ $10,000 staff ≈ $232.2K/month ... → ≈ $37.21 per 1,000 requests'.
issue.acceptance_test: No occurrence of '≈ ≈' remains in the 32-host bullet.

issue.quoted_clause: break-even is a price sensitivity across $15–25 per 1,000 requests (≈$0.015–0.025 per request) — per-price crossovers (~6.2–10.4M), not an interval
issue.observed: The phrase 'per-price crossovers (~6.2–10.4M), not an interval' is confusing because ~6.2–10.4M is itself an interval/range. The intended meaning is likely that the break-even is not a single point but a range of per-price crossovers.
issue.evidence: The same paragraph earlier says 'the break-even is a region, not a point' and reports a range ~6.2–10.4M req/mo. Calling that set of crossovers 'not an interval' contradicts the range notation.
issue.root_cause: Imprecise wording of the sensitivity result.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'break-even is a price sensitivity across $15–25 per 1,000 requests (≈$0.015–0.025 per request), producing a range of per-price crossovers (~6.2–10.4M req/mo), not a single point.'
issue.acceptance_test: The caption does not describe the ~6.2–10.4M crossover range as 'not an interval'; it clearly says it is a range, not a single point.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 'The Optimization Decision Map' opening paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: rather than applying a known technique by fashion
issue.observed: 'By fashion' is awkward and ambiguous. It likely means 'by trend' or 'because it is fashionable', but the current phrasing is not clear technical prose.
issue.evidence: The sentence intends to contrast diagnosis-driven optimization with adopting a technique because it is popular. 'By fashion' does not cleanly express that.
issue.root_cause: Word choice / phrasing issue.
issue.correction: Replace with 'rather than applying a known technique because it is fashionable' or 'rather than adopting a technique by trend'.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence clearly contrasts evidence-driven diagnosis with trend-driven adoption, without awkward phrasing.

issue.quoted_clause: under 100% prefix reuse only the incremental 11,795-token prefix is pre-filled, giving W(3) ≈ 14.16 s
issue.observed: Chapter 17 uses 11,795 tokens and 14.16 s for the 100% prefix-reuse T=3 service time, while Chapter 19 uses 11,600 tokens and 14.14 s. The 11,795 value is the final call's input length, not the incremental prefix that must be prefilled under 100% reuse.
issue.evidence: Ch 19 §4 states: 'only the incremental prefix (9,200 + 3×800 = 11,600 — the γ reasoning tokens were generated in the prior call, so their KV already exists) is pre-filled, giving W_reuse(3) ≈ 14.14 s.' Recomputation: 11,600/9,200×1.08 + 0.025×495 + 3×0.133 ≈ 14.13 s, rounded to 14.14 s. Using 11,795 gives ≈14.16 s.
issue.root_cause: The final call's input length was mistaken for the incremental prefill length; the rounding difference then propagated into Ch 17's Table 17-2 and mini-case.
issue.correction: Align Ch 17 with Ch 19 by using 11,600 incremental prefilled tokens and W_reuse(3) ≈ 14.14 s, or explicitly justify 11,795/14.16 s and update Ch 19 and Table 17-2. Recompute any affected host counts if the value changes.
issue.acceptance_test: Ch 17 and Ch 19 state the same incremental prefill token count and the same W_reuse(3); Table 17-2 matches the Ch 19 evaluator values.

issue.quoted_clause: the full end-to-end service time of a no-reuse agentic request is ~17.70 s at T = 3 (~14.14 s with prefix reuse) — the two are different quantities, and the latter is what sets concurrency and fleet size
issue.observed: W(T) is called the full end-to-end service time, but its formula includes prefill, decode, and a 133 ms/turn tool/retrieval leg; it excludes the 120 ms/turn per-invocation orchestration overhead (λ_step) that is part of L_agent. If that overhead occurs while the request/KV is resident, it should be included in the service time used for fleet sizing; if not, W should not be labeled full end-to-end.
issue.evidence: W(T) = Σ prefill + 25 ms/token×(O_final + Tγ) + T×λ_tool/retr, with λ_tool/retr ≈ 133 ms/turn. L_agent = λ_step + λ_tool, with λ_step ≈ 120 ms/turn. For T=3, the missing λ_step term is 3×120 ms = 360 ms; including it would make the no-reuse value ≈18.06 s, not 17.70 s. Ch 17 uses 17.70 s for fleet sizing.
issue.root_cause: Two latency models are used: an orchestration-overhead model (L_base + T·L_agent) and a model+tool service-time model (W). The text labels the latter 'full end-to-end' without including all end-to-end terms or explicitly excluding orchestration from the KV-residency population.
issue.correction: Either add T×λ_step to W and update Ch 17's agentic host counts, or rename W to 'model+tool service time' and define a separate W_e2e = W + T×λ_step (using one consistent tool/orchestration rate) for user-facing latency. State exactly which quantity is used as E[W_KV-resident] in the provisioning formula.

issue.page_hint: Ch 18 §2 Mental Model, Table 18-1 units note
issue.quoted_clause: cost = α·rate_tok·n_tok + β·rate_ms·n_ms (n_tok the request's token count, n_ms its per-request service latency; both terms USD per request)
issue.observed: rate_tok is defined as USD per 1M tokens, but the formula multiplies it by raw token count. This is dimensionally off by a factor of 1,000,000 unless rate_tok is actually USD/token or n_tok is in millions of tokens.
issue.evidence: For the FP16 row, $2.50/1M × 9,500 tokens should be $23.75 per request. The printed formula gives 2.50 × 9,500 = 23,750, which is 1,000,000× too large.

issue.page_hint: Ch 18 §3.1 Hardware capacity mapping table and note
issue.quoted_clause: # instances on one 8×H100 pool (this model alone) ... 70B dense 8-bit ... 2 (70 GB weights + 24.9 GB FP16 KV = 94.9 GB > 80 GB per GPU; FP8 KV still 82.5 GB) ... The last column counts instances of that model alone on the pool; the 8-bit rows' 2 is the GPUs one instance needs (94.9 GB > 80 GB per GPU), the one per-GPU reading in the table.
issue.observed: The column header says the value is the number of instances of that model alone on the pool, but the 8-bit and MoE 8-bit rows use 2 to mean the minimum number of GPUs required per instance. These are different quantities.
issue.evidence: A 70B 8-bit instance needs 2 GPUs because 70 GB weights + 24.9 GB canonical KV = 94.9 GB > 80 GB on one GPU. On an 8-GPU pool, up to 4 such 2-GPU instances can run (4×94.9 GB = 379.6 GB, within the 640 GB pool), so '2 instances' is not the maximum-alone instance count.
issue.root_cause: The table conflates placement minimum (GPUs per instance) with capacity count (instances per pool).
issue.correction: Split the column into 'minimum GPUs per instance' and 'max instances alone on 8×H100', or relabel the column and adjust the values. For the 8-bit row, show 2 GPUs/instance and 4 max instances (canonical KV, 2-GPU placement).
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can tell both how many GPUs one instance needs and how many instances of that model alone fit on the 8×H100 pool.

issue.quoted_clause: the same formula gives N_min = ceil(40 × 8.6 / 17) = 21 for the canonical peak, 21 + 1 N−1 reserve = 22

issue.quoted_clause: 35 GB of 4-bit weights in 64 GB RAM leaves ~29 GB for KV + runtime — 29/24.9 ≈ 1.16, i.e. room for ~1 concurrent canonical 9,500-token request's KV.
issue.observed: The budget says the remaining 29 GB is for KV + runtime, but the division uses all 29 GB as KV. This omits the runtime/OS memory reserve.

issue.quoted_clause: the billable tokens (what the API charges, = Σ over turns of the full accumulated context each turn sends — 41,990 input tokens for the T = 3 no-reuse trace of §4, not the single final context of 12,095) and the KV-resident tokens (what occupies the cache, = the same accumulated context under this no-reuse policy); the two differ by the Σ-per-call vs peak-resident distinction even without caching

issue.observed: The sentence is confusing and appears self-contradictory. If Plan and Decide are two evaluations of one model invocation, the Decide verdict is not a separate input to the next cycle's Plan. The state machine lists Plan and Decide as separate states, but the capacity model counts one LLM call per turn.
issue.evidence: §4's event ledger counts one model invocation per agent turn plus a terminal synthesis call. Each invocation emits either a tool call or a final answer, so planning and deciding are logical phases of the same call, not two calls.
issue.root_cause: The mapping between state-machine states and model invocations is not clearly stated.
issue.correction: Clarify: 'Plan and Decide are logical phases of one model invocation: the model reads the current context and either emits a tool call (plan to execute) or a final answer (decision to stop). The capacity model counts one LLM call per turn plus the terminal synthesis call.'
issue.acceptance_test: No reader infers that each agent turn requires two separate LLM calls.

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §5 Common Mistakes, Overlooking data movement cost
issue.quoted_clause: the retrieved-context portion of the ~9,200 in-tokens per query must be fetched from a vector database or cache over the network

issue.acceptance_test: The sentence distinguishes fetched retrieval content from tokenized model input and does not imply a vector store returns token IDs.

issue.observed: The result arrow and host count are duplicated, creating a typesetting/reading artifact.

issue.quoted_clause: However, many combinations are semantically redundant. After deduplication by normalized edit distance at a fixed threshold
issue.observed: The deduplication rule is normalized edit distance, which the section later defines as textual, not semantic. Calling the combinations 'semantically redundant' here contradicts the later caveat and can imply semantic equivalence was used.

issue.root_cause: Imprecise adjective in the worked arithmetic.

issue.quoted_clause: this null-model per-retrieval expectation (0.0052 ≈ 0.52%) already exceeds the §4.1 target of <0.3%
issue.observed: 0.0052 is the expected number of poisoned chunks per top-5 retrieval, while the §4.1 target is the fraction/probability of retrievals returning at least one poisoned chunk. The note compares them directly, although the later sentence clarifies the probability is 1-(1-p)^5 ≈ 0.005197.
issue.evidence: E[poisoned] = k p = 0.0052; P(≥1) = 1-(1-p)^5 = 0.005197. The target is a retrieval-level fraction, not an expected count.
issue.root_cause: Conflation of expectation and probability in a parenthetical note.
issue.correction: Reword to 'this null-model probability of at least one poisoned chunk per retrieval, 1-(1-p)^5 ≈ 0.005197 (0.52%), already exceeds...' or explicitly say the expectation approximates the probability for small p.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 26, §2.1 Workload-to-Strategy decision matrix, Fine-tuning row
issue.quoted_clause: Precision-aware optimizer (LoRA/QLoRA) before full FT; gradient checkpointing (Ch 7)
issue.observed: LoRA and QLoRA are parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, not optimizers. The cell's noun phrase misclassifies the mechanism.
issue.evidence: Standard usage: optimizers are parameter-update rules (e.g., Adam, Muon); LoRA adds low-rank adapters and QLoRA fine-tunes quantized base weights. The appendix separately lists Muon + AdamW as optimizers for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, showing the book distinguishes optimizers from training methods.
issue.root_cause: Compression of 'precision-aware fine-tuning' into 'optimizer'.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 26, §9 Patterns Library, Table 26-3, Inference Sharding row
issue.quoted_clause: One host saturates: TTFT p99 crosses the SLO as requests queue past the ~2.0 rps per-host ceiling
issue.observed: The row's problem is host saturation, but the mechanism is baseline tensor parallelism across the node's GPUs, which the capstone explicitly says is not a change and not a gain. If one host saturates, the relevant levers are adding replicas/hosts, changing offered load, or changing parallelism/batch configuration; merely placing the model across the node's GPUs is the existing baseline.
issue.evidence: §3 Pattern A: 'Sharding here is baseline configuration, not an incremental optimization (R-04)' and 'the capstone makes no change to the parallelism configuration between before and after'. Table 26-3's own Conditions of failure says 'Counted as a gain when the weights were already parallel'.
issue.root_cause: The pattern template conflates model-parallel fit (making a 70B model servable on one 8-GPU host) with scale-out response to saturation.
issue.correction: Rewrite Problem solved to 'A 70B-class model does not fit on one GPU / one host must serve the model with tensor parallelism' or, if the intended pattern is scale-out, rename to 'Replica scale-out' and make the mechanism 'add an independent serving host and load-balance; recompute KV slots, queue, and SLO-goodput'.
issue.acceptance_test: The row's symptom, mechanism, and capstone usage align: either Pattern A is a baseline fit pattern not claimed to solve saturation, or the saturation row points to a scale-out pattern with a named change.

issue.quoted_clause: lower engine load cannot raise SM utilization
issue.observed: This is stated as a universal mechanism, but SM utilization can be non-monotonic with load because of batching, kernel selection, contention, synchronization, and occupancy effects. The intended point is that, under the capstone's linear scaling assumption, the modeled 29% is lower than 45%.
issue.evidence: The same sentence says the ~29% is '45% × 1.3/2.0 ≈ 29%, scaled with engine load', which is an assumption, not a hardware law. GPU utilization metrics are not guaranteed monotone in offered load.
issue.root_cause: Overgeneralization from the illustrative linear model.
issue.correction: Qualify: 'under this linear scaling assumption, lower engine load is modeled to lower SM utilization' or 'in the capstone's model, lower engine load does not raise the modeled SM utilization'.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence no longer asserts a universal hardware law; it ties the direction to the stated scaling assumption.

issue.quoted_clause: a baseline that is bandwidth-bound in decode (box 2) → queueing once offered load approaches the host's ~2.0 rps ceiling (the ρ near 1 behind box 1's inflated compute) → the p99 tail the validate step measures
issue.observed: The capstone's measured metric is TTFT, and Step 1 attributes the inflated 320 ms compute term to prefill queueing at ρ near 1. Saying the baseline is 'bandwidth-bound in decode' can make the reader infer that decode bandwidth directly creates the TTFT tail, whereas the TTFT queue is a prefill/admission effect. The decode-bound statement is relevant to the canonical service-time ceiling, not to the short-prompt TTFT component.
issue.evidence: Step 1: 'the prefill queue already sits inside the 320 ms compute term'. Pattern A: decode is bandwidth-bound in low-batch regime, but the mini-case is a distinct short-prompt workload with prefill well under canonical 1.08 s.
issue.root_cause: Figure caption compresses two different causal chains: canonical service-time ceiling (decode) and capstone TTFT queue (prefill).
issue.correction: Reword to: 'the canonical host's service time is decode-influenced, so offered load near the ~2.0 rps ceiling creates queueing; in the capstone's short-prompt TTFT budget, the queue appears in the prefill/compute term' or separate the decode-bound service-time chain from the TTFT queue chain.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can tell from the caption that the p99 TTFT inflation is prefill/queue-related, while decode bandwidth only enters through the host's service-time ceiling.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A, 'How to read this appendix', mapping onto evidence taxonomy, and worked contrast
