issue.figure: Figure 1.1 (The KV cache: single-layer detail view)
issue.issue: The left-column step labels are off by one relative to the KV-write timing rule that the same caption and Ch. 2 state as a key detail, so the figure permits the wrong inference that a generated token's K/V is appended in the step that sampled it. Each of the four token boxes (token1 / from prefill, token2 / first decode, token3 / second decode, ... token_n / nth decode) has a rightward arrow into the orange 'append K/V per layer·head' box, making the sub-label read as the step in which that token's K/V is appended. But the caption says 'for a generated token, written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled; prompt-token K/V is written during prefill', and printed p.14 (§2) states 'A token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled.' token1 is the first sampled (generated) token, so its K/V is appended in the first decode step (when token1 is the input), not in prefill; likewise token2's K/V is appended in the second decode step, not the first. The figure's labels therefore tie each generated token to the step that produced it, not the step that appends it. Note the contrast with Figure 2.1 (PDF 35 / printed 15), which correctly gives the first token no 'populate' arrow into the cache (only the green 'initialize' arrow into decode), i.e. it does not claim the first token's K/V is written in prefill.
issue.evidence: Caption (PDF 27): 'for a generated token, written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled; prompt-token K/V is written during prefill.' Figure left column: 'token1 / from prefill', 'token2 / first decode', 'token3 / second decode', '... token_n / nth decode', each with an arrow into 'append K/V per layer·head'. §2 (PDF 34 / printed 14): 'A token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled.' Under the figure's visual logic (token box -> append box, sub-label = step), token1's append is placed in prefill, contradicting the rule; the same off-by-one applies to token2/token3/token_n (each generated token is labeled with its sampling step, not its append step).
issue.acceptance_test: After the fix, a reader using only the figure plus its caption must be able to state that (a) the prefill step appends the prompt tokens' K/V, and (b) each generated token's K/V is appended in the step in which that token is the input (one step after it is sampled) — i.e. token1 in the first decode step, token2 in the second, etc. Concretely, either relabel the left rows to the append step (prefill row = prompt tokens; first-decode row = token1; second-decode row = token2; nth-decode row = token_{n-1}) so the token feeding 'append K/V' in a row is the input of that row's step, or keep the production-step labels but add explicit 'sampled in X -> appended in Y' text per row. Verify that no row pairs a generated token with the step that sampled it as that token's append step, and that the figure no longer conflicts with Figure 2.1's treatment of the first token.

issue.figure: Figure 2.2 (Prefill and decode: two regimes split by the roofline ridge)
issue.issue: Internal numeric inconsistency on the same page: the figure's flat roof is labeled '989 TFLOPS' and the bottom annotation reads 'H100 SXM, BF16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 -> ridge at 295 FLOP/byte', but the caption's capacity sentence quotes the single-H100 peak as '0.980 PFLOPS'. 989 TFLOPS = 0.989 PFLOPS, not 0.980 PFLOPS (a ~9 TFLOPS / ~0.9% discrepancy, and 980 TFLOPS does not match the house H100 SXM dense spec of 989). The ridge arithmetic confirms 989 is the intended peak: 989e12 / 3.35e12 = 295.2 FLOP/byte, matching the printed '~295'. The conclusion is unaffected (the derived ~1.19 PFLOPS demand exceeds 0.989 just as it exceeds 0.980), but the figure and its caption disagree on the peak value, which violates the book's cross-element consistency standard.
issue.evidence: Figure label (top right): '989 TFLOPS'. Figure bottom annotation: 'H100 SXM, BF16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 -> ridge at 295 FLOP/byte'. Caption (PDF 43): 'the stated TTFT deadline implies ~1.19 PFLOPS demand, exceeding the compared single-H100 theoretical peak (0.980 PFLOPS)'. Recomputation: 989 TFLOPS = 0.989 PFLOPS; 989/3.35 = 295.2 (ridge consistent with 989, not with 980). 1.19 PFLOPS derives from 2*70e9*9200 / (1.2 s - 0.12 s) = 1.288e15 / 1.08 = 1.193e15, consistent with the TTFT budget on PDF 40 / printed 20.
issue.acceptance_test: Change the caption's '0.980 PFLOPS' to '0.989 PFLOPS' (or '989 TFLOPS') so it matches the figure's own '989 TFLOPS' label and the house H100 SXM dense spec; re-verify the comparison still reads correctly (1.19 PFLOPS > 0.989 PFLOPS, so one H100 is insufficient under the analytical deadline model). Confirm no other caption/figure pair on this page quotes a different H100 dense peak.

issue.issue: Caption and figure disagree on the name of the second workload dimension. The figure's left box reads 'Traffic / concurrency', but the caption's enumeration of the six dimensions reads 'Request rate & arrival pattern'. The right-side decision ('concurrency & batching') matches on both sides, so the mismatch is isolated to the dimension label. Using 'concurrency' as a workload (input) dimension is also imprecise, since concurrency is the decision-side concept the arrow points to.
issue.evidence: Figure left box, row 2: 'Traffic / concurrency'. Caption italic list: 'Request rate & arrival pattern → concurrency & batching'. Figure right box, row 2: 'concurrency & batching' (matches the caption's right side).
issue.acceptance_test: Make the figure's second left-box label and the second entry of the caption's six-dimension list the identical string (recommend 'Request rate / arrival pattern' in the figure, removing 'concurrency' from the input side). Re-render and confirm the two match verbatim.

issue.issue: The figure's three-layer metric taxonomy contradicts the prose on the preceding page (printed p.94, §6.1). The figure places 'queue depth' in the Resource metrics box and omits 'memory pressure', whereas the prose lists queue depth under Serving metrics ('a scheduler state') and lists memory pressure under Resource metrics. issue.evidence: Figure Resource box: 'HBM BW · MFU · KV occupancy · queue depth'; figure Serving box: 'TTFT · TPOT · goodput'. Prose p.94 Serving metrics: '... inter-token latency, queue depth (a scheduler state), and goodput'; prose p.94 Resource metrics: 'HBM bandwidth utilization, FLOP utilization / model FLOPs utilization (MFU), KV cache occupancy, and memory pressure.'
issue.acceptance_test: Move 'queue depth' out of the Resource box (into the Serving box, or mark it as a scheduler-state item on the serving side) and add 'memory pressure' to the Resource box so the figure's boxes match the prose's serving/resource lists; or, if the figure is intentionally an abbreviated/alternative grouping, add a caption sentence stating the figure shows representative metrics and that queue depth is treated as a serving/scheduler state in §6.1. Re-render and confirm no metric sits in a different layer than in the prose.

issue.issue: Visual-grammar mismatch: the figure is drawn as a vertical stack of equal-width bars with a single point-year per row, which reads as a layered substrate / causal sequence. The caption must explicitly rescue the reader from that false inference ('not a causal lineage and not a substrate stack: a later stage does not require the one before it, and the eras overlap'). Compounding this, the caption's claims that dates are 'approximate era markers' and that 'the eras overlap' are not visually encoded at all: each row shows one point year, not a span, so no overlap is depicted. The layout therefore both invites a wrong reading and fails to show the property the caption emphasizes.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 461: nine full-width bars stacked with no gaps (Transformer ~2017 ... Agent Fleet ~2026), each with a single year label on the right and no horizontal duration. Caption: 'the ascending order is a chronology of selected milestones, not a causal lineage and not a substrate stack: a later stage does not require the one before it, and the eras overlap.' The authors' own 'not a substrate stack' warning confirms the geometry induces that misreading.
issue.acceptance_test: Redesign so the geometry cannot be read as a stack/lineage and so era spans (and overlaps) are visible: use a horizontal time axis with each milestone drawn as a bar spanning its approximate era (start-end), rows ordered by time rather than by layer. After the change, a reader must not be able to infer 'Agent System requires Agent requires Tool-Using Model' from the layout, and at least one visible overlap between eras must appear.

issue.issue: Edge-label placement in the Pattern-Measurement-Feedback loop: the 'validate vs 800 ms target' arrow is drawn on the DERIVED->PATTERN edge (box 2 -> box 3). Read literally this puts SLO validation before the pattern is chosen and invites the category-error inference that the bandwidth-bound *diagnosis* (box 2) is being validated against a latency target. In this loop the measurement that checks the SLO logically follows pattern application (box 3) and belongs on the PATTERN->ASSUMPTION feedback edge; that edge is instead labeled 'adjust + pick pattern', which also misplaces 'pick pattern' (pattern selection is box 3's output, not the feedback action).
issue.evidence: Rendered page 445: green arrow box2->box3 labeled 'validate vs 800 ms target'; red arrow box3->box1 labeled 'adjust + pick pattern' / 'feedback'. Caption: 'the validate step compares the load test's measured TTFT p99 against the hypothesis criterion (TTFT p99 < 300 ms, S8 Step 3) under the capstone's p99 <= 800 ms TTFT target (S8 Step 0).'
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel/move edges so the SLO comparison is unambiguously tied to a measured p99 after the pattern, and pattern selection is unambiguously box 3's output: e.g., label the box2->box3 edge 'diagnosis drives selection' and put 'validate measured p99 vs 800 ms target' on the box3->box1 feedback edge (drop 'pick pattern' from that edge). A reader must not be able to read the diagram as 'the bandwidth-bound diagnosis is validated against 800 ms.'

issue.figure: Figure 8.1 (Where inference computation and data movement actually live)
issue.issue: The figure's structure visually contradicts its central conceptual claim and requires the long caption to rescue it. The caption explicitly says 'compute, memory and interconnect are separate groups in this figure, not levels of one ladder' and 'only the memory hierarchy is a smallest-to-largest ladder'. Yet all seven boxes are stacked in a single column with uniform inter-box connector marks, so at a glance the layout reads as one 7-rung hierarchy — with the blue 'tensor cores / ALU' (compute) box as a rung between registers and shared memory, and the two green interconnect boxes as the bottom rungs. The red gradient arrow is correctly scoped to the memory group (registers→HBM), but the chain connectors and single-column layout still imply a continuous ladder across all three groups. Per the standard 'if prose is required to rescue an ambiguous diagram, improve the diagram', the figure should carry the 'three distinct groups' point on its own.
issue.evidence: Caption clauses: 'not levels of one ladder' and 'only the memory hierarchy is a smallest-to-largest ladder'. Rendered layout: one vertical column, small connector marks between every adjacent pair of boxes (including registers↔tensor cores and HBM↔GPU interconnect), no visual grouping/bracket separating the blue compute box or the green interconnect boxes from the orange memory stack.
issue.acceptance_test: Redesign so the three categories are visually distinct without reading the caption: e.g., place the compute box in its own column/side position, add clear group separators or brackets around {memory hierarchy}, {compute}, {interconnect}, remove the uniform chain connectors between groups (keep them only within the memory stack), and keep the red capacity/speed/distance arrow spanning the memory group only. Confirm a reader who sees only the figure (not the caption) infers three groups, not one 7-level ladder.

issue.figure: Figure 17.1 — Sizing a fleet of one model (ideal ρ = 1 analytical ceilings; small ~5.5 req/s burst)
issue.issue: The shaded green band and the number printed inside it do not describe the same quantity, so a careful reader can infer a false value from the visual encoding. The green band is drawn between the orange dotted N-1 residual line (y = 6.0) and the blue dashed 4-host fleet line (y = 8.0), i.e. a vertical extent of 2.0 req/s (the reserve host's contribution). Yet the label inside that band reads 'N-1 residual (~6.0 ideal, ρ = 1)  headroom 2.5 req/s (8.0 − 5.5)'. The 2.5 is the gap from the burst peak (5.5, red curve) up to the fleet line (8.0), not the height of the shaded band (2.0). The 0.5 margin that actually sits between the band's bottom (6.0) and the peak (5.5) is unshaded and unlabeled as a region. Thus the figure shades a 2.0-tall region while annotating it with 2.5, and the band's true meaning (the 4th/reserve host's 2.0 req/s) is never stated.
issue.evidence: Read directly from the rendered page: orange dotted line at y=6 (legend 'N-1 residual (1 host drains, ideal)'), blue dashed line at y=8 (legend 'N = 4 fleet capacity (~8.0, ideal)'), red burst peak at y≈5.5 (label 'burst peak ~5.5 req/s'). The green fill spans 6→8. Caption text confirms the 0.5 margin is '6.0 − 5.5' and the full-fleet headroom is '8.0 − 5.5 = 2.5'; neither equals the 2.0 band height. All individual numbers are arithmetically correct; the defect is the mismatch between the shaded region's extent and the in-band annotation (figure-causality / visual-encoding error, not a numeric error).
issue.acceptance_test: After the fix, the vertical extent of every shaded band must equal the number printed in it, and the band's semantic role must be stated. Concretely, either (a) shade the headroom region from y=5.5 (burst peak) to y=8.0 (fleet line) so the band's 2.0+0.5=2.5 extent matches 'headroom 2.5 req/s (8.0 − 5.5)', or (b) keep the 6.0→8.0 band but relabel it as the reserve host's 2.0 req/s contribution and move the '2.5 headroom' annotation to a separate marker spanning the peak (5.5) to the 8.0 line. Verify by overlay: a reader must not be able to read the green band as 2.5 when it is 2.0 tall, nor as 2.0 when the in-band text says 2.5.

issue.issue: The left panel's x-axis stops at 100K tokens (10^2), but the causal-triangle crossover it annotates is ~106.8K, i.e. off the right edge. A reader can plausibly infer the blue line crosses within the frame (near 100K) rather than just past it, even though every label is technically correct.
issue.evidence: x-axis ticks are 10^0, 10^1, 10^2 (1–100K); the in-plot annotation reads 'causal-triangle quad term overtakes linear ~106.8K'; recomputing at the right edge (L=100K): causal quadratic 2·n_layers·L²·d ≈ 13.1 PFLOP < linear 2·N·L ≈ 14 PFLOP, confirming the crossing lies off-frame to the right of the plotted region.
issue.acceptance_test: Either extend the left x-axis to ~200K so both crossovers (53.4K and 106.8K) are visibly drawn, or add an explicit right-edge marker/arrow labeled 'causal crossover ≈106.8K (off right edge)' so the reader does not assume an in-frame crossing.

issue.quoted_clause: [canonical scenario][DERIVED] KV cache cost per token at FP16: for a Llama‑style 70B model, n_layers = 80, d_model = 8192, bytes per element = 2 (FP16). KV cache per token = n_layers × 2 × d_model × bytes = 80 ×2 × 8192 ×2 = 2,621,440 bytes ≈ 2.62 MB/token
issue.observed: The arithmetic is a full-MHA computation (K and V each at d_model = 8192), but it is attributed to a 'Llama-style 70B model'. Every widely deployed Llama-2/Llama-3 70B uses grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads of head_dim 128, i.e. n_kv_dim = 1024, not 8192. For such a model the KV footprint per token is 80 × 2 × 1024 × 2 = 327,680 bytes ≈ 0.33 MB/token — 8× smaller than the figure printed here. The book's canonical KV figure is (correctly, per house convention) the full-MHA reference; the defect is the model attribution, which invites the reader to believe a real Llama-70B deployment needs 24.1 GB of KV per 9.2K request.
issue.evidence: Llama-2 70B: 80 layers, hidden 8192, 64 attention heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128 → KV dim = 8 × 128 = 1024. Full-MHA reference: 80 × 2 × 8192 × 2 = 2,621,440 B = 2.62 MB/token (as printed). GQA-8 reference: 80 × 2 × 1024 × 2 = 327,680 B = 0.328 MB/token; 9,200 tokens → 3.0 GB, not 24.1 GB.
issue.root_cause: The canonical teaching geometry is a synthetic full-MHA 70B, but the prose names a real, GQA-based model family as its source, conflating the constructed geometry with a real checkpoint.
issue.correction: Rename the reference explicitly, e.g. 'for the canonical full-MHA 70B reference (n_layers = 80, d_model = 8192, no GQA — the constructed teaching geometry of Ch 4 Table 4-2)', and add one sentence noting that a real Llama-2/3 70B uses GQA with 8 KV heads and therefore has ~0.33 MB/token at FP16, i.e. ~8× less KV — which is exactly the GQA effect the book teaches elsewhere. Keep the 2.62 MB/token canonical value unchanged so downstream chapters stay consistent.
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 5 attributes the 2.62 MB/token full-MHA figure to a real Llama checkpoint; the text states the full-MHA assumption explicitly and states the GQA-8 alternative with its 8× factor.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5, §3(b) '[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]: tokens/s per dollar with prefill included'
issue.quoted_clause: under continuous batching (prefill of one request overlapping decode of another), on a combined prefill+decode basis the same host moves 50 × (1 + 9,200/300) ≈ 1,583 tok/s ≈ 285,000 tokens/$ (one hour of host time at that rate); the single-stream floor is 9,500/7.08 ≈ 1,342 tok/s ≈ 242,000 tokens/$ (one hour of host time)
issue.observed: The 1,583 tok/s figure is not a host throughput rate. It is the decode rate multiplied by the tokens-per-request ratio, i.e. it assumes each request's entire 9,200-token prefill is absorbed inside the 6.0 s of decode time. But the chapter itself states prefill of one request takes ~1.08 s of GPU time and that the host's prefill rate is ~8,518 tok/s (9,200 ÷ 1.08 s). If prefill and decode overlap, the host's combined rate is the sum of the two concurrent rates (≈ 8,518 + 50 ≈ 8,568 tok/s if prefill-bound), not the product of the decode rate with the token ratio; if they do not overlap, the rate is the serial 9,500 / 7.08 = 1,342 tok/s. The two printed figures therefore differ by a method error, not by a batching effect, and the paragraph's own conclusion ('The per-dollar figures therefore scale up substantially at batch') is supported by a number that is not a throughput at all. The 285,000 tokens/$ figure is also not comparable to the 9,000 tokens/$ figure in Table 5-2 (output tokens only) without an explicit basis statement.
issue.evidence: Serial: (9,200 + 300) / (1.08 + 6.0) = 9,500 / 7.08 = 1,341.8 tok/s → × 3600 / $20 = 241,500 tokens/$ (as printed). Overlapped: 9,200 / 1.08 = 8,518 tok/s prefill + 50 tok/s decode = 8,568 tok/s → × 3600 / $20 = 1,542,000 tokens/$. The printed 1,583 tok/s equals 50 × 31.67, which is a token-equivalent rate with no time basis. The printed pair (1,583 vs 1,342) differs by 18%, which is inconsistent with the text's claim that batching scales the figure up 'substantially'.
issue.root_cause: A token-count ratio was substituted for a time-based rate. The paragraph mixes a per-request token accounting with a host-level throughput accounting without stating the concurrency at which the host is saturated.
issue.correction: Replace the 1,583 tok/s derivation with a time-based one. State the concurrency C at which the host is evaluated and compute the combined rate as min-bound by prefill and decode resources: e.g. at C concurrent requests, decode contributes C × 50 tok/s and prefill contributes up to 8,518 tok/s, so the combined rate is min(C × 50 + 8,518, ...) subject to the KV ceiling of ~18 concurrent requests. If the intent is to keep the single-stream figure, say so and drop the 1,583 number. Also state explicitly that 9,000 tokens/$ (output only) and the combined tokens/$ are different metrics and must not be compared directly.
issue.acceptance_test: Every tokens/s figure in §3(b) is derived from a stated time basis and a stated concurrency; the combined prefill+decode rate is reproducible from the printed prefill rate and decode rate; no figure in the chapter is produced by multiplying a token ratio by a token rate.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a) 'Takeaway for the canonical RAG workload'
issue.quoted_clause: the bge‑large‑en option is not justified at this scale: its quality gain over all‑mpnet‑base‑v2 is not quantified for this model pair (the table gives use cases, not metrics), and an unquantified gain would have to clear a ~3× FLOP bar (≈43 vs ≈14 GFLOPs per 64‑token embedding in the table above, the same ratio as their parameter counts) — validate the gain on the target corpus before paying it.
issue.observed: The chapter applies a decision rule to bge-large that it does not apply to the recommendation it actually makes. bge-large is rejected because its quality gain over mpnet is unquantified and would have to clear a ~3× FLOP bar. The identical argument applies to the recommended mpnet over MiniLM: the quality gain is equally unquantified for that pair, and the bar is ~4.8× FLOP (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP), which is larger. The chapter nevertheless recommends mpnet, on the strength of a 'few to ~15% MAP' prior that is explicitly labeled an unverified hypothesis and is not tied to this model pair. The recommendation therefore rests on a weaker evidential basis than the one used to reject the alternative, and the stated criterion is applied asymmetrically.
issue.evidence: Table 5-1 rows: MiniLM 2.94 GFLOP, mpnet 14.08 GFLOP, bge-large 42.88 GFLOP per 64-token query. Ratios: mpnet/MiniLM = 4.79×; bge/mpnet = 3.05×. The text's own quality evidence for mpnet over MiniLM is 'an unverified prior of a few to ~15% MAP [HYPOTHESIS]', i.e. no pair-specific measurement — the same status as the bge gain it rejects.
issue.root_cause: The recommendation was fixed before the criterion was applied, and the criterion was then used only to remove alternatives rather than to test the recommendation.
issue.correction: Apply the bar symmetrically. Either (a) state the recommendation as a provisional shortlist entry explicitly conditional on a measured ΔMAP ≥ the stated threshold (with the threshold written as a MAP-per-FLOPS or MAP-per-storage figure so the reader can compute it), or (b) present the three candidates as a shortlist with the decision deferred to the §7 validation, and remove the word 'recommended' from Table 5-2's 'Selection status' row in favor of 'provisional shortlist, pending target-corpus validation'. If the recommendation is retained, the text must say why the ~4.8× bar is cleared while the ~3× bar is not.
issue.acceptance_test: The same evidential standard (measured or explicitly hypothesized pair-specific quality gain vs. a stated FLOP/storage bar) is applied to every candidate in Table 5-1, including the recommended one; the recommendation's justification is either a measurement or an explicitly stated assumption that is flagged as load-bearing.

issue.quoted_clause: reducing the embedding dimension may trade retrieval quality for lower storage and compute — e.g. a 384‑dim variant of the same model family can halve the index storage of a 768‑dim one (the encoder's compute is essentially unchanged, since only the final projection shrinks)
issue.observed: The paragraph's headline claims a compute saving from reducing dimension, then states in the same sentence that the encoder's compute is essentially unchanged. The two statements are only reconcilable if 'reducing dimension' means post-hoc truncation or Matryoshka-style training of one model at multiple output widths — in which case there is no compute saving at all, only a storage saving. The compute saving the chapter actually quantifies later (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP) comes from choosing a smaller model (MiniLM vs mpnet), which is a model-size change, not a dimension change. The paragraph conflates the two, and the parenthetical 'only the final projection shrinks' describes truncation, not a trained 384-dim variant, which would have a smaller encoder.
issue.evidence: Table 5-1: MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-dim, ~23M) vs all-mpnet-base-v2 (768-dim, ~110M) differ in encoder depth/width, not only in output dimension; the 4.8× FLOP gap is a parameter-count gap. The table's own footnote already separates the two effects ('the proxy overstates compute most for the smallest model').
issue.root_cause: Two distinct interventions (truncating a fixed model's output width; substituting a smaller model) are described with one vocabulary ('dimension'), so the compute claim inherits the wrong referent.
issue.correction: Split the claim into two: (i) truncating or Matryoshka-training a fixed encoder to a lower output width reduces index storage and query-time projection cost but leaves encoder compute essentially unchanged; (ii) substituting a smaller encoder reduces both storage and compute, and is a model-selection decision, not a dimension decision. Then state which of the two the ~4.8× FLOP figure belongs to.
issue.acceptance_test: The §3(a) dimension paragraph and the Table 5-1 footnote use the same distinction, and the 4.8× FLOP figure is attributed to model size rather than to output dimension.

issue.quoted_clause: It is only **~15% of the wall-clock time** (1.08 s prefill vs 6.0 s decode) ... vs. at 300 output tokens and ~25 ms TPOT, decode alone is ~7.5 s versus ~1.08 s prefill
issue.observed: The chapter uses two different batch-1 decode rates for the same canonical workload: 50 tok/s (20 ms/token, 6.0 s for 300 tokens) in §3(b), and 25 ms/token (40 tok/s, 7.5 s for 300 tokens) in the mini-case. The economics unit note acknowledges that 50 tok/s is an illustrative low-batch point above the canonical 40 tok/s, but the mini-case then silently switches to the canonical rate and presents 7.5 s without labeling the switch, so the reader sees two different decode durations for one workload with no marker at the point of use. The derived wall-clock shares also differ (85% vs 87%) and the per-request economics (9,000 tokens/$) are computed from the 50 tok/s point while the latency narrative in the mini-case uses 40 tok/s.
issue.evidence: §3(b): 300 tokens ÷ 50 tok/s = 6.0 s; 1.08 / (1.08 + 6.0) = 15.3%. Mini-case: 300 × 0.025 s = 7.5 s; 7.5 / (7.5 + 1.08) = 87.4%. Both are internally consistent; the defect is the unannounced change of rate between them.
issue.root_cause: The reconciliation note was placed in the economics paragraph rather than at the point where the second rate is used, so the mini-case inherits a number whose provenance is not visible there.
issue.correction: Use one canonical decode rate for the chapter's worked example (the canonical 25 ms/token / 40 tok/s from Ch 2) and treat 50 tok/s as a clearly labeled sensitivity variant, or carry the [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] label into the mini-case bullet. If both rates must appear, state in the mini-case which rate is in use and why.
issue.acceptance_test: Every decode-duration figure in Ch 5 is either the canonical 25 ms/token or carries an explicit [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] label at the point of use; the chapter contains no unlabeled second decode rate.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5, §3(b) opening and §8 mini-case closing paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: The architect must decide whether a base 70B‑class dense model, a smaller dense model, or a fine‑tuned variant best satisfies the latency, quality, and economic constraints.
issue.observed: The chapter's central claim is that workload characterization narrows the model space to a handful of viable candidates, and §6 repeats it ('narrow the model space from the full vendor catalog to a handful of viable candidates'). But the generation leg is never actually narrowed: only the 70B candidate is computed, and the mini-case's shortlist contains exactly one generation model. The smaller dense model (13B-class, named in §1 surface 2) and the MoE variant are never evaluated on the surfaces the chapter defines — no KV-per-token, no prefill time, no decode rate, no cost/token — so the reader is told that selection is a consequence of workload characterization but is shown a single-candidate evaluation for the leg that dominates cost. The MoE rejection appears only in the mini-case, as an assertion, with no arithmetic.
issue.evidence: §3(b) computes KV/token, prefill time, decode rate and tokens/$ for the 70B only. §8 shortlist: '768-dim all-mpnet-base-v2 for the retrieval leg, and the 70B FP16 base model for the generation leg'. §1 surface 2 promises 'a dense 70B, a distilled 13B, or a MoE variant'.
issue.root_cause: The worked example was scoped to a single canonical candidate; the comparative step that the chapter's thesis depends on was left implicit.
issue.correction: Add a compact candidate comparison for the generation leg using the same surfaces and the same arithmetic template as the 70B row: for a 13B-class dense model (e.g. 40 layers, d_model 5120, FP16 → ~26 GB weights) and for the MoE challenger referenced from Ch 3, compute KV/token, KV for 9.2K, prefill FLOPs and estimated prefill time, decode rate, and tokens/$ on the same 8×H100 host. Show which SLOs each fails or passes. If the MoE rejection is asserted in the mini-case, back it with the weight-residency arithmetic there or move it into §3(b).
issue.acceptance_test: The generation-leg section presents at least two candidates evaluated on the same surfaces with the same units, and the mini-case's shortlist is the output of that comparison rather than a restatement of the single worked candidate.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a) first [HYPOTHESIS] paragraph and §3(a) 'The decision hinges on...'
issue.quoted_clause: Any observed quality‑vs‑dimension relationship (reports range from a few to ~15% MAP difference) is domain‑ and corpus‑specific and must be validated on the target corpus.
issue.observed: A quantitative empirical range ('a few to ~15% MAP') is asserted with no citation, and it is then used twice as the load-bearing quality prior for the chapter's recommendation ('the top-of-range ~15% MAP gain'). The [HYPOTHESIS] label correctly marks it as unverified, but the book elsewhere distinguishes 'unverified because no measurement exists' from 'unverified because the measurement has not been done yet'; here published reports are said to exist ('reports range from...') yet none is cited, so the reader cannot check the range, its metric definition (MAP@10? MAP over what corpus?), or its direction. The same range is restated as 'an unverified prior of a few to ~15% MAP [HYPOTHESIS]' in the takeaway, where it becomes the justification for the recommendation.
issue.evidence: No footnote or reference accompanies the range in either location; the chapter's other empirical claims (H100 memory, price, engine behavior) are footnoted or explicitly labeled.
issue.root_cause: A quantitative prior was introduced to make the recommendation decidable without sourcing the literature it claims to summarize.
issue.correction: Either cite the specific studies behind the range (with metric definition, corpus, and year) and scope the claim to them, or restate the range as an explicit scenario assumption with no claim that published reports exist — e.g. 'assume a quality uplift of up to 15% MAP for the larger model; this is a scenario input, not a measurement'. Then make the recommendation's dependence on that input explicit.
issue.acceptance_test: Every numeric quality range in Ch 5 is either footnoted to a specific source with metric and corpus, or is labeled as a scenario assumption without an implied literature.

issue.quoted_clause: | Tokens per dollar (generation, runtime) | 9,000 tokens per dollar | 50 tok/s × 3600 s/hr ÷ $20/hr [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] |
issue.observed: The table's row label does not say which tokens are counted. The derivation shows it is output tokens only, at a single-stream rate. Two other tokens-per-dollar figures appear in the same chapter (≈242,000 and ≈285,000 tokens/$ on a combined prefill+decode basis), so a reader comparing Table 5-2 with §3(b) sees an apparent 26–32× discrepancy that is a metric-basis difference, not a finding. The table is the most likely place a reader will copy a number from.
issue.evidence: 9,000 = 50 output tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20; 242,000 and 285,000 are total-token rates from the same host. All three are labeled [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] but the metric basis is stated only in the prose.
issue.root_cause: The table compresses a metric whose denominator (output tokens vs all tokens) and operating point (single-stream vs batched) are not part of the row label.
issue.correction: Rename the row to 'Output tokens per dollar (single-stream, 50 tok/s)' and, if a combined figure is wanted, add a second row 'Total tokens per dollar (prefill + decode, stated concurrency)' with its own derivation cell. Keep the two rows adjacent so the basis difference is visible at a glance.
issue.acceptance_test: Every tokens-per-dollar figure in Ch 5 states, in the same place it appears, whether it counts output tokens or all tokens and at what concurrency; no two such figures in the chapter can be compared without reading their basis.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a) paragraph beginning 'On that basis the incremental cost stays well within...'
issue.quoted_clause: single‑core encoding fits only above ~92.5 GFLOP/s sustained per core (11.14 GFLOP ÷ 0.12 s)

issue.quoted_clause: but only ~1.1 ms on a ~10 TFLOP/s GPU, which is the basis the ~120 ms retrieval budget already assumes (vector search and reranking on a local GPU, Ch 4)

issue.acceptance_test: The GPU rate used in §3(a) is either sourced to the book's hardware figures or explicitly labeled as a conservative placeholder, and the reader can tell which.

issue.quoted_clause: [canonical scenario][DERIVED] | 70B FP16, 80 layers, 9.2K context
issue.observed: The label '[canonical scenario]' is used five times in this chapter but is not one of the book's defined evidence labels ([CANONICAL], [DERIVED], [ILLUSTRATIVE], [ASSUMPTION], [1P], [2°], [LAB], [FACT], [HYPOTHESIS], [UNRESOLVED], [ANALYTICAL]). It is also lower-case and hyphenated, unlike the bracketed uppercase vocabulary. If it is defined in Ch 4 it should be in the Ch 4 / Appendix A axis table; if it is not, it is an ad-hoc label that readers cannot resolve.
issue.evidence: Five occurrences in Ch 5: Table 5-2 (2 rows), §3(b) (3 paragraphs).
issue.root_cause: A local convenience label was introduced for the canonical scenario and propagated without being registered in the book's label vocabulary.
issue.correction: Either register '[CANONICAL SCENARIO]' in the Ch 4 / Appendix A axis table and use it consistently, or replace it with the existing pair '[CANONICAL][DERIVED]' (or '[ASSUMPTION][DERIVED]' where the canonical values are constructed rather than measured).
issue.acceptance_test: Every bracketed label used in Ch 5 appears in the Appendix A axis table; no ad-hoc label remains in the chapter.

issue.quoted_clause: (~200 GFLOP/s is the AVX‑512 theoretical peak, not a sustained rate)
issue.observed: A specific per-core peak is stated as fact without a source or a machine description. A 200 GFLOP/s AVX-512 per-core peak requires roughly 3.1 GHz with two 512-bit FMA units; mainstream server cores land nearer 120–160 GFLOP/s. The number is used only to characterize the gap to sustained rates, so the conclusion is insensitive to it, but the parenthetical reads as a specification.
issue.evidence: 2 FMA units × 16 FP32 lanes × 2 flops = 64 flops/cycle → 160 GFLOP/s at 2.5 GHz, 192 at 3.0 GHz, 200 at ~3.1 GHz.
issue.root_cause: A hardware figure was quoted without the clock and core configuration that determine it.
issue.correction: Either source the figure to a named microarchitecture and clock, or restate generically ('a modern AVX-512 core's theoretical peak is on the order of 150–200 GFLOP/s, depending on clock and core count per socket').
issue.acceptance_test: The per-core peak figure is either sourced or expressed as a range with its determining parameters.

issue.quoted_clause: | bge‑large‑en | 1024 | ~335M | ~43 GFLOPs | Dense-retrieval-optimal, technical docs |
issue.observed: 'Dense-retrieval-optimal' is an unqualified superlative in a table whose other columns are quantitative and sourced. It is also the exact kind of claim the chapter elsewhere refuses to make without measurement ('Dimension alone is not a cross-model quality metric'). The 'technical docs' use case is likewise unsourced.
issue.evidence: No citation accompanies the table; the chapter's own §3(a) and §7 state that no public study quantifies the quality differences among these models.
issue.root_cause: Marketing-style descriptors were carried over from model cards into a table the chapter treats as quantitative evidence.
issue.correction: Replace the superlative with a factual, sourceable description of the model's training objective or published benchmark context, or drop the column and keep the table purely quantitative (dim, params, FLOPs), with use-case guidance moved to prose where it can be hedged.
issue.acceptance_test: No cell in Table 5-1 contains an unsourced superlative; the table's columns are either quantitative or explicitly attributed.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5, §1 'Inference mode is a candidate, not a selection verdict'
issue.quoted_clause: AR fill-in-the-middle (FIM) models — autoregressive models trained to infill a marked span — are a necessary editing baseline.
issue.observed: 'Necessary' is a strong universal claim about a workload class (code editing) where FIM is one of several viable approaches (whole-file rewriting, instruction-tuned editing, agentic patch generation). The chapter's own framing elsewhere is careful to scope claims to workloads, so this reads as an overreach.
issue.evidence: No source; the claim is not workload-scoped in the sentence.
issue.root_cause: A recommendation from a specific editing workflow was generalized to a class of tasks.
issue.correction: Soften to a workload-scoped statement, e.g. 'for code-editing workloads where only a span changes, an FIM-trained model is the natural baseline to compare against, because it avoids re-generating unchanged context'.
issue.acceptance_test: No unqualified necessity claim survives in Ch 5; each is scoped to a named workload class.

issue.quoted_clause: supports ~436/24.1 ≈ 18 concurrent 9.2K‑token requests per host before KV pressure
issue.observed: The concurrency screen divides the KV budget by the initial (prefill-only) KV footprint, but each request continues to grow its KV during decode: 300 output tokens add 300 × 2.62 MB ≈ 0.79 GB, so the steady-state footprint is ≈ 24.9 GB and the true ceiling is ≈ 17.5 requests. The figure is also a KV-only bound presented without the caveat that other limits (compute, scheduler, per-request latency) may bind first.
issue.root_cause: The screen was computed at the prefill boundary rather than at the request's maximum footprint.
issue.correction: Compute the screen at the request's maximum footprint (input + output) and state that it is a KV-only upper bound.
issue.acceptance_test: The concurrency screen in Ch 5 uses the maximum per-request KV footprint and is labeled as a KV-only bound.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a) 'Takeaway for the canonical RAG workload'
issue.quoted_clause: and it introduces no per‑request latency that threatens the TTFT SLO
issue.observed: The reassurance is stated against a budget the chapter elsewhere says is already fully consumed: §3(b) computes prefill 1.08 s + retrieval 0.12 s = 1.20 s against a 1.2 s budget and calls it 'zero true headroom'. The takeaway's phrasing invites the reader to treat the retrieval leg as having slack, which the chapter's own arithmetic denies.
issue.evidence: §3(b): 'at ~1.08 s it leaves ~0.12 s against the 1.2 s budget — exactly the ~120 ms retrieval allocation, i.e. zero true headroom'.
issue.root_cause: The takeaway was written as a reassurance about the embedding model alone, without carrying the budget state established in §3(b).
issue.correction: Rewrite the clause to acknowledge the exhausted budget, e.g. 'adds ~1.1 ms of query-embedding time to a retrieval budget that is already fully consumed by search and reranking — acceptable only because the p95 ≤ 2 s target, not the 1.2 s design budget, provides the margin'.
issue.acceptance_test: No statement in Ch 5 implies slack in the 1.2 s TTFT budget that §3(b) has shown to be exhausted.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 7, §3, Table 7-1 (row 'fits 8×H100 at 128K?') and the italic note immediately below the table
issue.quoted_clause: fits 8×H100 at 128K? | passes aggregate bytes + TP=8 shard; per-rank runtime/workspace at 128K not established | 475.5 GB < 640 GB (59.4 GB/rank vs ~62.5 GB/rank after weights) ... the 128K row — also 8×H100, so TP=8 sharding is integral — clears gate 2's shard check but not its per-rank runtime/workspace sub-clause at 128K.
issue.observed: The row's own arithmetic supports a PASS, but the verdict (and the note) assert a FAIL of the per-rank runtime/workspace sub-clause. The row compares '59.4 GB/rank' (which already includes the 17.5 GB/rank of weights) against '~62.5 GB/rank after weights' (80 − 17.5). That comparison double-counts weights and is dimensionally incoherent. The correct per-rank check is: weights 17.5 + KV 41.94 (335.5/8) + runtime reserve 8 = 67.4 GB ≤ 80 GB, i.e. it passes with ~12.6 GB/rank of slack. Equivalently, KV-only per rank 41.94 GB ≤ 62.5 GB available after weights, leaving 20.6 GB/rank for the 8 GB/rank reserve.
issue.evidence: 475.5/8 = 59.4375 GB/rank (weights+KV). 335.54432/8 = 41.943 GB/rank KV. 17.5 + 41.943 + 8 = 67.44 GB ≤ 80 GB. The only reading under which the row fails is '59.4 + 8 = 67.4 ≤ 80' — i.e. it passes. The stated comparison (59.4 vs 62.5) subtracts weights twice.
issue.root_cause: The row mixes two different quantities (total per-rank residency vs post-weight capacity) in one comparison, and the verdict was written from an intuition ('128K is tight') rather than from the numbers printed beside it. A second, smaller inconsistency: the note says 'Both therefore carry the label "passes aggregate bytes only — placement/runtime not established,"' but the table's 128K row actually carries a different label ('passes aggregate bytes + TP=8 shard'), so the note misdescribes the table.
issue.correction: Rewrite the row's derivation as an explicit per-rank budget: '475.5 GB < 640 GB; per rank: weights 17.5 + KV 41.94 + runtime reserve 8 = 67.4 GB ≤ 80 GB (passes gate 2 at the ~8 GB/rank reserve; a context-scaled activation reserve would need measurement)'. If the intended verdict is 'not established', state the missing assumption explicitly (e.g. 'activation/workspace reserve grows with context length; at 128K the assumed 8 GB/rank reserve is unverified') and give the context length at which it would bind. Also fix the note's sentence so it does not claim a single shared label for two rows that carry different labels.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can recompute the 128K per-rank verdict from the printed numbers alone and reach the printed verdict; the table row label and the note's description of it are identical; no quantity in the row is compared against a capacity from which it has already been subtracted.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 7, §1 'Unit basis (locked)' paragraph; consequences at §4 point 3, §6 bullet 1, §8 mini-case
issue.quoted_clause: the H100's quoted 80 GB is treated as 80×10^9 B throughout (vendor 80 GB = 81,920 MiB ≈ 85.9×10^9 B would give 2×H100 = 171.8 GB and a 687 GB host pool — re-run this fit test on that basis before procurement). The 2×H100 fit verdict, the 640 GB envelope, the 436 GB KV budget and the ~17.5 concurrency all use this decimal basis.
issue.observed: The chapter makes its headline architectural verdict ('does not fit on 2×H100') explicitly dependent on a decimal-vs-binary capacity convention, and instructs the reader to re-run the fit test on the vendor-binary basis. But the verdict does not actually depend on the convention: with TP=2, per-rank residency is weights 140/2 = 70 GB + KV 24.1/2 = 12.05 GB (9.2K) or 12.45 GB (9.5K) = 82.05–82.45 GB per 80 GB rank, which fails under either basis. As written, a reader who follows the instruction ('re-run this fit test on that basis before procurement') recomputes 164.1 GB < 171.8 GB and concludes that 2×H100 fits — a wrong conclusion that the chapter's own per-rank arithmetic refutes.
issue.evidence: Per-rank, TP=2: 70 + 12.05 = 82.05 GB/rank > 80 GB (decimal basis); 70 + 12.05 = 82.05 GB/rank > 85.9 GB? No — under the binary basis a rank has 85.9 GB, so 82.05 < 85.9 would pass per rank too. So the per-rank argument is basis-independent only if the per-rank capacity is 80 GB; under the vendor-binary basis per-rank capacity is 85.9 GB and 82.45 < 85.9 passes. The verdict therefore IS basis-dependent under both aggregate and per-rank reasoning, and the chapter's own numbers do not settle it.
issue.root_cause: The chapter treats the capacity convention as a pure bookkeeping choice, when in fact it flips a published architectural verdict (2 vs 3+ GPUs) that recurs in §4, §6 and the mini-case. It also does not state which convention the vendor's own tooling reports, so the reader cannot resolve the question from the book.
issue.correction: Do not leave the verdict convention-dependent. Either (a) state the usable per-device capacity the reader will actually see (nvidia-smi total vs usable) and compute the verdict on that basis, or (b) present the verdict as basis-conditional and give both: 'decimal basis (80 GB = 80×10^9 B): 164.1 GB > 160 GB, does not fit; vendor-binary basis (80 GB = 81,920 MiB = 85.9×10^9 B): 164.1 GB < 171.8 GB aggregate, and per rank 70 + 12.45 = 82.45 GB < 85.9 GB — fits, subject to the runtime/workspace reserve of ~8 GB/rank, which would then have to come out of the remaining 3.45 GB/rank and therefore does NOT fit'. The second form shows that the verdict is stable once the runtime reserve is included, which is the architecturally meaningful conclusion. Add the same one-line basis qualifier at each of the three later occurrences of the 160 GB verdict.
issue.acceptance_test: Every occurrence of the 'does not fit on 2×H100' verdict in Ch 7 carries an explicit capacity basis, and a reader who adopts the opposite convention can still reach the same architectural conclusion (how many GPUs are needed) from the printed numbers.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 7, §7 'Technical note — per-rank fit (moved out of the caption)'
issue.quoted_clause: at 17.5 concurrent requests a rank reaches ~99.7% of its 80 GB capacity (17.5 + 8 + 54.25 = 79.75 GB) ... KV budget per rank: 436 ÷ 8 = ~54.5 GB ... Per-rank budget: 17.5 + 54.5 + 8 = 80 GB ≤ 80 GB.
issue.observed: Two different per-rank KV figures are used in the same note without distinction: 54.25 GB (in the 99.7% sentence) and 54.5 GB (in the bullet list and the budget sum). 54.25 is 17.5 × 3.1, i.e. it is the KV *consumed at 17.5 requests* computed from the rounded per-request figure, while 54.5 is the *budget* (436/8). The two sums then disagree about how full a rank is: 79.75 GB (99.7%) versus exactly 80 GB (100%). Using the byte-accurate per-request per-rank figure (24.90368/8 = 3.11296 GB), 17.5 requests consume 54.48 GB and the rank reaches 79.98 GB = 99.97% of 80 GB, not 99.7%. The '99.7%' figure is a rounding artifact presented as if it were the byte-accurate fill.
issue.evidence: 436/8 = 54.5 exactly. 24.90368/8 = 3.11296 GB/request/rank. 17.5 × 3.11296 = 54.477 GB. 17.5 + 8 + 54.477 = 79.977 GB → 99.97% of 80 GB. The note's own closing sentence ('Byte-accurate, 436 ÷ 24.9037 = 17.51') establishes that byte-accuracy is the intended standard for this note, which the 54.25/99.7% figures do not meet.
issue.root_cause: A budget quantity and a consumption quantity are conflated in one arithmetic chain, and a rounded intermediate (3.1) is carried into a load-bearing conclusion ('a hard ceiling, not a comfortable operating point') without the byte-accurate value being used.
issue.correction: Separate the two quantities explicitly: 'KV budget per rank = 436/8 = 54.5 GB; at 17.5 concurrent requests a rank holds 17.5 × 3.11296 = 54.48 GB of KV, so per-rank occupancy = 17.5 (weights) + 54.48 (KV) + 8 (runtime) = 79.98 GB = 99.97% of 80 GB'. Then state the conclusion once: the aggregate 17.5 is a hard ceiling with essentially zero per-rank headroom, and the conservative integer floor of 17 is the right planning number.
issue.acceptance_test: Every number in the technical note is byte-accurate or explicitly marked as rounded, and no two quantities in the note differ only by rounding without being distinguished (budget vs consumed).

issue.quoted_clause: realized savings land between these 2× and 4× reduction factors, once per-block scale/offset metadata and per-token variation are counted — rather than the single 2×–4× that weight-only quantization applies to weights ... Weight-only quantization's 2×–4× applies to weights; do not transfer an expectation across precisions or across tensors without naming the bit width.
issue.observed: The chapter asserts that weight-only quantization realizes a clean 2×–4× reduction while KV quantization does not, because of scale/offset metadata. This is contradicted by the chapter's own worked example two sections later: MXFP4 weights cost 0.53125 B/value (17 B per 32 values), i.e. a realized 3.57× reduction, not 4×; NVFP4 costs 0.5625 B/value (3.56×); the INT4-with-FP16-scaled-zero layout costs 8,912,896 B for the same matrix that MXFP4 costs 8,912,896 B for — i.e. the same 3.57×. Weight quantization therefore carries exactly the same per-block scale metadata overhead the text attributes exclusively to KV. The asymmetry is an artifact of the text, not of the formats.
issue.evidence: Ch 7 §3: 'MXFP4 adds one local-scale byte, producing 17 bytes per 32 values, or 0.53125 B/value' → 2/0.53125 = 3.765×? No: 2 B/value ÷ 0.53125 B/value = 3.765×. Either way it is not 4×. The chapter's own §3 example states 'a 70B-parameter teaching model that stores 98% of parameters in MXFP4 and 2% in BF16 ... needs 39.24375 GB of compact weight storage rather than 140 GB' → 140/39.24375 = 3.568×, i.e. the chapter itself computes a realized weight reduction of 3.57×, not 4×.
issue.root_cause: The 'raw bound vs realized saving' distinction is stated correctly for KV but then mis-generalized into a claim that weights are exempt from metadata overhead. The correct general principle is: every block-scaled format has a raw bit-width bound and a realized ratio that depends on the scale/zero-point layout, for weights and for KV alike.
issue.correction: Rewrite both passages to state the general rule once: 'Raw bit-width is an upper bound on the reduction; the realized ratio depends on the scale/zero-point layout and is smaller than the raw bound for both weights and KV. MXFP4 weights realize ~3.57× (0.53125 B/value), not 4×; FP8 KV realizes 2× exactly (1 B/value, no per-element scale) before any block metadata.' Then the Common Mistakes bullet becomes 'Do not transfer a reduction factor across precisions, across tensors, or across formats without naming the bit width AND the scale/zero-point layout.'
issue.acceptance_test: No passage in Ch 7 claims a realized 2×–4× reduction for weights that is contradicted by the chapter's own MXFP4/NVFP4/INT4 worked example; the raw-bound vs realized-saving distinction is stated once and applied symmetrically to weights and KV.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 7, §3 'Worked Example' opening paragraph; Table 7-1; §7 technical note bullet 'per-request KV per rank'
issue.quoted_clause: a canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, full-MHA 70B reference model (every query head carries its own K,V, so the per-token KV width equals the model's hidden dimension) ... per-request KV per rank: 24.9 ÷ 8 = ~3.1 GB (tensor-parallel attention shards each request's KV across the 8 ranks)
issue.observed: The canonical geometry fixes layers (80) and hidden_dim (8192) but never fixes the query-head count or head_dim, yet two load-bearing claims depend on them: (a) Table 7-1's 128K row asserts 'TP=8 shard' passes gate 2, and (b) the technical note asserts that TP=8 shards each request's KV across the 8 ranks. Both require the KV-head count to be divisible by 8 (e.g. 64 heads × 128 dim → 8 KV heads/rank). The chapter's only head-count statement (64 query heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128) appears in the GQA sensitivity note and belongs to LLaMA-2 70B, which is explicitly NOT the canonical model. A reader therefore cannot verify the TP=8 shard claim from the canonical geometry as stated.
issue.evidence: The canonical geometry as printed contains no head count. The GQA note supplies '64 query heads but only 8 KV-heads' for LLaMA-2 70B (a GQA model), while the canonical is declared full-MHA with hidden 8192 — for which the head count is unstated (64 heads × 128 dim is the natural completion, and it is what makes TP=8 integral).
issue.root_cause: The canonical geometry was specified by the two parameters needed for the KV byte formula (layers, hidden width) and the head geometry was left implicit, even though the chapter later makes head-partition claims that depend on it.
issue.correction: Add the head geometry to the canonical geometry statement: 'canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, 64 query heads, head_dim 128, full-MHA (n_KV-heads = 64)'. Then the TP=8 shard claim becomes checkable (64/8 = 8 KV heads per rank) and the GQA note can be presented as the same geometry with n_KV-heads reduced from 64 to 8, which also makes the '8× smaller' comparison a controlled one (same layers, same hidden width, same head_dim) rather than a comparison across two different models.
issue.acceptance_test: Every TP=8 / per-rank KV-sharding claim in Ch 7 can be verified from the canonical geometry as printed, and the GQA comparison differs from the canonical in exactly one stated parameter (n_KV-heads).

issue.page_hint: Chapter 7, §3 note below Table 7-1; §7 Fig 7.7 caption; §8 mini-case
issue.quoted_clause: We compute that concurrent capacity here — the ~436 GB KV budget and ~17.5 requests/host (byte-accurate 17.51; conservative integer floor 17; arithmetic in this section) — and carry it into Chapter 17's fleet sizing.
issue.observed: The chapter derives a memory-derived concurrency ceiling (17.5 requests per 8×H100 host) and explicitly hands it to Chapter 17's fleet sizing, but never reconciles it with the traffic figures the chapter itself quotes in its opening paragraph (~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak) or with the mini-case's concurrency figures (~100 concurrent typical / ~400 at peak). These are different quantities and the chapter never says so. A memory ceiling is not a demand-derived concurrency: at ~300 output tokens and a plausible 20–40 tok/s per request, 10 rps implies ~75–150 concurrent requests, and 40 rps peak implies ~300–600 — i.e. the demand-derived concurrency is roughly 5–30× the memory ceiling of 17.5 per host. If Chapter 17 sizes hosts from 17.5/host without a Little's-law demand check, the fleet will be materially over- or under-provisioned. (Chapter 17's arithmetic was NOT VERIFIED in this pass.)
issue.evidence: Chapter 7 opening: '~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak traffic served by a 70B FP16 model on an 8×H100 host'. Chapter 7 §8: '~2,000 registered users (~100 concurrent typical / ~400 at peak), ~10 requests/s'. Chapter 7 §3 note: '~17.5 requests/host ... carry it into Chapter 17's fleet sizing'. Fig 7.7 caption already hedges: 'This is an analytical upper bound, not a validated concurrent-request count'. The hedge lives in a figure caption while the unqualified number is what is handed to the next chapter.
issue.root_cause: Two different concurrency concepts (memory ceiling vs demand-derived concurrency) are denoted by the same word and the chapter forwards only one of them downstream, with the caveat demoted to a caption.
issue.correction: In §3 (not only in the Fig 7.7 caption), state the distinction and give the demand-side check: '17.5 is the memory ceiling per host — the maximum number of simultaneously-resident 9.5K sequences. The demand-side concurrency is set by Little's law (concurrency = rps × mean service time) and must be computed from the workload's service time; for the canonical ~10 rps average and ~300 output tokens, the demand-side concurrency is far below 17.5 per host, so the memory ceiling binds only at the peak.' Then state explicitly what Chapter 17 should consume: the demand-derived concurrency, with 17.5 as the per-host feasibility check.
issue.acceptance_test: The phrase 'concurrency' is never used in Ch 7 for two different quantities without a qualifier; the number handed to Chapter 17 is stated with its definition; a reader can compute the demand-side concurrency from the chapter's own traffic and output-length figures.

issue.quoted_clause: The next step — turning "5,000 employees" into ~2,000 registered users (~100 concurrent typical / ~400 at peak), ~10 requests/s, and a specific model-and-hardware choice — applies Chapter 4's workload-anatomy method, already developed before this chapter.
issue.observed: The mini-case poses no decision, supplies no competing interpretations, and resolves nothing: it re-states numbers already printed in Table 7-1 (24.9 GB, 24.1 GB, 140 GB, 165 GB, 224 GB) and then explicitly defers the actual decision to Chapter 4. There is no evidence set to interpret, no ambiguity to resolve, and no architecture consequence that follows from the reader's work. As written it is a summary of the chapter, not a case.
issue.evidence: Every number in §8 appears earlier in Table 7-1 or §3 with the same values and the same labels; the closing paragraph names the decision ('a specific model-and-hardware choice') and assigns it to another chapter.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case was written as a restatement rather than as an application; the chapter's own most interesting decision — the one the chapter's arithmetic makes decidable — was not used.
issue.correction: Convert it into a decision the reader must make with the chapter's tools. Suggested frame: the company offers only 2×80 GB servers and asks whether the 70B FP16 model can be deployed on them; the reader must (i) compute the residency floor at 9.2K and 9.5K, (ii) discover that the aggregate verdict is basis-sensitive while the per-rank verdict is not, (iii) decide between 2×H100 with FP8 KV, 3–4×H100 with FP16 KV, and 8×H100 with headroom for concurrency, and (iv) state the validation each option still requires. Add the competing option (FP8 KV at ~152 GB) so the reader must weigh a capacity lever against a quality/precision lever, and require the answer to name the gate (1/2/3) that remains open.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case contains at least one decision the reader must make, at least two candidate configurations, and a conclusion that is not already printed verbatim in Table 7-1; a reader who skips the chapter body cannot answer it from the mini-case alone.

issue.quoted_clause: the GQA FP16 line reaches that budget only at ~1.32M tokens
issue.observed: The GQA FP16 per-token constant is 2 × 80 × (8 × 128) × 2 B = 327,680 B = 0.32768 MB, not 0.33 MB. The 436 GB KV budget is reached at 436×10^9 / 327,680 = 1,330,566 tokens ≈ 1.33M. The printed 1.32M is what one gets by dividing by the rounded 0.33 MB/token figure (436e9/330,000 = 1,321,212). The caption is the one place in the chapter where a reader is asked to read a value off a chart, so a 1% error in the chart's own annotation is a defect in the figure's meaning, not just in prose.
issue.root_cause: A rounded per-token constant was carried into a derived threshold instead of the byte-accurate constant, in a caption whose purpose is to let the reader locate a value on the plotted axis.
issue.correction: Print '~1.33M tokens' and, if the chart's axis annotation carries the same value, update it to match. If the figure itself labels the crossing at 1.32M, the figure must be regenerated so that the plotted line and the caption agree.
issue.acceptance_test: The GQA crossing point quoted in the caption equals 436 GB ÷ 327,680 B/token to the printed precision, and the figure's own axis annotation (if any) shows the same value.

issue.quoted_clause: would give 2×H100 = 171.8 GB and a 687 GB host pool — re-run this fit test on that basis before procurement). The 2×H100 fit verdict, the 640 GB envelope, the 436 GB KV budget and the ~17.5 concurrency all use this decimal basis.
issue.observed: The paragraph names four quantities that depend on the basis but instructs the reader to re-run only 'this fit test'. Under the vendor-binary basis the other three also move: host pool 8 × 85.9 = 687.2 GB; KV budget 687.2 − 140 − 64 = 483.2 GB; concurrency 483.2 / 24.90368 = 19.40 (floor 19, not 17). A reader who re-runs only the 2×H100 test and keeps 436 GB / 17.5 will mix bases across the chapter's own ledger.
issue.root_cause: The caveat was scoped to the verdict that was topically visible at the point of writing, rather than to the full set of derived quantities the basis touches.
issue.correction: Either state the complete basis-dependent set in one place ('on the vendor-binary basis the pool is 687 GB, the KV budget 483 GB, and the per-host concurrency ceiling 19 (floor 19)'), or state the rule once — 'every capacity figure in this chapter is decimal; the binary-basis equivalents are obtained by multiplying the pool by 1.074 and re-deriving the budget and concurrency from it' — and cross-reference it from the three later figures that depend on it.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who adopts the opposite capacity convention can re-derive every capacity-dependent number in Ch 7 (pool, KV budget, concurrency, per-rank fill) from a single stated rule, without mixing bases.

issue.quoted_clause: When evaluating a model where the hidden dimension or layer count differs from LLaMA-70B, recompute the constant factor
issue.observed: The chapter's canonical geometry is explicitly a constructed full-MHA teaching model, and the chapter insists (twice) that it is not a named vendor model. Invoking 'LLaMA-70B' here as the reference point reintroduces exactly the confusion the chapter warns against: LLaMA-2 70B is GQA (8 KV heads), so its real per-token KV is ~0.33 MB, not 2.62 MB. A reader who takes 'LLaMA-70B' as the reference for the 2.62 MB/token constant will mis-derive the KV footprint for the most widely deployed 70B-class model.
issue.evidence: Ch 7 §3: 'The 70B reference is a constructed teaching geometry, not a named vendor model'; Ch 7 §3 GQA note: 'LLaMA-2 70B, for instance, has 64 query heads but only 8 KV-heads' → 0.33 MB/token.
issue.root_cause: A familiar model name was used as shorthand for the chapter's own reference geometry.
issue.correction: Replace 'differs from LLaMA-70B' with 'differs from this chapter's 80-layer / 8192-hidden reference geometry', and add one clause: 'note that LLaMA-2 70B shares the 80-layer/8192 geometry but is GQA, so its per-token KV is ~0.33 MB — see the sensitivity note above.'
issue.acceptance_test: No passage in Ch 7 uses a named vendor model as the implicit referent for the canonical 2.62 MB/token constant.

issue.quoted_clause: at 24.9 GB/request max-FP16 KV (9.5K max context, per Fig 7.6)
issue.observed: Fig 7.6 is 'Inference vs fine-tuning memory floor' — it shows the ~165 GB weights+KV floor and the ~1,120 GB training floor, not the per-request KV figure. The 24.9 GB/request value is derived in §3/Table 7-1. The reference resolves to a figure that does not carry the number, which is the kind of cross-reference that sends a reader to the wrong conceptual material.
issue.evidence: Fig 7.6 caption: 'The same 70B model has a weights+KV floor of ~165 GB ... but needs ~1,120 GB for full Adam fine-tuning'. Table 7-1: 'total inference KV (9.5K max) | ≈ 24.9 GB'.
issue.root_cause: Figure numbers were used as anchors for values that live in the table.
issue.correction: Change '(per Fig 7.6)' to '(Table 7-1, §3)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every 'per Fig X' / 'per Table X' in Ch 7 points to the element that actually prints the cited number.

issue.page_hint: Chapter 7, opening paragraph (color disclaimer) vs Fig 7.8 caption
issue.quoted_clause: Color is not semantic across this chapter's figures: the same concept (persistent KV/state storage) is rendered in different hues in FIGS 7.1–7.4 ... the FP16 KV cache (orange) is the only block that grows
issue.observed: The disclaimer scopes the color warning to FIGS 7.1–7.4, but Fig 7.8's caption relies on a color word ('orange') to identify the KV block, and Fig 7.8 is outside the disclaimed range. Either the disclaimer should cover all figures in the chapter, or Fig 7.8's caption should identify the block by position/label rather than hue (which also serves the grayscale-print requirement).
issue.evidence: Fig 7.8 caption: 'the FP16 KV cache (orange) is the only block that grows'.
issue.root_cause: The disclaimer was written for the figures that existed when it was added and was not extended when later figures were added.
issue.correction: Extend the disclaimer to 'FIGS 7.1–7.8' and, in Fig 7.8's caption, name the block by its label ('the FP16 KV block') with the color as a parenthetical only.
