issue.observed: The [ASSUMPTION] canonical label is attached to a normative instruction ('must be confirmed') rather than to a value or a span of text it characterizes. The label therefore appears to certify the instruction as an assumption, which is not what it means.
issue.evidence: Compare Ch 12 §3's usage, where the label attaches to the canonical values ('164 GB < 640 GB aggregate ([ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2))').
issue.root_cause: Label placement on a sentence whose content is a rule, not an assumption.
issue.correction: Move the label to the canonical inputs it refers to (the three numbers), or drop it from the normative sentence and keep it on the values in items 1–3.
issue.acceptance_test: Every [ASSUMPTION] canonical label in Ch 12 attaches to a value or a clearly delimited span, never to a normative instruction.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 §6 Architecture Consequence vs §3 and §8 mini-case; Table 12-1 verdict column
issue.quoted_clause: §6: "(Candidate (c) does not advance as a finalist; it is carried only as a labeled sensitivity case)"; mini-case: "it is provisionally moved to the quality-gate evaluation (Chapter 14) to measure whether a 7B-class model actually meets the workload's capability/quality threshold"; Table 12-1: "**gated, not a finalist** — ✗ quality gate open (Ch 14)"
issue.observed: Candidate (c)'s status is described three different ways: 'carried only as a labeled sensitivity case' (§6), 'provisionally moved to the quality-gate evaluation (Chapter 14)' (mini-case), and 'gated, not a finalist' (Table 12-1). 'Sensitivity case' is not a term defined in the book's evidence taxonomy, and 'not a finalist' is compatible with either 'evaluated in Ch 14' or 'excluded'. The reader cannot tell whether (c) is actually measured in Ch 14.
issue.evidence: §3 also says 'The candidate is therefore provisional: its fate depends on the measured quality gate, which Chapter 14 (the capability screen) administers.'
issue.root_cause: Three status vocabularies for one candidate, one of them undefined.
issue.correction: Use one status term for (c) across §3, §6, Table 12-1 and the mini-case (e.g. 'gated — carried into the Ch 14 quality screen, not a finalist'), and either define 'sensitivity case' in the taxonomy or drop it.
issue.acceptance_test: Candidate (c)'s status is stated with one term in all four locations, and the term is defined in the book.

issue.quoted_clause: "[ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] (the tier's model-size range is a book-defined characterization; the H100/H200 and NVLink/NVSwitch specs it cites are [1P] vendor datasheets)"
issue.observed: The parenthetical asserts that the bullet cites H100/H200 and NVLink/NVSwitch specifications from vendor datasheets, but the bullet contains no specifications — only product names and a model-size range. The provenance claim does not match the content it annotates.
issue.evidence: The bullet reads: 'one host with 1-8 GPUs, typically H100/H200 — multi-GPU servers joined by NVLink/NVSwitch (a 1-GPU host uses PCIe; no intra-host fabric is needed). Serves dense models up to ~70B-180B with real concurrency.'
issue.root_cause: Provenance annotation written for a version of the bullet that carried specifications.
issue.correction: Either add the specific datasheet-derived figures the annotation refers to (with citations) or rewrite the annotation to cover only what the bullet actually asserts.
issue.acceptance_test: Every [1P] annotation in Ch 13 §1 is attached to a specific specification that appears in the annotated text.

issue.quoted_clause: "Make these measurable: thresholds are examples to calibrate to your SLO headroom policy, e.g. de-escalate when 30-day p95 utilization < 40% AND SLO margin > 2× AND the smaller tier's failure domain is acceptable."
issue.observed: The figure caption carries a de-escalation policy with numeric thresholds and a three-part conjunctive rule. This is body content inside a caption: it is long, it will be read once and not again, and it competes with the caption's actual job (explaining the ladder and its triggers). It also duplicates the caption's own list of de-escalation considerations.
issue.evidence: The caption already enumerates 'utilization', 'failure domain', 'operations burden' and 'SLO margin' as considerations before adding the threshold rule.
issue.root_cause: Caption used as a catch-all for material that belongs in the body.
issue.correction: Move the threshold example into §2 (Mental Model) or §4 (Measurement) as a short 'calibrating the de-escalation trigger' paragraph, and shorten the caption to the ladder, the triggers, and the rung mapping.
issue.acceptance_test: Fig 13.1's caption contains no policy thresholds; the thresholds appear in the body with the reasoning for choosing them.

issue.quoted_clause: Ch 12 §1: "the three gates this chapter fixes"; Ch 12 mini-case: "the chapter notes it equals one host's cloud-equivalent"; Ch 13: "continuous batching on 8×H100 at ~9.5K tokens/request sustained roughly tens of thousands of tokens/s"
issue.observed: Three small wording issues: (i) 'fixes' should be 'defines' for gates the chapter introduces; (ii) the mini-case refers to 'the chapter' from inside itself — it should name the source (Ch 4/16) of the $15K budget and the $20/hr rate; (iii) Ch 13's 'roughly tens of thousands of tokens/s' is a vague restatement of a number the book states precisely elsewhere (~19,800 prefill tok/s per host), and it is used to support the claim that one host's goodput is exceeded.
issue.evidence: Ch 12 §3 and Table 12-2 both state ~19,800 tok/s per host; Ch 13 §3 uses 'tens of thousands' instead.
issue.root_cause: Loose editing; a precise number was replaced by an approximation in one place.
issue.correction: Fix (i) and (ii) as noted; in (iii) use the book's own per-host figure and name the screen it comes from.
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 12/13 refers to 'the chapter' from inside a chapter; the per-host throughput figure is stated identically wherever it appears.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §6 (Architecture Consequence), paragraph beginning 'These choices together would change the basis of the throughput figure'
issue.quoted_clause: ~35,000–48,000 tokens/s [ILLUSTRATIVE achievable range] at the canonical context (with flash, continuous batch; a mixed prefill+decode aggregate; upper end = the case-(ii) attention-adjusted ceiling, lower end = the mini-case's per-host figure) ... the single-host upper end is capped by the 100%-MFU parameter-matmul-only ceiling: 7.91×10¹⁵ FLOP/s ÷ 1.4×10¹¹ FLOP/token ≈ 56,500 tok/s under the linear-only case (i) — a 2N-only figure; at the canonical 9,200-token context the attention term (§3, case ii) lowers this to ≈48,000 tok/s (≈52,000 under the causal case (iii)) — so the illustrative range is ~35,000–48,000 at canonical context
issue.observed: The per-host throughput range is internally inconsistent with the chapter's own numbers on three separate bases, and its label ('achievable range') contradicts its own construction. (a) The upper end, 48,000 tok/s, is by construction the 100%-MFU ceiling (7.912e15 FLOP/s ÷ 1.6412e11 FLOP/token = 48,208), i.e. a theoretical maximum that no system attains; calling the range 'achievable' re-introduces exactly the MFU>1 error the chapter spends a paragraph forbidding. (b) The lower end, 35,000 tok/s/host, implies 35,000 × 1.4e11 = 4.90e15 FLOP/s ÷ 7.912e15 = 61.9% MFU under case (i) (72.6% under case (ii)), which contradicts §3's own 35% MFU planning screen (7.912e15 × 0.35 ÷ 1.4e11 = 19,779 tok/s/host) by a factor of ~1.8×. (c) The label 'mixed prefill+decode aggregate' is not supportable: at the canonical 9,500-token context the host's decode-bandwidth ceiling is ≈809 tok/s (see CH15-02), so a 35,000 tok/s aggregate is ≥97.7% prefill — it is a prefill rate, not a mixed rate. (d) 35,000 tok/s/host ÷ 9,200 tok/req = 3.80 rps/host, which contradicts §4's own '~2 rps per host' admission capacity (17 slots ÷ 8.6 s = 1.98 rps) by ~1.9×.
issue.root_cause: The chapter mixes three incompatible bases inside one quoted range — a theoretical 100%-MFU ceiling, an achievable mixed-workload rate, and a per-host figure imported from another chapter's mini-case — and then labels the union 'achievable'. The 35% planning screen established in §3 is never carried forward to §6, so the two efficiency assumptions (35% vs ~62–73%) coexist without reconciliation.
issue.correction: Split the statement into three explicitly labelled quantities: (i) the 100%-MFU prefill ceiling (56,500 case (i) / 48,000 case (ii) / 52,000 case (iii)) labelled as a theoretical bound, not an achievable rate; (ii) the planning-screen rate implied by §3's 35% MFU (≈19,800 tok/s/host case (i)); (iii) the mini-case's per-host figure, with its workload level and MFU assumption stated and reconciled against (ii). If a single range is retained, label it 'illustrative planning range' and state the MFU assumption behind each endpoint; do not call a 100%-MFU ceiling 'achievable'. Also drop or qualify 'mixed prefill+decode aggregate' unless the decode share is computed.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state, for each of the three numbers (56,500 / 48,000 / 35,000), its FLOP/token convention, its implied MFU, and whether it is a bound or an estimate; and can verify that no number in the range is labelled 'achievable' while being equal to a 100%-MFU ceiling. The 35,000 tok/s/host figure is either reconciled with §3's 35% screen or explicitly flagged as resting on a different (stated) efficiency assumption.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §3 (Worked Example), paragraph beginning 'The architectural conclusion, that there is no single bottleneck for the whole request, stands'
issue.quoted_clause: At the canonical peak, prefill shows a *workload capacity deficit* — aggregate compute demand above the host's peak (it needs more FLOPs/s than the host can supply, and leans on caching/queueing). Decode is primarily memory-bandwidth constrained, and maximum concurrency is constrained by KV residency. Each phase is established from arithmetic intensity and the roofline (Chapter 8), never from an impossible "MFU > 1."
issue.observed: The chapter promises a phase-by-phase establishment and delivers it for prefill (a demand/peak ratio of ~6.5×) but not for decode. Decode is asserted to be 'primarily memory-bandwidth constrained' with no demand/peak ratio at all, even though the chapter has already computed every input needed (140 GB weights, 24.9 GB KV per 9,500-token sequence, 12,000 output tok/s peak demand, 17-slot KV-limited concurrency). The natural completion is bytes/token = weights/B + KV_bytes = 140/B + 24.9 GB: at B = 17 that is 33.1 GB/token, so 12,000 tok/s demands ≈398 TB/s against a host peak of 8 × 3.35 TB/s = 26.8 TB/s — a ~14.8× deficit; even as B → ∞ the KV term alone (24.9 GB/token) gives 299 TB/s, a ~11× deficit. The per-host decode ceiling is therefore ≈809 tok/s, so decode alone needs ≈15 hosts at the theoretical bandwidth limit — comparable to the 19-host prefill screen. The 19-host screen is thus prefill-only and is presented as if it were the fleet answer. The same omission also hides prefill's KV-write traffic (368,000 tok/s × 2.62144 MB = 965 GB/s, ≈3.6% of host peak) and the fact that the decode FLOP ratio of 0.21 (§3) says nothing about decode headroom, because decode is not FLOP-limited.
issue.evidence: Recomputed: KV per sequence = 9,500 × 2,621,440 B = 24.90 GB; weights = 70e9 × 2 B = 140 GB; host HBM peak (H100 SXM) = 8 × 3.35 TB/s = 26.8 TB/s; bytes/token at B=17 = 140/17 + 24.90 = 33.14 GB; 12,000 × 33.14 GB = 397.7 TB/s → 14.8× over peak; per-host ceiling = 26,800 GB/s ÷ 33.14 GB = 809 tok/s; 12,000/809 = 14.8 hosts. Cross-check against the chunk's own §4 figure: 2 rps/host × 300 tok = 600 decode tok/s vs the 809 ceiling (74% duty) and 2 × 9,200 = 18,400 prefill tok/s vs §3's 35%-screen rate of 19,779 tok/s — §3 and §4 are mutually consistent, which confirms the missing decode check is the only gap.
issue.root_cause: The chapter's analytical template (demand ÷ peak, per phase) was applied to prefill's FLOP axis but not to decode's bandwidth axis, even though decode's binding resource is bandwidth and the chapter says so. The omission is then masked by the 0.21 FLOP ratio, which is on the wrong axis for decode.
issue.correction: Add the decode demand/peak check to §3, immediately after the prefill one, using the same template: bytes/token = W/B + KV_bytes_per_token; demand = 12,000 × bytes/token; compare with 8 × HBM bandwidth. State the resulting per-host decode ceiling and the implied host count for the decode phase, and state explicitly that the 19-host screen is prefill-derived and must be combined with (not substituted for) the decode requirement. Add the prefill KV-write term (965 GB/s) for completeness. Also state the H100 variant (SXM 3.35 TB/s vs PCIe 2.0 TB/s) since the result depends on it.
issue.acceptance_test: §3 contains a decode-phase demand/peak ratio computed on the bandwidth axis, with the batch size stated, and the text no longer presents the prefill-derived host count as the fleet answer without noting the decode requirement. A reader can reproduce the decode host count from the chapter's own inputs.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §4 (Measurement), paragraph beginning 'On the FlashAttention "traffic reduction" claim, be precise about the units'
issue.quoted_clause: That is a *rate*, not a byte count — FlashAttention finishes sooner, so a higher achieved rate over a shorter run still yields fewer total bytes per request.
issue.observed: The inference is invalid as stated. Bytes transferred = achieved rate × elapsed time. A higher achieved rate over a shorter run yields fewer bytes only if the speed-up exceeds the rate ratio; with the chapter's own illustrative numbers (400 GB/s vs 150 GB/s, a 2.67× rate ratio) the byte totals are equal only if FlashAttention finishes 2.67× sooner, and are otherwise ambiguous. The sentence asserts a general implication that does not hold, and it is immediately followed by the correct statement ('A bandwidth figure alone does not establish that fewer bytes/request were transferred'), so the paragraph contradicts itself. The byte reduction is real, but it follows from the mechanism (no materialized L×L intermediate), not from the rate comparison.
issue.evidence: bytes = rate × time. With rate_1 = 400 GB/s, rate_0 = 150 GB/s, bytes_1 < bytes_0 requires t_0/t_1 > 400/150 = 2.67. The chapter supplies no such bound. The correct causal chain is: no materialized intermediate → fewer bytes per request (mechanism) → shorter runtime → higher achieved rate (consequence), not the reverse.
issue.root_cause: The paragraph is trying to correct a units error (rate vs byte count) and over-corrects into a false implication, because the author did not separate 'the mechanism reduces bytes' from 'the measurement shows a higher rate'.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'A bandwidth figure is a rate, not a byte count: bytes = rate × time, so a higher achieved rate over a shorter run does not by itself establish fewer bytes. The byte reduction follows from the mechanism — the materialized L×L intermediate is not written and re-read — and must be confirmed as bytes/request (or read/write transaction counters) under a matched workload.'
issue.acceptance_test: The paragraph contains no sentence in which a rate comparison is used to conclude a byte reduction; the causal direction runs mechanism → bytes → runtime → rate.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §3 (Worked Example), paragraph beginning 'Compute demand versus peak — and why this is not an MFU'
issue.quoted_clause: The decode figure at 12,000 tokens/s is ≈ 1.68 ×10¹⁵ ÷ 7.91 ×10¹⁵ ≈ 0.21, i.e. ~21 % — again a groundable number, not a ceiling-defying one; the actual achieved value must come from the target serving benchmark.
issue.observed: The paragraph's whole purpose is to separate a demand ratio from an achieved MFU, and it does so correctly for prefill ('What it must not be called is "MFU = 6.5"'). The decode sentence then abandons that discipline: 'again a groundable number' invites the reader to treat 21% as an achieved MFU, and the ratio is presented without the label 'demand'. Worse, a sub-1.0 FLOP ratio for decode is easy to misread as evidence of decode headroom, when decode is bandwidth- and KV-limited and the FLOP axis is not the binding constraint (see CH15-02, where the decode bandwidth deficit is ~15×). The chapter's own opening paragraph warns against exactly this collapse ('whether either phase is actually compute- or bandwidth-bound is a property of the model × workload × kernel × hardware operating point'), so the unqualified 'Decode is primarily memory-bandwidth constrained' later in the same section also undercuts its own caveat.
issue.evidence: 12,000 × 1.4e11 = 1.68e15; 1.68e15/7.912e15 = 0.2123. The ratio is a demand/peak ratio on the FLOP axis. Decode's binding axis is bandwidth: 12,000 tok/s × 33.1 GB/token (B=17) = 398 TB/s vs 26.8 TB/s peak (CH15-02).
issue.root_cause: The demand/achieved distinction was established once and then not applied consistently; the decode ratio was written as a 'figure' rather than as a labelled demand ratio on a named axis.
issue.correction: Label the decode number explicitly as a demand-to-peak ratio on the FLOP axis, e.g. 'the decode FLOP demand is ≈21% of the host's FP16 peak — a demand ratio on the compute axis, not an achieved MFU, and not evidence of decode headroom, because decode is limited by bytes/token (bandwidth) and by KV residency, not by FLOPs.' Then add the bandwidth-axis ratio (CH15-02).
issue.acceptance_test: Every ratio in §3 is explicitly labelled as demand-vs-peak or achieved, and states which resource axis it is on. No reader can arrive at 'decode has 79% headroom' from the text.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §5 (Common Mistakes), third bullet, 'Using scaled-dot-product attention without FlashAttention'
issue.quoted_clause: and it pays off specifically when memory-bound; for moderate lengths (2,000–4,000 tokens) the HBM bandwidth reduction can translate to a ~1.3–1.8× throughput gain on H100 (illustrative — bench the specific kernel on the target hardware)
issue.observed: The referent of 'throughput gain' is unstated (attention-kernel throughput vs end-to-end request throughput), and the number is not derivable from either reading using the chapter's own arithmetic. End-to-end: the chapter computes in §3 that attention is ≈15% of total forward FLOPs at 9,200 tokens; at 2,000–4,000 tokens the same formula gives attention = 4·80·L²·8192 / (2·70e9·L + 4·80·L²·8192) = 3.7% (L=2,000) and 7.5% (L=4,000) of total FLOPs, so even a free attention kernel bounds the end-to-end gain at ≈4–8%, not 1.3–1.8×. Kernel-level: a 3–5× reduction in HBM traffic on a bandwidth-bound kernel should give roughly a 3–5× kernel speed-up, not 1.3–1.8×, unless the kernel is not bandwidth-bound at those lengths — which is itself an important and unstated fact (at L=2,000 the fp16 score matrix is 8 MB and at L=4,000 it is 32 MB, both within H100's 50 MB L2, so the naive path's intermediate may not reach HBM at all). The chapter also asserts elsewhere that the KV working set 'exceeds L2 at any batch ≥ 1', which is true for KV but not for the attention score intermediate at these lengths — the two L2 facts need to be kept apart.
issue.evidence: Attention FLOPs (full square) = 4·n_layers·L²·d = 4·80·L²·8192. L=2,000: 1.049e13; param-matmul = 2·70e9·2,000 = 2.8e14; attention share = 3.6%. L=4,000: 4.194e13 vs 5.6e14 → 7.0%. L=9,200: 2.219e14 vs 1.288e15 → 14.7% (matches the chapter's '≈15% of total'). Score-matrix bytes at fp16: L=2,000 → 8.0 MB; L=4,000 → 32.0 MB; H100 L2 = 50 MB.
issue.root_cause: The chapter has a precise attention-share model in §3 but does not carry it into §5, where a bare speed-up multiplier is asserted; and it conflates the L2 residency of the KV working set with that of the attention score intermediate.
issue.correction: State the referent ('attention-kernel throughput' or 'end-to-end request throughput'), and either derive the number from the chapter's own attention-share arithmetic or replace it with the derived bound (e.g. 'at 2,000–4,000 tokens attention is only 4–8% of forward FLOPs, so the end-to-end gain is bounded at roughly 4–8% even for a perfect attention kernel; the kernel-level gain is larger, and at these lengths the fp16 score matrix (8–32 MB) may fit in H100's 50 MB L2, which is why the benefit is length- and kernel-dependent').
issue.acceptance_test: The §5 claim names its referent, and its magnitude is either derived from §3's attention-share numbers or explicitly bounded by them; the L2 discussion distinguishes the KV working set from the attention score intermediate.

issue.page_hint: Ch15, 'The Optimization Decision Map', 'Two cautions' paragraph immediately below the table
issue.quoted_clause: Second, the last two rows (P/D disaggregation, interconnect tuning) are the expensive, structural levers — they are worth testing only after the cheaper in-kernel and in-scheduler mechanisms have been measured and shown insufficient
issue.observed: The parenthetical misidentifies the rows. The table's last two rows are row 7 ('multi-GPU execution dominated by communication' → interconnect/parallelism) and row 8 ('weight capacity or weight traffic limiting' → weight quantization). P/D disaggregation is row 6 ('prefill and decode interfering'). A reader who follows the reference lands on the weight-quantization row, which the chapter elsewhere explicitly calls a cheap, non-structural lever ('quantization is a candidate, not a win'), and misses the P/D row that carries the 'only after measuring' qualifier.
issue.evidence: Table row order as printed: (1) high TTFT + compute saturated during prefill; (2) high TPOT/ITL + HBM bandwidth saturated; (3) KV exhaustion / low concurrency; (4) long-context attention dominated by memory traffic; (5) low GPU util, request-lifecycle mismatch; (6) prefill and decode interfering (contains 'chunked prefill ... then P/D disaggregation'); (7) multi-GPU execution dominated by communication; (8) weight capacity or weight traffic limiting.
issue.root_cause: The sentence was written against an earlier row order (or from memory) and not re-checked after the table was edited.
issue.correction: Replace 'the last two rows' with an explicit row identification, e.g. 'the P/D-disaggregation row and the interconnect-tuning row (rows 6 and 7) are the expensive, structural levers', or reorder the table so the structural levers are last.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence's row references resolve to the rows it describes when the table is read as printed.

issue.page_hint: Ch15, 'The Optimization Decision Map', row 3 ('KV exhaustion / low concurrency')
issue.quoted_clause: GQA/MQA (architecture-fixed — not a runtime lever; requires a re-checkpointed model), KV quantization, PagedAttention, context reduction, eviction/offload, prefix reuse | capacity vs transfer latency | lower per-request KV or offload
issue.observed: 'Prefix reuse' is listed as a remedy for a memory-capacity bottleneck, but prefix caching does not reduce KV capacity demand: it eliminates prefill recomputation (a FLOP saving) while adding resident cached prefixes (a capacity cost). Listing it in the 'memory capacity' row invites the reader to believe that enabling prefix caching frees KV space for more concurrency, which is the opposite of its normal effect. The row's evidence column does list 'fragmentation', but the 'likely bottleneck' cell says only 'memory capacity', so the row conflates two distinct bottlenecks (raw capacity exhaustion vs fragmentation waste) that the chapter elsewhere insists on separating.
issue.evidence: Chapter's own §3/§6: prefix caching stores additional KV blocks; the only capacity-reducing levers listed are KV quantization (2.62 → 1.31 MB/token), context reduction, eviction/offload, and GQA/MQA. §6's concurrency gain (17.5 → 35.0) is attributed to FP8 KV quantization, not to prefix reuse.
issue.root_cause: The row was assembled as a list of 'KV-related techniques' rather than as a mapping from bottleneck to mechanism, which is the stated organizing principle of the map ('symptom → bottleneck → evidence → candidate mechanism chain').
issue.correction: Remove 'prefix reuse' from the memory-capacity row (it belongs in the prefill-compute row, where it already appears as 'prefix caching'), and split the row's bottleneck cell into 'raw KV capacity' and 'KV fragmentation / allocator waste', assigning PagedAttention to the latter and KV quantization / context reduction / eviction-offload / GQA-MQA to the former.
issue.acceptance_test: Every mechanism listed in a row of the map reduces the resource named in that row's 'likely bottleneck' cell; a reader can state which resource each listed mechanism relieves.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §6 (Architecture Consequence), final sentences of the paragraph beginning 'These choices together would change the basis of the throughput figure'
issue.quoted_clause: 70,000 tok/s on one host would be ~124% MFU (a 2N-only check), so that figure is the *two-host* aggregate of the mini-case below (≈35,000 tok/s/host at its ~2× second-host factor) ... A fourth decision, raised by the mini-case (Ch11 §11.8) and not yet validated
issue.observed: Two problems. (a) Cross-reference ambiguity: the same mini-case is called 'the mini-case below' and 'the mini-case (Ch11 §11.8)'. Chapter 11 precedes Chapter 15, so 'below' cannot refer to it; if Chapter 15 has its own end-of-chapter mini-case, the two references point at different objects and the reader cannot tell which supplies the 35,000 tok/s/host figure. (b) The phrase 'at its ~2× second-host factor' is uninterpretable: it could mean 'the second host contributes 2× the first' (total 3 hosts) or 'the factor is 2 hosts' (total 2 hosts). Only the latter reconciles with 2 × 35,000 = 70,000. (c) The imported figure conflicts with this chapter's own numbers: 35,000 tok/s/host ÷ 9,200 tok/req = 3.80 rps/host, versus §4's '~2 rps per host' admission capacity (17 slots ÷ 8.6 s = 1.98 rps) and §3's 19-host peak screen (19 × 1.98 = 37.6 rps). A two-host deployment at 3.8 rps/host covers ~7.6 rps, which is below even the canonical 10 rps average — so the mini-case's basis (workload level, context length, MFU) must be stated before its number can be used as the canonical deployment's throughput.
issue.evidence: 35,000/9,200 = 3.80 rps/host; §4: 17/8.6 = 1.98 rps/host; §3: 6.5/0.35 = 18.6 → 19 hosts; 19 × 1.98 = 37.6 rps vs the 40 rps canonical peak. 2 hosts × 35,000 = 70,000 tok/s = 7.6 rps of prefill.
issue.root_cause: A number imported from another chapter's worked example is used as a canonical-deployment figure without its workload level, context length, or efficiency assumption being carried along; and the cross-reference was written before the chapter's mini-case was placed.
issue.correction: Resolve the reference to one object (state 'the mini-case in Ch 11 §11.8' or 'the mini-case at the end of this chapter', consistently), replace 'at its ~2× second-host factor' with the explicit arithmetic ('2 hosts × 35,000 tok/s/host'), and state the mini-case's workload level, context length, and implied MFU so the reader can see whether it is comparable with §3's 19-host peak screen and §4's ~2 rps/host admission capacity. If the mini-case is not the canonical workload, say so and stop using its per-host figure as the canonical range's lower endpoint (see CH15-01).
issue.acceptance_test: Every cross-reference in §6 resolves to exactly one mini-case; the 70,000 tok/s figure is accompanied by its workload level and per-host MFU; and a reader can reconcile it with §3's 19-host screen and §4's ~2 rps/host without contradiction.

issue.quoted_clause: (3) KV cache management via FP8 KV quantization ... plus length-based eviction of *inactive* prefix-cache entries (never truncation of an active request's context — active KV is offloaded or recomputed, per §5) ... A fourth decision, raised by the mini-case (Ch11 §11.8) and not yet validated, is to design the request-routing layer for KV cache affinity: when a user re-submits a request, routing to the same host avoids cache warm-up penalties and keeps p99 latency under the target SLO
issue.observed: Decisions (3) and (4) are in direct conflict as written. Decision (3) evicts inactive prefix-cache entries by length; decision (4) relies on those same cached prefixes surviving so that an affinity-routed request finds a warm prefix. If the eviction policy removes the user's prefix, affinity routing yields no cache-warm-up benefit and the fourth decision's stated benefit ('keeps p99 latency under the target SLO') evaporates. The chapter is careful elsewhere to distinguish eviction of inactive prefixes from truncation of active context (§5), but it does not notice that its own two recommendations pull in opposite directions on the same objects.
issue.evidence: §5: '(a) Evicting an idle/inactive prefix-cache entry — a cached prefix not currently in service — is safe, because no active request depends on it and it can be recomputed on reuse.' §6 decision (3) selects length-based eviction of exactly those entries; §6 decision (4) selects affinity routing to preserve exactly those entries.
issue.root_cause: The two decisions were derived independently (one from the KV-capacity analysis, one from the mini-case) and never reconciled, although they govern the same cache objects.
issue.correction: State the interaction and resolve it: either (i) make eviction affinity-aware (evict by (length, affinity) so that a user's likely-to-be-reused prefix is retained), or (ii) scope decision (4) to prefixes that survive the eviction policy, or (iii) note that decision (4) is conditional on decision (3)'s eviction policy and mark it as unresolved. Also state that the p99 benefit of affinity routing is unvalidated (as the text already does) and that it competes with the capacity freed by eviction.
issue.acceptance_test: §6 contains an explicit statement of how the eviction policy and the affinity-routing policy interact, and no reader can apply both as written and expect the affinity benefit to materialize.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §4 (Measurement, final paragraph) vs §6 (Architecture Consequence, decision (2))
issue.quoted_clause: §4: 'beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises (implying a knee near batch 4)' ... §6: '(2) continuous batching, with the maximum decode-step batch granularity chosen empirically from the measured goodput/latency knee ... (a max batch size of 8 requests per decode step — an [ILLUSTRATIVE] configuration, not the recommendation; the knee must be measured on the target stack)'
issue.observed: The chapter's own §4 locates the goodput/latency knee near batch 4, and §6 then illustrates the chosen maximum decode-step batch as 8 — above the knee it just identified — while simultaneously saying the value must be chosen from the measured knee. Both numbers are labelled illustrative, but they are the chapter's only two statements about where the knee is, and they disagree. A reader who takes either at face value gets a different operating point, and the architecture-consequence section is where the reader expects the chapter's own analysis to have converged.
issue.evidence: §4: 'beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises (implying a knee near batch 4)'; §6: 'a max batch size of 8 requests per decode step'. The §4 sweep is (1, 4, 16, 32), so 8 is not even one of the measured points.
issue.root_cause: The illustrative configuration in §6 was chosen independently of the illustrative knee in §4, and neither was reconciled with the other or with the §4 sweep grid.
issue.correction: Make §6's illustrative value consistent with §4 (e.g. 'a maximum decode-step batch of 4–8 requests, with the value set by the measured knee; note that the §4 sweep grid (1, 4, 16, 32) should be extended to include the chosen value'), or drop the specific number from §6 and keep only the method. If 8 is retained, state why it is acceptable above the knee (e.g. as a hard cap on tail latency rather than an operating point).
issue.acceptance_test: The illustrative batch size in §6 does not exceed the illustrative knee in §4 without an explicit justification, and the §4 sweep grid contains the value §6 recommends.

issue.page_hint: Ch15, Fig 15.1 caption (FlashAttention), final sentences of the caption body
issue.quoted_clause: Both paths still do Θ(L²) HBM element accesses (with d fixed) — the gain is a constant factor set by on-chip capacity (d²/M), not a lower order.
issue.observed: The I/O-complexity statement is ambiguous in sign and loose in units. In the FlashAttention I/O analysis, the fused kernel's HBM traffic in the quadratic regime is Θ(L²d²/M) while the materialized path's is Θ(L²); the reduction factor is therefore M/d² (how much larger the on-chip budget is than d²), and d²/M is the retained fraction. Calling d²/M 'the gain' reads as a speed-up factor of 0.083 (i.e. a 12× reduction) to one reader and as a slowdown to another. The units are also inconsistent: d is a head dimension in elements while M is an SRAM size in bytes, so d²/M is not dimensionless unless element size is silently taken as 1. The caption's own scope note ('the exact number of K/V re-reads depends on the tile scheduling, sequence length, and SRAM size') is the right caveat, but it sits above a formula that states the opposite kind of certainty.
issue.evidence: FlashAttention I/O analysis (Dao et al.): fused kernel Θ(Nd²/M) HBM accesses vs Θ(Nd + N²) for the materialized path; the quadratic-term ratio is M/d². With d = 128 and M ≈ 192 KB (H100 shared memory per SM), d²/M ≈ 0.083 in element units — an idealized bound, not a realized traffic reduction, which is why the chapter elsewhere quotes a measured 3–5×.
issue.root_cause: The caption compresses a two-sided complexity statement into a single ambiguous symbol without stating which side is the numerator, and mixes element and byte units.
issue.correction: State the comparison explicitly and in consistent units, e.g. 'the fused kernel's HBM traffic in the quadratic regime is Θ(L²d²/M) versus Θ(L²) for the materialized path — a reduction factor of M/d², where M is the on-chip (SRAM) budget and d the head dimension; with d = 128 and M ≈ 192 KB the idealized bound is ≈12×, while realized reductions are smaller (see §5) because the materialized path's traffic depends on the number of softmax passes and on tile scheduling.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state which of the two paths has more traffic, by what factor, and in what units, without re-reading the caption; the caption's idealized bound is reconciled with the 3–5× figure quoted in §5.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §7 (What We Still Don't Know), fourth bullet
issue.quoted_clause: Can in‑flight KV cache compression (e.g. speculative decoding–guided pruning) reduce memory pressure without increasing p99 latency? Pruning less‑important key/value pairs based on attention weight magnitudes is promising, but the accuracy‑latency trade‑off needs empirical validation across model families.
issue.observed: The parenthetical names a mechanism that does not correspond to any established technique: speculative decoding is a draft-and-verify acceleration method, and 'speculative decoding–guided pruning' is not a recognized KV-compression approach. The sentence's own description ('pruning less-important key/value pairs based on attention weight magnitudes') describes attention-score-based KV eviction/pruning (e.g. H2O-, SnapKV-, Quest-, PyramidKV-style methods), which is a different family with a different literature and different failure modes. As written, the bullet either invents a technique or mislabels a real one, and it carries no source. This is also the only bullet in §7 whose subject is not a genuine open question but a mis-citation.
issue.evidence: The bullet's own explanatory clause describes attention-score-based KV pruning, not speculative decoding; no source is given for the named mechanism, in a section whose other bullets are framed as open questions rather than as claims.
issue.root_cause: Two adjacent concepts (speculative decoding, covered at length in the 'Two Mechanisms' subsection, and attention-score-based KV pruning) were conflated when the bullet was drafted.
issue.correction: Either name the concrete, citable family ('attention-score-based KV eviction/pruning — e.g. H2O- or SnapKV-style methods that retain the tokens with the highest accumulated attention weight — with a citation') and drop the speculative-decoding attribution, or, if there is a specific published speculative-decoding-guided KV-compression method, cite it by title, authors, and year. Keep the open question itself (accuracy vs p99 trade-off across model families), which is legitimate.
issue.acceptance_test: The bullet names a mechanism that exists in the literature with a citation, and the mechanism's description matches the technique it names.

issue.quoted_clause: the canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, full-MHA 70B reference model (a 70B-class dense FP16 model), 8×H100 host with 640 GB GPU memory
issue.observed: The chapter's regime claims ('Decode is primarily memory-bandwidth constrained', 'HBM bandwidth saturated' in the decision map) depend on the host's HBM bandwidth, but the chunk never states the H100 variant or its bandwidth. 640 GB implies eight 80 GB parts, which covers both H100 SXM (3.35 TB/s) and H100 PCIe (2.0 TB/s) — a 1.68× difference that changes every bandwidth conclusion in the chapter, including the decode ceiling computed in CH15-02 (809 tok/s at SXM, ~485 tok/s at PCIe). The chapter also does not say whether the 8 GPUs are NVLinked.
issue.evidence: H100 SXM: 80 GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s. H100 PCIe: 80 GB HBM2e, 2.0 TB/s. H100 NVL: 94 GB, 3.9 TB/s. The chunk's '640 GB GPU memory' is consistent with SXM or PCIe.
issue.root_cause: The hardware specification is inherited from Chapter 8 by implication rather than stated where the bandwidth reasoning is actually performed.
issue.correction: State the variant and its HBM bandwidth in the canonical-scenario paragraph (or add an explicit cross-reference to Chapter 8's canonical H100 specification), and note the interconnect (NVLink/NVSwitch) since §4's collective-measurement paragraph and the decision map's interconnect row depend on it.
issue.acceptance_test: The canonical scenario paragraph names the H100 variant, its per-GPU HBM bandwidth, and the interconnect, so that every bandwidth figure in the chapter can be recomputed from the chapter alone.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §4 (Measurement), sentence beginning 'A minimal benchmark runs 40 rps'
issue.quoted_clause: A minimal benchmark runs 40 rps — a saturation run on one host (6.5× the ~56,500 tok/s prefill ceiling at 100% MFU — theoretical peak), whose queue is expected to grow
issue.observed: The 56,500 tok/s figure is the case-(i) (2N-only) ceiling, but it is introduced here without that qualifier, while §6 states that at the canonical 9,200-token context the ceiling is ≈48,000 tok/s (case (ii)) and ≈52,000 (case (iii)). A reader who takes 56,500 as 'the prefill ceiling' at the canonical context will mis-state the host's headroom by 18%. The 6.5× ratio itself is correct for case (i) (368,000/56,500 = 6.51), so only the label needs fixing.
issue.root_cause: The case convention is introduced in §3 and not carried into §4, where the same ceiling is quoted without its convention.
issue.correction: Write 'the ~56,500 tok/s case-(i) (2N-only) prefill ceiling at 100% MFU — theoretical peak; at the canonical context the attention-adjusted ceiling is ≈48,000 tok/s (§6)', or simply reference §6's number.
issue.acceptance_test: Every occurrence of the prefill ceiling in the chapter carries its case convention, and the 6.5× ratio is stated with the same convention.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §3 (Worked Example), KV-cache-footprint paragraph, sentence beginning 'Doubling context to 19,000 tokens'
issue.quoted_clause: Doubling context to 19,000 tokens pushes per-user KV to ~49.8 GB (19,000 × 2.62 MB) and halves on-host concurrency to ~8.7 (436 GB ÷ 49.8 GB; conservative integer floor 8).
issue.observed: 436 ÷ 49.8 = 8.755, which rounds to 8.8, not 8.7; using the unrounded per-token value (19,000 × 2,621,440 B = 49.807 GB) gives 8.754, again 8.8. The neighbouring figure in the same paragraph, 436 ÷ 24.9037 = 17.507, is correctly rounded to 17.5. The two roundings in one paragraph are inconsistent (one rounds, one truncates). No downstream decision is affected — the conservative integer floor is 8 either way — so this is a presentation inconsistency rather than an error.
issue.root_cause: Mixed rounding conventions within a single paragraph.
issue.correction: Use '≈8.8' (or '≈8.75') to match the rounding used for 17.5, and keep the conservative integer floor of 8.
issue.acceptance_test: Both concurrency figures in the paragraph are rounded by the same rule.

issue.quoted_clause: §3: '6.5 hosts at 100% MFU → 6.5 ÷ 0.35 = 18.6 → 19 hosts at the 35% MFU planning screen (case (i))' ... §4: 'report p95 only at offered loads ≤ the host's admission capacity, ~2 rps per host: 17 slots ÷ 8.6 s'
issue.observed: The chapter derives two per-host capacity numbers that are close but not equal, and never reconciles them: the KV-slot route gives 17/8.6 = 1.98 rps/host, while the FLOP route gives 7.912e15 × 0.35 ÷ 1.4e11 ÷ 9,200 = 2.15 rps/host. Consequently 19 hosts cover 37.6 rps by the first route and 40.9 rps by the second — i.e. the 19-host screen is either marginally short of the 40 rps canonical peak or has 2% headroom, depending on which derivation is used. The chapter presents 19 hosts as a settled planning screen without noting that it sits within 6% of the peak under one reading.
issue.root_cause: Two independent capacity derivations (KV-residency-limited and FLOP-limited) are used in adjacent sections without a stated binding constraint, so the reader cannot tell which one sets the host count.
issue.correction: State which constraint binds at the canonical operating point and note the other as a co-limiter; if the KV-limited 1.98 rps/host binds, say so and note that 19 hosts covers 37.6 rps, i.e. the peak requires 21 hosts at that operating point (or that the peak is served with a small queueing margin).
issue.acceptance_test: The chapter names the binding per-host constraint, and the stated host count is shown to cover the 40 rps peak under that constraint.

issue.quoted_clause: Over‑provisioning batch size to chase throughput: Increasing batch size improves TFLOPS utilization but degrades p99 latency because tail requests wait for larger chunks to fill.
issue.observed: The stated mechanism — requests waiting for a batch to fill — describes static (fixed-batch) batching, not the continuous batching the chapter recommends in §6. Under continuous batching, a request joins the next scheduler iteration and never waits for a batch to fill; the latency cost of a larger batch comes from a longer per-step duration (higher ITL/TPOT for every in-flight request) and from increased queueing delay, not from fill-waiting. The chapter elsewhere (§4) gives the correct mechanism ('inter-request token interleaving ... scheduler fairness/queueing delay'), so §5 and §4 disagree on why the mistake happens.
issue.evidence: §4: 'beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises ... because kernel launch overhead is amortized but inter-request token interleaving increases per-step HBM traffic and scheduler fairness/queueing delay'. §5: 'tail requests wait for larger chunks to fill'.
issue.root_cause: The common-mistake bullet was written from the intuition of static batching and not reconciled with the continuous-batching model the chapter teaches.
issue.correction: Rewrite the mechanism: 'because a larger decode batch lengthens the per-step duration, so every in-flight request sees a higher ITL/TPOT, and because queueing delay grows with the number of requests sharing the step.' If the fill-waiting mechanism is worth keeping, scope it explicitly to static batching.
issue.acceptance_test: The mechanism named in §5 matches the mechanism named in §4 and is consistent with the continuous-batching model introduced in §6.

issue.quoted_clause: Neglecting kernel launch overhead: In dynamic‑batching setups, each new token generation can trigger a kernel launch. Without continuous batching or token‑level fusion, the kernel‑launch overhead (illustratively ~10–20 % of GPU time on H100-class parts at this traffic) can artificially depress measured MFU.
issue.observed: Continuous batching does not reduce the number of kernel launches per decode step; it reduces idle gaps between batches and lets the scheduler keep the device busy. The mechanisms that actually remove per-step launch overhead are CUDA-graph capture and kernel fusion (which the chapter names elsewhere as 'token-level fusion'). As written, the sentence credits continuous batching with a benefit it does not provide, in a chapter whose §6 recommends continuous batching as the fix for a different symptom.
issue.evidence: Per decode step, the launch count is set by the number of kernels in the model forward (tens to low hundreds), independent of how requests are batched; continuous batching changes when steps are issued, not how many kernels each step contains.
issue.root_cause: Two distinct overheads — launch overhead and idle-gap overhead — are conflated under the label 'kernel launch overhead'.
issue.correction: Separate them: 'each decode step issues a fixed set of kernels regardless of batch composition, so per-step launch overhead is a fixed cost that continuous batching does not remove; it is removed by CUDA-graph capture or kernel fusion. Continuous batching instead removes idle gaps between batches, which is a different saving.'
issue.acceptance_test: The bullet names the mechanism that actually reduces launch overhead, and does not credit continuous batching with it.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §4 (Measurement), sentence beginning 'beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises'
issue.quoted_clause: beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises (implying a knee near batch 4) because kernel launch overhead is amortized but inter‑request token interleaving increases per‑step HBM traffic and scheduler fairness/queueing delay
issue.observed: The stated cause is imprecise. Per-step HBM traffic does grow with batch (140 + 24.9B GB per step), but per-token traffic falls (140/B + 24.9 GB/token), so 'increases per-step HBM traffic' does not by itself explain a latency increase — it explains a throughput increase. The mechanism that raises latency is that a larger batch lengthens the step duration, so each in-flight request's inter-token latency grows (ITL = step time), with queueing delay as a secondary effect. The chapter's own bytes/token model (140/B + KV) makes this precise and should be used.
issue.evidence: bytes/token = 140/B + 24.9 GB: B=1 → 164.9; B=4 → 59.9; B=16 → 33.65; B=32 → 29.28. Step time = (140 + 24.9B)/26,800 s: B=4 → 25.2 ms; B=16 → 42.0 ms; B=32 → 82.6 ms. ITL grows with B even though bytes/token falls.
issue.root_cause: The chapter has a precise bytes/token model available but describes the batch-size latency effect in terms of traffic volume rather than step duration.
issue.correction: Replace the traffic clause with the step-duration clause: 'because a larger batch lengthens the decode step (per-step traffic 140 + 24.9B GB), so every in-flight request's inter-token latency grows even though bytes/token falls (140/B + 24.9 GB/token); queueing delay and fairness effects add to this.'
issue.acceptance_test: The stated mechanism is consistent with the chapter's own bytes/token and step-time arithmetic, and a reader can predict the direction of ITL change from the batch size.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §4 (Measurement), sentence beginning 'On the FlashAttention "traffic reduction" claim'
issue.quoted_clause: one often sees (the figures below are hypothetical, not a cited measurement) a FlashAttention‑class kernel reported at a *different achieved HBM bandwidth* than a naive SDPA kernel (illustratively FlashAttention‑class ~400 GB/s achieved vs naive SDPA ~150 GB/s achieved for 9,200‑token contexts)
issue.observed: The framing 'one often sees' presents the two numbers as typical reported values, but they are 12% and 4.5% of H100's 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth — far below what attention kernels typically achieve on that part, and low enough that a reader who treats them as 'typical' will badly underestimate the achievable rate and the size of the traffic reduction. The parenthetical 'hypothetical, not a cited measurement' contradicts the 'one often sees' framing in the same sentence. Either the framing or the numbers should change.
issue.root_cause: The sentence was written to make a units point (rate vs bytes) and inherited placeholder numbers that are inconsistent with the framing sentence.
issue.correction: Either drop 'one often sees' and keep the numbers explicitly as deliberately conservative placeholders ('for illustration, suppose a FlashAttention-class kernel sustains ~400 GB/s and a naive SDPA kernel ~150 GB/s — these are placeholders, not measurements, and are far below the H100's 3.35 TB/s peak'), or replace them with realistic achieved-bandwidth figures and cite them.
issue.acceptance_test: The framing sentence and the numbers agree: either the numbers are presented as placeholders with no 'one often sees' claim, or they are realistic and sourced.

issue.page_hint: Ch15, Fig 15.2 caption and the paragraph immediately following it ('The capacity response to batch size under peak load')
issue.quoted_clause: They are not competing on the same axis: the decode bottleneck is unaffected by caching.
issue.observed: The statement is true of the bottleneck (decode remains bandwidth-bound) but incomplete in a way that matters for the figure's own right-hand panel. Prefix caching frees KV capacity (fewer recomputed prefixes, more room for active sequences), which raises the achievable concurrency and therefore the decode batch size, which raises decode goodput — the very quantity plotted on the right. The chapter's own §3 establishes KV capacity as the binding constraint on concurrency, so the two levers are coupled through KV capacity even though they act on different phases. The figure's framing ('two levers, two serving phases') would be more useful with the coupling stated.
issue.evidence: §3: on-host concurrency is set by the 436 GB KV budget (17.5 requests at 9,500 tokens); §6: FP8 KV quantization doubles concurrency to 35.0. Any mechanism that frees KV capacity raises the batch size available to the decode path.
issue.root_cause: The 'independent levers' framing was adopted to prevent the reader from treating prefix caching and batching as substitutes, and the coupling through KV capacity was not added back.
issue.correction: Qualify the sentence: 'the decode bottleneck itself is unaffected by caching — but the two levers are coupled through KV capacity: prefix caching frees KV blocks, which can raise the achievable concurrency and therefore the decode batch size, so the right-hand curve can shift when the left-hand lever is pulled. The coupling is a capacity effect, not a compute effect.'
issue.acceptance_test: The text states whether the two levers are independent, and if coupled, names the coupling resource and its direction.

issue.page_hint: Ch15, 'The Optimization Decision Map', row 3 ('KV exhaustion / low concurrency')
issue.quoted_clause: KV exhaustion / low concurrency | memory capacity | KV bytes/token, context distribution, fragmentation, active sequences | GQA/MQA (architecture-fixed — not a runtime lever; requires a re-checkpointed model), KV quantization, PagedAttention, context reduction, eviction/offload, prefix reuse
issue.observed: PagedAttention is listed under a bottleneck labelled 'memory capacity', but it does not reduce the mathematical or allocated size of the KV state — it reduces fragmentation and allocator waste, so it raises usable capacity without lowering bytes/token. The chapter is explicit elsewhere that PagedAttention is a memory-management strategy rather than a size reduction, and §3's KV arithmetic is built on bytes/token. Listing it without that distinction risks the reader misconception that PagedAttention 'makes the KV cache smaller'.
issue.evidence: §3's concurrency arithmetic is bytes/token × requests ≤ 436 GB; PagedAttention changes only the packing efficiency of that budget, so it moves the achievable request count without changing 2.62 MB/token.
issue.root_cause: The row's bottleneck cell names only one of the two bottlenecks its own evidence column measures (fragmentation is listed as evidence but not as a bottleneck).
issue.correction: Annotate the mechanism cell, e.g. 'PagedAttention (reduces fragmentation waste, not bytes/token)', and/or split the row's bottleneck cell into 'raw KV capacity' and 'fragmentation / allocator waste'.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader cannot conclude from the map that PagedAttention reduces the per-token KV footprint; the map's bottleneck cell names every bottleneck its evidence column measures.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §6 (Architecture Consequence), decision (3), vs §5 (Common Mistakes), second bullet
issue.quoted_clause: §6: '(3) KV cache management via FP8 KV quantization (≈2.62 → ~1.31 MB/token — exactly 50% of FP16 by raw tensor byte-halving, cutting a 9,500-token per-user KV to ~12.45 GB ...)' ... §5: '**KV quantization** is a separate, orthogonal lever that cuts the per-token footprint without changing context length or the attention window; it introduces a numerical approximation (FP8 rounding) that must be quality-validated (Ch 14) before it is relied on'
issue.observed: §5 makes quality validation a precondition for relying on FP8 KV quantization; §6 adopts it as an architecture decision and derives a concurrency figure (17.5 → 35.0) from it without carrying the precondition. The decision map's weight-quantization row carries an explicit 're-run the SLO and quality test after the change' instruction, but the KV-quantization row does not, so the map and §6 are both weaker than §5 on this point.
issue.evidence: §5: 'must be quality-validated (Ch 14) before it is relied on (FP8 ≈2.62 → ~1.31 MB/token ...)'. §6: the same FP8 KV figure is used to compute 436/12.45 = 35.0 concurrent requests with no validation gate.
issue.root_cause: The decision section was written from the capacity arithmetic and did not carry the quality gate that the mistakes section established.
issue.correction: Add the gate to §6 decision (3) and to the map's KV-quantization cell, e.g. 'FP8 KV quantization — adopt only after the quality test (Ch 14) passes; the concurrency figure below assumes the quality gate is met.'
issue.acceptance_test: Every place FP8 KV quantization is relied upon for a capacity or latency figure carries the quality-validation precondition stated in §5.

issue.page_hint: Ch15 §6 (Architecture Consequence), sentence beginning 'the single-host upper end is capped by'
issue.quoted_clause: the single-host upper end is capped by the 100%-MFU parameter-matmul-only ceiling: 7.91×10¹⁵ FLOP/s ÷ 1.4×10¹¹ FLOP/token ≈ 56,500 tok/s under the linear-only case (i) — a 2N-only figure; at the canonical 9,200-token context the attention term (§3, case ii) lowers this to ≈48,000 tok/s
issue.observed: The sentence names 56,500 tok/s as the cap and then immediately lowers the cap to 48,000, so 'capped by' and the number that follows do not agree. The arithmetic is right; the sentence structure is not. A reader scanning for the host's ceiling can easily take 56,500 as the answer.
issue.root_cause: The sentence was extended (case i → case ii → case iii) without restructuring the lead clause.
issue.correction: Restructure: 'the single-host ceiling is set by the 100%-MFU FLOP bound: ≈56,500 tok/s under the linear-only case (i), reduced to ≈48,000 tok/s at the canonical 9,200-token context once the attention term is included (case ii), and ≈52,000 tok/s under the causal case (iii).'
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence's lead clause names the same number that the sentence's conclusion establishes as the cap.

issue.page_hint: Ch 16 §3 (Worked Example → Mode 2 — cloud GPU instances), paragraph beginning 'The cloud case is a family, not a single line.'
issue.quoted_clause: For example, a mid-case with ~6 reserved warm hosts + ~15 burst hosts held for ~4 peak hours/day, at $20/hr (burst) and the warm pool at a reserved rate, lands between the two endpoints
issue.observed: The mid-case as specified does not land between the two named endpoints ($87.6K and $306.6K). It exceeds the upper endpoint, and its burst term is longer than the billing month it is priced against, so the configuration is not physically realizable as written.
issue.evidence: Burst term: 15 hosts × 4 h/day × 260 workdays = 15,600 host-hours. The billing month contains only 730 h, and 4 h/day × 260 days = 1,040 h of burst per month > 730 h — the burst term alone is infeasible. Total: 4,380 (warm) + 15,600 (burst) = 19,980 host-hours × $20/hr = $399,600/mo = 1.30× the always-on-at-peak endpoint (21 × 730 × $20 = $306,600). Even if the warm pool were free, the burst term ($312,000) still exceeds the always-on endpoint. A month-consistent version (4 peak h/day × 21.67 business days = 86.7 h/mo) gives 15 × 86.7 = 1,300 burst h → 5,680 h → $113,600/mo ≈ $18.21/1K, which does fall between the endpoints. The chapter's own monthly-workday divisor (260 ÷ 12 = 21.67) is used correctly elsewhere in the same chapter.
issue.root_cause: The mid-case was constructed by multiplying a per-day burst duration by the annual workday count (260) instead of the monthly workday count (21.67), and the resulting total was never checked against the two endpoints it is asserted to fall between.
issue.correction: Restate the mid-case on a monthly basis: 4 peak h/day × 21.67 business days ≈ 86.7 h/mo; burst = 15 × 86.7 ≈ 1,300 host-hours; total ≈ 5,680 host-hours → ≈ $113.6K/mo ≈ $18.21/1K. State explicitly that the burst term is bounded by the 730-h month, and add one sentence asserting that the mid-case lies between $87.6K and $306.6K.
issue.acceptance_test: Recompute 6×730 + 15×(4×21.67) = 5,680 host-hours; × $20 = $113,600; assert 87,600 < 113,600 < 306,600 and assert burst hours ≤ 730. The printed mid-case must satisfy both assertions.

issue.page_hint: Ch 16 §8 mini-case — paragraphs 'The rate comparison hides the memory geometry…', 'The honest number:…', and the closing paragraph beginning 'Request volume is not the lever:'
issue.quoted_clause: The two hosts clear the rate comparison, not the full-context KV budget. ... The honest number: self-hosting two servers ~$40K/month all-in vs ~$104K/month API at current volume (5M × $0.0208) — a **~$64K/month saving in favor of self-hosting** ... the two hosts are sized for a ~4 rps peak — 2 × the canonical ~1.9 rps per host
issue.observed: The mini-case proves that the two-server configuration cannot hold the KV state for the stated workload, then prices it as a viable alternative, reports a $64K/mo saving in favor of self-hosting, and finally asserts a ~4 rps peak capacity for it. The capability failure and the cost conclusion are never reconciled; the closing decision rule ('self-host if the consumed engineer's time is worth less than ~$90K/month') therefore recommends buying a configuration the same mini-case has shown to be infeasible.
issue.evidence: Mini-case's own numbers: 4 replicas × 140 GB = 560 GB of the 640 GB pool; after the ~64 GB runtime reserve, ~16 GB of KV remains = 0.64 of one 9,500-token request (24.9 GB). At 2 rps × 8.6 s ≈ 17 requests in flight, the KV requirement is 17 × 24.9 = 423 GB — 26× the 16 GB available; the configuration can hold zero full-context requests. The '~4 rps peak' claim is contradicted by the same arithmetic: 4 rps × 8.6 s = 34.4 in flight × 24.9 GB = 857 GB of KV required versus 16 GB available. The '640 GB pool' framing also misstates where KV lives: with 2 GPUs per replica each replica has 160 GB HBM − 140 GB weights = 20 GB for KV + runtime, so KV cannot be pooled across the host's four replicas.
issue.root_cause: Two independent analyses (memory geometry and TCO) run in the same mini-case without a capability gate; the cost model silently assumes away the first analysis's conclusion, and the capacity claim is imported from the canonical TP=8 fleet rather than derived for the mini-case's TP=2 replica layout.
issue.correction: Add an explicit capability gate before the TCO comparison and make the cost conclusion conditional on it. Recommended wording: 'The two-server configuration fails the KV screen for 9,500-token requests (16 GB of KV against 423 GB required at 17 in flight), so the $64K/mo figure compares an infeasible option with a feasible one and is not a realizable saving; the API is the only mode that can serve this workload as specified.' Restate the geometry per replica (2 GPUs = 160 GB, 140 GB weights, 20 GB for KV + runtime) rather than as a pooled 640 GB host pool. Delete or re-derive the '~4 rps peak' claim and the 'more volume widens the gap' argument that depends on it.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case must contain an explicit statement of whether the two-server configuration can hold the in-flight KV for the stated request length, and the $64K/mo saving and the 'more volume widens the gap' claim must each be qualified by that statement. A reader must not be able to conclude that buying the two servers saves $64K/mo at the stated workload.

issue.page_hint: Ch 15 §8 mini-case — sentence introducing the queueing-delay and token-throughput results
issue.quoted_clause: drops from 320 ms (single host, batch‑1) to 140 ms (dual host, continuous batch) — both measured under saturation at the stated 12.5/50 rps offered load, and token throughput rises from ~8.5K to 70,000 tokens/s
issue.observed: The 'measured under saturation' claim is inconsistent with the mini-case's own token arithmetic, and a bounded p95 queueing delay is not a saturation measurement. The sentence also conflates a capacity rate with an achieved throughput at the stated load.
issue.evidence: At the 12.5 rps average with the canonical 9,500-token request, the offered token rate is 12.5 × 9,500 = 118,750 tok/s, which exceeds the two-host aggregate of 70,000 tok/s; the dual-host system can complete only 70,000/9,500 ≈ 7.4 rps of full-context requests, so it is under-served, not saturated, at 12.5 rps. Under the benign reading (the 50 rps peak arm), saturation is arithmetically plausible, but an overloaded queue grows without bound, so a stable p95 queueing delay of 320 ms cannot be a saturation measurement either. In both arms the 8.5K and 70,000 tok/s figures are capacity rates (the mini-case itself calls 8.5K 'the same prefill-dominated raw single-host rate'), not achieved throughput at the stated offered load.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case reports a capacity benchmark (tokens/s at saturation) and an offered-load condition (12.5/50 rps) in the same sentence without distinguishing them, and then attaches the word 'saturation' to a queueing-delay statistic that is only meaningful below saturation.
issue.correction: Separate the two claims: state the offered load the benchmark was driven at, state that the 8.5K and 70,000 tok/s figures are saturated capacity rates (tokens/s the host(s) can sustain), and state the queueing-delay measurement as taken at a load below saturation (or replace it with a saturation-queueing statement such as 'the queue grows without bound at 12.5 rps on one host'). If the benchmark was run at the 50 rps peak, say so and give the admitted completion rate (≈7.4 rps) alongside the token rate.
issue.acceptance_test: Every throughput figure in the mini-case must be labelled either as a saturated capacity rate or as an achieved rate at a stated offered load, and the queueing-delay figure must be attached to a load at which the queue is stable. A reader must be able to tell which of the two the 8.5K and 70,000 tok/s numbers are.

issue.page_hint: Ch 15, Table 15-1 — column header 'KV Cache / User (GB)' and the note beneath the table
issue.quoted_clause: | KV Cache / User (GB) | ... | ~24.9 | ... KV‑Cache/User uses the canonical ~2.62 MB/token × 9,500 ≈ 24.9 GB.
issue.observed: The column is labelled per user but its values are per request (one 9,500-token request's KV footprint). The chapter's own note repeats the mislabel. This contradicts the book's explicit distinction between users and in-flight requests.
issue.evidence: 24.9 GB = 2.62 MB/token × 9,500 tokens = the KV of a single request. The 'KV demand ÷ host KV budget' column multiplies this value by in-flight requests (17 / 86 / 344), confirming the per-request basis. The table's own note states: 'never equate in-flight concurrency with a number of registered or simultaneously-online users' — so a per-user reading is excluded by the book's own definition. At the canonical 5% concurrency, a user's KV is 0.05 × 24.9 ≈ 1.25 GB, not 24.9 GB.
issue.root_cause: The column header was written from the workload's user-centric framing rather than from the quantity actually tabulated (per-request KV footprint), and the note inherited the error.
issue.correction: Rename the column 'KV per request (GB)' (or 'KV / in-flight request (GB)') and correct the note to 'KV per request uses the canonical ~2.62 MB/token × 9,500 ≈ 24.9 GB; the KV-demand column multiplies this by the in-flight request count.' If a per-user figure is wanted, add it as a separate, clearly labelled column (≈1.25 GB at 5% concurrency).
issue.acceptance_test: No cell in Table 15-1 may be labelled 'per user' unless it is computed from the concurrency profile; the note beneath the table must use the same unit as the column header.

issue.page_hint: Ch 15, Table 15-1 — column header 'prefill demand ÷ 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling (56,500 tok/s)' and the adjacent 'Tokens' column
issue.quoted_clause: | Tokens | ... | 9,500 | ... | prefill demand ÷ 100%-MFU para­meter-matmul ceiling (56,500 tok/s) | ... | 0.33× | 1.63× | 6.51× |
issue.observed: The prefill-demand ratios are computed on 9,200 input tokens per request, but the adjacent 'Tokens' column states 9,500 and the note says 'Tokens is tokens per request — the 9,500-token canonical context length'. A reader recomputing from the table's own numbers gets different values, and the discrepancy is material in the peak row.
issue.evidence: Recomputation with 9,200 input tokens: 2 × 9,200/56,500 = 0.326 → 0.33×; 10 × 9,200/56,500 = 1.628 → 1.63×; 40 × 9,200/56,500 = 6.513 → 6.51× — all three printed values reproduce exactly. Recomputation with the table's stated 9,500 tokens: 0.336 → 0.34×; 1.681 → 1.68×; 6.726 → 6.73×. The typical row differs by 3.1% and the peak row by 3.4%, and the peak row's binding-constraint cell quotes '~6.5× demand over host peak'. The 56,500 tok/s ceiling itself is confirmed as the case-(i) linear-only ceiling (8 × 989 TFLOPS ÷ 140e9 FLOP/token = 56,514 tok/s), consistent with Ch 16's 19,780 tok/s/host at 35% MFU.
issue.root_cause: The column header states the denominator but not the numerator's token basis, and the table's 'Tokens' column mixes total context (9,500) with the prefill-relevant input count (9,200) without distinguishing them.
issue.correction: State the numerator basis in the column header, e.g. 'prefill demand (9,200 input tokens/req) ÷ 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling (56,500 tok/s)', and rename the 'Tokens' column to 'Context tokens/req (9,500 = 9,200 in + 300 out)' so the two token counts are visibly different quantities.
issue.acceptance_test: Every value in the prefill-demand column must be reproducible from the table's own printed numbers plus the stated numerator basis; recomputing with 9,500 tokens must not be the path a reader is led down.

issue.quoted_clause: **Caveat:** break-even is a price sensitivity across $15–25 per 1,000 requests (≈$0.015–0.025 per request) — per-price crossovers (~6.2–10.4M), not an interval — not apples-to-apples
issue.observed: The caption contradicts the body text on the nature of the break-even. The body insists repeatedly that the break-even is a region/range, not a point; the caption says the opposite.
issue.evidence: Body, §16.3: 'the break-even is a **region**, not a point: the figure marks the [ILLUSTRATIVE] price band, and the honest output is a range (here ~6.2–10.4M req/mo) rather than a single "the break-even is 7.5M" claim.' Body, Note 16.1-1: 'The self-host line crosses the managed line over a **range** of ~6.2–10.4 M requests/mo'. Caption: 'per-price crossovers (~6.2–10.4M), **not an interval**'. The caption's own Takeaway also states a point ('crosses the managed API at ~7.5M req/mo'), which the body forbids as a standalone claim.
issue.root_cause: The caption was written to compress the note and over-compressed: the intended point (the band is a set of per-price crossover points, not a statistical confidence interval) was expressed as a denial of the body's own framing.
issue.correction: Rewrite the caveat to agree with the body: 'break-even is a price sensitivity across $15–25 per 1,000 requests (≈$0.015–0.025 per request): the per-price crossovers span ~6.2–10.4M req/mo, so the break-even is a region rather than a single volume; the ~7.5M point is the canonical-price crossover only.'
issue.acceptance_test: The caption and the body must both describe 6.2–10.4M as a range/region of crossover volumes; no sentence in the chapter may describe the same quantity as 'not an interval'.

issue.quoted_clause: | 3 | Warmed capacity per region | N_region = ⌈λ_region·W_KV/(C·u·ρ)⌉ + N_spare (Table 17-1 formula, applied per region; each region is sized for λ_peak = 40 rps — the failover load — not its share λ_region; λ_region sets only the traffic split, which is what produces the ≥2× capacity term) | NOT SIZED (depends on rows 1–2) |
issue.observed: The formula and its own parenthetical rule contradict each other: the formula sizes each region on λ_region, while the rule states each region is sized on λ_peak = 40 rps. A reader applying the printed formula gets a smaller per-region fleet than the rule requires, and the ≥2× capacity term does not follow from the formula as printed.
issue.evidence: Applying the formula as printed with λ_region = α·40 gives N_region = ⌈α·40·8.6/(17·0.665)⌉ + N_spare, which for α < 1 is below the 31 working + 1 reserve hosts the failover rule requires. Applying the stated rule (λ_peak = 40 rps per region) gives ⌈344/11.305⌉ + 1 = 32 per region, so two regions = 64 hosts = 2× the 32-host single-region policy fleet — which is exactly the '≥2×' claim the row makes. The formula as printed cannot produce that number.
issue.root_cause: The row was written by copying the Table 17-1 formula verbatim and then adding a sizing rule that the copied formula does not implement; the two were never reconciled.
issue.correction: Write the formula to match the rule: N_region = ⌈λ_peak·W_KV/(C·u·ρ)⌉ + N_spare (each region sized for the full failover load λ_peak = 40 rps), and add a separate line or note showing the resulting ≥2× term (2 regions × 32 hosts = 64 vs 32 single-region). If λ_region is retained for the traffic split, label it as a traffic-share input only and show it nowhere in the sizing formula.
issue.acceptance_test: Substituting the row's own rule into the row's own formula must reproduce the ≥2× capacity term quoted in the same row and in the multi-region paragraph above the table.

issue.page_hint: Ch 16 §3, paragraph immediately after Table 16-1 ('None of A/A′/B/B′/C is scored as validated comparable')
issue.quoted_clause: The three statuses are: `validated comparable` (measured on matched availability/failover/warm-capacity/SLO-goodput), `planning-only incomparable` (this table), and `fails requirement` (a mode that cannot meet the 99.9% multi-region SLA).
issue.observed: The status vocabulary is internally inconsistent with the table it governs. By the book's own definition every row in Table 16-1 fails the requirement (all are single-region, none is priced for the 99.9% multi-region SLA), yet all are labelled 'planning-only incomparable'. Meanwhile the one row that demonstrably fails a requirement — row B, 6 hosts ≈ 11.9 rps against a 40 rps peak — has no status that fits it.
issue.evidence: Table 16-1 rows A, A′, B, B′, C all carry the status 'planning-only, incomparable' and the table's own qualification for B states 'cannot serve the canonical peak'. The multi-region paragraph states that 'every $/1K figure in this chapter … prices a single-region deployment' and that the canonical SLA is 'UNSIZED and NOT PRICED'. So 'fails requirement' as defined is true of every row, and the third status is simultaneously unused and universally applicable.
issue.root_cause: The status vocabulary was defined against the availability requirement only, while the table's rows are scored against several requirements (load-serving, availability, SLO-goodput); the definition was not re-checked against the rows it classifies.
issue.correction: Redefine the third status against the requirement the table actually tests, e.g. 'fails load-serving requirement (a mode that cannot serve the canonical offered load under its stated provisioning)', and apply it to row B (6 hosts ≈ 11.9 rps < 40 rps peak). Add a sentence stating that no row is scored against the multi-region availability requirement at all, so 'fails requirement' in the availability sense is not evaluated in this table.
issue.acceptance_test: Every row in Table 16-1 must map to exactly one status under the stated definitions, and the third status must be used at least once or explicitly declared out of scope for the table.

issue.page_hint: Ch 16 §8 mini-case — sensitivity sentence beginning 'Sensitivity: at $156K/yr fully loaded…'
issue.quoted_clause: Sensitivity: at $156K/yr fully loaded (0.5 FTE engineer → $6.5K/mo) self-host = 13.8 + 6.5 = $20.3K/mo — the verdict is robust to the rate; the $84K saving and the threshold margin are not.
issue.observed: The claim that the threshold is not robust to the staff rate is false. The opportunity-cost threshold is algebraically invariant to the wage rate; only the cash saving changes. The book also misses the useful insight that the threshold is wage-independent.
issue.evidence: Threshold derivation as printed: V* = API + wage − self-host = 104 + W − (13.9 + W) = 90.1K, independent of W. At W = 26K: 104 + 26 − 40 = 90.2K. At W = 6.5K: 104 + 6.5 − 20.4 = 90.1K. The cash saving does change (104 − 40 = 64K vs 104 − 20.4 = 83.6K ≈ 84K), so only the first half of the sentence is correct. The same invariance is visible in the Mode-1 staffing variant the mini-case already prints: 'On Mode 1's ~$10K/mo staff alloc the self-host cost is ~$23.8K/mo and the gap ~$80.2K/mo' — the implied threshold there is 104 + 10 − 23.9 = 90.1K, identical.
issue.root_cause: The sensitivity was run on the cash-saving line only; the threshold was not re-derived under the alternative rate, and the sentence generalized from one quantity to two.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'the verdict is robust to the rate: the cash saving moves from ~$64K to ~$84K, but the opportunity-cost threshold is unchanged at ~$90K/mo, because the wage appears on both sides of the comparison (104 + W − (13.9 + W)).' Add the invariance as an explicit teaching point — it tells the reader that the staffing rate changes the size of the prize, not the decision rule.
issue.acceptance_test: Recompute the threshold at both wage rates ($26K/mo and $6.5K/mo) and confirm the printed threshold is identical; the text must not claim the threshold moves with the wage rate.

issue.page_hint: Ch 16 §8 mini-case — closing paragraph beginning 'The architect's verdict:'
issue.quoted_clause: Until it does, start on the managed API now (conditional on the startup's $26K/mo 0.5 FTE engineer staffing basis) as the default while that opportunity cost is unmeasured, and revisit self-host the moment it is measured below ~$90K/month
issue.observed: The mini-case's final recommendation (start on the API) is not derived from its own analysis, which yields self-host unless the freed 0.5 FTE is worth more than ~$90K/mo. The prose never states the expected-value argument that would justify departing from the modeled answer, so the recommendation reads as a contradiction of the preceding paragraphs.
issue.evidence: The modeled answer with V = 0 (no alternative product value for the freed hours) is self-host with a $64K/mo saving. The threshold of $90.2K/mo corresponds to $1.08M/yr of product output for a 0.5 FTE, i.e. ~$2.16M/yr per FTE — a bar that the mini-case's own framing ('about $1.08M/year of product work the startup is not doing') makes look implausible for a startup. The chapter also states earlier in the same mini-case: 'The token arithmetic alone therefore does not send this startup to the API; it points to self-hosting.' The recommendation is therefore a risk/reversibility choice, not an analytical conclusion, and is not labelled as such.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case ends with a decision that its model does not produce; the gap between 'the model says self-host unless V > $90K' and 'default to the API' is left implicit rather than argued.
issue.correction: Either (a) state the recommendation as an explicit risk-aversion/reversibility choice with its cost ('starting on the API forgoes ~$64K/mo of modeled saving and is reversible; buying the servers is not'), or (b) change the default to self-host with the threshold stated as the check to run, noting that the threshold is high enough that self-host is the expected outcome unless the engineer is unusually valuable. Whichever is chosen, label the recommendation as a decision under an unmeasured input rather than as the model's conclusion.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case's final recommendation must be traceable to a stated argument (expected value or reversibility), and must not read as the output of the break-even arithmetic it follows.

issue.page_hint: Ch 15 §8 mini-case — MFU sentence beginning 'The MFU stabilizes at ~62 %…'
issue.quoted_clause: against the two-host 15.82 ×10¹⁵ FLOP/s peak (half of the ~124 % one-host figure in §6)
issue.observed: The parenthetical is not self-explanatory and appears to import a >100% utilization figure from §6. If §6 presents '~124%' as an MFU or utilization percentage, it exceeds 100% and contradicts Ch 8's MFU definition; if it is a token rate, the percentage and the rate are being conflated in one phrase.
issue.evidence: The only clean numerical fit for '124%' in this chapter is 70,000 tok/s ÷ 56,500 tok/s = 1.239 — i.e. §6's one-host figure appears to be a 70,000 tok/s rate expressed as a percentage of the 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling. A single host cannot exceed its own 100%-MFU ceiling, so such a figure is either a ceiling (not a measurement) or an error. The mini-case's own arithmetic is sound: 70,000 × 140e9 = 9.8e15 FLOP/s against 16 × 989e12 = 15.82e15 → 61.9% ≈ 62%, and 35,000 tok/s/host ÷ 56,500 = 62%. The problem is the cross-reference, not the MFU.
issue.root_cause: The parenthetical was written as a shorthand link to a §6 figure whose quantity and denominator are not restated, and the §6 figure itself has not been checked against the MFU definition.
issue.correction: Restate the parenthetical with quantity and denominator, e.g. 'the two-host aggregate equals the single-host rate quoted in §6, i.e. 35,000 tok/s per host = 62% of the 56,500 tok/s 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling'.
