Then audit §6: if it states a one-host rate of ~70,000 tok/s, it must be labelled a ceiling or an upper bound, not a measured rate, and any '124%' must be explicitly framed as 'above the 100%-MFU ceiling, therefore not achievable' rather than as a utilization figure.
issue.acceptance_test: No figure in Ch 15 or Ch 16 may be presented as an MFU/utilization percentage above 100%; the parenthetical must name the quantity and its denominator; §6's one-host figure must be checked and, if it is a ceiling, labelled as such.

issue.page_hint: Ch 16 §3 — the whole 'Worked Example' section, from 'Step 1 — fleet size' through the 'Feasible served-volume bound' paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: **Parametric multi-region worksheet (candidate only — the shape of the work, not a result).** ... The multi-region row is NOT priced — see the §16.3 multi-region statement (Ch 17 §17.6 applies it to the host counts)
issue.observed: §16.3 carries too much independent material for one section, and the multi-region worksheet inside it duplicates a role the book assigns to Ch 17 §17.6. The worksheet is a fleet-availability artifact, not a TCO artifact, and its eight rows are all 'NOT SIZED / NOT PRICED / NOT TESTED'.
issue.evidence: §16.3 contains: Step 1 fleet sizing (5-row table), Step 2 with three priced modes and two display equations, the multi-region availability paragraph, an 8-row parametric worksheet, Table 16-1 (5 rows), Table 16-2 (3 rows), a six-bullet sensitivity list, the feasible-served-volume bound, the x-axis-variation paragraph, and (after §6) Note 16.1-1 plus Fig 16.1. The chapter's own text says Ch 17 §17.6 'applies it to the host counts', so the sizing content of worksheet rows 1–3 and 6–7 is already owned by Ch 17. The worksheet's rows 4, 5 and 8 (weight/index availability, live-KV replication policy, incremental cost) are the only rows that are not host-count sizing.
issue.root_cause: The chapter absorbed the availability-scope material that belongs with fleet sizing and reliability, and the section was never subdivided once the content grew.
issue.correction: Split §16.3 into labelled subsections (3.1 fleet sizing; 3.2 pricing the three modes; 3.3 availability scope and what is not priced; 3.4 sensitivity and break-even; 3.5 the feasible served-volume bound) so the reader can navigate it. Move the multi-region worksheet to Ch 17 §17.6 (where the host counts are sized) or to an appendix, and keep in Ch 16 only the two facts the cost model needs: that multi-region is unpriced, and that the capacity-duplication term is on the order of ≥2× the single-region fleet.
issue.acceptance_test: §16.3 must be navigable by subsection; the multi-region worksheet must appear exactly once in the book, and its host-count rows must not restate content owned by Ch 17 §17.6.

issue.quoted_clause: Two systems with the same card count can differ 10× in cost per request when 3× the goodput per card composes with ~3.4× from better utilization and no idle coasting.
issue.observed: The decomposition double-counts utilization: goodput per card already contains utilization (goodput/card = capacity/card × utilization × SLO-pass rate), so '3× the goodput per card' and '3.4× from better utilization' cannot be independent multiplicative factors. The arithmetic (3 × 3.4 ≈ 10) works, but the model behind it does not.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own §16.4 defines 'Raw utilization = served ÷ provisioned; effective utilization = SLO-meeting goodput ÷ theoretical capacity', and §16.3's fleet sizing uses utilization as a derate on slot occupancy and scheduling efficiency. Under those definitions, a 3× goodput-per-card improvement already includes whatever utilization change produced it; multiplying by a further 3.4× utilization factor double-counts the same physical resource.
issue.root_cause: The bullet was written as an illustrative magnitude ('10×') and the factors were chosen to reach it, rather than being derived from a decomposition the chapter defines elsewhere.
issue.correction: Rewrite the bullet with a decomposition consistent with §16.4, e.g. 'Two systems with the same card count can differ 10× in cost per request: 3× from higher per-card capacity (better kernels, better quantization) × 3.4× from higher effective utilization (better batching, higher SLO-goodput per slot) — the two are independent levers, and the second is the one most often left on the table.'
issue.acceptance_test: The factors named in the bullet must map one-to-one onto the chapter's own definitions of capacity and utilization, with no quantity appearing in both factors.

issue.quoted_clause: | Regime | In‑Flight (λ·W) | Request Rate (rps) | Tokens | KV Cache / User (GB) | prefill demand ÷ 100%-MFU para­meter-matmul ceiling (56,500 tok/s) | KV demand ÷ host KV budget | kernel regime (§3) | binding workload constraint (§3) |
issue.observed: Nine columns, one of which carries a 60-character header, force the reader to scan a wide, header-heavy table on a US Letter page. The two ratio columns are the analytical payload; the header text that defines them is longer than the data.
issue.evidence: The header 'prefill demand ÷ 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling (56,500 tok/s)' is the longest cell in the table and is set in the same weight as the other headers, so the reader must read it before the numbers mean anything. The table also carries a long note beneath it (the illustrative load-pressure explanation) that is several times the length of the table's own content.
issue.root_cause: Column definitions were pushed into headers instead of being split between header, note and caption.
issue.correction: Shorten the headers to 'Prefill demand ÷ ceiling' and 'KV demand ÷ host budget', and move the definitions ('ceiling = 56,500 tok/s = 100% MFU of the parameter-matmul ceiling; demand = input tokens/s') into the note beneath the table. Consider dropping the 'Tokens' column (its value is constant across rows and is stated in the note).
issue.acceptance_test: Every column header in Table 15-1 fits on one line at the printed size, and the table's definitions live in the note rather than in the header row.

issue.page_hint: Ch 15, Table 15-1 — note beneath the table ('Illustrative load pressure')
issue.quoted_clause: **Illustrative load pressure** — kept in prose here, not as a table column — is a dimensionless labeled score (0–100), not MFU: the 12/38/52 values (light/typical/peak) are a demand-side/congestion *label* for teaching shape [ILLUSTRATIVE], on a stated scale in which the light regime sits near 12, the typical regime near 38 and the peak regime near 52
issue.observed: An unanchored 0–100 score is introduced and then requires roughly 200 words of defensive prose to prevent it being read as a utilization figure. The note itself concedes the score is redundant with the computed ratio columns ('for computed ratios, use the table's prefill-demand ÷ ceiling and KV-demand ÷ budget columns').
issue.evidence: The score has no derivation, no numerator or denominator, and no anchor to any measured or computed quantity; the note says so explicitly ('it has no FLOP numerator or denominator behind it'). The Ch 15 mini-case then has to add a further clarification ('the 38 in Table 15-1's illustrative load pressure note is that table's congestion label, not an MFU'). The two computed ratio columns already convey the shape: 0.33×/0.97× (light), 1.63×/4.91× (typical), 6.51×/19.6× (peak).
issue.root_cause: A teaching device was introduced to convey 'shape' that the table's own quantitative columns already convey, and the device then generated more explanatory text than the content it replaced.
issue.correction: Delete the 0–100 load-pressure score and the paragraph defending it, and let the two ratio columns carry the shape. If an ordinal label is retained for teaching purposes, cap it at one sentence and place it in the caption rather than in a 200-word note.
issue.acceptance_test: The note beneath Table 15-1 must not need to explain why a number is not a percentage; the table's quantitative columns must be sufficient to convey the light/typical/peak progression.

issue.quoted_clause: | Provisioning policy | 21-host ideal-active (case (i)/KV screen — **sensitivity comparison**, zero spare) | 22-host full-square case (ii) compute screen (zero spare) | 70% × 95% target + N−1, KV-only (32 hosts; 31 working + 1 reserve) | 70% × 95% target + N−1, case (ii) (34 hosts; 33 working + 1 reserve) |
issue.observed: The stub header 'Provisioning policy' mislabels the row-label column: the rows are 'Peak fleet', 'Self-host (capex+energy+staff)' and 'Per 1,000 requests' — metrics, not policies. The policies are the column headers.
issue.evidence: The four column headers are the four provisioning policies; the first column contains the line items. A reader scanning the table sees 'Provisioning policy' over 'Peak fleet' and has to re-read to understand the orientation.
issue.root_cause: The stub header was written from the table's subject (provisioning policies) rather than from the column's contents.
issue.correction: Change the stub header to 'Line item' (or 'Metric'), and consider moving the policy names into a short legend above the table so the headers can be shortened.
issue.acceptance_test: The stub header of every table in the chapter names the kind of quantity its rows contain.

issue.quoted_clause: 1. **Capital (capex)** — the one-time cost of the cards, servers, networking, racks, and cooling that make up the system. For self-hosted inference this dominates up front: an 8×H100 server with networking and infrastructure carries a large price. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
issue.observed: The evidence labels are attached to the whole bullet, which is a definition of a cost family rather than an illustrative or derived value. The label span is wider than the clause it is meant to qualify.
issue.evidence: The house convention binds a label to its clause or an explicitly split caption span. The definitional sentence ('the one-time cost of the cards, servers, networking, racks, and cooling') is a category definition and carries no provenance; the only illustrative content is the price of an 8×H100 server, which is not stated numerically in this bullet.
issue.root_cause: Labels were appended at bullet level for convenience rather than being bound to the specific clause carrying the scenario value.
issue.correction: Move the labels to the clause that carries the scenario value (the server-price sentence) or drop them from this bullet, since no number appears here; the $350K figure and its [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] label already appear in §16.2 and §16.3.
issue.acceptance_test: Every [ILLUSTRATIVE]/[DERIVED]/[ASSUMPTION] label in Ch 16 sits adjacent to a clause that contains a scenario value or a derivation, not to a definition.

issue.page_hint: Ch 16 §8 mini-case — 'The honest number:' paragraph and the 'On Mode 1's ~$10K/mo staff alloc' sentence
issue.quoted_clause: capex ~$11.6K + power ~$2.2K for two hosts leaves ≤ ~$26K for staff ... self-host = 13.8 + 6.5 = $20.3K/mo ... On Mode 1's ~$10K/mo staff alloc the self-host cost is ~$23.8K/mo
issue.observed: The capex-plus-power subtotal is truncated rather than rounded: 11.66667 + 2.22066 = 13.887 ≈ $13.9K, not $13.8K. The error propagates into two printed figures ($20.3K/mo and ~$23.8K/mo).
issue.evidence: Capex for two hosts = 2 × $350,000/60 = $11,666.67; power = 2 × $1,110.33 = $2,220.66; sum = $13,887.33 → $13.9K. With $6.5K staff: 13.9 + 6.5 = $20.4K/mo (printed $20.3K). With $10K staff: 13.9 + 10 = $23.9K/mo (printed $23.8K). The derived savings figures ($84K and $80.2K) are unaffected at the printed precision (104 − 20.4 = 83.6 ≈ 84; 104 − 23.9 = 80.1 ≈ 80.2).
issue.root_cause: A subtotal was truncated to one decimal instead of rounded, and the truncated value was then reused in two downstream sums.
issue.correction: Print $13.9K for the capex-plus-power subtotal and update the two dependent figures to $20.4K/mo and ~$23.9K/mo (and $80.1K for the Mode-1 gap).
issue.acceptance_test: 13.9 + 6.5 = 20.4 and 13.9 + 10 = 23.9 must both hold in the printed text; no subtotal in the mini-case may be a truncation of a repeating decimal.

issue.quoted_clause: Intel, *Intel Extension for PyTorch*, “Retirement Plan,” retrieved 28 October 2026: https://intel.github.io/intel-extension-for-pytorch/xpu/latest . ... Intel, *IPEX-LLM*, README at commit `de6bce27133ab250f13fd5d549c197519ce16d30`: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/intel/ipex-llm/de6bce27133ab250f13fd5d549c197519ce16d30/README.md
issue.observed: The IPEX retirement citation points at an unpinned '/latest' documentation URL, while the adjacent IPEX-LLM citation pins to a specific commit and the Ch 15 NCCL footnote pins to a specific tag. The unpinned link will drift, and the chapter's own evidence convention requires pinning.
issue.evidence: The same footnote states 'The pinned bytes match the 28 October archive' for the README, showing the author applies pinning; the retirement-plan URL is the one unpinned source in the chapter. The claim being supported ('active development and official quarterly releases stopped after release 2.8') is a dated, version-specific statement that a moving URL cannot support after the fact.
issue.root_cause: Inconsistent application of the book's own source-pinning convention within a single footnote.
issue.correction: Pin the retirement-plan citation to a dated snapshot (commit hash or an archived copy with a retrieval date), and state the release number unambiguously ('the last IPEX release was 2.8' rather than 'after release 2.8', which is ambiguous between IPEX and PyTorch version numbering).
issue.acceptance_test: Every URL in Ch 16's footnotes resolves to a pinned artifact or carries an explicit archival/retrieval date; no citation in the chapter points at a '/latest' path.

issue.quoted_clause: - **Using peak capacity for cost-per-request.** Peak sizing (40 rps) overstates cost if average (10 rps) utilization is what governs.
issue.observed: The chapter's own most consequential trap — that a break-even computed against a frozen fleet is not a scalable crossover — is argued at length in §16.3 and Note 16.1-1 but is absent from the Common Mistakes list, even though the list is where a reader will look for it.
issue.evidence: §16.3: '$155,816.93 ÷ $0.0208 = 7,491,198.56 ≈ 7.5M is a frozen-fleet crossover, not a generalized scalable crossover: it holds only while those 21 hosts and that $155,816.93/month are held fixed, and it must not be read as "the volume at which a growing deployment becomes cheaper."' Note 16.1-1 repeats the warning. The Common Mistakes list contains six items, none of which covers it.
issue.root_cause: The Common Mistakes list was assembled from the chapter's early sections and not updated after the sensitivity/feasibility material was added.
issue.correction: Add a Common Mistake: '**Reading a frozen-fleet break-even as a scalable crossover.** The ~7.5M figure divides a fixed 21-host monthly cost by a per-request API price; it says nothing about the volume at which a growing deployment becomes cheaper, because a growing deployment re-runs N_hosts and steps the self-host line upward (⌈λ·8.6/17⌉ hosts per step).'
issue.acceptance_test: Every trap the chapter explicitly warns about in its body appears as a Common Mistake, and vice versa.

issue.quoted_clause: A new deployment adds 500 registered users (traffic rises to ~12.5/50 rps at the same 5 % concurrency profile).
issue.observed: The user-to-traffic scaling in the mini-case is not checkable from the text: adding 500 users raises average traffic by 2.5 rps and peak by 10 rps, implying 0.005 rps per user, which must be reconciled with the canonical workload's user count and per-user rate.
issue.evidence: The canonical workload is 10 rps average / 40 rps peak. If the canonical user count is 1,000, the per-user rate is 0.01 rps and 500 additional users at the same rate would give 15 rps / 60 rps, not 12.5 / 50. The mini-case's figures are internally consistent with each other (50 rps × 8.6 s = 430 in flight; ⌈430/17⌉ = 26 hosts), so the discrepancy is confined to the user-count derivation. NOT VERIFIED against Ch 4's canonical user count from this chunk.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case states the traffic outcome without stating the per-user rate it assumes, so the reader cannot check the derivation.
issue.correction: State the per-user rate explicitly ('at the canonical 0.005 rps per registered user, 500 additional users take the average from 10 to 12.5 rps and the peak from 40 to 50 rps') or state the canonical user count alongside the traffic figures. Reconcile with Ch 4's canonical user count.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case's 12.5/50 rps figures must be reproducible from the canonical user count and a stated per-user rate, and must match Ch 4's canonical workload definition.

issue.quoted_clause: ![Fig 16.1 — **Takeaway:** ... **Geometry/source:** ... **Caveat:** ... **Availability-scope caveat (do not quote this chart as an achievable procurement winner):** ...]
issue.observed: The caption runs to roughly 250 words with four bolded mini-headings and restates material that appears in full in §16.3 and Note 16.1-1. A caption of this length is read once and then skipped, which defeats the purpose of putting the caveats next to the figure.
issue.evidence: The caption's 'Availability-scope caveat' paragraph duplicates the multi-region paragraph in §16.3 nearly verbatim; the 'Geometry/source' line duplicates Note 16.1-1's line definitions; the 'Caveat' line duplicates the break-even discussion. The figure's own takeaway (self-host above the API at 6.24M; cloud marker not capacity-matched) is the only part that must live in the caption.
issue.root_cause: Captions were used as a place to relocate caveats that had accumulated in the body, rather than as a compact statement of what the reader should take from the figure.
issue.correction: Reduce the caption to: takeaway (one or two sentences), geometry/source line (one line), and a single pointer — 'see §16.3 and Note 16.1-1 for the availability-scope caveats and the derivation'. Keep the full caveats in the body where they are already stated.
issue.acceptance_test: No caption in the book exceeds roughly 80 words; every caveat that appears in a caption also appears in the body, and the caption contains no material that exists only there.

issue.page_hint: Ch 16, note block immediately preceding Fig 16.1
issue.quoted_clause: **Note 16.1-1 (Fig 16.1) — line definitions and the cloud marker.**
issue.observed: The note is numbered '16.1-1' but is placed at the end of §16.6, and the caption refers to it as 'Note 16.1-1 below'. The numbering is ambiguous: it reads as a note to §16.1 (Concept) or to Fig 16.1, and the reader cannot tell which.
issue.evidence: The note's content is entirely about Fig 16.1 (the three plotted series, the cloud marker, the utilization convention, the feasible bound). It sits physically after §6 'Architecture Consequence' and immediately before the figure, which is the natural place for a figure note.
issue.root_cause: The note was numbered by figure rather than by section, in a chapter where the same digits also denote a section number.
issue.correction: Rename to '**Note to Fig 16.1 — line definitions and the cloud marker**' (or 'Note 16-1'), and update the caption's cross-reference accordingly.
issue.acceptance_test: Every note reference in Ch 16 resolves unambiguously to a single note, and no note number can be confused with a section number.

issue.quoted_clause: 70,000 tok/s × 2 × 70×10⁹ FLOP/token = 9.8 ×10¹⁵ FLOP/s
issue.observed: The '× 2' is unexplained and is easily misread as a factor of two hosts. It is the 2-FLOPs-per-MAC factor that converts 70e9 parameters into 140e9 FLOP/token for the linear layers.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own case-(i) convention is 140e9 FLOP/token (confirmed by Ch 16's 19,780 tok/s/host = 35% MFU of 56,514 tok/s, where 56,514 = 8 × 989 TFLOPS ÷ 140e9). The mini-case's arithmetic is correct: 70,000 × 140e9 = 9.8e15 against 16 × 989e12 = 15.82e15 → 61.9%. Only the presentation is ambiguous.
issue.root_cause: The FLOP/token convention is established in Ch 16 but not restated where the factor is used, and the bare '× 2' invites misreading.
issue.correction: Write the expression as '70,000 tok/s × 140e9 FLOP/token (2 FLOPs per parameter per token, case (i) linear-only) = 9.8 ×10¹⁵ FLOP/s', and add a one-clause reminder of the case-(i) convention.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state, from the mini-case alone, what the '× 2' multiplies and why the FLOP/token figure is 140e9.

issue.page_hint: Ch 17 §4 (Measurement, 'Which one drives KV residency?') vs §8 (Mini-Case, 'Initial sizing analysis' and 'Decision')
issue.quoted_clause: §4: "Do not substitute a p95/p99 for E[W] in Little's Law. Little's Law is a *mean* relation, E[L] = λ·E[W]; pairing a mean λ with a p95 W mixes moments and yields a number that is neither a mean population nor a percentile one."  §8: "At T = 3 (the 95th-percentile, and the honest stress-cohort sizing point — 'worst case' applies only to the 2% fallback route, F-01) ... N ≈ ⌈1,770/(13 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈1,770/8.645⌉ ≈ **205 working hosts**" and "the integer-slot FP8 bound under **no-reuse** is **99 working hosts at the 70% × 95% policy, plus one spare host for N−1 operation: 100 hosts in total**"
issue.observed: The chapter states a hard rule (percentile W must not be substituted into the mean Little's Law identity) and then bases its entire mini-case decision on the 95th-percentile turn count T=3, with no mean-based fleet count anywhere in the chapter. The chapter's own F-01 box supplies the distribution-weighted mean W ≈ 12.71 s but never converts it into a host count, so the reader is left with a single (stress-cohort) number presented as 'the Decision'.
issue.evidence: Recomputation from the chapter's own inputs: distribution 0.68/0.25/0.05/0.02 over T=1/2/3/fallback; I(1)=10,365, I(2)=11,230, I(3)=12,095, I(fallback)=9,500 tokens; κ=2.62144 MB/token → per-request KV 27.171 / 29.438 / 31.705 / 24.904 GB; distribution-weighted mean bytes ≈ 0.68(27.171)+0.25(29.438)+0.05(31.705)+0.02(24.904) ≈ 27.92 GB → C = 436/27.92 ≈ 15.6 → floor 15. With F-01's mean W ≈ 12.71 s at 100 rps: in-flight ≈ 1,271 → N = ⌈1,271/(15×0.70×0.95)⌉ = ⌈1,271/9.975⌉ = ⌈127.4⌉ ≈ 128 working hosts (FP16) — versus the 205 the chapter reports for the same traffic point. The stress-cohort figure is ~1.6× the mean-based figure. (The mean-based number is itself approximate because E[bytes×time] ≠ E[bytes]·E[time], which the chapter itself notes.)
issue.root_cause: The chapter separates 'mean' and 'stress cohort' ledgers in F-01 but never propagates the mean ledger into the sizing output; the mini-case's decision line inherits the stress cohort without qualification.
issue.correction: Add the distribution-weighted mean case as a first-class row of Table 17-2 (or a second mini-case column): mean W ≈ 12.71 s, mean per-request KV ≈ 27.9 GB, C ≈ 15 (floor), and the resulting N at 40/100/200 rps. Then state explicitly which number is the planning decision (e.g. 'size to the mean, hold the stress cohort as the tail-risk bound') and label the T=3 columns as the stress bound they are. Reconcile the §4 rule with the §8 practice by pointing at the new mean row rather than at F-01's caveat.
issue.acceptance_test: Table 17-2 contains a distribution-weighted-mean row whose N values are reproducible from F-01's mean W and the distribution-weighted mean bytes; the mini-case's 'Decision' paragraph names which row is the decision and which is the bound; no sentence in Ch 17 pairs a percentile W with a mean Little's Law identity without an explicit stress-cohort label.

issue.page_hint: Ch 17 §4 ('The KV population is its own derivation' paragraph)
issue.quoted_clause: "then adjusted for the **rank/replication layout** (tensor-parallel rank count, and whether KV is sharded across ranks or replicated) and the **admission policy** (whole-context admission with no fractional slots; a prefix-cache hit or a pre-reserved block changes the effective holding time, not the byte geometry)."
issue.observed: The claim that a prefix-cache hit changes 'the effective holding time, not the byte geometry' is incorrect for the mechanism the chapter elsewhere relies on. When a prefix is shared across requests, the marginal KV bytes attributable to a new request are the *delta* (the newly appended tokens), not the whole context; the cached prefix is resident once and reused. The chapter's own reuse scenario (§8, W=14.16 s) is built on exactly this mechanism, so the statement contradicts the chapter's use of prefix caching.
issue.evidence: In §8's reuse case the prefill of the final call is 11,795 tokens of which 9,200 are the cached prefix; the KV for those 9,200 tokens is resident once per shared prefix, not once per request. The chapter nevertheless keeps C = 13 (full 12,095-token context) for the reuse rows of Table 17-2, i.e. it charges every request for the whole context while simultaneously claiming the prefix is shared. The two statements cannot both be true; the reuse rows are conservative in bytes but the accompanying mechanism claim is wrong.
issue.root_cause: The 'byte geometry' sentence was written to prevent a specific transplant error (queue time into KV slots) and over-generalized into a claim about prefix caching, which is a different mechanism.
issue.correction: Split the sentence: (a) a pre-reserved block changes the *holding time* (and can change the admission granularity), not the per-request byte geometry; (b) a prefix-cache hit changes *both* — the marginal bytes per request (delta-only) and the effective holding time — and its capacity benefit depends on the prefix-hit rate and on whether the cached prefix is shared across concurrent requests or pinned to one. Then state which assumption the reuse rows of Table 17-2 use (full-context C, i.e. no byte credit for prefix sharing) and label it as conservative.
issue.acceptance_test: The chapter contains no sentence asserting that prefix caching leaves byte geometry unchanged; Table 17-2's reuse rows state explicitly whether any byte credit is taken for shared prefixes, and the §8 reuse narrative is consistent with that statement.

issue.quoted_clause: "Under case (i) the available headroom is only ~7%; under cases (ii) and (iii) the prefill leg alone exceeds the idealized ceiling, so headroom is negative — the real headroom is smaller than ~7% and may be negative."  vs  "the check pushes the real count upward — by at least the ~7% headroom deficit under case (i), and by more than that under cases (ii)/(iii), where the prefill leg already exceeds the ceiling."
issue.observed: The same 7% is described as 'available headroom' in one sentence and as a 'headroom deficit' in the next. Under case (i) the prefill leg consumes 93% of the ceiling, so the deficit is negative (there is 7% of headroom, not a 7% shortfall). The second sentence then uses the deficit to claim the host count must be pushed upward by 'at least ~7%', which does not follow from a positive 7% headroom.
issue.evidence: 18,400 ÷ 19,780 = 0.9302 → headroom 6.98%. A 7% headroom means the prefill leg could grow by 7% before the ceiling binds; it does not imply a 7% capacity shortfall. The upward push under case (i) is already captured by the policy screens reported elsewhere in the chapter (⌈18.60/0.665⌉+1 = 29 for case (i), versus 32 for the KV-only policy total), so the paragraph double-counts the effect it claims to add.
issue.root_cause: The paragraph was written as a 'the check pushes the count up' narrative and reuses the 7% figure with the wrong sign, without reconciling against the policy-level prefill screens already tabulated in Table 17-1's caption and Table 17-2's note.
issue.correction: Rewrite the paragraph to state the sign correctly: under case (i) the prefill leg leaves ~7% headroom at full utilization, so the prefill screen (18.60 hosts) does not bind against the KV screen (21 hosts); under cases (ii)/(iii) it binds. Then point to the already-reported policy-level screens (29 / 32 / 34) as the place where the prefill constraint enters the host count, instead of asserting an additional upward push.
issue.acceptance_test: The word 'deficit' is not applied to the case-(i) 7% figure anywhere in Ch 17; the 'Effect on the headline counts' paragraph cites the same 29/32/34 policy screens as Table 17-1 and Table 17-2 rather than introducing a separate, unsourced increment.

issue.page_hint: Ch 17 §4 (bullet list under 'At the canonical peak')
issue.quoted_clause: "This is the honest fleet size and matches the throughput/latency analysis in Chapter 20."
issue.observed: The chapter labels the KV-screen count (21 / 31 / 32) 'the honest fleet size', while (a) the same bullet reports that under case (ii) the prefill screen binds and the policy-level floor is 34, and (b) the chapter repeatedly states that the deployable count is max(capacity screen, measured N_SLO) and that the counts are 'analytical lower-bound screens, not measured SLO-goodput'. Calling one of several screens 'the honest fleet size' overstates the claim and conflicts with the chapter's own repeated qualifications.
issue.evidence: Same bullet: 'Under case (ii) the compute screen **binds above** the KV screen, so the capacity floor is **max(KV, compute) = 22 hosts** — and at the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy ⌈21.81/0.665⌉ + 1 = 34 hosts under case (ii) versus **32** for KV-only'. Table 17-1's caption: 'an **analytical lower-bound screen, not measured SLO-goodput**'. Table 17-2's note: 'the deployable fleet is the **maximum** of that capacity requirement and the measured tail-latency (N_SLO) requirement'.
issue.root_cause: A rhetorical summary sentence ('the honest fleet size') was left in from an earlier draft in which the KV screen was the only screen; the chapter later added the prefill screens and the N_SLO requirement without revising the sentence.
issue.correction: Replace with a scope-matched statement, e.g. 'the KV-residency screen alone gives 21/31/32; the binding screen depends on the FLOP-counting case (case (ii) gives 34 at policy), and the deployable count is the maximum of the capacity screens and the measured N_SLO requirement (Ch 14)'. Delete 'the honest fleet size'.
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 17 characterizes any single screen as 'the honest fleet size' or equivalent; the phrase 'honest' is not used to override the chapter's own lower-bound/SLO caveats.

issue.page_hint: Ch 17 §7 ('What We Still Don't Know', first bullet)
issue.quoted_clause: "Do larger fleets (N ≫ 4 — the canonical 21/31/32, or the 82/205/410 agentic fleets; N = 4 appears only in the failover example in §6) change the observed T distribution?"
issue.observed: The parenthetical asserts that N = 4 appears only in the §6 failover example. Fig 17.1's caption uses a 4-host fleet as its central worked example ('a 4-host fleet (~8.0 req/s)'), so the claim is false as written and will mislead a reader who cross-checks the figure.
issue.evidence: Fig 17.1 caption: 'a small ~5.5 req/s burst exceeds one host's ~2.0 req/s analytical bound, so a 4-host fleet (~8.0 req/s) is sized above it: 3 hosts clear the 5.5 req/s burst at ρ = 1; a 4th is the N−1 reserve'. §6: 'For N = 4 **in the no-spare case** ... a single-host loss reduces capacity from 100% to 75%'.
issue.root_cause: The bullet was written before Fig 17.1 was added, and the figure's N=4 example was not propagated into the cross-reference.
issue.correction: Rewrite as 'N = 4 appears in the Fig 17.1 burst-sizing example and in the §6 failover illustration; the canonical and agentic fleet sizes are 21/31/32 and 82/205/410', or drop the parenthetical enumeration entirely.
issue.acceptance_test: Every N value mentioned in Ch 17 prose can be located in the chapter's own figures, tables, or examples; no 'appears only in' claim contradicts a figure caption.

issue.quoted_clause: §8: "The proposed design uses NGINX with consistent hashing for session affinity and OpenTelemetry tracing on each host."  §6: "(b) if stateless, use least-connections or power-of-two-choices so load follows capacity — do not use consistent hashing."
issue.observed: The mini-case's design decision selects consistent hashing for session affinity, which the chapter explicitly forbids for stateless routing. The canonical workload is stateless: §3 states 'In the canonical scenario, requests are independent — no user session spans multiple hosts', and §2 states that stateless routing gives even distribution. The decision therefore adopts the option the chapter rules out, without stating a session-affinity requirement that would justify it.
issue.evidence: §3: 'Cross-host communication. In the canonical scenario, requests are independent — no user session spans multiple hosts.' §2: 'If sessions are stateless ... any host can serve any request, and load distribution becomes even.' §6: 'do not use consistent hashing' for the stateless case.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case's decision line appears to have been written from a generic 'production design' template rather than from the chapter's own routing rule; the session-affinity requirement is never established for the scenario.
issue.correction: Either (a) change the decision to least-connections / power-of-two-choices and state that the canonical workload is stateless, or (b) establish in the scenario that sessions must be sticky (e.g. multi-turn conversations with retained KV), and then justify consistent hashing against the §2 density-vs-evenness trade-off and the §5 mistake #2 skew analysis. If (b), the fleet sizing must also account for the reduced effective parallelism that affinity implies.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case's LB choice is consistent with §6's routing rule given an explicitly stated session model; if affinity is chosen, the chapter states the affinity requirement and its capacity consequence.

issue.quoted_clause: "## 4. Measurement"  ...  "We derive three planning quantities from the worked example and Chapter 19's illustrative turn-count distribution. These are not measurements from production traffic. A deployment must measure its own traffic distribution before using these quantities for provisioning."
issue.observed: The section is titled 'Measurement' but contains no measurement: it opens by stating that its contents are not measurements, and the section actually contains (i) four KV-capacity derivations, (ii) a four-rate reconciliation box, (iii) a five-symbol time-budget table, (iv) a network budget, (v) two counter-scenarios, and (vi) a feasibility check. The opening claim of 'three planning quantities' is also inaccurate. A reader scanning headings will expect measured data and instead find derivations, and the section's role in the book's causal chain (derivation → what must be measured) is obscured.
issue.evidence: Section 4 subsections: 'Per-host throughput and KV cache budget', 'Load-balancer overhead factor', 'Cross-host interconnect budget', 'Request traffic and model collectives are different populations', 'Counter-scenarios: KV is not always the driver', 'Simultaneous feasibility check (prefill + decode coexistence)'. The only measurement content in the chapter is deferred to Ch 14 ('Before treating 2 req/s/host as deployable, measure the p95 TTFT, p95 TPOT, and SLO-goodput on a representative host (Chapter 14)').
issue.root_cause: The section was renamed to 'Measurement' to signal rigour, but its content is analytical; the honest framing (derivation with an explicit measurement agenda) was lost.
issue.correction: Rename to 'Derivation and the measurement agenda' (or 'Planning quantities and what must be measured'), and add a short closing subsection listing the specific telemetry the chapter says must be collected (per-host resident-sequence count, measured W_KV-resident distribution, p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT, SLO-goodput, measured ρ, measured φ and D) with the Ch 14 reference for each. Correct 'three planning quantities' to match the actual content.
issue.acceptance_test: No section heading in Ch 17 promises measurement where the content is derivation; the section's opening sentence enumerates the quantities it actually produces; a reader can list every measurement the chapter says is required before the counts are trusted.

issue.quoted_clause: 'Viability at peak': "Peak traffic is 40 rps; with the canonical ~8.6 s per-request service time ... Little's Law puts ≈ 40 × 8.6 ≈ **344 requests in flight**, against a KV capacity of ~17.5 per host (conservative integer floor 17). **A single host is not viable at peak even for the non-agentic canonical workload** — the fleet needs roughly ⌈344/17⌉ = **21 hosts** at 40 rps (**31 working hosts** at the 70% × 95% provisioning policy, **32 total with N−1** — Table 17-1)"  'Scaling forecast (service-time-aware)': "the in-flight concurrency at the 40 rps peak ... is λ_peak × W ≈ 40 × 8.6 ≈ **344 requests**, not 40. With FP16 KV (baseline C≈17.5, conservative integer floor 17), the fleet needs ⌈344/17⌉ = **21 hosts** at full utilization (**31** at the 70% × 95% provisioning policy, **32 total with N−1** — Table 17-1)."
issue.observed: Two adjacent paragraphs in §3 derive the identical quantity (344 in flight; 21 / 31 / 32 hosts) with the same inputs and the same formula, differing only in wording. The second adds no new computation, no new assumption, and no new consequence; it re-states the first with a 'not 40' emphasis. This is redundant repetition (class C), not reinforcement, and it sits in the chapter's most-read section.
issue.evidence: Both paragraphs use λ_peak = 40 rps, W = 8.6 s, C = 17 (floor), u = 0.70, ρ = 0.95, N_spare = 1, and cite Table 17-1. The only content unique to the second paragraph is the qualitative statement that agentic turns make it worse, which the preceding 'Threshold for fleet expansion' subsection has already established.
issue.root_cause: The 'Scaling forecast' paragraph was added when the service-time-aware framing was introduced, without deleting the earlier 'Viability at peak' paragraph that already carried the same arithmetic.
issue.correction: Merge the two into one paragraph that (i) states the 344 in-flight figure, (ii) states the 21/31/32 counts, and (iii) states the agentic direction of travel once, with a forward pointer to §8 for the agentic numbers. Keep the 'not 40' emphasis as a single clause.
issue.acceptance_test: No two paragraphs in Ch 17 §3 derive the same host count from the same inputs; a reader encountering 344/21/31/32 in §3 encounters it once.

issue.quoted_clause: "These are the honest arithmetic bounds the full service-time model produces — the naive '1–5 hosts' rps estimate — never tied to a traffic level — is off by ~16–205× (82 hosts ÷ 5 ≈ 16.4 at the 40-rps peak; 205 ÷ 1 = 205 at the 100-rps peak; each ratio is per its own traffic point)"
issue.observed: The '1–5 hosts' baseline is never derived anywhere in the chapter, and the two ratios use two different denominators (5 at 40 rps, 1 at 100 rps) with no stated basis for either. The parenthetical's 'each ratio is per its own traffic point' does not repair this: the denominator is the thing that changes, not the traffic point. As written, the comparison is not reproducible and reads as a rhetorical amplification of the chapter's own result.
issue.evidence: No occurrence of a '1–5 host' estimate appears in §1–§7 of the chunk. The two ratios are 82/5 = 16.4 and 205/1 = 205; a single consistent baseline (e.g. the same naive estimate at both traffic points) would give 82/x and 205/x, whose ratio is 2.5, matching the traffic ratio 100/40 = 2.5.
issue.root_cause: The comparison was constructed rhetorically after the fact rather than from a stated baseline model, and the two denominators were chosen to widen the range.
issue.correction: Either derive the naive baseline explicitly (e.g. 'a naive sizing that equates peak rps with per-host capacity gives ⌈40/2.0⌉ = 20 hosts at 40 rps and ⌈100/2.0⌉ = 50 hosts at 100 rps — under-sizing by 4× and 4× respectively') or delete the ratio and keep only the qualitative statement that an rps-only estimate under-sizes by roughly the service-time factor. If a range is retained, use one denominator per traffic point derived from the same naive rule.
issue.acceptance_test: Every ratio quoted in Ch 17 §8 has both operands derivable from text in the chapter; the naive baseline, if used, is stated once as a rule and applied identically at each traffic point.

issue.page_hint: Ch 17 §8 (Mini-Case, 'Initial sizing analysis') vs Ch 19 references
issue.quoted_clause: "The tool leg here uses the ~133 ms/turn tool/retrieval rate; Chapter 19's `T·L_agent` (~660 ms at T=3) is the *orchestration-only* incremental overhead at a different per-turn rate, and a single model should use one rate consistently."
issue.observed: The chapter acknowledges that two different per-turn tool/orchestration rates are in play (0.133 s/turn here vs 0.22 s/turn implied by Ch 19's T·L_agent ≈ 660 ms at T=3) and states that 'a single model should use one rate consistently' — i.e. it identifies a defect in the book's own model and leaves it in place. The two rates differ by ~65%, and the tool term is ~2% of W(3) = 17.70 s, so the numerical impact on the fleet counts is small; the impact on the book's coherence is not: the same agentic scenario is costed with two different orchestration rates in two chapters.
issue.evidence: Ch 19's T·L_agent ≈ 660 ms at T=3 → 220 ms/turn. Ch 17's evaluator uses 3 × 0.133 = 0.399 s → 133 ms/turn. Ratio 1.65. The chapter's own W(3) = 17.70 s is built on the 133 ms rate; substituting 220 ms/turn gives W(3) ≈ 18.03 s, in-flight 1,803 at 100 rps, N = ⌈1,803/8.645⌉ = 209 (vs 205) — a ~2% change, confirming the numerical stakes are low but the modelling inconsistency is real.
issue.root_cause: Ch 17's evaluator script and Ch 19's β(T) model were parameterised independently; the discrepancy was documented rather than reconciled.
issue.correction: Reconcile in one place: state the canonical per-turn tool/retrieval rate (and whether it includes orchestration), and have both Ch 17's evaluator and Ch 19's β(T) reference it. If the two quantities are genuinely different (retrieval service time vs orchestration overhead), say so explicitly and state which one enters W_KV-resident and which enters W_e2e, then show the effect on W(3) (≈ +0.33 s, ≈ +2% on the host count).
issue.acceptance_test: A single per-turn tool/retrieval rate is used wherever an agentic service time is computed in Ch 17 and Ch 19, or the two rates are explicitly distinguished with their separate roles and their numeric effect on W stated.

issue.page_hint: Ch 17 §2 (Mental Model) vs §4 ('Request traffic and model collectives are different populations')
issue.quoted_clause: §2: "Each backend host runs an identical copy of the model and serves requests independently."  §4: "A distributed model introduces different events. Tensor-parallel participants exchange partial results at layer boundaries; expert-parallel participants dispatch and combine routed tokens."
issue.observed: The chapter's mental model — the frame through which the reader is meant to understand everything that follows — assumes a fleet of independent, identical model replicas. The chapter then introduces collectives (TP/EP) that only exist when a single model spans multiple hosts, without reconciling that topology with the mental model. The reader is never told which fleet topology the canonical 21/31/32 counts assume (replica-per-host) or how a TP-spanning-host fleet would change the sizing arithmetic (the KV screen, the per-host C, and the load-balancer model all change).
issue.evidence: §2's two invariants (throughput ≈ N × per-host; memory = N × per-host) hold only for the replica-per-host topology. §4's collective paragraph explicitly notes that collectives 'follow the actual TP or EP communication group and execution schedule, not the total number of serving hosts', which is incompatible with the §2 frame unless the topology is fixed. The canonical host is 8×H100, so TP=8 is already inside the host; the chapter never states whether the fleet's TP group is confined to a host.
issue.root_cause: The mental model was written for the simple replica fleet and the collectives paragraph was added later as a caveat, without extending the model.
issue.correction: State the topology assumption explicitly in §2 ('the canonical fleet is replica-per-host: each 8×H100 host holds one complete TP=8 model; no TP group crosses a host boundary') and add one sentence in §4 explaining what changes if a TP group does cross hosts (the per-host C and the load-balancer's role change; the KV screen becomes a per-group screen; collectives enter the critical path). This also gives the reader the transfer rule for a future disaggregated-serving topology.
issue.acceptance_test: The fleet topology (replica-per-host vs model-spanning) is stated once in §2 and referenced wherever host counts are derived; §4's collective paragraph opens by naming the topology it applies to.

issue.page_hint: Ch 17 §8 (Mini-Case, 'KV compression changes the answer' and 'Decision') vs §7 (last bullet)
issue.quoted_clause: §8: "under the 100%-reuse point it is **79 + 1 = 80**" ... "the reuse columns are the 100%-reuse point and no intermediate saving is assumed."  §7: "can a fleet-wide prefix cache (same-model, same-prefix hits only) or retrieval cache reduce the effective δ per request? The savings could be substantial but require cross-host cache-invalidation protocols for that prefix/retrieval cache, which are not yet well understood."
issue.observed: The reuse column of Table 17-2 (66 / 164 / 328 hosts FP16; 32 / 79 / 158 hosts FP8) is presented as a usable sizing alternative, but the mechanism it depends on — a fleet-wide prefix cache with cross-host invalidation — is listed in the same chapter as not yet well understood. The chapter therefore offers a 100%-reuse operating point whose enabling mechanism is unresolved, without marking the reuse rows as conditional on an unproven capability.
issue.evidence: §7: 'cross-host cache-invalidation protocols ... are not yet well understood'. §8: 'Prefix caching can reduce repeated prefill work and share identical cached prefixes when the engine supports that representation.' The reuse rows also assume 100% hit rate, which the chapter elsewhere refuses to assume for any other parameter (e.g. it refuses to assume an intermediate prefix hit ratio but does assume the extreme one).
issue.root_cause: The reuse scenario was computed from the evaluator's declared 100%-reuse case without carrying the §7 caveat into the table's scope note.
issue.correction: Mark the reuse rows in Table 17-2 as conditional: 'requires a fleet-wide shared prefix cache with cross-host invalidation semantics that the book treats as unresolved (§7); the 100% hit rate is the evaluator's declared extreme case, not an expected operating point'. Consider adding one intermediate hit-rate row (e.g. 50%) to show the sensitivity, or state that the reuse column is a bound rather than a plan.
issue.acceptance_test: Table 17-2's reuse rows carry a scope note naming the unresolved mechanism and the extreme hit-rate assumption; the mini-case's 'Decision' paragraph does not present the reuse count as an available alternative without that qualification.

issue.quoted_clause: | $W_{\mathrm{e2e}}$ (end-to-end) | the **full service time** as the user experiences it: queue + GPU execution + tool/orchestration + inter-turn gaps | ≈ 10 s planning round for the canonical non-agentic round; grows with turns | λ·W_e2e — requests in flight (user view) |
issue.observed: The canonical non-agentic request has no tool or orchestration leg (the chapter's own §3 says the canonical request is 'the non-agentic canonical request'), so the 10 s figure is unexplained by the definition given in the same row. The 1.4 s difference from W_GPU-exec = 8.6 s is never attributed to a component, and the table's W_queue row says queue time is 'unmeasured here'. The reader cannot tell whether the 10 s includes an assumed 1.4 s of queueing, an orchestration allowance, or a rounding of a Ch 4 planning round.
issue.evidence: Table row W_GPU-exec: '≈ 8.6 s (1.08 s prefill + 7.5 s decode, canonical 9.2K/300)'. Table row W_queue: 'unmeasured here'. §4 prose: 'The end-to-end time ($W_{\mathrm{e2e}}$ ≈ 10 s planning round, the quantity earlier drafts labeled W_plan) is the workload-level Little's-law basis used to derive the arrival rate from the population (Chapter 4)'. The 10 s figure is used in the chapter only to distinguish populations, but it is the one number in the table with no derivation.
issue.root_cause: The 10 s value was inherited from Ch 4's planning round without decomposing it against the chapter's own five-symbol taxonomy, and the taxonomy was introduced later.
issue.correction: Decompose the 10 s explicitly (e.g. '8.6 s GPU execution + ~1.4 s of queueing and orchestration allowance carried from the Ch 4 planning round') or replace the cell with '≈ 8.6 s + queue/orchestration allowance (Ch 4 planning round: 10 s)'. Also remove the meta-reference to 'earlier drafts', which does not belong in a published book.
issue.acceptance_test: Every value in the five-symbol table is either derived in Ch 17 or attributed to a named chapter with its composition stated; no cell contains a number whose components cannot be enumerated.

issue.quoted_clause: "In the worked example, the fleet is currently sized by KV capacity (§17.3), not by a fabricated tokens/s number: at T = 3 (the 95th-percentile sizing point, per the chapter's own rule), FP16-KV C ≈ 13.8/host (436 GB ÷ (12,095 × 2.62 MB ≈ 31.7 GB) ≈ 13.8; conservative integer floor 13) sets the continuous ceiling."
issue.observed: The §4 LB subsection silently switches the sizing point from T=0 (the canonical non-agentic case used for the 21/31/32 headline counts in §3) to T=3, and calls T=3 'the chapter's own rule'. The chapter's own rule (F-01) is the opposite: Little's Law needs the distribution-weighted mean, and the T=3 cohort is explicitly labelled a stress bound. The subsection also says the fleet 'is currently sized by KV capacity (§17.3)', but §3's sizing is at T=0, not T=3.
issue.evidence: §3: 'the fleet needs roughly ⌈344/17⌉ = **21 hosts** ... **31 working hosts** ... **32 total with N−1**' (T=0, C=17). §4 LB subsection: 'at T = 3 ... C ≈ 13.8/host ... floor 13' and 'C × u × ρ = 13 × 0.70 × 0.95 = 8.645'. F-01: 'Little's Law needs the **mean** E[W_KV-resident]; a percentile substituted into a mean equality yields a stress bound, not a measured/typical population.'
issue.root_cause: The LB subsection was written against the agentic sizing point (from §8) and pasted into §4 without reconciling with §3's canonical T=0 sizing or with F-01.
issue.correction: State which sizing point the LB subsection is illustrating and why (e.g. 'the agentic T=3 stress point of §8, where the effective slot count is 8.645'), and remove 'per the chapter's own rule'. If the intent is to illustrate the canonical case, use C = 17 and 11.305 and cross-reference §3.
issue.acceptance_test: Every C value used in Ch 17 §4 is labelled with its turn-count point (T=0 or T=3) and its source; no sentence calls the 95th-percentile point 'the chapter's own rule'.

issue.page_hint: Ch 17 §4 ('Per-host throughput and KV cache budget', bullet list)
issue.quoted_clause: "For T = 0 (baseline, I = 9,500): C = 436 GB / (9,500 ×2.62 MB) ≈ 436/24.9037 ≈ **17.5 concurrent requests per host** (byte-accurate; floor 17 — rounding rule in §17.3)."
issue.observed: The printed substitution does not produce the printed divisor: 9,500 × 2.62 MB = 24,890 MB = 24.89 GB, not 24.9037 GB. The divisor 24.9037 comes from the byte-accurate κ = 2,621,440 B. The same pattern recurs for the other three rows (10,365 × 2.62 = 27.156 vs printed 27.17; 12,095 × 2.62 = 31.689 vs printed 31.71; 12,960 × 2.62 = 33.955 vs printed 33.97). The results are unaffected, but a reader who checks the substitution will find the printed arithmetic does not close.
issue.root_cause: The bullets were written with the rounded κ in the formula slot and the byte-accurate product in the numeric slot.
issue.correction: Use one κ consistently in the substitution: write '9,500 × 2.62144 MB ≈ 24.9037 GB' (and 27.171 / 31.705 / 33.974 for the other rows), or state 'κ ≈ 2.62 MB/token (2.62144 MB byte-accurate)' and show the byte-accurate products.
issue.acceptance_test: Every printed divisor in Ch 17 §4's bullet list is reproducible from the printed multiplicand and the stated κ to the printed precision.

issue.quoted_clause: "under **100% prefix reuse** only the incremental 11,795-token prefix is pre-filled, giving W(3) ≈ **14.16 s**"
issue.observed: 11,795 tokens is the *final* context length (I(3) = 9,200 + 3×865 + 300), not an incremental quantity. The incremental amount beyond the cached 9,200-token prefix is 2,595 tokens. The arithmetic is correct (11,795/9,200 × 1.08 = 1.385 s of prefill), but the label 'incremental' inverts the meaning and would mislead a reader who tries to reuse the sentence as a method.
issue.evidence: §8: 'the T=3 trace has four model calls (inputs 9,200 + 10,065 + 10,930 + 11,795 = 41,990)'. Under 100% prefix reuse the first three calls' prefills are skipped and only the final call's 11,795-token input is prefilled: 11,795/9,200 × 1.08 = 1.3846 s; W = 1.3846 + 0.025×495 + 3×0.133 = 14.16 s ✓.
issue.root_cause: Terminology slip: 'incremental' was used to mean 'the last call's input' rather than 'the newly appended tokens'.
issue.correction: Rewrite as 'under 100% prefix reuse only the final call's 11,795-token context is prefilled (the 9,200-token prefix is served from cache), giving W(3) ≈ 14.16 s', and add the incremental figure (2,595 tokens) where the delta is meant.
issue.acceptance_test: The word 'incremental' is not applied to a full context length anywhere in Ch 17; the reuse computation states which call's input is prefilled and which is cached.

issue.quoted_clause: "With the illustrative φ = 0.05 — halved from §17.6's φ = 0.1 to model a lower cross-host fraction at the grown 100-rps traffic"
issue.observed: φ = 0.1 is introduced in §4 ('Cross-host interconnect budget'), not §6; §6 restates it in the 'Cross-host data infrastructure' paragraph. The cross-reference points at the wrong section for the definition.
issue.evidence: §4: 'If a fraction φ of requests require cross-host data ... B_agg = φ · λ · D = 0.1 × 40 × 5 MB = 20 MB/s'. §6: 'The minimum bandwidth is B_min = φ · λ · D (the fleet aggregate derived in §17.4.4 ...)'. §8 refers to '§17.6's φ = 0.1'.
issue.root_cause: Section renumbering between drafts; the §17.4.4-style sub-section references elsewhere in the chapter (§6, §8) suggest the chapter once had numbered subsections that no longer exist.
issue.correction: Point to §4 ('Cross-host interconnect budget') for the definition of φ, and audit the chapter's other sub-section references ('§17.4.4', '§17.3', '§17.4', '§17.6', '§17.8') against the current section structure — several refer to subsections that no longer exist as headings.
issue.acceptance_test: Every §-reference in Ch 17 resolves to a heading that exists in the current chapter; the definition of φ is cited from the section that defines it.

issue.page_hint: Ch 17 §4 (sensitivity band in the 'At the canonical peak' bullet)
issue.quoted_clause: "at the weights-only floor 5.2 ms/step (B → 0, no KV reads) W ≈ 2.6 s (in-flight ≈ 106, ~7 hosts at full util)"
issue.observed: B → 0 is not a physically realizable operating point: a decode step always reads the KV of at least the sequence being decoded. The label 'weights-only floor' is correct, but the parenthetical '(B → 0, no KV reads)' presents a non-physical limit as if it were a scenario, and the derived W ≈ 2.6 s / ~7 hosts inherits that status. A reader could quote '~7 hosts' as a legitimate sizing option.
issue.evidence: The floor is correctly derived as 140 GB ÷ 26.8 TB/s = 5.22 ms, and the sensitivity band is otherwise sound (21 ms → W 7.4 s → 295 → 18 hosts; 25 ms → 8.6 s → 344 → 21; 40 ms → 13.1 s → 523 → 31). Only the B → 0 endpoint is unreachable.
issue.root_cause: The band was constructed as a bracket of the step time and the lower endpoint was not checked for physical realizability.
issue.correction: Mark the 5.2 ms endpoint explicitly as a non-physical lower bound ('B = 1, i.e. the KV of a single sequence is still read; the true floor is 5.2 ms + one sequence's KV read'), and state that the realizable minimum step time is bounded below by the weights read plus at least one sequence's KV.
issue.acceptance_test: Every point in the sensitivity band is labeled either as a realizable operating point or as a mathematical bound, and the realizable lower bound is stated.

issue.quoted_clause: "at the 40 ms TPOT SLO pole W ≈ 13.1 s (in-flight ≈ 523, ~31 hosts on the KV screen). Sizing at the 25 ms budget is a tighter internal target than the 40 ms SLO pole, so name the sizing pole once and state it once: sizing at the SLO pole gives ~31 hosts"
issue.observed: The number 31 is used in the chapter for two unrelated quantities: 31 hosts at full utilization on the 40 ms SLO pole, and 31 *working* hosts at the 70% × 95% policy on the 25 ms budget pole. The chapter's own instruction ('name the sizing pole once and state it once') is not followed, and the coincidence makes the two easy to conflate — a reader could conclude that the policy-sized fleet is the same as the SLO-pole-sized fleet.
issue.evidence: §4 bullet: '⌈344/17⌉ = **21 hosts** (**31 working** at the 70% × 95% policy, **32 total with N−1**)'. Sensitivity band: '~31 hosts on the KV screen' at the 40 ms pole (523/17 = 30.8 → 31, full utilization, no u/ρ, no spare).
issue.root_cause: Two independent derivations coincidentally produce 31, and the chapter does not flag the collision even though it flags two other coincidences (29 and 32) elsewhere.
issue.correction: Either state the collision explicitly ('note that the SLO-pole full-utilization count (31) coincidentally equals the policy working count at the 25 ms pole — different quantities') or change the sensitivity band's presentation to give the policy-level count at the 40 ms pole (⌈523/11.305⌉ = 47 working) so the two are not confusable.
issue.acceptance_test: Every host count in Ch 17 is accompanied by its pole (25 ms budget vs 40 ms SLO), its utilization treatment (full vs u×ρ), and its spare treatment; coincidentally equal counts are flagged where they occur.

issue.quoted_clause: "**Scope:** every capacity line is an **ideal ρ = 1 analytical service ceiling — no SLO claim**; the same formula gives N_min = ceil(40 × 8.6 / 17) = 21 for the canonical peak, 21 + 1 N−1 reserve = 22 (coincidentally equal to the case (ii) prefill screen ⌈21.81⌉ = 22 at zero spare — same number, different derivation)"
issue.observed: Two problems in the caption's scope statement. (a) The scope names only ρ = 1; the 21 = ⌈40 × 8.6 / 17⌉ also requires u = 1 (no utilization derate), which is not stated, so a reader could read the caption as claiming the 21/22 figures are the policy numbers (which are 31/32). (b) The flagged 'coincidence' compares a *total* (21 working + 1 spare = 22) with a *working* count (case-(ii) prefill screen at zero spare = 22 working, 23 total), so the two 22s are not the same quantity; the caption says 'same number, different derivation' without noting the different semantics.
issue.evidence: Table 17-1 policy: u = 0.70, ρ = 0.95 → 31 working, 32 total. Fig 17.1's 21/22 correspond to u = ρ = 1. Case-(ii) prefill screen at zero spare = ⌈21.81⌉ = 22 working hosts; with the spare it is 23.
issue.root_cause: The caption was written to describe the figure's own ideal-ceiling lines and does not distinguish the figure's operating point from the chapter's policy operating point, nor working from total counts.
issue.correction: Extend the scope line to 'ideal ρ = 1, u = 1 analytical service ceiling — no SLO claim; the policy operating point (u = 0.70, ρ = 0.95) gives 31 working / 32 total (Table 17-1)'. Reword the coincidence as 'the KV screen with one spare (22 total) coincides numerically with the case-(ii) prefill screen at zero spare (22 working) — different quantities, different derivations'.
issue.acceptance_test: Fig 17.1's caption states both derate factors it assumes; every host count in the caption is labeled working or total.

issue.quoted_clause: §2: "the **throughput invariant**: total system throughput ≈ N × throughput_per_host, reduced by a factor ρ that captures load‑balancer overhead, health‑check traffic, and imperfect distribution (typically ρ ∈ [0.95, 0.98] depending on LB sophistication)."  §4: "**These LB-efficiency values are [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] engineering thresholds, not universal vendor-independent constants**"
issue.observed: The ρ range is stated in §2 as a typical property of load balancers, without the [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] label that §4 attaches to the same values. A reader who stops at the mental model will take 0.95–0.98 as a property of the technology rather than a scenario assumption. Separately, the §2 invariant omits u: the chapter's actual per-host usable capacity is throughput_per_host × u × ρ, so the mental model understates the derate by one factor.
issue.evidence: Table 17-1: u = 0.70 and ρ = 0.95 are both 'independent' multipliers in the denominator. §4: 'a well-configured software LB (NGINX) typically achieves ρ ≈ 0.95, and a hardware L7 switch may achieve ρ ≈ 0.98, *but both must be measured on the target topology, workload, and sample duration before being trusted*'.
issue.root_cause: The mental model was written before the evidence-label discipline and the u factor were formalized in Table 17-1.
issue.correction: Add the [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] label to the ρ range in §2 and state the invariant as 'total system throughput ≈ N × throughput_per_host × u × ρ', with u and ρ defined by pointer to Table 17-1.
issue.acceptance_test: Every numeric range presented as a property of a technology in Ch 17 carries the same evidence label as in §4; the §2 invariant matches the denominator of the chapter's authoritative formula.

issue.page_hint: Ch 17 §7 ('What We Still Don't Know', third bullet)
issue.quoted_clause: "**Optimal fleet size for cost vs. latency.** The cost of adding a host is roughly the cost of 8×H100 (multi‑hundred‑thousand dollars). The marginal latency improvement from the Nth host diminishes (diminishing returns). A cost‑per‑latency‑improved curve would help the architect justify fleet size to stakeholders."
issue.observed: In the chapter's own model, adding hosts does not improve latency at all: the service time W is a property of the request (prefill + decode + tool), and N is chosen so that per-host concurrency stays at the u target. Latency improves with N only through reduced queueing delay, which the chapter explicitly excludes from W_KV-resident and never models. The bullet therefore asks for a 'cost-per-latency-improved curve' on an axis the chapter has not established, and the 'diminishing returns' claim is asserted rather than derived.
issue.evidence: §4: 'the ~8.6 s used below is a **conditional scenario proxy** for E[W_KV-resident]' and 'The end-to-end W_e2e ... is the user-view in-flight count and is **not** the W in this KV formula'. The chapter's own sensitivity band shows latency (W) varying with the step-time pole, not with N.
issue.root_cause: The open-questions list was written from general fleet-planning intuition rather than from the chapter's model, which contains no queueing component.
issue.correction: Reframe the bullet around what the chapter's model actually leaves open: the queueing delay that appears when offered load exceeds per-host capacity (the N_SLO requirement, deferred to Ch 14), and the cost-per-unit-of-goodput curve rather than a cost-per-latency curve. State that, under the chapter's model, N affects latency only through queueing, which is unmeasured.
issue.acceptance_test: Every open question in Ch 17 §7 names a quantity the chapter's model actually contains or explicitly names the missing component (e.g. queueing) that would be needed to answer it.

issue.quoted_clause: §8: "At T = 3 (the 95th-percentile, and the honest stress-cohort sizing point — 'worst case' applies only to the 2% fallback route, F-01)"  F-01: "The columns above are honestly labeled as the stress cohort; they are *not* claimed to be the distribution *mean*, nor a strict worst case if the 2% fallback jobs do multiple failed invocations plus the final answer beyond the cap."
issue.observed: The mini-case asserts that 'worst case' applies only to the 2% fallback route; F-01 then says the T=3 columns are not a strict worst case precisely because the 2% fallback jobs may do multiple failed invocations plus the final answer beyond the cap. The two statements are in tension: if the fallback route can exceed the T=3 cohort's resource footprint, then the T=3 columns are not an upper bound on the fleet's requirement, and the chapter's 'stress cohort' framing understates the tail.
issue.evidence: F-01: 'nor a strict worst case if the 2% fallback jobs do multiple failed invocations plus the final answer beyond the cap'. The fallback route's W is given as 17.40 s in the F-01 ledger (0.02 × 17.40), which is below the T=3 value of 17.70 s — so the fallback's *mean* W is lower, but its *tail* (multiple failed invocations) is not quantified anywhere.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case's parenthetical was written to reassure the reader that the T=3 point is conservative; F-01 was written later and states the opposite caveat.
issue.correction: Align the two: either quantify the fallback route's worst-case footprint (failed invocations plus the final answer) and show that it is bounded by the T=3 cohort, or remove the 'worst case applies only to the 2% fallback route' claim and state that the T=3 cohort is a stress point that is not a proven upper bound on the tail.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case's characterization of the T=3 cohort and F-01's characterization of the same cohort are consistent; if the fallback tail is not quantified, no sentence claims the T=3 cohort bounds it.

issue.page_hint: Ch 17 §2 (Mental Model) and §3 ('Threshold for fleet expansion')
issue.quoted_clause: §2: "If sessions are stateless (the model is reloaded or KV cache is discarded between requests), any host can serve any request"  §3 heading: "**Threshold for fleet expansion.**"
issue.observed: Two localized wording/structural defects. (a) 'the model is reloaded' as a synonym for statelessness is wrong in this context — reloading a 140 GB model per request is not a stateless-routing option; the intended meaning is that no per-session state (KV, tool outputs, retrieval context) is retained. (b) The §3 subsection titled 'Threshold for fleet expansion' never states a threshold: it introduces the agentic turn distribution and the resulting C values, but the actual expansion threshold (the λ at which one host ceases to suffice, ≈ C/W ≈ 2.0 req/s) is never given in that subsection.
issue.evidence: §4 gives the threshold implicitly ('C/W ≈ 2.0 req/s' in the queueing counterexample) and Fig 17.1's caption uses 'one host's ~2.0 req/s analytical bound', but §3's 'Threshold' subsection does not. The chapter's opening question is 'when does one host cease to suffice', so the threshold belongs where the heading promises it.
issue.correction: (a) Rewrite as 'If sessions are stateless (no KV, tool output, or retrieval context is retained between requests)'. (b) Either rename the §3 subsection to 'Agentic turns: the KV-per-request driver' or add the threshold explicitly: 'one host ceases to suffice above λ ≈ C/W ≈ 17/8.6 ≈ 2.0 req/s of admitted traffic (KV screen); the canonical peak of 40 rps is 20× that'.
issue.acceptance_test: The §3 subsection heading matches its content, and the chapter states the single-host sufficiency threshold in the same place as the question it answers.

issue.quoted_clause: **The mixed fleet needs more hosts than the single-model fleet under the shared placement (58 vs 31 — 27 extra hosts; 39 vs 21 — 18 extra — on the no-derate pair).** ... In our example, consolidation wins because the MoE and 8-bit models capture the same request classes at lower cost, and the FP16 tier handles the tail without contention.
issue.observed: §18.3.3 establishes that the shared-pool mixed fleet requires 18–27 MORE hosts than the single-model fleet, and explicitly says the token-rate saving "must be weighed against *that* placement's extra hosts' amortization and energy: total cost = host amortization + energy + token cost, not token cost alone." §18.5 then asserts, without performing that weighing, that "consolidation wins." Using the book's own only per-host cost figure ($155,817/mo ÷ 21 hosts ≈ $7,420/host/mo average; §18.3.2 basis note), 18 extra hosts ≈ $133,560/mo against a canonical-volume token saving of ≈$69,654/mo (§18.3.3 Volume basis) — i.e. the chapter's own numbers point the other way, and even the marginal (non-staff) host cost plausibly exceeds the saving.
issue.evidence: Recomputed: 155,817/21 = $7,420/host/mo; 18 × 7,420 = $133,560; 27 × 7,420 = $200,340; canonical-volume token saving $69,654/mo (§18.3.3). The chapter never states a marginal per-host cost, so the required comparison cannot be closed from the text as written.
issue.root_cause: The chapter computes a token-rate delta and a host-count delta on different bases, then lets §18.5 assert a verdict that the §18.3.3 arithmetic does not support. The verdict was written before the placement arithmetic existed and was never revised.
issue.correction: In §18.5, replace the unconditional "consolidation wins" with the conditional result the chapter's own numbers support: the mixed fleet wins on token rate but loses on total cost under the shared placement unless the extra hosts' amortization is offset by higher utilization or a cheaper hardware basis; state the sign explicitly as undetermined until a per-host marginal cost is supplied, and show the break-even (e.g. required marginal host cost ≤ $69,654/18 ≈ $3,870/host/mo). Alternatively, adopt the dedicated placement (20/32 hosts) as the worked example's placement, which is the only one whose host count is at or below the single-model fleet, and say so.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state, from §18.5 alone, which placement the chapter adopts, what the total-cost comparison is, and what the verdict is — and the verdict is consistent with §18.3.3's host counts and §18.3.2's per-host cost.

issue.page_hint: §18.3.2 (Basis note / bases box) and §18.3.3 (Mixed-fleet hourly cost)
issue.quoted_clause: The §18.3.2 per-1M price rows are per-model nominal rates for routing comparison ... priced on three different bases (self-amortized capital+energy, public-cloud list, energy-only): routing-comparison proxies, not procurement-comparable. ... the mixed-fleet *savings* conclusion in §18.3.3 depends only on the relative per-model rates, not on the absolute self-host basis.
issue.observed: The headline saving ($23.75/hr vs $12.59/hr; $8,147/mo) is computed by comparing the FP16 tier priced on "capital + energy" against the 8-bit and MoE-8-bit tiers whose Basis cell reads only "[ILLUSTRATIVE] example rate, Q4 2026 — not retrieved" — i.e. no cost basis is stated for two of the three routed tiers. The claim that the savings "depends only on the relative per-model rates" is exactly what the mixed-basis caveat denies: relative rates across different bases are not comparable. The bases box also names a "public-cloud list" basis that no row in the table uses.
issue.evidence: Table 18-2 Basis column: "capital + energy" (FP16), "[ILLUSTRATIVE] example rate" (8-bit), "[ILLUSTRATIVE] example rate" (MoE 8-bit), "energy only" (4-bit). Bases box enumerates three bases including "public-cloud list", which appears nowhere in the table. §18.3.3 then multiplies tokens by these rates across bases.
issue.root_cause: The evidence-label vocabulary ([ILLUSTRATIVE]) was substituted for the cost-basis field, so the table lost the information that makes the comparison meaningful; the reconciliation prose was added without re-deriving the comparison on a single basis.
issue.correction: Give every row an explicit cost basis (e.g. "self-amortized capital+energy, 8×H100, 3-yr amortization, 70% util") and either (a) re-price all four rows on one basis so the $23.75 vs $12.59 comparison is basis-homogeneous, or (b) state that the saving is a ratio of illustrative rates and therefore not a cost estimate at all, and remove the "$8,147/month" headline or relabel it as an illustrative rate-ratio illustration. Delete the "public-cloud list" basis from the box or add the row that uses it.
issue.acceptance_test: Every row of the §18.3.2 table carries a named cost basis; the §18.3.3 subtraction uses rows that share a basis, or is explicitly labelled as a rate-ratio illustration with no dollar claim.

issue.quoted_clause: | # instances on one 8×H100 pool (this model alone) | ... | 70B dense 8-bit | ... | 2 (70 GB weights + 24.9 GB FP16 KV = 94.9 GB > 80 GB per GPU; FP8 KV still 82.5 GB) ... The last column counts instances of that model alone on the pool; the 8-bit rows' **2** is the GPUs one instance needs (94.9 GB > 80 GB per GPU), the one per-GPU reading in the table.
issue.observed: The column header declares a unit (instances of that model alone on the 8×H100 pool) that two of the four rows violate: the 8-bit rows report 2 GPUs-per-instance, and the 4-bit row reports ~5 instances computed on a co-resident basis (see CH18-29). The explanatory note is itself incoherent ("the one per-GPU reading in the table" states no referent) and contradicts the header it is meant to clarify. A reader sizing a pool from this column would conclude that two 8-bit instances fit on the pool; in fact 8-bit alone on the pool would fit ≈6 instances (576 GB usable ÷ 94.9 GB).
issue.evidence: Recomputed 8-bit alone: (640 − 64 reserve) ÷ (70 weights + 24.89 KV) = 576/94.89 = 6.07 → 6 instances, not 2. Recomputed 4-bit alone: 576/35 = 16.4 → 16 instances, not ~5.
issue.root_cause: The column was repurposed mid-draft from "instances on the pool" to "GPUs required per instance" for the 8-bit rows, and the note was patched rather than the table restructured.
issue.correction: Split into two columns: "GPUs per instance (canonical 9.5K request)" and "instances on one 8×H100 pool (this model alone, canonical KV)", with each row's value computed on the stated basis. Delete the garbled note sentence and replace it with a one-line unit statement per column.
issue.acceptance_test: Every cell in the table has a unit that matches its column header; a reader can compute the pool's instance count for any row without consulting the prose.

issue.page_hint: §18.3.1, co-residency bullet list vs the paragraph immediately following it
issue.quoted_clause: Two 70B 4-bit GGUF (≈70 GB total; ... and hold no canonical KV reservation, so the sole-resident 436 GB KV assumption of the table above still governs the active tiers) ... **290 GB < the canonical 436 GB KV budget, so the FP16 tier cannot co-reside at the canonical profile.** KV, not weights, is the binding term: as the FP16 row above notes, that tier's KV alone is the canonical 436 GB; with the §18.3.1 co-resident weights (~350 GB) the pool's KV falls to ~226 GB and C to ~9
issue.observed: The bullet states that the 436 GB KV assumption "still governs the active tiers"; the very next paragraph states that with the co-resident weights the pool's KV falls to 226 GB and C to 9. Both cannot be true. The 436 GB figure is the FP16-tier-alone budget (640 − 140 − 64) and is void once the 8-bit, MoE-8-bit and 4-bit weights are resident. The bullet's clause is the one that survives into the reader's memory and it is the wrong one.
issue.evidence: 640 − 350 (co-resident weights) − 64 (reserve) = 226 GB; ⌊226/24.89⌋ = 9. The 436 GB figure is only valid for the FP16 tier alone: 640 − 140 − 64 = 436, ⌊436/24.89⌋ = 17.
issue.root_cause: The co-residency list was added after the table's KV budget was derived, and the bullet was written to preserve the earlier figure rather than to reflect the new configuration.
issue.correction: Delete the clause "so the sole-resident 436 GB KV assumption of the table above still governs the active tiers" and replace it with the co-resident figure: "the pool's KV budget under this configuration is 640 − 350 − 64 = 226 GB, i.e. C = 9 concurrent canonical requests (§18.3.3)". Also fix the sentence "the FP16 tier cannot co-reside at the canonical profile" — the FP16 tier IS co-resident in this list; what cannot happen is co-residing at the canonical KV profile.
issue.acceptance_test: The chapter contains exactly one KV budget for the co-resident configuration (226 GB) and one for the FP16-alone configuration (436 GB), each attached to the configuration it describes.

issue.page_hint: §18.3.1, paragraph after the co-residency bullet list
issue.quoted_clause: That is ~350 GB of weights, leaving ~290 GB for KV cache and for smaller specialized models (e.g., 22B, 8B) for classification or routing.
issue.observed: 640 − 350 = 290 GB, but the chapter's own reserve (64 GB, defined two paragraphs earlier and used in every other budget in the section) is not subtracted. The correct figure is 226 GB, which is the number the next paragraph uses. The 290 GB figure also silently ignores the weights of the "smaller specialized models (e.g., 22B, 8B)" it proposes to place in the same pool (22B FP16 ≈ 44 GB, 8B ≈ 16 GB), which would reduce KV further.
issue.evidence: 640 − 350 − 64 = 226 (matches the next paragraph). 640 − 350 = 290 (printed).
issue.root_cause: The reserve was omitted in one subtraction and included in all others; the specialized-model clause was added without re-deriving the residual.
issue.correction: Print 226 GB, state that it is net of the 64 GB reserve, and either remove the "smaller specialized models" clause or quantify it (e.g. "a 22B FP16 router at 44 GB would leave 182 GB of KV, C = 7").
issue.acceptance_test: Every KV residual in §18.3.1 is computed as 640 − weights − 64 and matches the figure used downstream.

issue.quoted_clause: Under the **dedicated** placement the ledger reverses: that same 20/32 group is at or slightly below the single-model fleet's 21/31.
issue.observed: The comparison is stated as "at or slightly below", but the policy pair is 32 vs 31 — above, not below — and the no-policy pair is 20 vs 21 — below. The sentence collapses two different comparisons into one directional claim, and the direction it asserts for the policy case is wrong.
issue.evidence: 20 vs 21 (no derate): mixed is 1 host lower. 32 vs 31 (policy): mixed is 1 host higher.
issue.root_cause: The sentence was written for the no-policy case and then extended to the policy case without rechecking the sign.
issue.correction: Rewrite: "Under the dedicated placement the ledger roughly balances: 20 hosts vs 21 for the single-model fleet without the utilization derate, and 32 vs 31 with it — the mixed fleet's advantage is at most one host, not a reduction."
issue.acceptance_test: No directional comparison in §18.3.3 or §18.5 states a sign that the printed numbers do not support.

issue.quoted_clause: A chat UI tolerates ~200 ms of added service latency per request ...
