issue.evidence: Same paragraph: 'on the book's whole-slot convention (floor 436 ÷ 24.9 = 17 slots/host) ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts'. 8 × 17 = 136; 8 × 17.51 = 140.1. The 140 figure is repeated in the Outcome paragraph.
issue.root_cause: A fractional slot count was carried into the conclusion after the convention was applied to the 21-host figure.
issue.correction: Use 136 (8 × 17) everywhere, and state the convention once so the reader can reproduce both numbers.
issue.acceptance_test: All slot counts in §3.3 use the floored per-host slot count; 140 does not appear.

issue.quoted_clause: either size B to ≥21 hosts (≥17 at 40% MFU prefill) and re-run the comparison ... the canonical peak screens (21 hosts KV / 19–22 prefill / 32 policy)
issue.observed: The scope note introduces a third canonical screen — '32 policy' — that is never defined, never used, and never reconciled. The Outcome then prescribes sizing B to ≥21 hosts, which satisfies the KV and prefill screens but not the 32-host policy screen the same section cites. The reader cannot tell what the policy screen contains (redundancy? headroom? failure domain?) or why 21 is acceptable.
issue.evidence: Scope note: '(21 hosts KV / 19–22 prefill / 32 policy)'. Outcome: 'either size B to ≥21 hosts (≥17 at 40% MFU prefill)'. Check 2 discusses failure domain (one host down) but never ties it to the 32-host figure.
issue.root_cause: A canonical screen was referenced without definition, and the worked conclusion was written against a subset of the screens.
issue.correction: Define the policy screen (what it adds over the KV and prefill floors) and either reconcile the ≥21 recommendation with it or state explicitly that 21 is the KV/prefill floor and the policy screen (32) governs the committed design.
issue.acceptance_test: Every screen named in §3.3 is defined in §3.3, and the recommended sizing satisfies or explicitly defers each named screen.

issue.quoted_clause: Instead, they opt for a targeted refinement: add a context-aware classifier that distinguishes intent-preserving prompts from injection attempts, aiming to bring PIES below 150 while keeping the false-positive rate under 1.5%.
issue.observed: The stated goal is already satisfied: PIES is 143 at Cycle 2 (Table 24-1), below the <150 target. The decision therefore has no stated unmet objective on the PIES axis, and the Red Team's recommendation to tighten thresholds 'to ~110' is likewise aimed at a metric already in compliance. The decision rationale is incoherent as written.
issue.evidence: Table 24-1: PIES 217 / 143 / 138, target < 150. §8 scenario: 'PIES has dropped from 217 to 143'. §4.1 target: '< 150 (after hardening; illustrative target, not a release gate)'.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case's decision was drafted around the false-positive rate but expressed in terms of a metric that was already compliant.
issue.correction: Restate the goal as 'hold PIES below 150 while reducing the false-positive rate below 1.5%', and make the Red Team's proposal (tighter thresholds → PIES ~110, FP 4.1%) explicitly a trade of a compliant metric for a non-compliant one.
issue.acceptance_test: The decision point names a metric that is currently out of target, and the proposed change's effect on that metric is the stated reason for the choice.

issue.quoted_clause: The loop (red team → probe → exposure → guardrails → metrics → green team) is operational, but it needs decision gates to be actionable: (1) a release-blocking severity criterion ... (2) test-corpus ownership ... (3) regression thresholds. Without these, the cycle is a ritual, not a gate.
issue.observed: The caption critiques the figure it captions, telling the reader that the depicted cycle is insufficient and that the missing elements live outside the diagram ('failed metrics spawn change-request backlog items (tracked outside this figure)'). A figure that is described as a ritual is not doing the explanatory work the chapter needs; the reader is left with a diagram the book itself disowns.
issue.evidence: Caption text as quoted; the italic note beneath repeats the same disclaimer ('tracked outside this figure').
issue.root_cause: The figure was drawn as a loop and the decision-gate content was pushed into prose rather than into the diagram.
issue.correction: Add the three gates to the diagram (a severity gate on the promotion path, a corpus-ownership node, a regression check on the loop edge) and the change-request link, then let the caption describe what the reader should learn. If the figure must stay simple, retitle the caption so it does not assert the diagram is inadequate.
issue.acceptance_test: The rendered figure shows the decision gates and the backlog link; the caption describes the diagram rather than listing what it lacks.

issue.quoted_clause: samples 1,000 retrievals per cycle (n = 1,000 certifies the <0.3% target at 95% confidence only when zero poisoned retrievals are observed; one observed event puts the 95% upper bound at ≈0.47% (one-sided) / ≈0.56% (two-sided), so that cycle cannot certify the target; 0.001 resolution)
issue.observed: The stated bounds are correct (verified below), but the text omits the zero-event bound, which is the number that actually shows how marginal the 'certification' is: with n = 1,000 and zero events the one-sided 95% upper bound is 1 − 0.05^(1/1000) ≈ 0.2996%, i.e. 0.0004 percentage points below the 0.3% target. A reader will not see that a 1,000-sample audit can essentially never certify a 0.3% target except by observing zero events, and then only barely.
issue.evidence: Recomputation (Clopper–Pearson / Poisson): x=0 → 0.5·χ²(0.05; 2)/1000 = 2.996/1000 = 0.2996%; x=1 → 0.5·χ²(0.05; 4)/1000 = 4.744/1000 = 0.4744% (one-sided) and 0.5·χ²(0.025; 4)/1000 = 5.572/1000 = 0.5572% (two-sided). All three match the printed values.
issue.root_cause: The zero-event case was described qualitatively ('certifies') rather than with the number that reveals the margin.
issue.correction: Add the zero-event bound (≈0.30%) and state the implication: certification requires zero observed events and is marginal at n = 1,000, so the sample size should be justified against the target rather than asserted.
issue.acceptance_test: The zero-event upper bound is printed and the sample-size choice is justified against the 0.3% target.

issue.quoted_clause: The Red Team can submit up to 50 poisoned chunks per evaluation cycle. Probability that a randomly retrieved chunk is poisoned: p = 50/48000 ≈ 0.00104
issue.observed: p is a per-cycle quantity, but the chapter recommends running 5–10 cycles (§5) and quarterly integrity audits (§7). Over N cycles the poison count grows linearly (10 cycles → 500 chunks → p ≈ 0.0104, ~10× the exposure), so the null model is not stationary across the evaluation program and the '52 expected hits per window' figure silently assumes a freshly poisoned corpus each cycle.
issue.evidence: §3.2: 'Q = 10,000 queries per evaluation window'; §5: 'Run at least 5 cycles'; §7: 'Schedule quarterly RAG integrity audits'. No text states whether the corpus is reset between cycles.
issue.root_cause: A single-cycle snapshot was presented as the program's exposure model.
issue.correction: State the per-cycle assumption explicitly and add one sentence on accumulation (and on whether the corpus is reset or the poison is removed between cycles).
issue.acceptance_test: The null model states the corpus state at the start of each evaluation window and how it evolves across cycles.

issue.page_hint: Ch 24, §4.2 closing line vs §3.1 scope note
issue.quoted_clause: All raw logs are stored in a local `redteam-logs/` directory with timestamps and session hashes for reproducibility.
issue.observed: 'For reproducibility' overstates what timestamps and session hashes provide — they make the log auditable and traceable, not the metric reproducible, which §3.1 explicitly denies ('The 217 is not reproducible from the text alone'). The two statements sit in tension within one chapter.
issue.evidence: §3.1 caveat (2): 'Not reproducible. The 217 is not reproducible from the text alone ... the count is an author-chosen operational rule, not a property of the deployment and not a deterministic cross-run class count.'
issue.root_cause: A storage description was given a stronger purpose claim than the chapter's own caveat supports.
issue.correction: Say 'for audit and traceability', and state what would be required for reproducibility (fixed generation order, normalization denominator, representative-selection and tie-break rules, test fixture) — the items §3.1 already lists.
issue.acceptance_test: The logging sentence and the §3.1 caveat use compatible language about reproducibility.

issue.observed: The bullet wraps a list in a code span that itself contains unescaped backticks (only the triple-backtick delimiter is escaped). In Markdown this breaks the code span and will render as stray backticks and literal text rather than a clean list of eight delimiters. Separately, the chapter mixes U+2011 non-breaking hyphens ('Prompt‑Injection', 'style‑steganography', 'Poisoned‑hit', 'Red‑team', 'Tool‑use', 'Cross‑entry‑point', 'Human‑in‑the‑loop') with ASCII hyphens used for the same terms elsewhere in the same tables ('prompt-injection', 'guardrail-trigger rate'), which will show as inconsistent typography and will break search and index generation.
issue.evidence: Raw source shows the nested-backtick construct; the hyphen inconsistency is visible between the §4.1 metric names and the §3.1/§7 headings.
issue.root_cause: Markdown escaping was applied inconsistently, and text was pasted with non-breaking hyphens from a word processor.
issue.correction: Render the eight delimiters as a plain inline list (or a small table) with no code-span wrapper; normalize all hyphens in Ch 23–24 to ASCII hyphens (or to a single declared typographic convention) and re-check the index.
issue.acceptance_test: The rendered page shows eight clean delimiters with no stray backticks; a search for U+2011 across the manuscript returns zero hits.

issue.page_hint: Ch 24, Fig 24.1 caption vs Ch 23, Fig 23.1 caption and note
issue.quoted_clause: ![Fig 24.1 - Red Team / Green Team cycle. ...] ... ![Fig 23.1 — From vague ask to architectural bounds. ...] [ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual
issue.observed: Caption dash style is inconsistent (hyphen in Fig 24.1, em dash in Fig 23.1 and in both table captions). Fig 23.1's caption and the italic note beneath it both end with the label '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual' and both restate the same flow, so the label is duplicated and the note largely repeats the caption.
issue.evidence: Fig 23.1 caption ends '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual'; the italic note beneath also ends '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual' and re-describes 'broad ask → five question gates → quantified bounds → the decisions those bounds unlock'.
issue.root_cause: Caption and note were authored independently; the house label convention was applied to both.
issue.correction: Use the em dash in all figure captions; keep one evidence label per figure (on the caption) and trim the note to what the caption does not say.
issue.acceptance_test: All figure captions use the same dash; no figure carries two evidence labels.

issue.quoted_clause: Roughly how many questions per second at the busiest minute? ... If everyone on the sales floor asked at once, maybe 40 a second.
issue.observed: The answer conflates a burst of requests with a sustained rate: 'everyone asked at once' describes a one-off burst of N requests, not N requests per second sustained. The canonical peak (40 rps) is then used throughout the book as a rate (Ch 24: 40 rps × 8.6 s = 344 in-flight), so the derivation of the book's most reused number is imprecise at its source.
issue.evidence: Ch 24 §3.3 uses 40 rps as a rate for both prefill demand (40 × 1.288 PFLOP) and KV residency (40 × 8.6 s).
issue.root_cause: The elicitation question asked for a rate but the answer supplied a burst count, and the chapter did not close the gap.
issue.correction: Have the architect elicit a sustained rate ('how many requests per second, sustained, at the busiest minute?') and, if the customer only knows a burst count, convert it explicitly (burst size ÷ burst duration) and record the conversion as an assumption.
issue.acceptance_test: The 40 rps peak traces to an explicit rate statement or a documented burst→rate conversion.

issue.quoted_clause: 6 role‑play templates (`You are a rogue AI`, `Ignore previous instructions`, `You are now DAN`, `Pretend you are unbound`, `system:`, `user: override`)
issue.observed: Two of the six entries ('system:', 'user: override') are role/prefix-override patterns, not role-play templates; the category label is inaccurate for the contents, which matters because the class count (217) and the dedup rule are defined over these categories.
issue.evidence: The list mixes persona framings ('You are now DAN') with instruction-override and prefix-spoofing patterns ('Ignore previous instructions', 'system:').
issue.root_cause: The generator's category names were not checked against their members.
issue.correction: Rename the category (e.g., 'instruction-override templates') or move the two prefix patterns into the delimiter category and restate the 768 count accordingly.
issue.acceptance_test: Every generator category name accurately describes all of its members, and the 768 total is reproducible from the restated categories.

issue.quoted_clause: Fleet-level effect: the peak KV-residency screen moves from 21 hosts to ~11 (344 in-flight ÷ 35.0 concurrent per host = 9.8, +N−1); ADR 0015 R1 must be re-screened on adoption.
issue.observed: The ADR draft states the fleet-level effect as a move from 21 hosts to ~11 hosts, and never states which prefill case the FP8-KV lever relieves. The scenario instruction immediately above asks the reader to 'state which case this ADR's FP8-KV lever relieves, and note FP8 KV does not shrink the case (ii) prefill screen' — the draft never answers it.
issue.evidence: Re-derivation from the book's own screens: KV screen = 21 hosts (case-independent); prefill screen = 19 hosts (case i) / 22 hosts (case ii) (ADR 0015 R1, restated in this mini-case's Alternatives #1). Fleet size is the max of the two screens. With FP8 KV the KV screen becomes ceil(344/35.0)+1 = 11, so the fleet becomes max(11,19) = 19 hosts under case (i) and max(11,22) = 22 hosts under case (ii). The printed '21 hosts → ~11 hosts' is therefore not a fleet-level effect under either case; it is only the KV screen alone, and the fleet does not shrink to 11 in either case.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case conflates a single screen with the fleet-level binding constraint, and the scenario's own diagnostic question (which case does the lever relieve?) is left unanswered in the draft ADR.
issue.correction: Rewrite the Fleet-level effect bullet as: 'the KV-residency screen moves from 21 hosts to ~11 (ceil(344/35.0)+1); the fleet is bounded below by the prefill screen, so the fleet becomes 19 hosts under case (i) (prefill-bound) and remains 22 hosts under case (ii) (prefill-bound, unaffected by FP8 KV). FP8 KV therefore relieves the KV screen only, and only in case (i).' Add an explicit 'Case affected: (i) only' line to the Context or Decision.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case draft contains an explicit statement of which case the lever relieves, and the host-count statement equals max(KV screen, prefill screen) for both cases (19 and 22), with the arithmetic shown.

issue.page_hint: Ch 25 §8 (mini-case), Scenario paragraph and ADR 0017 → Context
issue.quoted_clause: The concurrency ceiling is now limiting throughput below the target request rate. ... To reach the target request rate we need either more host capacity or more KV residency per host.
issue.observed: The scenario and the ADR Context both assert that KV concurrency is currently limiting throughput below the target request rate. The book's own numbers say the opposite: the canonical fleet is already sized for the peak.
issue.evidence: Peak in-flight requirement = 40 rps × 8.6 s = 344 requests (book's own figure). KV screen = ceil(344/17.5)+1 = ceil(19.66)+1 = 21 hosts (ADR 0015 R1, restated in this mini-case). Capacity at 21 hosts = 21 × 17.5 = 367.5 concurrent ≥ 344 required. So the KV concurrency ceiling is not binding at the canonical 40 rps peak with the canonical 21-host fleet; the fleet is sized to meet it. The mini-case's own Alternatives #1 then says 'the canonical peak already needs 21 hosts on the KV screen ... so "adding a second host" misunderstands the scale', which contradicts the Context's premise.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case's motivating premise was written from a per-host view (one host holds 17.5, target needs 344) without reconciling it against the fleet-level screen the same chapter quotes.
issue.correction: Restate the premise accurately: 'per-host KV concurrency (17.5) is the binding constraint on how much of the fleet's KV budget can be used; at the canonical 21-host fleet the KV screen is exactly met (367.5 ≥ 344), so FP8 KV is a cost/capacity-efficiency lever (19 hosts under case (i)), not a remedy for an unmet target.' Alternatively, if the intent is that the fleet is currently under-provisioned, state the current fleet size and the unmet demand explicitly.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case's Context contains no sentence asserting that the target request rate is currently unreachable; the fleet-level arithmetic (hosts × per-host concurrency vs 344 in-flight) is shown and is consistent with the 21-host screen.

issue.quoted_clause: Render the KV cache in FP16 for the long-context decode path, keeping prefill and the retrieval/prompt phase in FP16.
issue.observed: The Decision splits the KV cache by phase ('FP8 for the long-context decode path, keeping prefill ... in FP16'). The KV cache is *produced* during prefill and *consumed* during decode; it is a single stored state, not a per-phase one. As written, the decision is not implementable and implies a prefill-time FP16 KV that then becomes FP8.
issue.evidence: Mechanism: prefill computes K and V for the prompt and writes them into the cache; decode appends one token's K/V per step and reads the whole cache. The precision choice is a storage-format choice applied at write time (and inherited by all later reads). There is no 'FP16 prefill KV' that coexists with an 'FP8 decode KV' for the same sequence.
issue.root_cause: Phase-scoped phrasing of a state-scoped decision.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'Store the KV cache in FP8 (E4M3 with per-tensor/per-head scales) for all sequences, including the prefill-produced K/V; the prefill computation itself remains in BF16/FP16 and the K/V tensors are quantized on write into the cache.' Optionally note that K is more quantization-sensitive than V and that per-head scaling is the usual mitigation.
issue.acceptance_test: The Decision names the storage format of the cache and the write-time quantization point; no sentence implies two coexisting KV precisions for one sequence.

issue.quoted_clause: This chapter recommends that each ADR include at least two derived quantities — quantities computed from raw data, not merely observed.
issue.observed: The definition ('computed from raw data') does not describe either of the two examples given. Both examples are analytical derivations from published specifications (parameter count × bytes/param), not computations over measured data.
issue.evidence: Item 1: W = 70 × 10^9 × 2 B = 140 GB — derived from a model specification, not raw data. Item 2: 2 B/param → 1 B/param → ~70 GB — likewise a specification-derived calculation. The chapter's own evidence taxonomy (Ch 4 / Appendix A) separates [DERIVED] from measurement; the sentence conflates 'derived' with 'measured'.
issue.root_cause: The recommendation's definition was written for measurement and then illustrated with analytical derivations.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'each ADR should include at least two derived quantities — quantities computed from stated inputs (specifications, measurements, or a mix) rather than asserted — and should state which of the two kinds each one is.' Then mark item 1 as analytical-from-specification and item 2 as analytical-from-specification, and add one genuinely measured quantity (e.g. the p99 TTFT from the Ch 14 load test) to show the contrast.
issue.acceptance_test: The definition sentence is satisfied by both listed examples as printed, or the examples are re-labelled to match the definition.

issue.page_hint: Ch 25 §6, ADR 0015 → Context (parenthetical on request volume)
issue.quoted_clause: at the canonical 6.24M requests/mo (business-hours basis: 10 rps average × 8 h × 260 workdays, Ch 16 arithmetic — so the monthly denominator averages ~2.4 rps, while the 21-host capacity screen is peak-sized at 40 rps)
issue.observed: The stated basis does not produce the stated volume. 10 rps × 8 h × 3600 s/h × 260 workdays = 74.88M requests, which is 12× the printed 6.24M requests/mo. The parenthetical is an annual figure presented as the monthly basis.
issue.evidence: 10 × 8 × 3600 × 260 = 74,880,000 requests per year; 74.88M / 12 = 6.24M requests per month — so the printed monthly volume is correct and the parenthetical is missing the annual→monthly step. Cross-check: 6.24M / (30 × 86400 s) = 2.407 rps, matching the printed '~2.4 rps' monthly average. The $/1K figures are therefore correct (155.8/6.24 = 24.97; 87.6/6.24 = 14.04; 129.8/6.24 = 20.80) and are not affected; only the derivation as printed is wrong.
issue.root_cause: Period slip in the volume derivation (per-year workdays used to justify a per-month denominator).
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'at the canonical 6.24M requests/mo (business-hours basis: 10 rps average × 8 h × 260 workdays per year = 74.88M requests/yr = 6.24M requests/mo; the monthly denominator therefore averages ~2.4 rps across the full month, while the 21-host capacity screen is peak-sized at 40 rps)'.
issue.acceptance_test: The parenthetical's arithmetic, evaluated as printed, yields 6.24M requests/mo; a reader recomputing it gets the printed number without an unstated ÷12.

issue.page_hint: Fig 25.1 caption (Ch 25 §6) vs Ch 25 §1 and Table 25-1
issue.quoted_clause: an ADR is a fixed five-field record — Title & status, Context (the situation), Decision (the choice), Consequences (the effects), Alternatives (the rejected options) — and it is *kept, not edited*
issue.observed: 'Kept, not edited' contradicts the chapter's own status-tracking practice. §1 says ADRs are 'living, reviewed in pull requests'; Table 25-1's fix for 'No status tracking' is to 'update the ADR status and add a superseding ADR link'; and the ADR 0015 falsification path says a successor 'lifts the HOLD and supersedes this one' — a status edit.
issue.evidence: The distinction the figure needs is between rewriting the historical reasoning (forbidden) and updating the record's lifecycle metadata (status, supersession link, review date) (required). The caption as written forbids the latter.
issue.root_cause: The caption compressed 'the original record is not rewritten' into 'not edited', losing the lifecycle-metadata distinction.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'and it is *kept, not rewritten*: the reasoning of a superseded ADR is preserved verbatim, while only its status, supersession link and review date are updated.'
issue.acceptance_test: The figure caption and Table 25-1 can be read together without contradiction; the caption explicitly permits status/supersession updates.

issue.page_hint: Ch 25 §1 (status list), §3.1 (template '## Status' line), §6 (ADR 0015 Status field)
issue.quoted_clause: **Title** and status (proposed, accepted, superseded, deprecated) ... ## Status <proposed | accepted | superseded | deprecated>  (date) ... **Status:** **HOLD** — screened, not committed.
issue.observed: HOLD is used as a Status value in ADR 0015 and defended in the DECISION STATE callout ('Writing HOLD into the Status field is the correct, auditable record'), but HOLD is not in the enumerated status vocabulary in §1 and is not an option in the copy-ready template's Status line. A reader copying the template cannot record the very state the chapter calls correct.
issue.evidence: §1 enumerates four statuses; the template offers exactly those four; ADR 0015 uses a fifth. The callout asserts HOLD is 'the correct, auditable record' without reconciling it with the format the chapter defines.
issue.root_cause: The HOLD state was introduced by the canonical-scenario material without being added to the format definition.
issue.correction: Add HOLD to the status vocabulary in §1 and to the template's Status line, with a one-line definition ('HOLD — screened, not committed; exit criteria recorded'), and note in §1 that HOLD is a first-class status rather than a misuse of 'proposed'. Alternatively, define HOLD as 'proposed' plus an explicit 'exit criteria' block and say so.
issue.acceptance_test: Every status value used anywhere in Ch 25 appears in the §1 list and in the template's Status line.

issue.page_hint: Ch 25 §7 (What We Still Don't Know), 'Tooling gaps' bullet
issue.quoted_clause: **Tooling gaps:** [1P][FACT] — no widely adopted tool exists for ADR graph visualization or impact analysis (a factual tooling observation, not an open hypothesis).
issue.observed: A claim of universal absence is labelled [1P][FACT] with no first-party source and no date. '[1P]' denotes a first-party specification or artifact; no first-party artifact can attest that no tool exists. The claim is also undated in a field where tooling changes quarterly.
issue.evidence: The claim is a survey assertion, not a first-party fact. It is also the only [1P][FACT] in a section that otherwise lists open hypotheses, and the section's own framing ('the open items have no FACT instrumentation yet') sits awkwardly with a FACT-labelled absence claim.
issue.root_cause: The label was chosen to signal 'this is not speculation', but the taxonomy's provenance axis does not have a slot for 'surveyed absence'.
issue.correction: Either (a) relabel as [FACT] with a dated observation ('as of <month year>, no tool with broad adoption provides ADR dependency-graph visualization; the common practice remains hand-maintained indexes') and cite the survey or the absence of one, or (b) move it into the open-question list as 'Is there a maintained tool for ADR dependency-graph analysis, and what would it need to model?'
issue.acceptance_test: The bullet carries a date and a source, or is reclassified as an open question; no [1P] label is attached to a claim of absence.

issue.quoted_clause: **70B FP16 model footprint** — $W = N \times \text{bytes-per-param} = 70 \times 10^9 \times 2 \text{ B} = 140$ GB parameters
issue.observed: The derived quantity is labelled 'FP16' although ADR 0016's decision is BF16, and the same 140 GB figure is labelled '[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]' in ADR 0016's Evidence Tags but bare '[DERIVED]' here. The number is right (both formats are 2 B/param); the labels are not.
issue.evidence: ADR 0016 Decision: 'Render the serving model in BF16.' The chapter's own point is that the footprint is format-invariant, so naming the quantity after one of the two formats invites exactly the misreading the ADR exists to prevent.
issue.root_cause: The measurement section was written before the ADR's decision was fixed, and the label set was not carried over.
issue.correction: Rename to '**70B weight footprint at 16-bit (FP16 or BF16)**' and use the same evidence label as ADR 0016 ('[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]'), or state explicitly that the quantity is invariant across the two candidate formats.
issue.acceptance_test: The quantity's name and label match ADR 0016's decision and Evidence Tags; no reader can infer that the footprint depends on the FP16/BF16 choice.

issue.quoted_clause: The fleet runs a 70-billion-parameter dense model for RAG Q&A serving on an 8×H100 host (640 GB). ... The fleet serves the canonical RAG Q&A workload on an 8×H100 host.
issue.observed: Both passages describe 'the fleet' as a single 8×H100 host, while the canonical fleet in the same chapter is 21 hosts (32 under the N−1 policy). The per-host figure is being used with fleet-level nouns.
issue.evidence: ADR 0015 R1: 21 hosts (KV screen) / 32 hosts (N−1 policy). §8 mini-case: 'the canonical peak already needs 21 hosts on the KV screen'.
issue.root_cause: Per-host and fleet-level quantities share the same noun phrase.
issue.correction: Rewrite as 'serving on 8×H100 hosts (640 GB of HBM per host; the canonical fleet is 21 hosts — see ADR 0015 R1)' in §3, and 'on 8×H100 hosts' in the mini-case scenario.
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 25 uses 'the fleet' to denote a single host.

issue.quoted_clause: This alone often reveals overlooked options or clarifies why the chosen path is genuinely optimal.
issue.observed: Articulating alternatives does not establish optimality; it establishes that alternatives were considered and why they were rejected. The claim overstates what the practice can deliver.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own worked records demonstrate the point: ADR 0015 explicitly declines to rank the three delivery modes ('NOT COMPARABLE — scopes unmatched'), and ADR 0016's FP8 alternative is 'deferred', not rejected on merit. Neither record claims optimality.
issue.root_cause: Rhetorical strengthening of a modest, correct claim.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'This alone often reveals overlooked options, or makes explicit that the chosen path is the best of the options actually considered — which is a weaker and more defensible claim than optimality.'
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 25 asserts that an ADR establishes optimality.

issue.quoted_clause: The format was popularized by Michael Nygard and has been adopted by teams ranging from startups to enterprises managing complex AI/ML stacks.
issue.observed: A historical attribution and a broad adoption claim are stated without a citation, a date, or an evidence label, in a chapter that otherwise applies the book's evidence taxonomy rigorously (ADR 0016 Evidence Tags, §7 [1P][FACT]).
issue.evidence: The Nygard attribution is checkable against a primary source (Nygard, 'Documenting Architecture Decisions', 2011). The adoption claim ('startups to enterprises') is an unsourced generalization about the whole industry.
issue.root_cause: The chapter's evidence discipline was applied to the worked records but not to its own narrative claims.
issue.correction: Cite the primary source for the format's origin (with year) and either source the adoption claim or replace it with a bounded statement ('the format has been adopted in both small-team and large-organisation settings').
issue.acceptance_test: Every factual attribution in §1 carries a citation or an evidence label consistent with the book's taxonomy.

issue.page_hint: Ch 25 §3.1 (template, '## Evidence' block) and §4 (final paragraph of Measurement)
issue.quoted_clause:
- <claim> — FACT/DERIVED/HYPOTHESIS
  [1P]/[2°]/(to be verified) ... Each derived quantity should be tagged with its evidence source [1P]/[2°]/(to be verified)
issue.observed: '(to be verified)' is used as if it were a member of the book's evidence-label vocabulary, but the vocabulary defined in Ch 4 / Appendix A uses [UNRESOLVED] on the status axis. The template therefore teaches a label the book does not define, and the §4 sentence mixes a placeholder with two defined provenance labels.
issue.evidence: House taxonomy: provenance [1P] [2°] [LAB] [ILLUSTRATIVE]; status [FACT] [DERIVED] [ASSUMPTION] [HYPOTHESIS] [UNRESOLVED]. '(to be verified)' is not among them.
issue.root_cause: A template placeholder was promoted into the label list in prose.
issue.correction: In the template, write '[1P]/[2°]/[LAB] + status: FACT/DERIVED/ASSUMPTION/HYPOTHESIS/UNRESOLVED' and, in §4, replace '(to be verified)' with '[UNRESOLVED]'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every label string that appears in Ch 25 is a member of the Ch 4 / Appendix A vocabulary.

issue.quoted_clause: Ch. 8's "memory-bound" = low arithmetic intensity ... (Ch. 15) ... (Ch. 16/17/20) ... (Ch. 15, Ch. 17)
issue.observed: Cross-references in the mini-case use 'Ch. N' with a period, while the rest of the chapter uses 'Ch N' without one ('Ch 16', 'Ch 17', 'Ch 22', 'Ch 7', 'Ch 4', 'Ch 14'). The mini-case also quotes Ch 8's term 'memory-bound' while the chapter's own prose uses 'bandwidth-bound'.
issue.evidence: Inconsistent citation form within one chapter; and two different terms for the same regime ('memory-bound' vs 'bandwidth-bound') with the quoted form attributed to another chapter.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case was drafted separately from the chapter body and did not inherit its citation and terminology conventions.
issue.correction: Normalize to 'Ch N' throughout Ch 25, and either adopt 'bandwidth-bound' throughout with a one-time note that Ch 8 uses 'memory-bound', or use 'memory-bandwidth-bound' consistently.
issue.acceptance_test: All chapter cross-references in Ch 25 use one form; the decode-regime term is used identically in Ch 25 and in the quoted Ch 8 passage.

issue.page_hint: Ch 25 §3 (ADR 0016 → Evidence Tags) and §8 (ADR 0017 → Evidence Tags)
issue.quoted_clause: [canonical scenario][DERIVED] — weight residency is unchanged by the FP16↔BF16 choice. ... [canonical scenario][DERIVED] — at ~2.62 MB/token a 9,500-token request needs ~24.9 GB FP16 KV
issue.observed: The provenance label is written in lower case ('[canonical scenario]') whereas the book's canonical vocabulary uses the upper-case token '[CANONICAL]'.
issue.evidence: House vocabulary: [CANONICAL] [DERIVED] [ILLUSTRATIVE] [ASSUMPTION] [1P] [HYPOTHESIS]. A case-sensitive label-matching tool (or a reader building a label index) will not match '[canonical scenario]'.
issue.root_cause: Free-text spelling of a defined label token.
issue.correction: Use '[CANONICAL]' in both places.
issue.acceptance_test: All label tokens in Ch 25 match the Ch 4 / Appendix A vocabulary exactly, including case.

issue.quoted_clause: the Consequences of ADR-001 may become part of the Context of ADR-002, which supersedes it while the original stays on file.
issue.observed: The figure uses the identifier form 'ADR-001'/'ADR-002' while the chapter's records use 'ADR 0015', 'ADR 0016', 'ADR 0017'. Two identifier formats for the same object type in one chapter.
issue.evidence: §3: 'ADR 0016 — Model Precision'; §6: 'ADR 0015 — Delivery mode...'; §8: 'ADR 0017 — KV Cache Precision'. The figure's hyphenated form also implies zero-padding to three digits, which the chapter's own numbering (0015–0017) does follow, so the difference is purely the separator.
issue.root_cause: Figure artwork and body text were authored with different identifier conventions.
issue.correction: Pick one form (recommend 'ADR-0016', matching the figure's zero-padded convention and the §6 'ADR 0015 R1' style reference) and apply it in the body, or change the figure to 'ADR 0015'/'ADR 0016'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every ADR identifier in Ch 25, including inside the figure, uses one separator convention.

issue.quoted_clause: so the KV read is a secondary ~15% term (~15% of batch-1 decode reads; halving it cuts total read traffic ≈7.5% at batch 1) and intensity is ~1 FLOP/byte.
issue.observed: The bullet states '~15%' twice in one sentence, and packs five distinct quantitative claims (KV share of batch-1 reads, traffic reduction at batch 1, batch-1 intensity, KV-dominant share at C≈17.5, traffic reduction and intensity change at C≈17.5) into a single ~120-word bullet that mixes two operating points.
issue.evidence: The arithmetic is correct (24.9/164.9 = 15.1%; 12.45/164.9 = 7.6%; 140 GFLOP/164.9 GB = 0.85 FLOP/byte; 17.5 × 24.9 = 435.6 GB vs 140 GB; 575.6 → 357.8 GB = −37.8%; 2450/575.6 = 4.26 → 2450/357.8 = 6.85 FLOP/byte). The problem is presentational: the reader must hold two operating points (batch 1 and C≈17.5) in one bullet, and the duplicated '~15%' reads as an editing artifact.
issue.root_cause: Two operating-point analyses were merged into one bullet during drafting.
issue.correction: Split into two bullets — 'At batch 1 (weight-dominated)' and 'At the ADR's operating point C ≈ 17.5 (KV-dominated)' — each with its own numbers, and delete the duplicated '~15%'. A small two-row table (operating point | weight bytes | KV bytes | total | traffic change | intensity) would read faster than prose.
issue.acceptance_test: Each operating point's numbers appear in one place; no figure is stated twice in the same sentence.

issue.quoted_clause: Adopting GQA would cut KV per token by ~8× (the largest single capacity lever in this book, Ch 16)
issue.observed: The '~8×' is not checkable from the text: the target group count is never given, and the reader is not told whether the comparison is against the canonical 64 KV-heads or against a hypothetical 8-head GQA model.
issue.evidence: The canonical geometry is 64 KV-heads (stated in the same bullet). 64 → 8 KV-heads (GQA-8) gives exactly 8×; 64 → 4 (GQA-16) gives 16×. The lever magnitude therefore depends entirely on the target group count, which is the actual architectural decision.
issue.root_cause: The comparison was compressed to a ratio without the parameter that determines it.
issue.correction: Write: 'Adopting GQA with 8 KV-heads (GQA-8) would cut KV per token by 8× (64 → 8 heads); GQA-16 would give 16×. The group count is itself a model-architecture decision and must be fixed before the KV budget can be sized.'
issue.acceptance_test: The KV reduction factor is stated together with the target KV-head count and the baseline head count.

issue.quoted_clause: ## Architecture Decision Context  (from Ch 22's loop) ... These five are the *core* fields. ... the template adds Evidence, decision owner, validation, rollback, review trigger, and falsification path — without changing the core.
issue.observed: The template renames the core 'Context' field to 'Architecture Decision Context' and the chapter asserts the template 'does not change the core'. A reader mapping the template back to the five core fields has to guess that the renamed block is the Context field.
issue.evidence: §1's five core fields: Title and status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives considered. The template's blocks: Status, Decision, Architecture Decision Context, Alternatives considered, Evidence, Trade-offs & consequences, Decision owner, Validation plan, Rollback plan, Review trigger, Falsification path. 'Trade-offs & consequences' is likewise a renamed 'Consequences'.
issue.root_cause: The template was extended from Ch 22's loop vocabulary without an explicit mapping back to the ADR core fields.
issue.correction: Add a one-line mapping note under the template: 'Core-field mapping: Status → Title & status; Architecture Decision Context → Context; Decision → Decision; Trade-offs & consequences → Consequences; Alternatives considered → Alternatives considered.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can map every template block to one of the five core fields without inference.

issue.quoted_clause: A100 and H100 GPUs natively support BF16 and TF32 on their Tensor Cores. There is no "next GPU generation" required and no explicit-casting penalty; the premise that these formats wait for future hardware is itself the kind of error an ADR should catch.
issue.observed: TF32 is a matmul *compute* format (19-bit: 8-bit exponent, 10-bit mantissa) used inside Tensor Core instructions; it is not a weight-storage format and is not an alternative to FP16 or BF16 for holding weights. Listing it in a storage-precision ADR invites the reader to treat TF32 as a third candidate precision.
issue.evidence: The ADR's decision is about the format in which weights are stored and served; the relevant hardware facts are BF16 Tensor Core support (Ampere and later) and FP8 support (Hopper and later). TF32's role is in the training matmul path, which the ADR's 'operational consistency' rationale already references separately.
issue.root_cause: A hardware-capability fact was listed without checking whether the format is a candidate for the decision at hand.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'A100 and H100 Tensor Cores support BF16 natively (Ampere onward), so no hardware change is required and no runtime casting penalty applies.' If TF32 is mentioned, add one clause: 'TF32 is a matmul compute format, not a weight-storage format, and is therefore not a candidate for this decision.'
issue.acceptance_test: Every format named in ADR 0016 is a candidate for the decision being recorded, or is explicitly marked as not a candidate.

issue.page_hint: Ch 25 §8 (mini-case), ADR 0017 → Context; and Ch 25 §6, ADR 0015 → R2
issue.quoted_clause: Ch. 17 shows that ~40 rps at the canonical ~8.6 s service time implies ~344 in-flight requests ... R2 | TTFT ≤ 2 s (p95), ~25 ms/token decode
issue.observed: The 8.6 s service time is used to size the fleet, but the chapter never shows how it decomposes against the stated SLO (TTFT ≤ 2 s p95 plus ~25 ms/token decode over 300 output tokens, which alone implies 7.5 s of decode and a ~9.5 s SLO envelope). A reader cannot tell whether 8.6 s is a measured mean, a p95, or an SLO-derived figure, and whether it is consistent with the R2 SLO.
issue.evidence: 300 tokens × 25 ms = 7.5 s decode; 8.6 s − 7.5 s = 1.1 s implied TTFT, which is inside the 2 s SLO but is nowhere stated. The distinction matters because the fleet screen is driven by in-flight count (rate × service time), so a mean-vs-p95 mismatch here propagates into the 21-host screen and the 344-request figure.
issue.root_cause: A canonical service-time value is imported from Ch 15/17 without its measurement basis or its relation to the SLO decomposition being restated where it is used for sizing.
issue.correction: State the decomposition at first use in Ch 25: 'the canonical ~8.6 s service time (≈1.1 s TTFT + 300 × ~25 ms decode, measured at the Ch 14 load test) implies ~344 in-flight requests at 40 rps', and note whether it is a mean or a percentile.
issue.acceptance_test: The 8.6 s figure is accompanied by its TTFT/decode decomposition and its statistic (mean vs p95) at the point where it is used for fleet sizing.

issue.quoted_clause: **Reasoned quality optimization:** the discipline of improving an architecture decision's quality by forcing the articulation of alternatives and evidence, so the trade-off surface is explicit rather than tacit.
issue.observed: The bullet label ('Reasoned quality optimization') does not name what the bullet is about, and the sentence is a definitional gloss of its own label rather than a consequence. The other bullets in the list are consequences with a subject and a verb ('New engineers can audit...', 'Engineers no longer need to re-derive...').
issue.evidence: The bullet's actual content — that alternatives and evidence are made explicit — is a genuine consequence, but it is stated as a tautology ('the discipline of improving ... quality by forcing ...').
issue.root_cause: A term was imported as a heading without being turned into a claim.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: '**Explicit trade-off surface:** forcing the articulation of alternatives and evidence turns tacit reasoning into a reviewable artifact, so a decision can be challenged on its reasoning rather than on its outcome.'
issue.acceptance_test: Each bullet in §6 states a consequence with a subject and a predicate; no bullet is a definition of its own label.

issue.quoted_clause: "a cache miss is served by the engine at ~250 ms" ... "250 ≈ 120 + 80 + 50" ... "a cache hit returns at a fixed ~50 ms (query encoding + cache lookup, no corpus retrieval and no LLM prefill)"
issue.observed: The two-point latency model charges the ~50 ms term to the HIT path as "query encoding + cache lookup" and to the MISS path as the same 50 ms term, but the miss path must pay BOTH the semantic-cache lookup (encoding + nearest-neighbour search) AND the corpus retrieval that the baseline paid. The miss path is therefore 120 + 80 + 50 (retrieval) + 50 (lookup) = 300 ms, not 250 ms.
issue.evidence: Recomputation from the chunk's own stated components: baseline = model compute 320 + I/O 80 + retrieval 50 = 450 ms (§8 Step 1). With the cache installed, a miss incurs the cache lookup (explicitly priced at ~50 ms in §3 Pattern B: "its hit path pays query encoding + cache lookup (the ~50 ms term of §26.8 Step 2)") plus the 50 ms corpus retrieval. Miss = 120 + 80 + 50 + 50 = 300 ms. Then p99 = 300 ms (not 250), mean = 0.35×50 + 0.65×300 = 212.5 ms (not 180), and the headline reduction = (450 − 300)/450 = 33.3% (not ≈44%). The chunk's own §8 Step 1 already computes the analogous sensitivity for the retrieval term ("excluding that term from the baseline only ... would report 37.5%"), which shows the author is aware that component accounting drives the headline — but the lookup term was never given the same treatment.
issue.root_cause: The model conflates two distinct 50 ms components (corpus retrieval vs. semantic-cache lookup) into a single undifferentiated "50 ms" slot, so the cache's own overhead is invisible on the miss path. This is an event-trace accounting error, not a rounding error.
issue.correction: Give the two 50 ms terms separate names and separate lines in the miss path: miss = 120 (compute) + 80 (I/O) + 50 (corpus retrieval) + 50 (cache lookup) = 300 ms; hit = 50 (cache lookup, retrieval skipped). Recompute mean (212.5 ms), p99 (300 ms) and the headline reduction (≈33%), and add a sensitivity line showing the headline under the alternative assumption that the lookup is free or merged into the 80 ms I/O term. If the author intends the lookup to be free, that must be stated as an explicit assumption, because it is the assumption that makes the cache look good.
issue.acceptance_test: The two-point model in render/capstone_calc.py enumerates every component on both paths; the miss path's component list contains both a retrieval term and a cache-lookup term; the printed mean, p99 and percentage equal the values recomputed from that list; and the §3 headline, the §8 Step 2 numbers, the Fig 26.2 takeaway and Table 26-2 all carry the same p99 and the same percentage.

issue.quoted_clause: "Under that assumption compute falls from the inflated 320 ms to ~120 ms, so 250 ≈ 120 + 80 + 50 — and the ~120 ms is a scenario input, not a derived queueing result."
issue.observed: The 200 ms reduction in the compute term (320 → 120 ms) is attributed to "queue drain" when offered load falls from ρ≈1 to ρ≈0.65. This is impossible under any queueing model consistent with the baseline: if the observed 320 ms at ρ≈1 contains queueing delay, then the underlying service time S satisfies S ≤ 320 ms and the observed time at ρ=0.65 must be ≥ S. The chunk asserts the observed time at ρ=0.65 is 120 ms < S. The compute term therefore falls below its own service-time floor.
issue.evidence: M/M/1 with S = 320 ms: at ρ = 0.65 the expected response time is S/(1−ρ) = 320/0.35 ≈ 914 ms, i.e. queueing delay alone is ≈594 ms — the opposite sign from the chunk's claim. Even under a much more favourable model (batching absorbing bursts), the observed time at ρ=0.65 cannot be less than the service time observed at ρ=1. The chunk's own §8 Step 1 says the 320 ms "is the declared worst-case component sum ... carrying prefill-queue inflation at ρ near 1", so the queue component is explicitly inside the 320 ms. The entire −44% headline rests on this one unexplained 200 ms.
issue.root_cause: The queueing model was never written down. A 200 ms queue-drain was asserted to produce a desired headline rather than derived from a stated arrival/service model, and the ρ values were attached afterwards.
issue.correction: Either (a) supply an explicit queueing model (service-time distribution, arrival process, batching policy, and the queueing term's contribution at ρ = 1 and ρ = 0.65) and derive both 320 ms and 120 ms from it, or (b) restate the comparison honestly: the baseline is an overloaded operating point (ρ ≈ 1) and the cached configuration is a stable one (ρ ≈ 0.65), so the comparison is "overloaded vs. stable", not "cache effect". The chunk already contains the sentence that supports (b) — "a matched-load run (2.0 rps with and without the cache) would isolate the smaller path-substitution effect this model does not claim" — and that sentence should govern the headline rather than a footnote.
issue.acceptance_test: Either a queueing derivation appears in the chapter (or an appendix) from which both 320 ms and 120 ms follow, or the headline percentage is restated as an overloaded-vs-stable comparison with the matched-load caveat promoted into the headline and into §3 and the Fig 26.2 takeaway.

issue.page_hint: Ch 26 §3 (Worked Example — Capstone Scenario; Capstone Execution)
issue.quoted_clause: "Take the canonical deployment: ~2,000 registered users with ~5% concurrently active at peak (~100 concurrent users, a population measure) ... The result: one 8×H100 serving host + a 35% semantic response cache + circuit breaker yields an illustrative p99 TTFT ≈ 250 ms versus the ~450 ms uncached single-node baseline"
issue.observed: §3 frames the capstone as the canonical deployment and then reports a single-host result, but the arithmetic behind that result comes from §8's explicitly non-canonical short-prompt workload at ~2 rps. The canonical peak offered load quoted in the same section is ~40 rps, which one host (ceiling ~2.0 rps) cannot serve even after a 35% cache and a 7% shed. §3 never states that the single-host result applies to the short-prompt leg at ~2 rps, so a reader can conclude that one host serves the canonical deployment.
issue.evidence: From the chunk: canonical peak ≈ 40 rps (Ch 4, quoted in §3 Pattern C); per-host ceiling ≈ 2.0 rps (Ch 17/20, quoted in §3 and §8); canonical fleet = 21 hosts (implied by 21 × 2.0 ≈ 42 rps). After a 35% cache, engine load at the canonical peak would be ≈26 rps against a 2.0 rps ceiling — a 13× oversubscription. §8 Step 1 states the opposite boundary explicitly: "The capstone declares a distinct short-prompt workload — it is not the canonical 9.2K-input/1.08-s-prefill case of Ch 4" and "request rate ~2 rps". §3's own sentence "the per-host ceiling is ~2.0 rps (Ch 17/20), both of which still hold here" acknowledges the ceiling but never reconciles it with the ~40 rps peak it quotes two paragraphs earlier.
issue.root_cause: Two different workloads (canonical long-context at ~40 rps; short-prompt at ~2 rps) are narrated under one scenario heading, and the headline result is stated at the level of the more favourable one without a scope sentence.
issue.correction: In §3, split the scenario explicitly into (i) the canonical deployment (40 rps peak, 21 hosts per Ch 17) and (ii) the short-prompt leg the capstone actually models (~2 rps, one host), and attach the scope to the headline: "p99 TTFT ≈ 250 ms applies to the short-prompt leg at the declared ~2 rps offered rate on one host; the canonical 40 rps peak requires the Ch 17 fleet." Add a one-line reconciliation of the ~40 rps peak with the single-host result so the reader cannot carry away "one host serves the canonical workload".
issue.acceptance_test: Every numeric headline in §3, §8 and the Fig 26.2 takeaway names the workload (short-prompt vs canonical) and the offered rate it applies to; a reader who reads only §3's Capstone Execution paragraph can state the offered load at which the single-host result holds and the fleet size the canonical peak requires.

issue.page_hint: Ch 26 Table 26-2 (cost row) and its note
issue.quoted_clause: "| Cost | $ per query (marginal generation work; DERIVED from FACT inputs, §26.8 — not itself a FACT) | < $0.015 | $0.0076 (API-basis marginal: $0.01164 × 0.65; self-host all-in is a separate basis, §26.8) |"
issue.observed: Two defects in one row. (a) The Configuration column declares the basis as "marginal generation work" while the Modeled example cell computes an API-basis marginal ($0.01164 × 0.65). R-01, stated in this same chapter, says "marginal generation work, metered API spend, and all-in TCO are separate units, never collapsed" — the row collapses two of them under one label. (b) The $0.01164/request API price is derived at the canonical 9,200-in/300-out token mix, but §8 Step 1 declares the capstone workload to be a short-prompt workload ("a much smaller prompt", "not the canonical 9.2K-input/1.08-s-prefill case"). Applying a 9,200-token-mix price to a short-prompt request overstates the per-request cost by roughly the input-token ratio.
issue.evidence: Recomputation: 9,200 × $1.20/1M + 300 × $2.00/1M = $0.01104 + $0.00060 = $0.01164 ✓ (the price itself is arithmetically correct); $0.01164 × 0.65 = $0.007566 ≈ $0.0076 ✓. The problem is the basis and the token mix, not the arithmetic. The chunk's own note states: "both are per-request managed-API prices at the canonical 9,200/300 token mix and 6.24M requests/mo" — while §8 Step 1 states the workload is not the canonical one. A short-prompt request at, say, 1,000 in / 300 out would cost 1,000 × $1.20/1M + 300 × $2.00/1M = $0.0018, i.e. ~6× less than $0.01164.
issue.root_cause: The cost cell was populated from the canonical scenario's price table without re-deriving it for the declared short-prompt workload, and the row's basis label was written before the cell's arithmetic.
issue.correction: Split the cost row into two rows with explicit bases: (A) marginal generation work — expressed as a fraction of uncached generation work (65% of baseline), unit-free; (B) metered API spend — recomputed at the short-prompt token mix actually modelled, with the mix stated in the cell. Keep the all-in self-hosted TCO as a third, separate line (or an explicit pointer to Ch 16) and do not label any of them "marginal generation work" unless they are. If the intent is to keep the canonical-mix price, state that the cost row is quoted at the canonical mix and is therefore not the cost of the modelled workload.
issue.acceptance_test: Every cost figure in Table 26-2 carries exactly one basis from {marginal generation work, metered API spend, all-in self-hosted TCO}; the API figure's token mix equals the token mix of the workload modelled in §8; and no cell multiplies a fixed-fleet all-in $/request by a fraction of requests.

issue.quoted_clause: "The canonical C ≈ 17.5 and ~2.0 rps ceiling are held as conservative planning caps: a shorter prompt only lowers per-request KV (which would raise C) and shortens service time (which would raise the ceiling), so the canonical values sit on the safe side of this workload's real limits." ... "at the offered ~2 rps against the ~2.0 rps analytical ceiling (ρ near 1) the prefill queue already sits inside the 320 ms compute term"
issue.observed: The same 2.0 rps figure is used in two incompatible ways in the same paragraph. As a "conservative planning cap" it implies the short-prompt workload's true ceiling is HIGHER than 2.0 rps, so an offered load of 2.0 rps would sit at ρ < 1 and the queue would NOT be inflated. As "the ~2.0 rps analytical ceiling" it implies ρ ≈ 1 and an inflated queue. Both cannot hold, and the choice determines whether the baseline's 320 ms compute term contains queueing delay — which is the entire basis of the −44% headline (see CH26-02).
issue.evidence: The chunk's own reasoning: "a shorter prompt ... shortens service time (which would raise the ceiling)". The per-host ceiling is C/W (17.5 / 8.6 s ≈ 2.03 rps). For a short prompt, C rises and W falls, so the true ceiling is strictly above 2.03 rps. Therefore at 2.0 rps offered, ρ < 1 strictly, and the baseline is not queue-inflated. The chapter simultaneously asserts ρ ≈ 1 ("the prefill queue already sits inside the 320 ms compute term") and ρ < 1 (conservative cap).
issue.root_cause: The chapter wanted a defensible "we did not re-derive the canonical numbers" boundary, and separately wanted a queue-inflated baseline to make the cache look effective; the two requirements were not reconciled.
issue.correction: Choose one and state it: (i) the short-prompt workload's ceiling is re-derived (or bounded) and the baseline is placed at a stated ρ < 1 with a queueing term computed from it; or (ii) the canonical 2.0 rps is used as the true ceiling and the baseline is explicitly at ρ ≈ 1, in which case the baseline has no steady state and the comparison must be framed as "overloaded vs. stable". Do not call the same number both a conservative cap and the binding ceiling.
issue.acceptance_test: The chapter states one value for the short-prompt workload's per-host ceiling, one ρ for the baseline operating point, and one ρ for the cached operating point; the ρ values are consistent with the ceiling value and with the queueing claim made about the 320 ms term.

issue.quoted_clause: "the p99 and cost denominators are completed useful requests, and the ~7% fallback share is labeled a separately-tracked degraded outcome" ... Table 26-1: "| Circuit Breaker | timeout count / 30s | fallback activation rate | recovery grace-period latency | degraded-outcome (shed) rate over completed useful requests |"
issue.observed: The shed rate is defined with a denominator that excludes the shed requests by construction. A request shed by the breaker is, by definition, not a completed useful request, so "shed rate over completed useful requests" is either identically zero or undefined. The chapter elsewhere insists on denominator integrity (R-10), so this is an internal contradiction in the metric definition rather than a stylistic slip.
issue.evidence: R-10 as stated in §2: "a degraded or fallback answer is not an SLO success — the denominator is completed useful requests". That rule correctly governs the SLO-success denominator (p99 TTFT over completed useful requests). It does not govern the shed-rate denominator, which must be over admitted or arrived requests (or over all requests offered to the breaker). The chunk uses one denominator for two different quantities.
issue.root_cause: A single denominator was propagated from the SLO metric to the degradation metric without re-deriving which population each metric's denominator must contain.
issue.correction: Define the two metrics with distinct, explicit denominators: (i) SLO compliance / p99 TTFT — over completed useful requests (shed requests excluded, and reported as a separate count so the exclusion is visible); (ii) shed rate — over all requests admitted to the model service in the window (or over all arrivals), stated as such. Add a line to Table 26-1 and to Table 26-2's note giving the denominator for the 7% figure.
issue.acceptance_test: Table 26-1 and Table 26-2 state a denominator for every rate; the shed-rate denominator includes shed requests; the p99-TTFT denominator excludes them; and the 7% figure's denominator is named wherever it appears (§3, Table 26-2, Fig 26.2 takeaway).

issue.quoted_clause: "Table 26-2's ~7% fallback rate is the modeled share of requests shed to the intent classifier during such excursions (FACT target < 10%)" ... "alerts fire when DERIVED quantities cross safety boundaries (e.g., the p99 TTFT SLO, the fallback-rate FACT target < 10% of Table 26-2, or the queue-depth limits of Ch 15)"
issue.observed: A threshold is labelled a FACT. A target is an acceptance criterion, not a runtime quantity; the chapter's own Table 26-2 note says the opposite: "The Verification target column states thresholds to be met, not FACTs." The same slip appears in §4, where the p99 TTFT SLO (a measured FACT) is listed among "DERIVED quantities".
issue.evidence: §2 defines FACT as "a verified runtime quantity (e.g., request rate, cache hit ratio, query latency p99)" and DERIVED as "a computed quantity from FACTs". A configured threshold of <10% is neither. The chapter's own evidence-label vocabulary (Ch 4 / Appendix A) has no category for "target"; the correct treatment is an unlabelled acceptance criterion, or an explicit [ASSUMPTION] if the threshold itself is a scenario input.
issue.root_cause: Label vocabulary applied to the wrong span: the label was attached to a threshold rather than to the measured quantity it bounds.
issue.correction: Remove "FACT" from "FACT target" in §3 and §4 (write "verification target < 10%"), and in §4 separate the two lists: FACTs that are measured (p99 TTFT, hit ratio, shed rate) versus DERIVED quantities computed from them (throughput per shard, cost per query, fleet-wide rps).
issue.acceptance_test: No threshold, target, guardrail or SLO value in Ch 26 carries a FACT or DERIVED label; §4's alert list names the metric's status correctly.

issue.quoted_clause: "Step 1's 45% SM-utilization baseline is measured at the uncached ~2.0 rps offered rate, and the ~29% is the same definition at the cached ~1.3 rps engine load (45% × 1.3/2.0 ≈ 29%, scaled with engine load)"
issue.observed: The note says the 45% baseline "is measured", but §8 Step 1 states the opposite for the same number: "These are assumed baseline inputs, not gathered FACTs (R-07): no author-run load test produced them". The word "measured" here contradicts the chapter's own R-07 discipline and the note's closing sentence ("they are not FACTs measured on a deployed system").
issue.evidence: §8 Step 1: "SM utilization 45%" is listed among "The baseline inputs for this worked example" and is explicitly labelled assumed. Table 26-2's note: "Step 1's 45% SM-utilization baseline is measured at the uncached ~2.0 rps offered rate". Both cannot be true; the note's own later clause ("they are not FACTs measured on a deployed system") shows the intended reading.
issue.root_cause: The note was written to describe the measurement procedure a real deployment would follow, and the procedural verb "measured" leaked into a description of an assumed value.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: "Step 1's 45% SM-utilization baseline is an assumed input at the uncached ~2.0 rps offered rate; the ~29% is the same definition scaled to the cached ~1.3 rps engine load (45% × 1.3/2.0 ≈ 29%). A real deployment measures both under a single SM-utilization definition."
issue.acceptance_test: Every occurrence of the 45% and 29% SM-utilization values in Ch 26 uses the same status word (assumed / modeled), and no sentence describes either as measured.

issue.quoted_clause: "~2,000 registered users with ~5% concurrently active at peak (~100 concurrent users, a population measure)" ... "the canonical ~40 rps peak (Ch 4) would if concentrated on one host" ... "the canonical request's total end-to-end time is ~8.6 s"
issue.observed: The chunk's own three canonical quantities do not close under Little's law: 40 rps × 8.6 s service time implies ≈344 concurrent in-flight requests, but the chunk states ~100 concurrent users at peak. Either the concurrency figure, the peak-rate figure, or the service-time figure is scoped differently (users vs. requests vs. sessions), and the chapter never says which.
issue.evidence: Little's law: L = λW = 40 × 8.6 = 344 requests in flight. The chunk's population figure is 2,000 × 5% = 100 concurrent users. 344 requests from 100 users implies 3.44 concurrent requests per user, which is not stated and is unusual for a chat/RAG workload. §8 Step 3 compounds this by treating "~100 to ~150" concurrent users as the population that scales with the offered rate ("holding ~2.0 rps while the concurrent population grows from ~100 to ~150 implies a ~33% lower per-concurrent-user rate"), which is only coherent if concurrency is measured in requests.
issue.root_cause: Population measure (registered users, concurrently active users) and concurrency measure (in-flight requests) are used interchangeably across the chapter and across the canonical scenario.
issue.correction: State the three canonical quantities with their units and their relationship in one place (Ch 4 or here): registered users, concurrently active users, in-flight requests, peak rps, service time. If the canonical peak of ~40 rps is a fleet-wide figure over 21 hosts, say so and give the per-host figure. If the ~100 concurrent users is a user-population figure, state the implied in-flight request count and the requests-per-user ratio.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can compute, from the chapter's own numbers, the in-flight request count implied by the canonical peak rate and service time, and can reconcile it with the stated concurrent-user figure without consulting another chapter.

issue.quoted_clause: "Deeper continuous batching on the single host instead of sharding cannot raise throughput here: resident-request capacity is KV-bound at C ≈ 17.5 (Ch 15), so admitting more requests only lengthens the waiting queue and adds prefill interference"
issue.observed: The rejection is argued from a KV-capacity argument that applies only to admitting MORE concurrent requests, not to deeper batching (larger batch per step) at a fixed resident count. Deeper batching can raise throughput by improving per-step GPU efficiency at the same resident-request count; the chapter's own §2.1 matrix lists "Continuous batching" as the first strategy for high-throughput chat, and Ch 8 is cited elsewhere as the source of the batching regime argument. The claim "cannot raise throughput here" is therefore stronger than the argument supports, and it is stated as a universal-sounding rejection of a lever the book elsewhere recommends.
issue.evidence: The chunk's own ceiling arithmetic: throughput = C/W with C KV-bound at 17.5 and W ≈ 8.6 s → ≈2.0 rps. If deeper batching reduces W (better SM utilisation at the same C), throughput rises without any change in C. The chunk's argument only establishes that C cannot be raised. The alternative is also mis-framed as "instead of sharding", when sharding is baseline configuration (R-04) and therefore not an alternative at all.
issue.correction: Restrict the rejection to what the argument supports: "admitting more concurrent requests cannot raise throughput here, because resident-request capacity is KV-bound at C ≈ 17.5; deeper batching at fixed C can still improve per-step efficiency, but it trades p99 TTFT for throughput and is rejected here on the latency criterion (the p99 TTFT SLO binds), not on a capacity argument." Drop the "instead of sharding" framing.
issue.acceptance_test: The rejection of deeper batching cites the SLO/latency trade-off (not a capacity impossibility), and the chapter contains no sentence asserting that continuous batching cannot raise throughput in a KV-bound regime.

issue.quoted_clause: "| Inference Sharding (Pattern A) | One host saturates: TTFT p99 crosses the SLO as requests queue past the ~2.0 rps per-host ceiling | Place the model across the node's GPUs with tensor parallelism (baseline configuration here, R-04) | ... |"
issue.observed: The pattern template's stated problem and its mechanism do not match. The triggering symptom is a queue past the per-host ceiling; the mechanism offered is intra-host tensor parallelism, which does not add resident-request capacity and cannot relieve a queue caused by insufficient capacity — the chunk itself says so in §3 ("an independent replica adds KV slots and capacity, which is precisely what relieves a queue caused by insufficient resident-request capacity"). As written, the template teaches the reader that TP is the answer to a saturation problem it cannot solve.
issue.evidence: §3, Alternatives considered: "A second serving host with load balancing is not rejected on the single phrase 'KV-bound': an independent replica adds KV slots and capacity, which is precisely what relieves a queue caused by insufficient resident-request capacity." §3 also states the weights are already TP across the 8 GPUs in the baseline, so the mechanism is already present and cannot be the remedy for the stated symptom.
issue.root_cause: One pattern entry was written to cover two distinct decisions — model placement across devices (TP/PP) and capacity scaling (replica count) — under a single name.
issue.correction: Split the entry into two templates: (i) "Model placement / tensor parallelism" — problem solved: the model does not fit on one device; mechanism: shard weights and KV across devices; trade-off: inter-GPU communication; failure condition: counted as a gain when already present (R-04). (ii) "Replica scaling / load balancing" — problem solved: TTFT p99 crosses the SLO as requests queue past the per-host ceiling; mechanism: add replicas and balance across them; trade-off: KV slots and capex vs. tail latency; failure condition: benefit claimed without a load-curve test. Then point Pattern A at (i) and the deferred second host at (ii).
issue.acceptance_test: Every row of Table 26-3 has a mechanism that can relieve its own stated triggering symptom; the Inference Sharding row's symptom and mechanism are consistent, and the second-host option appears as a named pattern.

issue.quoted_clause: "The Patterns Library complements this by cataloging recurring structural solutions — sharding strategies for RAG pipelines, caching layers for LLM serving, circuit breaker patterns for inter-service communication, and more." ... "from the micro (which cache invalidation strategy?) to the macro (how does sharding affect fleet-wide latency?)" ... "a compendium of patterns, checklists, and mental models"
issue.observed: §1 describes a library that §9 does not deliver. The catalog contains five entries: Inference Sharding, Semantic Response Cache, Circuit Breaker, Fine-tuning, RAG model selection. There is no RAG-pipeline sharding pattern (the sharding pattern is model placement across GPUs), no general inter-service circuit breaker (the breaker is specific to model-service saturation), no cache-invalidation pattern (the micro example given in §1), and no checklist (Table 26-1 is a FACT set, not a checklist).
issue.evidence: §9's own inventory: "Each entry is a pattern template with seven table columns covering eight fields ... Patterns A–C from §3 are the first three entries ... The two model-selection patterns that Ch 5 files here close the catalog." Five entries total. §1's "and more" and "checklists" have no referent.
issue.root_cause: The chapter's opening was written as a generic description of a patterns library rather than as an inventory of what this chapter actually contains.
issue.correction: Rewrite §1's second paragraph to describe the actual catalog (five templates: model placement, response caching, load shedding, fine-tuning, model selection) and drop the RAG-pipeline-sharding, inter-service-circuit-breaker, cache-invalidation and checklist references, or add the missing patterns. If the intent is to promise a broader library, state that explicitly and mark the additional entries as forthcoming.
issue.acceptance_test: Every pattern named in §1 appears in Table 26-3, and every category named in §1 (checklists, micro-level decisions) has a corresponding artefact in the chapter.

issue.quoted_clause: Fig 26.2 caption: "The causal chain the figure encodes: a baseline that is bandwidth-bound in decode (box 2) → queueing once offered load approaches the host's ~2.0 rps ceiling (the ρ near 1 behind box 1's inflated compute) → the p99 tail the validate step measures" ... §2: "The loop operates as: instrument → observe FACT → compute DERIVED → validate HYPOTHESIS → adjust pattern."
issue.observed: Two problems. (a) The figure's causal chain attributes the baseline's latency to decode being bandwidth-bound, but the quantity in question is TTFT, which is dominated by prefill and by queueing ahead of the first token; decode bandwidth governs TPOT/ITL, not TTFT. A reader could conclude that the 320 ms compute term is a decode-bandwidth effect. (b) §2 defines the loop as FACT-first (instrument → observe FACT → compute DERIVED → validate HYPOTHESIS → adjust), while Fig 26.2's chain is ASSUMPTION-first (ASSUMPTION → DERIVED → PATTERN → ASSUMPTION) with FACTs entering only at the validate step. The chapter's named mental model and its own diagram describe different loops.
issue.evidence: §8 Step 1's baseline decomposition is model compute 320 ms + I/O 80 ms + retrieval 50 ms, and the text attributes the 320 ms to "prefill-queue inflation at ρ near 1" — a prefill/queue effect, not a decode-bandwidth effect. §8 Step 2 separately says the miss path's compute falls because the queue is "queue-light (ρ ≈ 0.65)". The Fig 26.2 caption's own parenthetical ("the ρ near 1 behind box 1's inflated compute") is the prefill/queue story; the "bandwidth-bound in decode" clause is a different mechanism imported from the TPOT discussion.
issue.root_cause: The figure was drawn to carry the chapter's general narrative (decode regime → queueing → tail) rather than the specific causal chain the worked example actually uses (prefill queue → TTFT tail), and the loop definition was written independently of the figure.
issue.correction: In the Fig 26.2 caption, replace the decode-bandwidth clause with the prefill/queue clause that the worked example uses, and add a sentence distinguishing the two regimes explicitly (TTFT is prefill- and queue-dominated; decode bandwidth governs TPOT/ITL). Reconcile §2's loop with the figure: either state that the figure shows the ASSUMPTION-seeded instantiation of the loop (with the FACT-seeded loop as the steady state), or redraw the figure to show instrument → FACT → DERIVED → HYPOTHESIS → adjust.
issue.acceptance_test: The Fig 26.2 caption's causal chain names the same mechanism that §8 Step 1/Step 2 use to explain the 320 ms term; and a reader who reads §2 and the figure can state one loop, not two.

issue.quoted_clause: "A genuine user-scaling test would grow the offered rate with the population (~3.0 rps at 3,000 users) and recheck the queue and TTFT consequences."
issue.observed: The proposed genuine scaling test is infeasible on the configuration under test. The scenario is a single 8×H100 host with a stated sustainable ceiling of ~2.0 rps; 3.0 rps exceeds it by 50%, so the test would measure an overloaded host, not a scaling behaviour. The chapter does not say whether the test adds a second host (which is the deferred alternative of §3) or what the expected result would be.
issue.evidence: §8 Scenario: "the rps is the ~2 rps the host can actually sustain, not a multiple of it." §8 Step 1: "request rate ~2 rps (within the ~2.0 rps per-host analytical planning ceiling)". 3.0 rps > 2.0 rps ceiling. §3's Alternatives considered explicitly defers the second host to "a load-curve/SLO-goodput question", so the chapter has not yet established the capacity for the test it proposes.
issue.root_cause: The scaling test was specified from the population arithmetic (~3.0 rps) without checking it against the host capacity the same section establishes.
issue.correction: State the test as it must be run: either (a) add the second replica first (naming it as the deferred alternative and stating the expected KV-slot and queueing consequences), or (b) run the test at 3.0 rps and state explicitly that the host is over its ceiling, so the measured TTFT p99 is a saturation result and not a scaling result. Add the acceptance criterion for the added capacity.
issue.acceptance_test: Every load rate named in §8 Step 3 is compared against the stated per-host ceiling in the same sentence, and any rate above the ceiling is accompanied by the capacity change it requires.

issue.page_hint: Ch 26 §8 Step 3; §3 Capstone Execution; Fig 26.2 takeaway
issue.quoted_clause: "[canonical scenario][HYPOTHESIS] — 'at the assumed ~2.0 rps sustained offered rate and 35% cache-hit ratio, sharding + caching will keep TTFT p99 < 300 ms as the fleet scales from the canonical ~2,000 users to the capstone's ~3,000 users.'" ... "Suppose a staged load test at ~3,000 users reports TTFT p99 = 285 ms"
issue.observed: The hypothesis as written is not the hypothesis the staged test validates. The test holds the offered rate flat at ~2.0 rps while the user count grows, so it tests configuration robustness, not scaling — the chapter says so ("The staged test therefore covers configuration robustness under constant load ... not user scaling"). A hypothesis that is not falsifiable by the test that is supposed to test it cannot be "accepted" by it. Separately, the chapter reports two different p99 values for the capstone outcome: 250 ms (model, §3 and Fig 26.2 takeaway) and 285 ms (illustrative load test), without stating which is the capstone's result.
issue.evidence: §8 Step 3: "The offered rate stays flat at 1.5× users because it is a declared scenario input capped at the host's ~2.0 rps sustainable ceiling ... not a per-user rate." and "The staged test therefore covers configuration robustness under constant load — cache and breaker behavior at the assumed inputs — not user scaling." The hypothesis text nevertheless says "as the fleet scales from the canonical ~2,000 users to the capstone's ~3,000 users". The 250 ms vs 285 ms divergence appears in §3 ("p99 TTFT ≈ 250 ms"), §8 Step 2 ("p99 TTFT ≈ 250 ms"), the Fig 26.2 takeaway ("p99 TTFT ~250 ms") and §8 Step 3 ("TTFT p99 = 285 ms").
issue.root_cause: The hypothesis was written to describe the scenario's narrative (a growing startup) rather than the discriminating test, and the model output and the illustrative measurement were never reconciled.
issue.correction: Restate the hypothesis so that it is falsifiable by the staged test: "at the assumed ~2.0 rps sustained offered rate and 35% cache-hit ratio, the cached configuration keeps TTFT p99 < 300 ms on one 8×H100 host". Move the user-scaling question into a separate, explicitly untested hypothesis with its own required setup (per CH26-14). Add one sentence reconciling 250 ms (model) and 285 ms (illustrative measurement) — e.g. the model is the expectation, the measurement is the observed value, and the difference is the model's residual error.
issue.acceptance_test: Each HYPOTHESIS in §8 states the load level at which it is tested; the staged test's acceptance criterion is derivable from the hypothesis text; and the chapter names one capstone p99 value in each context (model vs. measurement) with the relationship between them stated.

issue.quoted_clause: "**Pattern A — Inference Sharding.** [canonical scenario][DERIVED]" ... "[canonical scenario][HYPOTHESIS] — adding a second host ..." ... "[canonical scenario][DERIVED] — a cache hit ratio of 35% reduces ..."
issue.observed: The label "[canonical scenario]" is used repeatedly but is not one of the book's defined evidence labels. The house vocabulary is [CANONICAL] / [DERIVED] / [ILLUSTRATIVE] / [ASSUMPTION] / [1P] / [HYPOTHESIS] plus the three-axis taxonomy; "canonical scenario" is a scenario descriptor, not a status or provenance label, and it is set in lower case inside brackets, unlike every other label in the chapter.
issue.evidence: §2 itself uses the defined form: "the canonical 70B teaching model ... carries [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]" and "the canonical 70B teaching model is not a [1P] model". The chapter never defines "[canonical scenario]" anywhere, and the label is applied to clauses whose status is already given by the second tag ([DERIVED], [HYPOTHESIS]) — so it adds a third, undefined dimension to the label stack.
issue.root_cause: A scenario tag was introduced locally to mark "this comes from the canonical scenario", without being registered in the book's label vocabulary or reconciled with the three-axis scheme.
issue.correction: Replace every "[canonical scenario]" with the defined "[CANONICAL]" (upper case, as in the house vocabulary), or remove it where the second tag already carries the status and the scenario is named in the surrounding prose. If a scenario tag is genuinely wanted as a third axis, define it in Ch 4 / Appendix A alongside the others and use it consistently book-wide.
