issue.acceptance_test: Every bracketed label in Ch 26 appears in the book's defined label set; a grep of the manuscript for "[canonical scenario]" returns zero hits; and the label stack on any clause uses only registered labels.

issue.quoted_clause: "the ~50 ms term of §26.8 Step 2" ... "the load test of §8 Step 3" ... "§26.8 states those rules but does not perform the re-sizing" ... "the canonical ~436 GB KV budget from Chapter 15" ... "the §26.2.1 matrix" ... "§2.1"
issue.observed: The chapter mixes three cross-reference conventions for the same targets: "§26.8" and "§8" for the mini-case section, "§26.2.1" and "§2.1" for the decision matrix, and "Chapter 15" alongside "Ch 15" for chapter references. A reader following "§26.8 Step 2" must work out that this is §8 Step 2 of Chapter 26.
issue.evidence: Occurrences in the chunk: "§26.8 Step 2" (§3 Pattern B), "§8 Step 3" (§3 Capstone Execution), "§26.8's cost-basis rules" and "§26.8 states those rules" (§3), "§26.8" in Table 26-2's cost row and note, "§26.2.1" in the Fig 26.1 provenance note and §8 Step 0, "§2.1" in the same provenance note, "Chapter 15" in §3 Pattern A, "Ch 15" in §4 and §9.
issue.root_cause: The chapter was assembled from sections written at different times with different reference conventions, and no normalisation pass was run.
issue.correction: Pick one convention for intra-chapter references (e.g. "§8 Step 2", "§2.1") and one for chapter references ("Ch 15"), and normalise every occurrence in the chapter. If the book-wide convention is the "§26.8" form, use it consistently here too.
issue.acceptance_test: A grep of Ch 26 for "§26." and for "Chapter " returns only the chosen convention; every intra-chapter reference resolves to a heading that exists in the chapter.

issue.page_hint: Ch 26 §2.1 (decision matrix), Short-prompt RAG Q&A row
issue.quoted_clause: "| Short-prompt RAG Q&A | Short (<2K) | Short (<500) | Tail latency / queueing (p99 TTFT) | Semantic response cache, circuit breaker (Ch 26) |"
issue.observed: A row of Chapter 26's own matrix points to Chapter 26. The two strategies it names are Patterns B and C, which live in §3 and §9 of this chapter.
issue.evidence: §9: "Patterns A–C from §3 are the first three entries." §3: "Pattern B — Semantic Response Cache", "Pattern C — Circuit Breaker".
issue.root_cause: The matrix was drafted with chapter-level pointers for every row and the self-referencing row was not updated.
issue.correction: Change the pointer to "§3 Patterns B, C; §9" (or "this chapter, §3/§9").
issue.acceptance_test: No pointer in Table 26-2/26-3 or in the §2.1 matrix points to the chapter that contains it; every pointer resolves to a specific section.

issue.quoted_clause: "The two model-selection patterns that Ch 5 files here close the catalog." ... "| Fine-tuning for specific workloads | ... | Ch 5, §5.3 |"
issue.observed: Fine-tuning is not a model-selection pattern; it is an adaptation pattern. The sentence mis-describes one of the two entries it introduces. Separately, the pointer "Ch 5, §5.3" is ambiguous: it reads as §5.3 of Chapter 26 (which is "Common Mistakes") rather than §5.3 of Chapter 5.
issue.evidence: Table 26-3's two closing rows are "Fine-tuning for specific workloads" (problem: "A sustained domain workload that retrieval cannot close"; mechanism: "Adapt the model only after the break-even query volume is measured") and "RAG model selection" (problem: "'Which model is best?' asked before the workload is characterized"). Only the second is a model-selection pattern.
issue.root_cause: The two entries were filed under one description when they were added from Ch 5.
issue.correction: Rewrite as "The two patterns filed here from Ch 5 — workload adaptation (fine-tuning) and model selection — close the catalog." Disambiguate the pointer as "Ch 5 §5.3".
issue.acceptance_test: The §9 preamble describes each of the five catalog entries accurately, and every pointer in Table 26-3 is unambiguous when read in isolation.

issue.page_hint: Ch 26 Fig 26.1 caption and provenance note
issue.quoted_clause: Caption: "The canonical scenario's workload, rendered as a six-axis fingerprint. The three scored workload families from the §26.2.1 matrix sit in distinct regions: RAG Q&A is quality- and context-heavy with short outputs; chat is traffic- and latency-sensitive with long outputs; batch inference is cost-sensitive and latency-tolerant." Note: "In axis order (context length, traffic, quality, cost, latency, output tokens) the scores are long-context RAG Q&A 0.95 / 0.20 / 0.70 / 0.55 / 0.40 / 0.45, chat 0.35 / 0.95 / 0.50 / 0.75 / 0.90 / 0.55, batch 0.55 / 0.60 / 0.30 / 0.85 / 0.35 / 0.90"
issue.observed: The caption's characterisations are only partly supported by the scores it cites. (a) "chat ... with long outputs" — chat's output-token score is 0.55, below batch's 0.90 and only 0.10 above RAG's 0.45; the §2.1 matrix likewise gives chat "Med-Long (>1K)" and batch "Long". Chat is not the long-output family in this scoring. (b) The caption's first sentence ("The canonical scenario's workload, rendered as a six-axis fingerprint") describes one workload, while the rest of the caption describes three families; the provenance note says the canonical scenario is the anchor for the RAG family, so the first sentence is misleading as a caption for a three-family figure.
issue.evidence: Output-token axis: RAG 0.45 < chat 0.55 < batch 0.90. Cost axis: batch 0.85 > chat 0.75 > RAG 0.55 ✓ ("cost-sensitive"). Latency axis: chat 0.90 > RAG 0.40 > batch 0.35 ✓ ("latency-tolerant" for batch). Traffic: chat 0.95 ✓. Context: RAG 0.95 ✓. Quality: RAG 0.70 > chat 0.50 > batch 0.30 ✓ ("quality-heavy" for RAG). Only the output-token characterisation is unsupported.
issue.root_cause: The caption was written as a narrative gloss over the bars rather than as a description of them, and the first sentence was inherited from an earlier single-workload version of the figure.
issue.correction: Change "chat is traffic- and latency-sensitive with long outputs" to "chat is traffic- and latency-sensitive with medium-long outputs (batch inference is the long-output family)", and replace the first sentence with one that names the three families and states that the canonical scenario anchors the long-context RAG family.
issue.acceptance_test: Every comparative claim in the Fig 26.1 caption is true of the cited scores (in particular, no family is described as the extreme on an axis where another family scores higher); the caption's first sentence describes the same set of subjects as the rest of the caption.

issue.quoted_clause: "[ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] — model-service latency p99 degrades past the 800 ms SLO under concurrent load; downstream network jitter p99 = 120 ms (scenario inputs to be measured)."
issue.observed: The 120 ms downstream-jitter figure is introduced as a scenario input and then never used: it does not appear in any budget, threshold, trip condition, or derived quantity in the chapter. A reader cannot tell whether the breaker's 5-timeout trip threshold is sensitive to it, or whether it is a leftover from an earlier draft.
issue.evidence: Grep of the chunk: "120 ms" occurs once, in this sentence. The breaker's mechanism is "trip after 5 consecutive timeouts" and its FACT set is "timeout count / 30s; fallback activation rate; recovery grace-period latency" — none of which references the jitter distribution.
issue.root_cause: An input was added to make the scenario feel complete without being wired into the mechanism it is supposed to inform.
issue.correction: Either use it — e.g. state that the 5-timeout trip threshold is chosen relative to the 120 ms jitter p99 (a timeout budget of X ms is ~N× the jitter p99, so a single jitter spike does not trip the breaker) — or delete it. If retained, it should appear in the breaker FACT set as a measured quantity (e.g. downstream timeout rate) and in Table 26-1.
issue.acceptance_test: Every scenario input introduced in §3 appears in at least one budget, threshold, or FACT set; no input is introduced and abandoned.

issue.quoted_clause: "How does fleet-wide model versioning interact with per-shard caching, and what FACTs govern safe rollouts?"
issue.observed: "Per-shard caching" is not a term used anywhere else in the chapter or in the patterns library. The chapter's caching concepts are the semantic response cache (Pattern B), prefix caching (referenced in §2.1), and prompt caching. The open question therefore names a mechanism the reader has not been introduced to, which is exactly the failure mode the chapter's own §7 preamble tries to avoid ("each becomes a testable HYPOTHESIS once its FACT instrumentation and pass criterion are specified").
issue.evidence: Table 26-3's caching entry is "Semantic Response Cache"; §2.1's matrix mentions "prefix caching"; no "per-shard cache" concept is defined in the chunk.
issue.root_cause: The open question was drafted against a different vocabulary than the chapter settled on.
issue.correction: Rewrite the question in the chapter's own terms — e.g. "How does fleet-wide model versioning interact with the semantic response cache and with prefix caching, and what FACTs govern safe rollouts (cache-key revision, corpus snapshot, model revision)?" — and make sure the named mechanisms exist in the chapter.
issue.acceptance_test: Every mechanism named in §7 is defined earlier in the book; no term in §7 is unique to §7.

issue.quoted_clause: "**Rule key (R-codes).** The pattern templates cite the book's standing rules by code; the codes and their text: **R-01** ... **R-03** ... **R-04** ... **R-05** ... **R-07** ... **R-10** ... **R-13** ..."
issue.observed: The list is presented as "the codes and their text" but is non-contiguous (R-02, R-06, R-08, R-09, R-11, R-12 are absent), and no pointer tells the reader where the full rule set lives. A reader who wants to know whether R-06 exists, or what R-02 says, has nowhere to go.
issue.evidence: The chapter cites seven codes spanning R-01 to R-13 with six gaps; the phrase "the codes and their text" implies completeness.
issue.root_cause: The list was assembled from the codes this chapter happens to cite, but written as if it were the complete key.
issue.correction: Either (a) retitle as "the rules cited in this chapter" and add a pointer to the book's full rule key (chapter and section), or (b) reproduce the complete key. Also add the pointer so the codes are navigable.
issue.acceptance_test: The R-code list states whether it is complete and gives a resolvable pointer to the full set; every R-code cited in Ch 26 appears in that list.

issue.quoted_clause: "**Quantization decision record.** The architecture decision record names the active constraint, affected tensors, and proposed deployment configuration. ... [ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual"
issue.observed: This paragraph is a self-contained treatment of the quantization ADR (it names three chapters and an acceptance-condition set) but sits inside §2.1, whose declared subject is the workload-to-strategy decision matrix, with no subheading of its own. It interrupts the matrix's argument and is invisible to anyone scanning headings.
issue.evidence: §2.1's opening: "The matrix below is the first-pass mapping from a new workload's dominant constraint to the strategy class worth evaluating first". The quantization paragraph follows the matrix and the Fig 26.1 provenance note with no heading, and its content (ADR structure, resource ledger, acceptance conditions) is unrelated to the matrix.
issue.root_cause: A separate topic was appended to the matrix section rather than given its own heading or its own place in the chapter.
issue.correction: Give it a numbered subheading (e.g. "2.2 Quantization decision record") or move it to the chapter's measurement section, where the ADR/acceptance-condition material sits naturally next to Table 26-1. If it stays in §2.1, add a one-line transition explaining why the quantization ADR belongs in the workload-to-strategy discussion.
issue.acceptance_test: Every paragraph in §2.1 either belongs to the matrix discussion or sits under its own subheading; the chapter's heading structure exposes the quantization material to a scanning reader.

issue.quoted_clause: "Dashboards surface FACT trends; alerts fire when DERIVED quantities cross safety boundaries (e.g., the p99 TTFT SLO, the fallback-rate FACT target < 10% of Table 26-2, or the queue-depth limits of Ch 15)."
issue.observed: The three examples given are not DERIVED quantities: p99 TTFT is a measured FACT (as §2 itself lists it: "query latency p99"), the fallback rate is a FACT, and queue depth is a FACT. The sentence's own first clause ("Dashboards surface FACT trends") already assigns these to the FACT side, so the paragraph contradicts itself.
issue.evidence: §2: "FACT — a verified runtime quantity (e.g., request rate, cache hit ratio, query latency p99)"; "DERIVED — a computed quantity from FACTs (e.g., throughput per shard, cost per query, fleet-wide rps)". Table 26-1's FACT columns are exactly p99 latency, hit ratio, timeout count, SM utilization.
issue.root_cause: The alert list was written as a list of thresholds without checking each item's status, and the FACT/DERIVED distinction was applied to the sentence rather than to the items.
issue.correction: Rewrite the sentence to separate the two: dashboards surface FACT trends (p99 TTFT, hit ratio, shed rate, queue depth, SM utilization); alerts fire when a FACT crosses a threshold OR when a DERIVED quantity (throughput per shard, cost per query, fleet-wide rps, SLO compliance) crosses a boundary. Use the chapter's own DERIVED examples so the distinction is demonstrated rather than asserted.
issue.acceptance_test: Every item in §4's alert list is correctly classified as FACT or DERIVED, and the list contains at least one item of each kind.

issue.quoted_clause: "sharding distributes the model across the node so decode lands in the bandwidth-bound regime (the low-batch regime of Ch. 8; batch size, context precision, kernel, and hardware decide whether it stays there)"
issue.observed: Causal misattribution: sharding (tensor parallelism) does not cause decode to be bandwidth-bound. Decode is bandwidth-bound because the per-step work is dominated by reading the weights and the KV cache at low batch — a property of the arithmetic intensity of the decode step, not of how the model is partitioned. The parenthetical correctly qualifies the regime but the main clause asserts a false causal link.
issue.evidence: §3 Pattern A states the same regime correctly: "decode latency is bandwidth-bound in the low-batch decode regime of Ch. 8 ... whether decode binds on bandwidth or compute depends on batch size, context precision, kernel, and hardware" — with no causal role for TP. TP's role is stated separately: "per-token throughput is governed by the node's aggregate HBM bandwidth and approaches 8× the single-GPU rate only to the extent tensor-parallel communication and other overheads are negligible".
issue.root_cause: Two independent facts (TP placement; low-batch decode regime) were compressed into one causal sentence.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: "sharding distributes the model across the node's GPUs so the aggregate HBM bandwidth available to a decode step is 8× a single GPU's; at the low batch sizes of this scenario, decode is bandwidth-bound (Ch 8), so that aggregate bandwidth is what governs per-token latency." This also makes the TP→bandwidth link explicit rather than implied.
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 26 asserts that sharding or tensor parallelism causes a compute/bandwidth regime; the regime is attributed to batch size, precision, kernel and hardware, and TP is attributed to aggregate bandwidth and communication overhead.

issue.quoted_clause: "| Fine-tuning | N/A | N/A | Memory + interconnect | Precision-aware optimizer (LoRA/QLoRA) before full FT; gradient checkpointing (Ch 7) |"
issue.observed: The pointer for gradient checkpointing is Ch 7, which this chapter uses for KV/quantization memory accounting (Ch 7, 22 for KV bytes/token; Ch 7 for the representation and memory accounting of quantization). Gradient checkpointing is a training-time activation-memory technique; the chapter's own Training row points to Ch 10 for parallelism. The pointer is likely wrong.
issue.evidence: §2.1's own quantization paragraph: "Chapter 7 establishes the representation and memory accounting". §2.1's Training row: "Parallelism split (DP/TP/PP/FSDP) sized to model and cluster (Ch 10)". Gradient checkpointing appears in neither.
issue.root_cause: The row's pointer was filled with the chapter that covers "memory" rather than the chapter that covers training.
issue.correction: Verify where gradient checkpointing is treated in the book and point there (likely Ch 10, or a training chapter if one exists); if it is not treated anywhere, either add a short treatment or replace the pointer with a chapter that does cover the technique.
issue.acceptance_test: Every technique named in the §2.1 matrix is treated in the chapter it points to; a reader following the Fine-tuning row's pointer finds gradient checkpointing discussed.

issue.quoted_clause: "The architect instruments all three scenario quantities, observes the derived quantities in real time, and validates each HYPOTHESIS against measured traffic. The result: one 8×H100 serving host + a 35% semantic response cache + circuit breaker yields an illustrative p99 TTFT ≈ 250 ms versus the ~450 ms uncached single-node baseline ... (scenario outcome, not a measured benchmark)."
issue.observed: The paragraph narrates a completed measurement activity ("instruments ... in real time, and validates each HYPOTHESIS against measured traffic") that the chapter explicitly says did not happen: §8 Step 1 states "no author-run load test produced them", and §8 Step 3 states the 285 ms figure is "illustrative values to show how a hypothesis is tested, not a real experiment the book ran". The parenthetical "(scenario outcome, not a measured benchmark)" partially retracts the narration but does not fix it.
issue.evidence: §8 Step 1: "These are assumed baseline inputs, not gathered FACTs (R-07): no author-run load test produced them, so they are labeled an assumed baseline for a worked example (an input to the math), not a measured runtime quantity a FACT would be." §8 Step 3: "in this scenario these are illustrative values to show how a hypothesis is tested, not a real experiment the book ran."
issue.root_cause: The capstone was written in the voice of a completed engagement and then annotated with disclaimers rather than rewritten in the voice of a worked example.
issue.correction: Rewrite the paragraph in the indicative-of-a-template voice: "In a real engagement the architect would instrument ..., observe ..., and validate ... . The worked example below carries that loop with assumed inputs; the resulting configuration is recorded as Table 26-2 (scenario outcome, not a measured benchmark)." Keep the disclaimers but stop narrating an activity that did not occur.
issue.acceptance_test: No paragraph in Ch 26 narrates a measurement, deployment or validation as having occurred unless the chapter states that it did; the tense of the capstone narrative matches the chapter's evidence labels.

issue.quoted_clause: "The offered rate stays flat at 1.5× users because it is a declared scenario input capped at the host's ~2.0 rps sustainable ceiling (the Scenario above), not a per-user rate."
issue.observed: The sentence is garbled: "stays flat at 1.5× users" states the opposite of what is meant (the rate stays flat while the user count grows 1.5×). The reader has to reconstruct the intended meaning from the following sentences.
issue.evidence: The next two sentences make the intent clear: "The user count does not raise what one host sustains: holding ~2.0 rps while the concurrent population grows from ~100 to ~150 implies a ~33% lower per-concurrent-user rate." (Check: 2.0/100 = 0.020 rps per concurrent user; 2.0/150 = 0.0133; ratio 0.667 → 33% lower ✓.)
issue.root_cause: Compressed rewrite of a longer explanation.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: "The offered rate stays flat at ~2.0 rps while the user count grows 1.5×, because the rate is a declared scenario input capped at the host's ~2.0 rps sustainable ceiling (see the Scenario above) rather than a per-user rate."
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence parses on first reading and states which quantity is flat and which grows.

issue.quoted_clause: "The reproducible two-point model that yields these numbers is `render/capstone_calc.py`; a real deployment must measure the actual cache-hit latency distribution (not a point mass), the prefill queue at 1.3 rps, and the per-query cost"
issue.observed: A repository-relative path is given as the reproducibility reference. A reader holding the book cannot resolve `render/capstone_calc.py` without knowing the repository layout; the book elsewhere (per the chapter's own reproducibility conventions) should point to a resolvable location (URL plus version/commit) for the artifact.
issue.evidence: The path is given with no URL, no repository name, no commit or version, and no pointer to the book's reproducibility appendix.
issue.root_cause: An internal development path was substituted for a published artifact reference.
issue.correction: Give the artifact's resolvable location (repository URL + path + commit/release tag) and cross-reference the book's reproducibility appendix, consistent with how other first-party artifacts are cited in the book.
issue.acceptance_test: Every artifact path printed in the book resolves for a reader who has only the book; the path is accompanied by a version identifier.

issue.quoted_clause: "The Solution Architect's Toolkit answers two concerns — scalability and reliability — and is organized as pattern templates plus measurement rather than as three separate taxonomies"
issue.observed: The stated scope ("two concerns — scalability and reliability") does not match the chapter's own catalogue, two of whose five patterns are about quality and cost (fine-tuning: "quality delta vs RAG"; RAG model selection: "cost/token", "retrieve-vs-generate surface"), and whose measurement section is explicitly about cost ("Measure cost per query as a first-class derived quantity"). The sentence also reads as a rebuttal to a prior review rather than as a description of the chapter.
issue.evidence: Table 26-3's Minimal FACT sets include "quality delta vs RAG" and "cost/token"; §5 Mistake 3 is entirely about cost; §3's Capstone Execution is largely about cost bases.
issue.root_cause: The scope sentence was narrowed to answer a framing objection and never re-opened against the chapter's actual content.
issue.correction: Restate the scope to match the content — e.g. "The toolkit answers three concerns — scale, reliability, and cost/quality trade-offs — and is organised as pattern templates plus measurement" — and drop the "rather than as three separate taxonomies" clause, which references an alternative structure the reader never saw.
issue.acceptance_test: The stated scope of the toolkit covers every concern addressed by the five patterns and by §4–§6; no sentence in §2 defends against a structure the book does not present.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A, opening blockquote, 'four families at a glance' list, 'Signal in One Paragraph', §1, §5, service-status addendum (multiple pages)
issue.quoted_clause: the four-family comparison that this appendix's figures (Fig A.1, A.2) and its First-hand Sources list (A.10) rest on ... 1. **DeepSeek-V4** (A.3) ... 2. **Kimi K3** (A.4) ... 3. **Qwen3.8-Flash-Next** (A.5) ... 4. **GLM-5.3-Flash** (A.6) ... The capability story — reasoning, post-training, test-time compute — lives elsewhere (A.8) ... the 2026-09-27 Ornith-1.5-397B observation in A.6 ... the ~14× end is V4-Flash's ~7%-of-V3.2 single-token KV, A.7 ... see A.10 ... the A.10 First-hand Sources list
issue.observed: Every internal section pointer in the appendix is stale. The appendix's own headings are unprefixed numbers: '## 1. DeepSeek-V4', '## 2. Kimi K3', '## 3. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next', '## 4. GLM-5.3-Flash', '## 5. What This Means for the Handbook's Canonical Arithmetic', '## 6. Where 2026 Capability Actually Comes From', '## 7. The Frontier Question', '## 7A. Alternative inference in detail', '## 8. First-hand Sources'. Against that: (a) 'A.10' is cited four times for First-hand Sources, but First-hand Sources is §8 — A.10 does not exist; (b) 'A.8' is cited four times for the capability/post-training material, but §8 is First-hand Sources and the capability material is §6; (c) the four-family list points DeepSeek→A.3, Kimi→A.4, Qwen→A.5, GLM→A.6, whereas those families are §1, §2, §3, §4 respectively (off by two); (d) 'the 2026-09-27 Ornith-1.5-397B observation in A.6' — the observation is in §4 (GLM), not §6; (e) 'the ~14× end is V4-Flash's ~7%-of-V3.2 single-token KV, A.7' — that figure is in §1 and §5, not §7.
issue.evidence: Direct read of the chunk's heading sequence versus every 'A.#' pointer. No pointer in the chunk resolves to the material it names; one (A.10) names a section that does not exist. The pattern (off-by-two for the family list, +2 for the sources list, +2 for the capability list) is consistent with a single earlier draft numbering that had two more sections before the family list and two more before the sources list — i.e. one renumbering event that was never propagated.
issue.root_cause: Appendix section renumbering (likely when the unnumbered preamble sections 'The Signal in One Paragraph' and 'How to read this appendix' were inserted, and/or when the post-snapshot notes were added) was applied to the headings but not to the ~14 in-text pointers. The 'A.' prefix on the pointers also does not match the printed heading labels, so the pointers are doubly non-resolving.
issue.correction: Renumber the pointers to the printed labels and re-verify each: A.10 → §8 (First-hand Sources); A.8 → §6 (capability); A.3/A.4/A.5/A.6 in the family list → §1/§2/§3/§4; 'A.6' for the Ornith observation → §4; 'A.7' for the V4-Flash KV figure → §1 (or §5). Then grep the whole manuscript for 'A\.[0-9]' to catch any pointer outside this chunk. Consider adopting a single explicit label form (e.g. 'A §8' or 'App. A §8') and using it consistently, since the current 'A.10' form implies a numbering that does not exist.
issue.acceptance_test: Every 'A.#' string in the built PDF resolves to a heading whose number matches, and no pointer names a nonexistent section; verified by a mechanical cross-reference check over the appendix's headings and in-text pointers.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A, §7A 'Alternative inference in detail', subsection 'A language-generation trajectory' (closing paragraph)
issue.quoted_clause: The architectural consequence is conditional, and it is the reason this section sits in the model-understanding chapter rather than in a serving chapter.
issue.observed: The section's own justification for its location is now false. The heading states the section was '(moved from Ch 3)', and the section's opening line says it is 'The paper-by-paper treatment behind Ch 3 §1's alternative-inference scope note' — but the section now sits in Appendix A, not in the model-understanding chapter. The sentence therefore asserts a placement rationale that contradicts the page it is printed on.
issue.evidence: Heading '## 7A. Alternative inference in detail (moved from Ch 3) {.unnumbered}' plus the closing sentence quoted above, in the same chunk.
issue.root_cause: The section was relocated from Ch 3 to Appendix A without rewriting the sentence that explains why it belongs in Ch 3.
issue.correction: Either (a) rewrite the sentence to explain the new placement — e.g. that the material is durable mechanism background that Ch 3 §1 only scopes, and is collected here for reference — or (b) move the section back to Ch 3, where its own stated rationale places it. Option (b) also resolves APPA-03 and APPA-04 below.
issue.acceptance_test: No sentence in the built PDF asserts a chapter placement that differs from the section's actual location; a read-through of §7A finds no stale placement rationale.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A §7A, subsection 'Deriving attention FLOPs for a whole-clip video workload (Wan2.2 TI2V-5B)'; video-systems table row 'Wan2.2 TI2V-5B'
issue.quoted_clause: The worked example in Ch 8 §6 (From video dimensions to repeated attention work) uses this model only. ... Fig 8.3 shows the data path. ... *(Fig 8.3 in Ch 8 shows the data path.)*
issue.observed: The appendix contains a full Wan2.2 TI2V-5B derivation (geometry, 4N²d attention FLOPs, 27.434 PFLOP trajectory total, memory boundary, sensitivity) while simultaneously pointing the reader to 'the worked example in Ch 8 §6' for the same model and referring to 'Fig 8.3 in Ch 8' for the data path. Either Ch 8 §6 contains the same derivation (duplication across the book) or the appendix's copy is orphaned from the figure it cites. The appendix's own text also contains the sentence 'Fig 8.3 shows the data path.' immediately followed by the parenthetical '*(Fig 8.3 in Ch 8 shows the data path.)*', which is a duplicated statement within two sentences.
issue.evidence: Both passages are in this chunk; the duplication of the Fig 8.3 pointer within adjacent sentences is directly visible. Whether Ch 8 §6 duplicates the derivation cannot be settled from this chunk alone (Ch 8 not supplied) — hence medium confidence and an explicit verification step.

issue.correction: Open Ch 8 §6 and compare. If Ch 8 §6 carries the same derivation, keep the full derivation in Ch 8 §6 (where Fig 8.3 lives) and reduce the appendix subsection to a two-sentence pointer with the headline numbers, or vice versa — but not both. Delete the redundant parenthetical '*(Fig 8.3 in Ch 8 shows the data path.)*'.
issue.acceptance_test: The Wan2.2 TI2V-5B attention-FLOP derivation appears exactly once in the book; the appendix subsection either contains it or points to it unambiguously; no two adjacent sentences make the same Fig 8.3 statement.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A §7A (whole section) vs. post-snapshot note 'Diffusion language generation — 2026-10-28'
issue.chapter: Appendix A §7A / Appendix A post-snapshot notes
issue.quoted_clause: ## 7A. Alternative inference in detail (moved from Ch 3) ... Public artifacts now support more than one diffusion-language deployment pattern. LLaDA and Dream provide open checkpoints and generation code for masked/refinement-based language generation.
issue.observed: Two substantial treatments of diffusion language generation appear inside the same appendix: §7A ('From corruption to learned generation', 'A language-generation trajectory', 'State reuse follows dependency boundaries') and the post-snapshot note 'Diffusion language generation — 2026-10-28'. Both cover LLaDA, DiffusionGemma, block editing, and the SGLang Gemma4Renoise path; §7A adds MDLM, flow matching, Fast-dLLM/dKV-Cache, Block Diffusion, DFlash. The overlap is not merely topical — the same artifacts are characterized twice, once as durable mechanism and once as a dated release catalog. Separately, §7A is durable (paper-by-paper) mechanism material sitting inside an appendix whose own framing is 'a dated field guide, not an evergreen ranking' and whose stated scope is the four 2026 families.
issue.evidence: Both passages are in this chunk. §7A's own closing sentence (APPA-02) states the section was designed to sit in the model-understanding chapter, confirming it is not frontier-snapshot material.
issue.root_cause: A durable-mechanism section was relocated into a dated, scope-limited appendix without reconciling it against the appendix's existing diffusion note or against the appendix's stated scope.
issue.correction: Decide one home for the diffusion mechanism material. Preferred: keep the durable paper-by-paper treatment in Ch 3 (where §7A's own rationale and Ch 3 §1's scope note point) and reduce the appendix's post-snapshot diffusion note to a short, dated pointer listing only what changed after 2026-08-30 (release dates, engine restrictions), with a cross-reference to Ch 3. If §7A stays in the appendix, then the post-snapshot diffusion note must be cut to the delta only, and the appendix's scope statement must be widened to say it also collects durable background.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A, 'The four families at a glance' → Fig A.1 definition paragraph vs. the italic sparsity paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: 'active' ... means the parameters that participate in the forward pass for a given token: the routed experts dispatched for that token, the shared/always-on experts, and the attention and embedding/head parameters that run for every token. ... Qwen's N-gram embedding table is excluded from the active-fraction denominator below — see the Fig A.1 note ... the separate 51 B n-gram embedding and 4 B MTP modules are excluded from both numerator and denominator, so this is a *backbone* fraction
issue.observed: Two adjacent statements disagree about the Qwen numerator. The definition paragraph says the n-gram embedding table is excluded from the denominator only; the italic paragraph says the 51 B n-gram embedding is excluded from both numerator and denominator. The distinction is material: under the appendix's own definition (embedding parameters that run for every token count as active), including the 51 B n-gram table in the numerator would give 57 B / 125 B ≈ 45.6% rather than 4.8% — a factor of ~9.5 in the headline number. The appendix also states elsewhere (§3) that the n-gram tables are 'held off the accelerator and prefetched from host memory', i.e. they do participate in the forward pass, which is precisely the case the definition paragraph says counts as active.
issue.evidence: Both quoted clauses are in this chunk; 6/125 = 4.8% and 57/125 = 45.6% are the two readings. The Fig A.1 caption itself says 'the Qwen bar is its 125 B backbone only', consistent with the 'both numerator and denominator' reading, so the definition paragraph is the outlier.
issue.root_cause: The 'active' definition was written for the general case and then applied to Qwen's unusual split (backbone + separately offloaded n-gram table) without amending the definition to carve out the exception; the two statements were never reconciled.
issue.correction: Amend the definition paragraph to state the exception explicitly and consistently: the numerator excludes the separately offloaded n-gram embedding table and the MTP module for Qwen only, and the resulting figure is a backbone-only ratio, not a fraction of the deployed parameter inventory. Alternatively, report both (4.8% backbone-only and 45.6% including the n-gram table) so the reader can see how much of the 'extreme sparsity' signal is an artifact of the denominator choice. Also state in the definition that 'active' is not a proxy for per-token FLOPs (already stated as clause (b)) — the Qwen case is a live example of why.
issue.acceptance_test: The definition paragraph and the sparsity paragraph agree on whether the 51 B n-gram table is in the numerator; a reader can compute 4.8% from the stated inputs without ambiguity.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A §7A, 'Deriving attention FLOPs for a whole-clip video workload', final paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: 'Five-second clip,' '121 frames,' and '27,280 latent tokens' describe related but different quantities.

The latent spatial-temporal cell count is 109,120, and the appendix states this correctly two paragraphs earlier ('There are 109,120 latent spatial-temporal cells, each with 48 channels. Patching reduces the number of transformer positions'). Calling the post-patch count 'latent tokens' contradicts the appendix's own careful distinction between latent cells and transformer positions, and the same section elsewhere says 'all 27,280 tokens'.
issue.evidence: Both statements are in this chunk; N = 31 × 22 × 40 = 27,280 and cells = 31 × 44 × 80 = 109,120.
issue.root_cause: Loose reuse of 'latent' as a synonym for 'video-derived' in a passage whose point is that these quantities are different.
issue.correction: Replace '27,280 latent tokens' with '27,280 transformer tokens (patch positions)' or '27,280 patch tokens', consistent with the geometry paragraph.
issue.acceptance_test: The phrase 'latent tokens' does not appear where the post-patch count is meant; 'latent' is used only for the 109,120-cell grid.

issue.figure: Figure 1.1 — KV cache detail view (token -> append K/V -> stored K / stored V -> read for attention)
issue.issue: The drawing does not encode the one-step delay between sampling a generated token and writing its K/V. The figure alone therefore supports an off-by-one reading that the caption explicitly forbids, and the caption's central distinction is carried entirely by prose rather than by the diagram.
issue.evidence: Caption (printed p. 7): 'for a generated token, written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled: prompt-token K/V is written during prefill.' Figure labels: 'token1 / from prefill', 'token2 / first decode', 'token3 / second decode', '... token_n / nth decode', each with an identical arrow into the orange box 'append K/V per layer-head'. Nothing in the drawing distinguishes 'token sampled at step t' from 'token processed as input at step t+1'; the prefill token and the decode tokens are drawn with the same arrow semantics and the same box treatment. A reader scanning the figure can conclude that each decode step appends the K/V of the token it just sampled, which is wrong by one step.
issue.acceptance_test: Redraw so write timing is legible without the caption: label the append arrows 'written during prefill' (token1) and 'written at step t+1' (token2, token3), or add a step axis / step counter to the token column. Acceptance: a reader shown only the figure (caption obscured) states correctly that a generated token's K/V is written one step after it is sampled, and that prompt-token K/V is written during prefill.

issue.figure: Figure 1.1 — secondary annotations ('from prefill', 'first decode', 'second decode', 'nth decode', 'layer L . h1...h_h', 'next token q')
issue.issue: The smallest in-figure annotations appear to fall at or below the 8 pt print floor, and they carry essential semantics (which token is which; which layer/head the stored tensors belong to; what the query is).
issue.evidence: At 150 dpi the secondary annotation glyphs render at roughly 0.6-0.7x the x-height of the 10.5 pt body text set on the same page (compare 'not the expert count: GQA/MQA shrink the per-token KV width...' immediately below the caption). 'layer L . h1...h_h' and 'next token q' are the smallest and are the least redundant strings in the figure: they are the only place the reader learns the cache is indexed per (layer, head) and that the attention step consumes a query. The primary labels ('token1', 'append K/V', 'stored K - keys', 'read for attention') are visibly larger and legible.
issue.acceptance_test: Measure the smallest annotation at 100% on the printed page, or extract font sizes from the figure source: every figure glyph, including 'layer L . h1...h_h' and 'next token q', must be >= 8 pt. If any is below, raise the figure's minimum type size and re-verify that the figure still fits the text block without shrinking the primary labels.

issue.figure: Figure 1.1 — color coding of the store path vs. the read path
issue.issue: The read path and the store path are distinguished by hue alone, and the hues used are close in luminance, so the distinction largely disappears in grayscale. The distinction survives only because both paths are text-labeled.
issue.evidence: The 'store K' and 'store V' arrows are mid-gray; the 'read V' and 'read K' arrows and the 'read for attention' box are green; the 'stored K - keys' and 'stored V - values' boxes are lavender. A green of roughly (46,125,50) converts to a luminance near 93/255, and a mid-gray arrow near (100,100,100) converts to near 100/255 - a difference of about 3% of full scale, i.e. not perceptible. The lavender box border and the green box border likewise land within a few percent of each other in grayscale. The figure is therefore not self-explanatory in a grayscale print or for a reader with color-vision deficiency, except through the words 'store' and 'read'.
issue.acceptance_test: Convert the figure to grayscale at 300 dpi and confirm that the read path is distinguishable from the store path without relying on hue. If it is not, differentiate by line style (e.g. solid store arrows, dashed read arrows) or by box shape, so that hue becomes redundant rather than load-bearing.

issue.issue: Possible notation collision: 'h' is used here to index attention heads, while 'h' is a common symbol for hidden dimension elsewhere in transformer literature and possibly elsewhere in this manuscript. NOT VERIFIED against the rest of the book (only pages 27-28 were in this batch).
issue.evidence: Figure boxes read 'layer L . h1...h_h'; the caption reads 'each enumerated per head (h1...h_h)'. If the manuscript elsewhere uses 'h' for hidden size (e.g. hidden state h, or a hidden dimension of 8,192 for the canonical dense model), the same glyph denotes two different quantities within one page, which is exactly the kind of drift a reader cannot resolve from context.
issue.acceptance_test: Grep the manuscript for 'h' used as a hidden-dimension symbol and for 'h1...h_h' / 'h_h'. If both exist, rename the head index in Figure 1.1 and its caption (e.g. 'head 1...head H' or 'm1...m_H') and add the chosen symbol to the notation list. If 'h' is not used for hidden size anywhere, close this item with no change.

issue.figure: Figure 1.1 — green box 'read for attention / next token q'
issue.issue: The label conflates the query with the next token and leaves the query's origin unshown, so the box can be read as 'the next token's query is read out of the cache', which is false: the cache supplies K and V only; the query is produced by the projection of the token currently being processed.
issue.evidence: The only two arrows entering the green box are labeled 'read V' (from 'stored V - values') and 'read K' (from 'stored K - keys'). The second line of the box label, 'next token q', sits directly beneath 'read for attention' with no arrow showing where q originates, and the figure has no arrow returning from the attention box to the token column, so the chain terminates without showing that the attention output produces the next token.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel the box to make the query's role explicit (e.g. 'attention over cached K, V / query q_t from current token') and add an arrow from the token column into the box labeled 'project to q', or a return arrow labeled 'produces next token'. Acceptance: no reader can describe the cache as supplying the query.

issue.figure: Section 1.3 prose immediately above Table 1-1 (worked example)
issue.issue: The worked example's stated token arithmetic is internally inconsistent: the printed operands do not sum to the printed total, and the operand contradicts the canonical scenario, the bullets below it, and Table 1-1 on the same page.
issue.evidence: Printed text: 'If average request is ~2K input + ~300 output = 9.5K tokens per request'. 2K + 300 = 2.3K, not 9.5K. The canonical-scenario sentence two lines above reads 'prompt of ~1,200 tokens plus ~8K retrieved context (~9.2K prompt)'; the bullet below reads 'Input tokens/s: 9,200 tokens/req x 10 req/s = 92,000 tokens/s'; Table 1-1 on the same page lists 'input tokens / request ~9,200' with derivation '1,200 prompt + 8K context'. The only self-consistent reading is 9.2K + 300 = 9.5K, so the operand is wrong, not the total. (Note: at 150 dpi the operand glyphs are small; if the source string is in fact '~9.2K input' and the rendered page is correct, this finding is void - but the source must be checked, because a reader seeing '~2K input' alongside '= 9.5K' will conclude the book cannot do arithmetic.)
issue.acceptance_test: Grep the source for '9.5K tokens per request' and confirm the preceding operand is '~9.2K input'. Then re-derive: 9,200 + 300 = 9,500; 9,200 x 10 = 92,000; 9,200 x 40 = 368,000; 9,200 / 300 = 30.7 (~30x). All four must hold on the printed page. If the source reads '~2K input', rewrite to '~9.2K input + ~300 output = 9.5K tokens per request'.

issue.figure: Table 1-1 - Token throughput of the canonical workload (worked example, not reference)
issue.issue: The table is split across the page boundary at the foot of printed page 8 with no closing rule visible; the continuation (presumably the tokens/s rows that the prose bullets compute) falls on printed page 9, which was not in this batch. A split table without a repeated header row is a publication-quality defect.
issue.evidence: The last visible row on printed p. 8 is 'output tokens / request | ~300 | canonical scenario (Ch. 4, Table 4-2)', rendered flush to the bottom margin with no bottom rule, indicating the table continues. The header row ('metric | value | derivation') and the caption ('Table 1-1 - Token throughput of the canonical workload (worked example, not reference)') appear only above the split. This is only a defect if the throughput rows are not in the table; if they are (on the continuation page), the caption is acceptable but the split still leaves the caption describing a quantity that is not on the page.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'Table 1-1 - Token throughput of the canonical workload (worked example, not reference)'. Visible rows: 'input tokens / request ~9,200' and 'output tokens / request ~300'. The word 'throughput' conventionally denotes a rate (tokens/s), which is what the prose bullets compute but what the visible rows do not tabulate.
issue.acceptance_test: After resolving TAB-1.1-03, confirm the caption names the quantities actually tabulated. If the table contains only per-request counts, retitle to 'Token counts per request in the canonical workload (worked example, not reference)'; if it contains both counts and rates, keep the caption but ensure the rate rows are not separated from the caption by a page break.

issue.issue: The derivation cell states the same source twice in two different formats, and the duplication forces an unnecessary line wrap in a column that is otherwise short.
issue.evidence: The cell reads, on two lines, 'canonical scenario (Ch. 4, Table 4-2)' and 'Table 4-2 (1,200 prompt + 8K context)'. The reference 'Table 4-2' appears twice; the second line's informational content is only the arithmetic decomposition '1,200 prompt + 8K context'.
