issue.issue: The caption contains an unbalanced parenthesis and an orphaned clause, so the sentence that is supposed to define the KV cache's role cannot be parsed without the reader reconstructing the intended structure.
issue.evidence: Printed text reads verbatim: "...and the KV cache is a persistent state — written (append) and read (read past K,V, the backward read arrow from the KV cache back to attention across steps — not a processing stage." The parenthesis opened after "read (" is never closed; the parenthetical mixes an arrow label ("read past K,V"), an appositive ("the backward read arrow from the KV cache back to attention"), and the temporal qualifier ("across steps"), and the closing em-dash clause "— not a processing stage" is left syntactically orphaned. This is the caption of the book's first figure and the sentence that establishes the single most consequential distinction in the chapter (cache = persistent state, not a processing stage).
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite so that every parenthesis balances and each clause has one owner, e.g.: "...and the KV cache is a persistent state — written (the 'append K,V' arrow) and read (the 'read past K,V' arrow, which returns past K/V to attention) across steps — not a processing stage." Verify by re-reading the caption aloud for grammatical closure and by confirming that no '(' remains unmatched in the caption source.

issue.figure: FIGURE 1.2 — edge label on the Embedding → Attention arrow
issue.issue: The forward edge from Embedding to Attention is labeled "attend", which misattributes the attention operation to the wrong edge and invites a reading that contradicts the caption's own insistence that the past-token read path is the backward arrow.
issue.evidence: The Attention box's two sub-lines read "Q,K,V (this token)" and "vs. all past tokens". The only edge carrying past tokens is the green "read past K,V" arrow from KV Cache back into Attention. Labeling the Embedding→Attention edge "attend" therefore suggests that the attending happens on the forward edge, i.e. that the past tokens arrive with the embedding — which is exactly the misconception the caption spends a paragraph disarming ("the backward read arrow from the KV cache back to attention across steps"). The edge actually carries the current token's hidden state, from which Q (and the current token's K, V) are projected.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel the Embedding → Attention edge to name what it carries (e.g. "hidden state" or "Q from this token"), leaving "attend" as the operation described inside the Attention box. Confirm that after the change no edge label implies that past tokens enter via the forward path.

issue.figure: FIGURE 1.2 — box sub-labels ("user prompt", "characters", "BPE, byte-level", "corpus-driven", "order = position", "ID to d-dim vector", "one vec/token", "Q,K,V (this token)", "vs. all past tokens", "read + write", "per layer × head")
issue.issue: The box sub-labels appear to be set at roughly 65–75% of the caption's type size, which places them at or below the documented 8 pt print floor for figure in-text annotations. These are the labels that carry the figure's actual content (the per-box qualifiers), so they are the last thing that should be shrunk.
issue.evidence: At 150 dpi the sub-label glyphs measure visibly smaller than the caption's body-size text on the same page (e.g. "user prompt" and "per layer × head" versus "Conceptually only: what is drawn is..."). If the caption is set at 9–10 pt, the sub-labels land at approximately 6–7.5 pt. NOTE: this is an estimate from the rendered page, not a measurement of the source font size — the exact value must be confirmed in the figure source or by measuring the built PDF at 100% zoom.
issue.acceptance_test: Measure the rendered cap-height of the smallest annotation in Fig 1.2 in the built PDF at 100% zoom (or read the font size from the figure source). If any annotation is below 8 pt, raise the sub-label size to at least 8 pt and re-check that the box widths still accommodate the longest strings ("ID to d-dim vector", "per layer × head") without clipping or extra wrapping.

issue.figure: FIGURE 1.2 — box fills/borders and the "read past K,V" arrow
issue.issue: Color is used for two incompatible purposes at once, and there is no legend, so the reader cannot infer what the palette encodes. In grayscale the six box fills collapse to near-identical light grays and the palette carries no information at all.
issue.evidence: Green/teal is used both as the fill+border of the Tokenizer and Embedding boxes (i.e. as a "token-space" category) and as the sole distinguishing color of the "read past K,V" arrow (i.e. as "the backward read"). The remaining forward arrows ("split", "emit", "lookup", "attend", "append K,V") are all neutral gray. The six box fills (gray, mint, peach, mint, blue, lavender) all convert to approximately the same light gray value in grayscale, and the borders all convert to similar mid-gray, so in a black-and-white print the only surviving distinction is the bold box title. The figure remains interpretable in grayscale because every box is titled, but the color grouping (Tokenizer/Embedding as a pair) is lost and the green arrow's special status survives only as "slightly darker arrow".
issue.acceptance_test: Either (a) re-color the "read past K,V" arrow with a hue not used by any box, or (b) add a one-line legend stating what the palette encodes, and confirm that the figure remains fully interpretable when converted to grayscale (all six boxes still distinguishable by title, and the backward arrow still identifiable as the only non-gray arrow).

issue.figure: FIGURE 1.2 — left half (Text → Tokenizer → Token IDs → Embedding) vs. right half (Attention → KV Cache)
issue.issue: The diagram silently mixes prompt-level operations with per-token operations without marking where one level ends and the other begins, while the caption describes the whole thing as "the one-token-to-state construction".
issue.evidence: "split", "emit", and "lookup" are prompt-level operations performed once over the whole input (the Text box is labeled "user prompt / characters"). "attend", "append K,V", and "read past K,V" are per-token, per-step operations. The figure title ("How a token travels: text → tokenizer → IDs → embedding → attention → KV cache") therefore describes a chain that changes cardinality halfway across, and the caption's "one-token-to-state construction" gloss does not resolve it. A reader can plausibly infer that the whole prompt is embedded once and then attended as a unit, or that the tokenizer emits one token at a time into the embedding stage.
issue.acceptance_test: Mark the level boundary in the figure — e.g. a light bracket or a small annotation under the Token IDs → Embedding edge reading "per prompt" and under the Attention → KV Cache edge reading "per token, per step" — or state the distinction in one clause of the caption. Confirm that a reader can answer "which of these boxes run once per request and which run once per generated token?" from the figure alone.

issue.figure: Reference to "the figure" in the paragraph beginning "One detail the figure makes explicit is when a token's K/V enters the cache."
issue.issue: The paragraph attributes an explicitness to an unnamed "the figure" that Fig 1.2 does not in fact possess, and the ambiguity is resolvable only by guessing which of the two figures in scope is meant.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 14 opens: "One detail the figure makes explicit is when a token's K/V enters the cache." The paragraph then explains the input-vs-sampled distinction ("A KV token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled") and cites "the green initialize path in Fig 2.1". Fig 1.2 (printed p. 10) shows a single token in isolation and therefore cannot show the input-vs-output distinction at all; that distinction requires the step-to-step loop, i.e. Fig 2.1 (printed pp. 11–13). The nearest preceding figure reference on the page is Fig 1.2, so "the figure" is genuinely ambiguous.
issue.acceptance_test: Replace "the figure" with the explicit figure number ("Fig 2.1") in the first sentence of that paragraph, and confirm that the sentence's claim — that the figure makes the cache-entry timing explicit — is true of the figure actually cited.

issue.figure: FIG 1.2 (p. 10) vs. Fig 2.1 (pp. 11–13, not in this batch)
issue.issue: Possible cross-figure color-semantics collision: green appears in Fig 1.2 as the "read past K,V" (backward read) arrow, while printed p. 14 refers to a "green initialize path in Fig 2.1". If both are green, the same hue encodes two unrelated meanings across two consecutive figures.
issue.evidence: Fig 1.2 uses a distinctly green arrow for the backward read from KV Cache to Attention. Printed p. 14 states: "that first token is the input that seeds the decode loop (the green initialize path in Fig 2.1)". NOT VERIFIED: Fig 2.1 falls on printed pp. 11–13 and was not rendered in this batch, so I cannot confirm its actual color usage. This finding is conditional on that inspection.
issue.acceptance_test: Render and inspect Fig 2.1 (printed pp. 11–13). If its initialize path is also green, either recolor one of the two so that a given hue carries one meaning across both figures, or add a shared legend for the two figures. If the hues are already distinct, close this item with no change.

issue.issue: The green 'initialize' path crosses the two black KV-cache arrows ('read' downward, 'append' upward) without any junction or bridge marker. The green horizontal segment runs at the vertical level just above the DECODE band's top edge, spanning from the figure's right margin to the 'previous token' box; the black read/append arrows run vertically from the bottom of the PERSISTENT KV CACHE box down to the top of the decode band's 'transformer' box, so they intersect that horizontal segment. In a diagram whose only color-coded distinction is the green path, an unmarked crossing of a green line over two black arrows invites the reader to read a connection (e.g. 'the initialize path feeds the cache read') that the caption explicitly denies.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 35: the green horizontal segment at approximately y=345 px (image is ~580 px wide for 8.5 in, i.e. ~68 px/in) spans x≈122–478; the black read arrow (x≈278) and append arrow (x≈300) both span y≈300–352 and therefore cross it. No crossing marker, no 'no connection' bridge, no directional break. The caption's only disambiguation is the sentence 'The initialize path (labelled initialize) seeds the loop with the first sampled token', which is prose rescue for a visual ambiguity.
issue.acceptance_test: Re-render the figure at 300 dpi and confirm the two crossings persist. Then re-route the initialize path so it does not intersect the read/append arrows — e.g. run it below the KV-cache box and enter 'previous token' from the left, or run it along the far right and drop into 'previous token' from above-left of the band. If a crossing is retained, add explicit bridge markers at both intersections and state in the caption that crossings are not junctions. Acceptance: a grayscale 300-dpi render shows zero unmarked line-line crossings.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.1 — annotation 'conceptual per-step per-layer cache I/O'
issue.issue: The italic gray annotation 'conceptual per-step per-layer cache I/O' has three independent defects: (a) it is the smallest and lightest text in the figure (light-gray italic, visibly smaller than the other arrow labels 'populate', 'read', 'append', 'initialize', 'loop'), so it is the first element to disappear at print size or in a low-quality grayscale reproduction; (b) it is placed far to the right of the read/append arrows it annotates (roughly 50–170 px away), immediately adjacent to the green initialize path, so it reads as a label for the green path or for the 'logits + sampling' box rather than for the cache I/O arrows; (c) its baseline sits only a few pixels above the green initialize horizontal segment, so the two nearly touch. The annotation is also redundant: the caption already states 'each step reads the cached K/V, appends the new K/V'.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 35: annotation occupies approximately x=350–450, y=330–343, in light-gray italic; the green horizontal segment is at y≈345–347 across the same x-range; the read/append arrows it describes are at x≈278 and x≈300. Contrast of the annotation is visibly lower than every other label in the figure.
issue.acceptance_test: Either delete the annotation (the caption carries the same fact) or (i) move it immediately adjacent to the read/append arrows, (ii) set it in the same black roman face and size as the other arrow labels (>= 8 pt at final print size), and (iii) verify >= 3 mm clearance from the green initialize path. Acceptance: a 300-dpi grayscale render shows the annotation at >= 8 pt, in black, with no element within 3 mm, and positioned so that its referent is unambiguous without the caption.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.1 — PERSISTENT KV CACHE box vs. the two process bands
issue.issue: The figure uses one visual grammar for two different kinds of object. The PREFILL band, the DECODE band, and the PERSISTENT KV CACHE are all drawn as bordered rounded rectangles with the same fill family, and the KV cache is placed vertically between the two bands with arrows entering and leaving it. A reader scanning the figure can therefore read it as a three-stage pipeline — PREFILL -> KV CACHE -> DECODE — i.e. as a processing stage rather than as persistent state. That is precisely the misconception the caption spends two sentences disarming ('conceptual groupings for teaching, not runtime components: a real serving stack has per-layer, per-request KV ...'). The figure should carry that distinction in its own visual grammar rather than delegating it entirely to prose. The visual hierarchy compounds the risk: the KV cache is the largest, boldest, most centrally placed element, so the figure's emphasis points at the cache rather than at the two phases the caption calls out as the TTFT and TPOT determinants.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 35: PREFILL band (x≈85–470, y≈143–195), PERSISTENT KV CACHE (x≈160–405, y≈235–290, bold uppercase label), DECODE band (x≈85–470, y≈350–405) — all three share the same rounded-rectangle-with-border treatment; the cache is the only element with a bold, letter-spaced, all-caps label.
issue.acceptance_test: Give the PERSISTENT KV CACHE a distinct visual treatment (storage glyph, distinct fill/hatch, or a different outline weight) so that it cannot be parsed as a third processing stage, and verify in a grayscale render that the store is distinguishable from the two process bands without relying on color. Acceptance: a reader shown only the figure (no caption) describes the KV cache as state that persists across the two phases, not as a pipeline stage.

issue.issue: The caption's closing sentence appears garbled in the built PDF. As rendered it reads: '...not runtime components: a real serving stack has per-layer, per-request KV prefills "prefill band" object. [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]'. The clause 'per-request KV prefills "prefill band" object' is not grammatical, the quoted phrase '"prefill band"' appears nowhere else in the caption, and the sentence has no predicate. This is the caption of the book's canonical pipeline figure — the one figure that Chapter 2 and later chapters refer back to — so a broken sentence here is a reader-facing defect in the most-reused visual artifact in the book. It is also the sentence that carries the figure's most important caveat (the bands and the single cache box are teaching abstractions, not runtime components), so the caveat is currently not reliably legible.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 35, caption lines 6–8: 'The two bands and the single PERSISTENT KV CACHE box are conceptual groupings for teaching, not runtime components: a real serving stack has per-layer, per-request KV prefills "prefill band" object. [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]'.
issue.acceptance_test: Extract the caption from the built PDF text layer (pdftotext -f 35 -l 35) and from the .tex source. If the string 'per-request KV prefills "prefill band" object' is present in either, rewrite the closing sentence to a grammatical form that preserves both the caveat and the label, e.g. '...not runtime components: a real serving stack holds per-layer, per-request KV caches, and the "prefill band" is a teaching abstraction.' Acceptance: the caption's final sentence has a subject and a predicate, the quoted phrase '"prefill band"' is either defined or removed, and the caveat survives verbatim in meaning. NOTE: this finding is based on the rendered page only; the source text was not inspected in this pass.

issue.issue: The caption states 'Color is figure-local decoration — each box is tinted.' Both halves are inaccurate as rendered: the inner boxes are white/unfilled with thin borders (they are not tinted), and the green 'initialize' arrow is not decoration — it is the figure's only color-coded distinction, separating the one-shot initialization path from the steady-state loop path. A reader who accepts the caption's blanket statement may conclude that the green carries no information and that the initialize/loop distinction rests on the labels alone, which is not the design intent.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 35: all inner boxes (prompt, tokens + positions, transformer, logits + sampling, first token, previous token, token + position, next token) render as white fills with thin gray borders; the only saturated color in the figure is the 'initialize' arrow and its label.
issue.acceptance_test: Check the .tex source for the box fill definitions. If the boxes are untinted, delete 'each box is tinted' and replace the sentence with something like 'Color distinguishes the one-shot initialize path from the steady-state loop path; all other elements are monochrome.' Acceptance: the caption's color statement is true of the rendered figure and does not assert that color is uninformative.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.1 — absence of a scale/emphasis qualifier
issue.issue: The figure encodes no relative cost, and the caption's disclaimer covers only 'not runtime components', not 'not to scale'. The two bands are drawn at equal visual weight and the KV cache is drawn larger and more prominently than either band, so a reader can infer either that prefill and decode cost the same, or that the KV cache is the dominant resource. The caption asserts the opposite emphasis ('PREFILL ... is the dominant contributor to TTFT'; 'DECODE ... measured by TPOT'). The figure and the caption therefore disagree in emphasis without the figure disclaiming it.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 35: PREFILL band and DECODE band are drawn with identical box sizes and identical styling; the PERSISTENT KV CACHE box is ~245 px wide and ~55 px tall with a bold label, visually the dominant element; no qualifier about scale appears in the caption.
issue.acceptance_test: Add an explicit 'not to scale' qualifier to the caption, and/or annotate the two bands with the metric each one drives ('dominant TTFT contributor' on PREFILL, 'dominant TPOT contributor' on DECODE) so that the figure's emphasis matches the caption's claims without asserting a universal compute-bound/bandwidth-bound regime. Acceptance: the figure cannot be read as implying equal cost for the two phases or as implying the KV cache dominates runtime cost.

issue.issue: The green initialize path's vertical segment runs immediately outside the right edge of both process bands (roughly 8 px at the rendered scale, i.e. on the order of 0.1 in or less at print size). The line therefore reads as a band boundary or as a bracket belonging to the bands rather than as a separate connector, and it is the segment that carries the figure's only color-coded distinction.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 35: the green vertical segment is at x≈478; the PREFILL and DECODE band rectangles both terminate at x≈470.
issue.acceptance_test: Re-route the initialize path with >= 3 mm clearance from the band outlines (or route it on the left side of the figure, where the 'loop' path already runs, with the two paths separated vertically). Acceptance: in a 300-dpi grayscale render the green path is unambiguously a connector and not a band edge.

issue.issue: Printed page 15 carries only the figure and its caption; roughly the bottom quarter of the page (on the order of 2 inches) is blank, and the following section does not begin on the page. For a book whose page budget is tight and whose figures are the primary teaching artifacts, this is wasted page real estate and it also means the reader meets the figure with no adjacent prose to prime the labels.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 35: figure occupies y≈120–460, caption y≈485–600, page bottom margin begins at y≈620 with the footer at y≈735; no body text follows the caption on the page.
issue.acceptance_test: Reflow so that the figure, its caption, and the opening prose of the following section share the page, or move the figure to a page where it can be followed by text. Acceptance: no trailing blank block of more than ~1 inch below the last element on the page.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.2 — Prefill and decode: two regimes split by the roofline ridge
issue.issue: The roofline is drawn as a single rising line with no horizontal plateau. The compute-bound region (blue, horizontal hatch) is shaded all the way to the top of the plot (1e+15 FLOP/s), but the figure's own annotation states the machine's ceiling is 989 TFLOPS (9.89e14). A reader therefore sees the compute-bound regime as permitting performance up to 1e15 FLOP/s, i.e. above the stated hardware peak. The classic roofline shape (rising ridge + flat ceiling) is missing, and the flat ceiling is the single most important visual fact about the compute-bound regime.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 43: the black ridge line terminates at the top frame near x≈295; to its right the blue 'compute-bound' fill continues to the 1e+15 gridline with no horizontal boundary. The annotation 'H100 SXM, BF16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 → ridge at 295 FLOP/byte' fixes the ceiling at 9.89e14 FLOP/s, and the floating '989 TFLOPS' text sits at the top of the plot where the plateau should be. The caption's claim that 'prefill sits in the compute-bound regime' is therefore drawn against a region whose upper bound contradicts the stated peak.
issue.acceptance_test: Redraw so that a horizontal ceiling line at 9.89e14 FLOP/s runs from the ridge (AI≈295) to the right edge of the plot, with the compute-bound hatch filling only below that line; attach the '989 TFLOPS peak (BF16 dense)' label to that line. Re-render at 150 dpi and confirm (a) no blue hatch above 9.89e14, (b) the ceiling line is visually continuous with the rising ridge, (c) the prefill marker lies below the ceiling.

issue.issue: The drawn ridge line is geometrically inconsistent with the stated hardware bandwidth. On a log–log roofline the ridge must satisfy y = AI × BW, i.e. slope exactly 1 in log–log, passing through (AI=1, y=3.35e12) and (AI=295, y=9.89e14). As rendered, the line's lower-left endpoint sits at approximately y≈1e12 at AI=1 and reaches 1e15 at AI≈295, which implies BW≈1e12 B/s — a factor of ~3.4 below the annotated 3.35 TB/s. The figure is the book's central quantitative device for the prefill/decode regime split, and a reader who checks the arithmetic against the drawn line will find it does not hold.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 43: black line lower-left endpoint ≈ (x=1 tick, y=1e+12 gridline); upper-right endpoint ≈ (x≈295, y=1e+15). Independently: 989e12 / 3.35e12 = 295.2 FLOP/byte (ridge AI, consistent with the annotation), and the ridge height at AI=1 must be 3.35e12 FLOP/s, i.e. ~0.52 decade above the 1e+12 gridline. The drawn endpoint is ~0.5 decade below that.
issue.acceptance_test: Regenerate the ridge from the annotated constants (y = AI × 3.35e12, capped at 9.89e14) rather than hand-placing endpoints, then verify on the rendered page that the line passes through (1, 3.35e12) and (295, 9.89e14) to within the line width, and that its log–log slope is 1.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.2 — 'prefill' marker (x-position) vs caption and prose
issue.issue: Three different values are in play for the canonical prefill arithmetic intensity, and they do not agree: (a) the caption says the canonical prefill point is '~2K FLOP/byte'; (b) the printed prose on the facing page (printed p.20) repeats 'the canonical prefill point ~2K FLOP/byte'; (c) the figure's 'prefill' triangle is drawn at roughly 4×10^3 FLOP/byte. Worse, ~2K is itself inconsistent with the canonical scenario the book states (70B-class dense model, 1,200 + 8K = 9,200 input tokens): for a dense model, prefill arithmetic intensity ≈ 2·N_params·N_tok / (2·N_params + KV bytes) ≈ N_tok, i.e. ≈9×10^3 FLOP/byte for a 9.2K-token prefill (≈7.8×10^3 if the 24 GB of KV writes are included; ≈9.1×10^3 with attention FLOPs added). A ~2K FLOP/byte prefill corresponds to roughly a 2,000-token prefill, not the canonical 9.2K.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 43: 'prefill' triangle at x ≈ 4×10^3 (between the 1000 and 10000 ticks, ~0.6 decade past 1000). Caption: 'the canonical prefill point ~2K FLOP/byte'. Printed p.20 (PDF p.40): 'the canonical prefill point ~2K FLOP/byte'. Canonical scenario (printed p.20): 70B-class dense, FP16, 1,200 + 8K retrieved context = 9.2K input tokens. Derivation: FLOPs = 2 × 70e9 × 9200 = 1.288e15; bytes ≈ 140 GB weights + 24.1 GB KV write (9200 × 2.62 MB/token) + ~1 GB activations ≈ 165 GB; AI ≈ 7.8e3 FLOP/byte (≈9.2e3 ignoring KV writes).
issue.acceptance_test: Fix one canonical prefill arithmetic-intensity value, state it once in the caption, and place the marker at exactly that x-coordinate (2×10^3 → 0.30 decade past the 1000 tick; 9.2×10^3 → 0.96 decade). Then re-derive it in the text from the canonical scenario (AI ≈ N_prefill_tokens for a dense model) and confirm the prose on printed p.20, the caption, and the marker agree to the stated rounding. If the canonical scenario's prefill length is intended to be ~2K tokens, change the scenario instead and propagate.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.2 — 'roofline ridge ~295' label vs unlabeled black line
issue.issue: The red label 'roofline ridge ~295' sits above the dashed vertical line, but 'roofline ridge' is the natural name for the black diagonal line (the roofline), which is itself unlabeled. A reader can plausibly read the red label as naming the black line, in which case the black line would be claimed to be at AI≈295 — i.e. a vertical line — which is nonsense. The two lines carry two different meanings (a performance ceiling vs. an intensity location) and neither the caption nor the figure disambiguates them.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 43: red text 'roofline ridge ~295' positioned above the plot at the dashed line's x; the black diagonal line has no text label anywhere in the figure or caption. Caption refers to 'the roofline ridge' and 'the ~295 ridge' without saying which drawn element is which.
issue.acceptance_test: Label the black line directly (e.g. 'roofline: y = AI × 3.35 TB/s, capped at 989 TFLOPS') and rename the red annotation to 'ridge AI ≈ 295 FLOP/byte' with a short leader to the dashed line; add one clause to the caption stating that the solid line is the roofline and the dashed line marks the ridge's arithmetic intensity.

issue.issue: The red italic 'decode' annotation is placed immediately adjacent to (and appears to touch or be crossed by) the black roofline line, at the point where the line is steepest. This is the one place in the figure where the reader must distinguish 'the decode operating point' from 'the roofline', and the collision degrades both.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 43: the word 'decode' occupies roughly x∈[178,205] px, y≈315 px; the black ridge line passes through approximately y≈319→310 px over that same x-range, i.e. the glyphs sit on the line's path.
issue.acceptance_test: Move the 'decode' text label to the left of the marker (or below-left, inside the memory-bound region) with clear separation of at least one text-line height from the ridge line, and re-render to confirm no glyph touches the line.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.2 — bottom-left annotation 'H100 SXM, BF16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 → ridge at 295 FLOP/byte'
issue.issue: This annotation is set in small type directly on top of the diagonally hatched peach memory-bound fill, immediately above the x-axis and beside the '1e+11' tick label. Small dark text over 45° hatching is the lowest-contrast region in the figure, and the annotation is the only place the reader learns the machine constants. It also restates, redundantly and in a second location, the two facts already given by the floating '989 TFLOPS' label and the 'roofline ridge ~295' label.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 43: the annotation runs along the bottom-left inside the plot frame, over the hatch pattern, at a visibly smaller size than the axis labels; the same two numbers (989 TFLOPS, 295 FLOP/byte) appear twice more elsewhere in the figure.
issue.acceptance_test: Move the hardware-constants annotation out of the hatched region — either below the x-axis as a figure note or into the caption — and delete whichever of the two in-figure labels becomes redundant once the ceiling line is drawn (see FIG-2.2-01). Confirm at 150 dpi that the text sits on a plain background with no hatch behind it.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.2 — italic note 'markers = regime, not measured MFU (real kernels run below the roof)'
issue.issue: This is the figure's most important epistemic caveat — it tells the reader that the two markers are regime indicators, not measurements — yet it is rendered in small, light-gray italic type on the hatched peach fill in the upper-left of the plot. It is the least legible text in the figure and it carries the heaviest interpretive load. The caveat is also not repeated in the caption, where it would be read reliably.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 43: two-line italic gray note at approximately x∈[165,300] px, y≈170–185 px, over the diagonal hatch; visibly lower contrast and smaller than every other annotation. The caption discusses regimes and operating points but does not state that the markers' vertical positions are not measured MFU.
issue.acceptance_test: Set the note in the same size and weight as the other figure annotations, in a dark neutral color, on an unhatched background (e.g. in the white region above the ridge line), and add the equivalent clause to the caption ('the markers indicate regime; their vertical positions are illustrative, not measured MFU').

issue.issue: The '989 TFLOPS' text floats in the upper-right of the plot with no leader line and no boundary to attach to, in the middle of the compute-bound region. It can be read as a data point, as a label for the whole region, or as the value of the ridge line's right endpoint. Because the roofline's flat ceiling is missing (FIG-2.2-01), the label has nothing to name.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 43: '989 TFLOPS' at approximately x∈[355,410] px, y≈160 px, inside the blue hatched region, with no connecting element to the black line or to any gridline.
issue.acceptance_test: After adding the ceiling line, place '989 TFLOPS peak (BF16 dense)' immediately above that horizontal line at its left end (near AI=295), with the text baseline parallel to the line; verify no overlap with the 'prefill' marker or the region label.

issue.issue: The prefill triangle is placed at roughly 5×10^14 FLOP/s, i.e. about half the 989 TFLOPS ceiling. That vertical placement silently encodes a specific assumed MFU (~50%), which the caption does not license and the figure's own note disclaims. A reader who trusts the vertical coordinate will infer a performance figure the book has not derived.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 43: triangle at y ≈ 4.9e14 (≈0.31 decade below the 1e+15 gridline), against a stated ceiling of 9.89e14. The caption says only 'prefill lands at high intensity — the compute-bound side'.
issue.acceptance_test: Either place the prefill marker on the ceiling line (making it a pure regime marker) or annotate its vertical coordinate explicitly (e.g. 'illustrative MFU ≈ 50%') and state in the caption that the vertical position is illustrative.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.2 — color semantics and grayscale behavior
issue.issue: Red carries two unrelated meanings in this figure: the 'decode' marker and the dashed ridge-AI line. In grayscale the decode marker (solid red circle) sits on the peach memory-bound fill and loses contrast against it, and the red dashed line becomes a mid-gray dashed line that could be confused with a gridline. The figure survives grayscale only because shape (circle vs triangle) and dash pattern carry the distinctions; the color assignments themselves do not.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 43: red circle on peach/orange hatched fill; red dashed vertical line; blue triangle on blue hatched fill; blue 'compute-bound' text on blue hatch. Grayscale separation depends entirely on shape and hatch direction (diagonal vs horizontal), which is adequate but not by design.
issue.acceptance_test: Convert the figure to grayscale and confirm that (a) the decode marker is distinguishable from the memory-bound fill, (b) the dashed ridge line is distinguishable from gridlines, (c) the two region labels remain legible on their hatched fills. If any fails, add shape/dash redundancy (e.g. hollow vs filled markers, a distinct dash pattern for the ridge line) rather than relying on hue.

issue.issue: The y-axis is labeled 'attainable performance', which invites the reading that the plotted values are achievable performance figures, while the figure's own note says the markers are not measured MFU and the caption calls the whole thing '[ILLUSTRATIVE]'. The axis is in fact a roofline ceiling, not an attainable-performance measurement.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 43: y-axis label 'attainable performance (FLOP/s)'; figure note 'markers = regime, not measured MFU (real kernels run below the roof)'; caption '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual roofline developed in Ch 8'.
issue.acceptance_test: Rename the y-axis to 'roofline ceiling (FLOP/s)' (or 'performance bound (FLOP/s)') and confirm the caption and axis label use the same term for the same quantity.

issue.figure: FIGURE 3.4 (Dense vs MoE parameter allocation and KV cache behavior)
issue.issue: Caption's active-parameter arithmetic does not close: it states '~12.8B is active per token: the always-on attention/shared weights (~1.4B) plus the two routed experts (11.2B + 5.7B)'. 1.4 + 11.2 + 5.7 = 18.3B, not 12.8B. The figure itself says 'active experts = 23 GB resident (2 x 11.4)' = 11.4B routed params, so the correct decomposition is 1.4 + 5.7 + 5.7 = 12.8B. The '11.2B' term is wrong (it appears to be a stray 2 x 5.6 or a mis-keyed '5.7').
issue.evidence: Figure legend: 'active experts = 23 GB resident (2 x 11.4)' and '1 expert = 5.78 params = 11.4 GB (FP16)'. 23 GB / 2 bytes = 11.5B params for two experts, i.e. 5.7B each. Caption's own total (12.8B) is consistent with 1.4 + 2 x 5.7, and inconsistent with its printed breakdown.
issue.acceptance_test: Caption reads '~12.8B is active per token: the always-on attention/shared weights (~1.4B) plus the two routed experts (5.7B + 5.7B)', and the three terms sum to 12.8B. A reviewer recomputing the sum from the printed caption obtains 12.8B exactly.

issue.issue: Internal numeric inconsistency in the per-expert line: 5.78B params at FP16 (2 bytes/param) = 11.56 GB, not 11.4 GB. Further, 8 x 5.78B = 46.24B params = 92.5 GB, which does not match the figure's '91 GB experts' (8 x 11.4 GB = 91.2 GB, implying 5.7B params/expert). One of the two numbers (5.78 or 11.4/91) is wrong.
issue.evidence: Figure text: '1 expert = 5.78 params = 11.4 GB (FP16)'; 'MoE total resident = 94 GB = 91 GB experts + 3 GB always-on'; 'inactive experts = 68 GB (6 x 11.4)'; 'active experts = 23 GB resident (2 x 11.4)'. 91/8 = 11.375 GB/expert = 5.69B params/expert.
issue.acceptance_test: Either the line reads '1 expert = 5.7B params = 11.4 GB (FP16)' with 8 x 5.7B x 2 B = 91.2 GB, or it reads '5.78B params = 11.56 GB' with the totals updated to 92.5 GB experts / 95.5 GB total. All three printed quantities (per-expert GB, expert subtotal, total resident) must be mutually consistent to within the stated rounding.

issue.figure: FIGURE 3.4 (KV panels: 'Dense KV = 12 GB' vs 'MoE KV = 0.6 GB')
issue.issue: The two KV figures are only comparable if they refer to the same token count, but neither the figure nor the caption states the context length. The caption asserts 'the KV bytes per token follow each model's own attention shape' without giving bytes/token or the token count, so the 20x ratio (12 GB vs 0.6 GB) is presented as an unexplained number. The reader cannot verify the comparison, and the caption's claim that routing does not change KV is the chapter's key point.
issue.evidence: Recomputation at 8-bit KV: dense (80 layers, hidden 8192, full MHA) = 2 x 80 x 8192 x 1 B = 1.31 MB/token; MoE (32 layers, hidden 4096, 8 KV heads x 128 = 1024 KV dim) = 2 x 32 x 1024 x 1 B = 64 KB/token. 12 GB / 1.31 MB = ~9.2K tokens; 0.6 GB / 64 KB = ~9.8K tokens. Both are consistent with a ~9.2K-token context, but that number appears nowhere.
issue.acceptance_test: The figure states the shared context length (e.g. 'at 9.2K tokens') and the per-token KV bytes for each shape (1.31 MB/token dense, 64 KB/token MoE), so that 12 GB and 0.6 GB can be independently recomputed from the printed values.

issue.figure: FIGURE 3.4 (dense 70B panel: 4x5 grid of blue squares)
issue.issue: The dense-model grid is a decorative 20-square block with no stated meaning (no 'not to scale' note, unlike the MoE side), while the MoE grid encodes per-expert identity and active/inactive state. A reader may infer that the dense grid encodes something countable (e.g. 20 units of parameter mass) that it does not.
issue.evidence: Caption applies 'not shown to scale' only to the MoE expert set ('~94 GB, not shown to scale'). The dense grid has 20 identical squares with no legend entry.
issue.acceptance_test: Either add a 'not to scale' note to the dense grid, or replace it with a single labeled block ('140 GB resident & active') so that only the MoE grid carries per-unit encoding.

issue.issue: The figure asserts a specific execution model for Wan2.2 A14B ('Not two experts within one forward'; 'Only high-noise expert runs' / 'Only low-noise expert runs'), i.e. that the two experts run in separate forward passes selected by denoising stage. This is a first-party architectural claim about a specific released model and must be sourced; the caption's Scope line ('official rounded counts ... not an inferred per-expert split') explicitly disclaims the very per-expert split the figure draws.
issue.evidence: Figure text: 'Denoising schedule progresses / Not two experts within one forward'; stage boxes 'Only high-noise expert runs' and 'Only low-noise expert runs'. Caption: 'Scope: official rounded counts (about 27B total, about 14B active), not an inferred per-expert split; schematic (no step counts).' The figure's stage boxes ARE a per-expert split.
issue.acceptance_test: Either (a) the caption's Scope line is rewritten to state that the per-expert stage assignment is schematic/illustrative and is not an official statement, or (b) the caption cites the first-party source for the stage-wise expert routing and the Scope line no longer disclaims a per-expert split. The two statements must not conflict.

issue.issue: The diagram mixes two connector semantics with no legend: dashed blue arrows (checkpoint -> stage, i.e. 'which checkpoint is loaded/selected') and a solid black arrow (high-noise stage -> low-noise stage, i.e. temporal progression of the denoising schedule). The reader must guess which arrow means 'selection' and which means 'time'.
issue.evidence: Rendered page shows two dashed blue vertical arrows from the checkpoint boxes and one solid horizontal black arrow between the stage boxes; no key is provided in figure or caption.
issue.acceptance_test: Add a one-line key to the figure (or caption) distinguishing dashed = checkpoint selection, solid = denoising-schedule progression.

issue.issue: Roughly the top quarter of the printed page is empty before the figure begins, and the figure block is then followed by a large gap before the caption. The page reads as under-filled relative to the rest of the chapter.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 63: content starts at approximately 25% down the page; the figure's own title line is the first ink.
issue.acceptance_test: The figure is floated to the top of the page (or the preceding text is allowed to fill the page) so that no more than ~10% of the page height is blank above the first element.

issue.issue: Active/inactive expert state in the MoE grid is encoded by fill color (orange vs gray) with no shape or hatch difference. In grayscale the orange and gray squares differ only in luminance, and the dense-model blue squares are a third luminance class; a reader printing in grayscale must rely on the E1-E8 labels plus the legend to decode state.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 67: MoE grid uses orange fill for E1/E4, light gray for E2/E3/E5/E6/E7/E8, blue for the dense grid; no pattern or outline differentiation.
issue.acceptance_test: Active experts carry a distinct outline or hatch in addition to fill, so that active/inactive state survives grayscale reproduction and color-vision deficiency.

issue.issue: The figure introduces a second, competing taxonomy that contradicts the one established one chapter earlier, and the relationship between the two is never stated. FIG 4.1 (PDF 93 / printed 73) presents 'the six workload dimensions' (Quality requirements; Traffic/concurrency; Token profile; Latency SLO; Economic constraints; Operational constraints) as the book's workload-characterization vocabulary. FIG 5.1's top box, also labelled 'Workload characterization', lists only three items: 'tokens · cost · SLO'. A reader who has just absorbed the six-dimension frame will read the three-item box as a contradiction (or, worse, as a silent narrowing of the framework). Separately, the caption calls the five boxes 'the model-selection dimensions', introducing a third label for what are visibly derived from the Chapter 4 dimensions (latency -> Latency SLO; KV cache -> Token profile; S/Tok -> Economic constraints). The book never says whether the five surfaces are a subset of the six dimensions, a refinement of them, or an orthogonal axis.
issue.evidence: Page 73 figure header 'WORKLOAD DIMENSION' with six rows; caption: 'The six workload dimensions and the architectural decision each one drives'. Page 92 figure box 1: 'Workload characterization' / 'tokens · cost · SLO'; caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions'. No cross-reference to Chapter 4 or to FIG 4.1 appears on page 92.
issue.acceptance_test: Either (a) relabel the top box 'Workload characterization (subset shown: tokens · cost · SLO)' and add a caption clause stating that only the dimensions that bind model selection are drawn, or (b) replace the three items with the Chapter 4 vocabulary. In addition, add one caption sentence defining the relation between the six workload dimensions and the five selection surfaces (e.g. 'the five surfaces are the subset of the six dimensions that constrain model choice; the remaining dimension, Operational constraints, is out of scope for this figure'). Verify that a reader who has read p. 73 can state whether the five surfaces are a subset, a refinement, or a separate axis.

issue.issue: The abbreviation 'S/Tok' in the 'Five selection surfaces' box is undefined on the page and has two plausible readings that are not equivalent, one of which duplicates an adjacent term. Reading A: 'seconds per token' (i.e. TPOT / decode latency), which duplicates the adjacent surface 'latency'. Reading B: '$ per token' (cost per token), which duplicates the 'cost' item in the box immediately above ('tokens · cost · SLO'). Because the figure is the reader's first encounter with the token, and because the caption's whole argument is that the five surfaces are a distinct set, an ambiguous member of that set weakens the figure's central claim. The book elsewhere uses 'TPOT' for time-per-output-token, so a reader is likely to reach for that reading and then find the surface list redundant.
issue.evidence: Figure box 2 sub-label: 'quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate'. Figure box 1 sub-label: 'tokens · cost · SLO'. Caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions'. No expansion of 'S/Tok' appears in the caption, the figure, or the visible page text.
issue.acceptance_test: Replace 'S/Tok' with an unambiguous phrase ('cost per token' or 'seconds per output token'), or define the abbreviation in the caption and in the glossary. Confirm that the resulting five-item list contains no item that restates 'latency' or 'cost' from the box above. Verify against the Chapter 5 body text that the chosen expansion matches the term the chapter actually uses.

issue.issue: The word 'quality' denotes two different things inside one figure, and the caption asserts they are distinct without disambiguating them. 'quality' is one of the five selection surfaces in the drawn box; 'retrieval quality' and 'final answer quality' are two of the five end-to-end evaluation gates listed in the caption. The caption's claim that the surfaces are 'deliberately distinct from the end-to-end evaluation gates' is therefore made using an identical word for one surface and two gates, with no clause saying which 'quality' the surface refers to. A reader can plausibly conclude that the 'quality' surface IS the retrieval-quality gate, which is precisely the confusion the caption says it is excluding.
issue.evidence: Figure box 2 sub-label: 'quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate'. Caption: 'they are deliberately distinct from the end-to-end evaluation gates (retrieval quality, reranking, embedding recall, grounding, and final answer quality) that a RAG system must also pass'.
issue.acceptance_test: Rename the surface so it cannot collide with a gate name (e.g. 'answer-quality bar' or 'quality requirement'), and/or add a caption clause naming which quality each refers to. Verify that no reader can map the surface 'quality' onto either 'retrieval quality' or 'final answer quality' without re-reading the caption.

issue.issue: The drawing implies that all five selection surfaces apply to both legs, but the surfaces are not leg-symmetric. A single 'Five selection surfaces' box fans out through two arrows labelled 'split' to 'Retrieval leg' and 'Generation leg', which reads as 'these five surfaces are then evaluated for each leg'. Two of the five are generation-leg concepts: an embedding model has no autoregressive KV cache, and it has no per-token decode cost of the kind 'S/Tok' denotes. The figure therefore permits the inference that the embedding model has a KV cache, which is a substantive architectural error rather than a stylistic one.
issue.evidence: Figure: 'Five selection surfaces' -> two arrows labelled 'split' -> 'Retrieval leg' (embedding · 768-dim) and 'Generation leg' (70B FP16 · serving). Surface list includes 'KV cache' and 'S/Tok'. Caption describes the surfaces as applying to 'model selection' generally and does not qualify which surfaces bind which leg.
issue.acceptance_test: Annotate the two split arrows with the surfaces that bind each leg (e.g. 'quality · latency · cost/token' for retrieval; 'quality · latency · KV cache · cost/token' for generation), or add a caption sentence stating that the surfaces are evaluated per leg and that KV cache and per-token decode cost apply only to the generation leg. Verify that no reader concludes the embedding model holds a KV cache.

issue.figure: FIGURE 4.1 (Six-dimension workload characterization mapped to architectural decisions)
issue.issue: The caption contradicts itself about the cardinality of the mapping. The first paragraph states that 'The arrows are non-exclusive: in practice a dimension often influences several decisions at once'. The second paragraph then describes the figure as 'The six workload dimensions and the architectural decision each one drives' — singular 'the architectural decision', 'each one drives' — which asserts exactly the one-to-one mapping the first paragraph disclaims. The figure's own note ('primary mapping shown; cross-influences omitted') is consistent with the first paragraph, so the second paragraph is the outlier. The result is that the caption simultaneously teaches and un-teaches the same point in consecutive paragraphs.
issue.evidence: Caption paragraph 1: 'Each arrow means the dimension constrains/informs the corresponding architectural choice - it is a heuristic influence, not a deterministic one-to-one mapping. The arrows are non-exclusive: in practice a dimension often influences several decisions at once'. Caption paragraph 2: 'The six workload dimensions and the architectural decision each one drives: Quality requirements -> model size/type; ...'.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite paragraph 2 to use non-exclusive language, e.g. 'The six workload dimensions and the primary architectural decision each one informs: ...', and confirm that no sentence in the caption asserts a one-to-one mapping. Verify the revised caption against the figure note 'primary mapping shown; cross-influences omitted (see caption)'.

issue.issue: The caption's parenthetical is missing a separator and reads as a run-on: 'two legs (retrieval/embedding generation/70B)'. The intended reading is '(retrieval/embedding, generation/70B)', matching the drawn boxes 'Retrieval leg - embedding · 768-dim' and 'Generation leg - 70B FP16 · serving'. As printed, 'embedding generation' can be parsed as a single phrase, which is confusing in a figure whose whole point is that the two legs are distinct.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'Model selection for RAG workload - five selection surfaces -> two legs (retrieval/embedding generation/70B) -> the system decision.'
issue.acceptance_test: Render as 'two legs (retrieval/embedding, generation/70B)'. Verify the parenthetical maps one-to-one onto the two drawn leg boxes.

issue.issue: The 'Generation leg' box is drawn with a visibly heavier and darker border than every other box in the figure (including its sibling 'Retrieval leg'). The emphasis is unexplained by the caption or the prose. It matters more than a cosmetic inconsistency because, in grayscale, all five box fills fall in a narrow light band (green, pink, purple, tan, blue-gray all convert to roughly 78-82% gray), so the border weight is the only visual differentiator between the two legs once color is removed. An unexplained emphasis cue that survives grayscale is a semantic claim the reader cannot decode.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 92: 'Generation leg' box outline is thicker and darker than 'Retrieval leg', 'Workload characterization', 'Five selection surfaces', and 'RAG system decision'. No caption clause refers to emphasis, the canonical model, or the 70B leg being the subject of the chapter.
issue.acceptance_test: Normalize all five box borders to the same weight and color, or state the reason for the emphasis in the caption (e.g. 'the generation leg is the subject of this chapter'). Verify that in a grayscale rendering the two legs are distinguished by their labels and by nothing else.

issue.issue: The five selection surfaces are drawn as a single run-on line of dot-separated words ('quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate'), which renders them as an undifferentiated list. The caption's argument depends on the reader being able to count and individuate the five surfaces and hold them apart from the five evaluation gates, but the drawing provides no visual structure that supports that count. Five discrete chips (or a two-column mini-list) would make the 'five' verifiable at a glance and would also make the leg-specific applicability (see FIG-5.1-03) expressible.
issue.evidence: Figure box 2 sub-label is one continuous line of five items; caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions; they are deliberately distinct from the end-to-end evaluation gates'.
issue.acceptance_test: Render the five surfaces as five visually discrete items. Verify that a reader can count five without reading the caption, and that the count matches the caption's enumeration.

issue.issue: The diagram's structure reads as two parallel legs converging on a decision, with no depiction of the retrieved context entering the generation leg. The 'context' arrow runs from 'Retrieval leg' directly to 'RAG system decision', bypassing 'Generation leg'. The caption frames the figure as a selection map rather than a pipeline, which makes the parallel reading defensible, but the drawing alone permits the inference that the two legs are independent selections whose outputs are combined only at the end - i.e. that the retrieved context is not an input to generation. That is the defining structural property of RAG and the figure is the natural place a reader would look for it.
issue.evidence: Figure: arrow labelled 'context' from 'Retrieval leg' to 'RAG system decision'; arrow labelled 'answer' from 'Generation leg' to 'RAG system decision'; no arrow from 'Retrieval leg' to 'Generation leg'. Caption: '...this figure is a selection map, not an evaluation pipeline.'
issue.acceptance_test: Either route the 'context' arrow into the 'Generation leg' box (with 'answer' continuing to the system decision), or add a caption clause: 'the two legs are selected in parallel; the retrieved context is supplied to the generation leg at serving time (not shown)'. Verify that no reader concludes the legs are independent of one another.

issue.figure: FIGURE 4.1 (Six-dimension workload characterization mapped to architectural decisions)
issue.issue: The row 'Traffic / concurrency' -> 'concurrency & batching' uses the word 'concurrency' on both sides of the arrow, which reads as circular: concurrency determines concurrency. The intended distinction is between observed/offered load and the serving-side concurrency target and batching policy. The same row also conflates two different quantities (an arrival rate and a concurrency level) in one label, whereas the other five rows each name one dimension.
issue.evidence: Figure row 2: left box 'Traffic / concurrency', right box 'concurrency & batching'. Caption: 'Traffic/concurrency -> concurrency & batching'.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel the left box to name the input unambiguously (e.g. 'Offered load / arrival rate') and the right box to name the decision (e.g. 'concurrency target & batching policy'). Verify that no row of the figure reads as self-referential.

issue.figure: FIGURE 4.1 (Six-dimension workload characterization mapped to architectural decisions)
issue.issue: The caption's second paragraph is a verbatim restatement of the figure's six drawn mappings, adding no information beyond what the drawing already shows, while the first paragraph (which does carry the argument) is the one a reader is most likely to skim. The result is that the caption's intellectual content is diluted by a legend that duplicates the visual. If the restatement is retained for accessibility, it should be compressed to a single sentence; otherwise the caption should lead with the semantics of the arrows and the non-exclusivity caveat.
issue.evidence: Caption paragraph 2 lists all six mappings in the same order and with the same wording as the drawn boxes ('Quality requirements -> model size/type; Traffic/concurrency -> concurrency & batching; Token profile -> KV cache size & prefill demand; Latency SLO -> TTFT/TPOT & batch window; Economic constraints -> host count & cost ceiling; Operational constraints -> multi-region vs. single-region deployment').
issue.acceptance_test: Compress the restatement to one sentence or remove it, keeping the arrow-semantics and non-exclusivity sentences. Confirm the figure remains self-explanatory without the restatement and that the caption still carries the non-exclusivity caveat.

issue.figure: FIGURE 4.1 (Six-dimension workload characterization mapped to architectural decisions)
issue.issue: In-figure annotation type sizes are at or near the legibility floor and should be measured before release. The italic note 'primary mapping shown; cross-influences omitted (see caption)' and, on page 92, the box sub-labels ('tokens · cost · SLO'; 'quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate'; 'embedding · 768-dim'; '70B FP16 · serving'; 'base + RAG + guardrails') and the arrow labels ('drives', 'split', 'context', 'answer') are all set noticeably smaller than the bold box titles. At the 150 dpi render they are readable but thin, and the longest sub-label on page 92 is the most at risk. These are in-text annotations within figures, so the 8 pt floor applies to them.
issue.evidence: Rendered pages 93 and 112: annotation text is visibly smaller than the bold box titles; the page-92 sub-label 'quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate' is the longest single-line annotation in the batch.
issue.acceptance_test: Measure rendered glyph heights for every in-figure annotation at 100% print scale on both pages; all must be >= 8 pt, and the longest sub-label must not wrap, shrink, or clip. Re-render at 150 dpi and confirm the note on p. 73 and the five sub-labels on p. 92 remain legible without magnification.

issue.figure: FIGURE 4.1 and FIGURE 5.1 (both pages are figure-only pages)
issue.issue: Both pages in this batch are float pages whose lower region is empty: on printed page 73 roughly the bottom 18% of the page below the caption is blank, and on printed page 92 roughly the bottom 22%. The result is two consecutive pages with a large dead band at the foot, which reads as an unfinished layout rather than a deliberate figure page. Because the two pages are adjacent in the same chapter sequence, the effect compounds.
issue.evidence: Rendered PDF 93 / printed 73: caption ends at approximately 82% of page height, remainder blank. Rendered PDF 112 / printed 92: caption ends at approximately 78% of page height, remainder blank. No body text follows either caption on the page.
issue.acceptance_test: Reflow so that the figure plus caption shares a page with the following body text, or vertically center the float block so the trailing band is distributed. Verify that the reflow introduces no widow/orphan, no stranded heading, and no caption separated from its figure.

issue.figure: FIGURE A.1 — Extreme sparsity: single-digit active (2026)
issue.severity: P1 (major; numerically wrong in the headline figure of Appendix A)
issue.issue: The Kimi K3 bar is labelled 3.7% but its own annotation reads "280B/104B active", which is 104/280 = 37.1% — a factor-of-ten discrepancy. The bar length (drawn to ~3.7 on a 0–10 axis) matches the label, so the drawing and the label agree with each other and disagree with the annotation. Two mutually exclusive readings exist: (a) the fraction is wrong and should be ~37.1% (in which case the axis maximum of 10, the bar length, the figure title, and the caption are all wrong); or (b) the annotation is wrong and the denominator is 2.8T (104/2800 = 3.71%, which reproduces 3.7% exactly), in which case the printed "280B" is missing a digit. As printed, the figure is internally inconsistent and the reader cannot determine which quantity is claimed.
issue.evidence: Printed values: DeepSeek V4-Flash 4.6% = 13/284 = 4.577% ✓; Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 4.8% = 6/125 = 4.80% ✓; GLM-5.3-Flash 5.6% = 18/320 = 5.625% ✓; Kimi K3 3.7% vs 104/280 = 37.14% ✗ (and 104/2800 = 3.71% ✓). The three other rows all reconcile to three significant figures, so the Kimi row is the sole outlier and the error is not a rounding-convention difference.
issue.acceptance_test: Recompute all four fractions from the printed total/active pairs and confirm each equals the printed percentage to the printed precision. Resolve the Kimi row to a single unambiguous pair (either "2.8T/104B active" with 3.7%, or "280B/104B active" with 37.1%); if the latter, rescale the x-axis (max ≥ 40), redraw the bar, and update the title and caption (see FIG-A.1-02). The figure must not ship with a bar whose annotation and label disagree by 10×.

unique.severity: P1 (major; numerically wrong in the headline figure of Appendix A)

issue.severity: P1 (major; the figure's title and caption assert a claim the figure's own data may falsify)
issue.issue: The figure title asserts "Extreme sparsity: single-digit active (2026)" and the caption asserts "active fraction in single digits". If FIG-A.1-01 resolves to 37.1% for Kimi K3, both claims are false for one of the four surveyed families, and the appendix's opening thesis ("one that improves efficiency (more context, cheaper tokens) rather than raw capability", printed p. 432) rests on a pattern that one of the four models does not exhibit. The title is doing argumentative work, not merely labelling work, so it must be true of every plotted family.
issue.evidence: Title: "Extreme sparsity: single-digit active (2026)". Caption: "four open models, total vs activated parameters, and active fraction in single digits — fractions are [DERIVED] from the 1P model-card counts". Plotted values: 4.6%, 3.7% (or 37.1%), 4.8%, 5.6%.
issue.acceptance_test: After FIG-A.1-01 is resolved, re-derive the title and caption claim from the four plotted values. If any family is ≥10% active, restate the title and caption to the actual range (e.g. "active fractions: 4.6%–37%") and revise the A.1 opening paragraph so the thesis is not contradicted by the figure two paragraphs below it.

issue.figure: FIGURE A.2 — Vendor-reported ratios: % remaining (appears twice, under the same figure number)
issue.severity: P1 (major; production defect — one figure number, two different renderings, two consecutive pages)
issue.issue: FIGURE A.2 is printed twice, on consecutive pages, under the same number, with materially different visual treatments and different footnote text. The p. 438 rendering is monochrome (black model names, black arrows, red warning box) with the footnote "*Metric scopes differ. x% remaining = (100 − x)% reduction, per every row." The p. 439 rendering is colour-coded (red/blue/green model names and matching arrows) with the footnote "*Metric scopes differ. 7% remaining = 93% reduction." The two captions are near-duplicates with slightly different wording. This is a duplicate figure, not a legitimate cross-reference, and it also breaks the book's visual language (the same figure is monochrome on one page and colour-coded on the next).
issue.evidence: p. 438: "FIGURE A.2: Vendor-relative KV/compute ratios. Vendor-reported percentages remaining relative to each model's own reference, not a shared baseline. Every row states its metric scope in figure: ..." with footnote "x% remaining = (100 − x)% reduction, per every row." p. 439: "FIGURE A.2: Vendor-relative KV/compute ratios. Vendor-reported percentages remaining relative to each model's own reference, not a shared baseline. Every row states its metric scope in figure: ..." with footnote "7% remaining = 93% reduction." Row data are identical in both (V4-Flash 100%→~7% / ~10%; V4-Pro 100%→~10% / ~27%; GLM-5.3-Flash 100%→~23% / ~33%).
issue.acceptance_test: Exactly one FIGURE A.2 exists in the built PDF. Verify by searching the PDF for the string "FIGURE A.2" and confirming a single occurrence, and by confirming the surviving rendering carries one footnote (recommend the general form "x% remaining = (100 − x)% reduction, per every row", which covers all five rows, rather than the single-row exemplar). If the colour-coded version is retained, add a one-line legend or drop the per-row colour, since the colour currently encodes nothing the reader is told about.

unique.severity: P1 (major; production defect — one figure number, two different renderings, two consecutive pages)

issue.severity: P2 (major; the figure and its own caption state different validation thresholds)
issue.issue: The green arrow from box 2 to box 3 is labelled "validate vs 800 ms target", but the caption states that the validate step compares measured TTFT p99 against "the hypothesis criterion (TTFT p99 < 300 ms, §8 Step 3) under the capstone's 8.80 ms TTFT target (§8 Step 0)". issue.figure: n/a — no figure on this page; displayed equations in §A.9-5 "Geometry: from pixels to tokens"
issue.issue: The token-count equation does not substitute its own stated intermediate values. The page defines H_i = 704/16 = 44 and W_i = 1280/16 = 80, and separately states "There are 109,120 latent spatial-temporal cells, each with 48 channels" (31 × 44 × 80 = 109,120, consistent). But the displayed equation reads N = T_i·H_i·W_i / 2 × 2 = 31 × 22 × 40 = 27,280. Substituting the page's own H_i = 44 and W_i = 80 into the printed left-hand side gives 31 × 44 × 80 × 2 = 218,240, not 27,280. The printed right-hand side (31 × 22 × 40) is consistent with a 2×2 spatial patch (44/2 = 22, 80/2 = 40, matching the stated "denoiser patches the latent video by (1, 2, 2)"), so the result is almost certainly the intended one and the printed formula is the defect: the correct expression is N = T_i · (H_i/2) · (W_i/2) = 31 × 22 × 40 = 27,280. As printed, the equation is dimensionally and numerically self-contradictory, and a reader who checks the substitution will conclude either that the token count is 8× too large or that the cell count is wrong. Figure annotation box: 'mean = 0.85s / p99 (interpolation) = 1.33s / population p99 = 5.0 s / SLO 2 s (TTFT budget)'. Prose (printed p. 96) distinguishes the interpolated p99 (1.33 s) from the population p99 (5.0 s) and says the population p99 'paints a very different picture' — so the 'p99 SLO is met' claim is true only for the interpolated reading and must say so.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite the parenthetical as '(interpolated p99 = 1.33 s <= 2 s; population p99 = 5.0 s > 2 s)' and confirm the caption's claim of a met p99 SLO is explicitly qualified as holding under the interpolated reading only.

issue.issue: The caption's final caveat appears to read 'the shading marks violations of the one 1 s SLO, not a second threshold', but the SLO drawn in the figure and used everywhere else on the page is 2 s. If the printed numeral is '1 s', the caption contradicts the figure, the annotation box ('SLO 2 s'), and the caption's own earlier phrase 'the 2 s request-latency line'.
issue.evidence: Caption (rendered at 150 dpi): '...the shading marks violations of the one 1 s SLO, not a second threshold.' Figure annotation: 'SLO 2 s (TTFT budget)'. Caption earlier: '1% of requests exceed the 2 s request-latency line'. Prose (printed p. 96): 'the p99 SLO is met' against a 2 s line. The numeral is ambiguous at 150 dpi and must be checked against the source.
issue.acceptance_test: Read the numeral in the source caption; it must be '2 s'. If it is '1 s', correct it. Then confirm every occurrence of the SLO value on printed pp. 96-97 (prose, figure annotation, caption) reads 2 s.

issue.issue: The in-plot label names the 2 s line a 'TTFT budget', but the caption explicitly distinguishes the request-latency SLO from TTFT ('the 2 s request-latency line — a superset of TTFT violations'). Labeling the request-latency line as a TTFT budget lets the reader conclude that the 2 s line is a TTFT threshold, which is the opposite of the caption's careful distinction and would corrupt the TTFT-vs-request-latency reasoning the chapter is building.
issue.evidence: Figure annotation: 'SLO 2 s (TTFT budget)'. Caption: '1% of requests exceed the 2 s request-latency line — a superset of TTFT violations'. Prose (printed p. 96): 'the p99 SLO is met' and 'the population p99 paints a very different picture' — both about request latency, not TTFT.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel the in-plot marker 'SLO 2 s (request latency)' (or 'request-latency SLO 2 s'), and confirm no figure label on this page equates the 2 s request-latency line with a TTFT budget.

issue.issue: The percentile markers are not unambiguously associated with their labels: a red label near the top of the plot reads as 'sample p5' (truncated/ambiguous at print size), the blue 'p95 0.99' label sits far to the left of the blue dash-dot line at ~1.33 s, and blue is used both for a percentile marker and for the 2 s SLO line. A reader cannot reliably map each dashed line to its statistic, which is the entire point of the figure.
issue.evidence: Rendered page shows: green 'p50 0.80' with a green dashed line at ~0.80; red 'p90 0.94' with a red dashed line at ~0.94; a red label reading 'sample p5' (or 'sample p95') above a red dashed line near ~1.0; blue 'p95 0.99' at the far left; a blue dash-dot line at ~1.33 s; and a blue 'SLO 2 s' label with a blue dash-dot line at 2 s. The figure's own annotation box states p99 (interpolation) = 1.33 s, so the line at 1.33 s is the p99 marker, not p95. In grayscale, green/red/blue dashed lines of similar dash pattern are not reliably separable.
issue.acceptance_test: Redraw with one marker per statistic, each label placed immediately adjacent to its own line, and a distinct visual treatment for the SLO line (e.g. heavy dash-dot, or a labeled arrow) that does not reuse a percentile color. Verify at 150 dpi that every dashed line has an adjacent label naming its statistic and value, and that the p95 marker is at 0.99 s and the p99 (interpolated) marker at 1.33 s.

issue.issue: The legend entry 'full-MHA FP16 (raw byte-halving, 50%)' labels the byte-halved (8-bit) series as FP16, while the corresponding GQA series is correctly labelled 'GQA FP8 (raw byte-halving, 50%)'. As drawn, the legend contains two series labelled FP16 with different values, and a reader could conclude the book measures two distinct FP16 KV footprints.
issue.evidence: Legend: 'full-MHA FP16 (bound, ~2.62 MB/tok)' (red), 'full-MHA FP16 (raw byte-halving, 50%)' (orange), 'GQA FP16 (~0.33 MB/tok)' (blue), 'GQA FP8 (raw byte-halving, 50%)' (green). Caption: 'FP16 = 2.62 MB/token, FP8/8-bit = 1.31' and 'The FP8 value is raw byte-halving (50% of FP16)'. The orange series therefore represents 1.31 MB/token, i.e. FP8, not FP16.
issue.acceptance_test: Rename the orange legend entry to 'full-MHA FP8 (raw byte-halving of FP16, 50%)' and confirm the legend contains exactly one FP16 series per attention geometry, with the byte-halved series labelled FP8 in both geometries.

issue.issue: The drawn connector direction implies the wrong mechanism: the fan lines run downward from the query-head glyphs into the K/V box, which reads as 'query heads produce the K/V head'. In GQA the causality is the reverse — one KV head is shared by (read by) a group of query heads. The subtitle's arrow ('many query heads <- few shared KV heads') points the other way, so the figure's own subtitle and geometry disagree, and a reader could infer that GQA derives KV from query heads.
issue.evidence: Rendered figure: three groups of blue query-head squares above three orange 'K/V' boxes, with thin lines converging downward into each K/V box; subtitle 'many query heads <- few shared KV heads' (arrow pointing left/upstream). Caption: '8 query heads share one KV head' — sharing, not derivation.
issue.acceptance_test: Redraw the connectors with arrowheads pointing from the K/V box up to the query-head group (or as a bidirectional 'shared read' bracket labelled 'shared by 8 query heads'), and confirm the subtitle arrow and the drawn arrowheads agree in direction.

issue.issue: The caption contradicts the drawn content: it says 'snapshot 3 retains KV1+KV3', but the third KV box in the figure contains KV1, KV2 and KV3, and the caption's own next clause says the KV row is cumulative. The drawn figure is correct; the caption's parenthetical is wrong and, as written, implies KV2 is evicted — a materially different memory behavior in a chapter about state lifetime.
issue.evidence: Figure bottom row: boxes labelled 'KV1', 'KV1 KV2', 'KV1 KV2 KV3'. Caption: 'recurrent snapshots are successive, not jointly retained, while the KV row is cumulative (snapshot 3 retains KV1+KV3)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Change the caption parenthetical to '(snapshot 3 retains KV1+KV2+KV3)' and confirm it is consistent with the drawn third box and with the 'cumulative' clause.

issue.issue: The caption asserts 'Bar widths are proportional to bytes', but the two bars are drawn with identical total width while representing 17 B (MXFP4) and 18 B (NVFP4). The figure therefore contradicts its own stated encoding rule, and a reader who trusts the caption will read the two formats as byte-identical in overhead.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'Bar widths are proportional to bytes.' Rendered figure: MXFP4 bar (16 B values + 1 B scale) and NVFP4 bar (8 B + 8 B + 2 B scales) span the same x-extent. The in-figure labels give the true totals: 'Local: 17 B / 32 = 0.53125 B/value = 4.25 bit/value' and 'Local: 18 B / 32 = 0.5625 B/value = 4.5 bit/value'.
issue.acceptance_test: Either redraw the bars so total widths are proportional (17:18) and add a scale ruler, or change the caption to 'Bar segments are labeled with byte counts; total bar widths are equal for comparison' — and verify the caption's statement matches the drawing exactly.

issue.issue: The annotation '9.5K x 3.1 GB (GQA FP16)' uses a multiplication sign where a mapping is meant, and the parallel annotation '9.5K = 24.9 GB (FP16 bound)' uses '='. The two annotations for the same x-position are therefore written in two different, one of them wrong, relations.
issue.evidence: Rendered annotations: '9.5K = 24.9 GB (FP16 bound)' and '9.5K x 3.1 GB (GQA FP16)'. Values check out: 2.62 MB x 9,500 = 24.9 GB; 0.33 MB x 9,500 = 3.1 GB.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite both annotations with a single consistent relation (e.g. '9.5K -> 24.9 GB (full-MHA FP16)' and '9.5K -> 3.1 GB (GQA FP16)') and confirm the arithmetic still matches 2.62 and 0.33 MB/token.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.1 (label '8 query heads : 1 KV head (x 8 groups)')
issue.issue: The figure draws three groups (plus an ellipsis) while the label asserts 'x 8 groups'. The reader cannot tell whether the canonical configuration has 8 groups (64 query heads, 8 KV heads) or whether 'x 8' refers to the heads within each group — the same '8' is doing two jobs in one label.
issue.evidence: Rendered figure: three groups of 8 blue query-head squares, each fanning to one orange K/V box, followed by '...'. Label: '8 query heads : 1 KV head (x 8 groups)'. Caption: 'the load-bearing number is the n_q : n_kv ratio (8 : 1 here)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite the label as '8 query heads : 1 KV head per group (8 groups in the canonical model; 3 shown)' or draw all 8 groups, and confirm the caption's n_q : n_kv statement is unchanged.

issue.issue: The caption defines 'Arrows = token input / state flow', but the KV-history row has no arrows at all, so the cumulative growth KV1 -> KV1KV2 -> KV1KV2KV3 is conveyed only by box contents. The reader must infer the accumulation direction, and the figure's own legend does not cover the row where the memory-growth claim lives.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'Arrows = token input / state flow; snapshots are schematic.' Rendered figure: arrows appear only in the recurrent-update row (token -> update, update -> update); the three KV boxes at the bottom are unconnected.
issue.acceptance_test: Add left-to-right accumulation arrows between the KV boxes (or extend the caption's arrow key to state that the KV row is shown by cumulative box contents), and confirm the arrow key covers every arrowed element in the figure.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.3 (Quantization choices are not execution guarantees)
issue.issue: The 'compatible dispatch' arrow fans out to three execution-path boxes (Native FP4 math, Fused dequant, Reconstruct) with solid arrowheads to all three, which can be read as 'all three run'. The caption's actual claim is that only supported combinations can load and execute — i.e. the paths are alternatives.
issue.evidence: Rendered figure: one arrow labelled 'compatible dispatch' splitting into three solid arrows into 'Native FP4 math', 'Fused dequant', 'Reconstruct'. Caption: 'Only supported combinations can load and execute. No compatible kernel: reject; fallback is not guaranteed.'
issue.acceptance_test: Mark the three terminal boxes as mutually exclusive alternatives (e.g. a brace or 'one of' label on the fan-out, or dashed alternative arrows) and confirm the drawing cannot be read as simultaneous execution.

issue.issue: The figure presents 'Error-control method: AWQ / GPTQ' and 'Numerical representation: INT4 + scheme / MXFP4 / NVFP4' as two parallel, universally applicable inputs to the packed tensor, with no indication that AWQ/GPTQ are weight-only calibration methods and do not apply to KV-cache quantization. In a chapter that also covers KV quantization, this invites the reader to apply AWQ/GPTQ to KV state.
issue.evidence: Rendered figure: two side-by-side input boxes feeding 'Packed tensor: values + scales (+ zero points, if used)'. Caption: 'quantization (calibration) method, numerical representation, packed tensors and checkpoint container describe different parts of a deployment' — no scope qualifier on the calibration method.
issue.acceptance_test: Add a scope qualifier to the error-control box (e.g. 'AWQ / GPTQ (weight-only)') and, if KV quantization is in scope for the figure, add a separate KV path or an explicit note that calibration methods do not apply to KV state.

issue.issue: The caption clause 'and common 1D NVFP4 two (18 B per 32 values) plus a separate FP32 scale per tensor' leaves it grammatically ambiguous whether the FP32 per-tensor scale applies to NVFP4 only (as the figure states) or to both formats. MXFP4 has no FP32 global scale, so the ambiguity is substantive.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'MXFP4 adding one local-scale byte (17 B per 32 values) and common 1D NVFP4 two (18 B per 32 values) plus a separate FP32 scale per tensor.' Figure: 'NVFP4 global FP32 scale: 4 B per tensor, not per block.' (no global-scale note on the MXFP4 row).
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite as '...and common 1D NVFP4 two (18 B per 32 values), plus (NVFP4 only) a separate FP32 global scale per tensor', and confirm the MXFP4 row carries no global-scale annotation.

issue.figure: FIGURE 6.2 (in-plot label '1% stragglers > 5 s (cross the SLO)')
issue.issue: The label says the stragglers are '> 5 s', while the prose and caption place the cluster AT 5.0 s ('a 1% straggler cluster at 5.0 s'; 'plus 1% at 5 s'). '> 5 s' implies the cluster lies beyond 5 s, which would change the population p99 and the shape of the tail.
issue.evidence: Figure label: '1% stragglers > 5 s (cross the SLO)'. Prose (printed p. 96): 'with a 1% straggler cluster at 5.0 s'. Caption: 'plus 1% at 5 s'.
issue.acceptance_test: Change the label to '1% stragglers at ~5 s (cross the SLO)' and confirm it matches the prose's 'at 5.0 s'.

issue.figure: FIGURE 6.2 page layout (also applies to printed pp. 114, 120, 127)
issue.issue: Figure pages are vertically centered, producing large empty bands above the figure title and below the caption (roughly 1 inch of dead space above the figure on printed pp. 97, 114 and 120, and roughly 1.5 inches of trailing white below the caption on printed pp. 120 and 127). The pages read as under-filled and the figure is not anchored to the top margin where the eye expects it.
