issue.acceptance_test: Re-anchor figure floats to the top of the text block (or allow the following body text to flow onto the page) so that no figure page carries more than ~0.5 inch of unexplained leading whitespace above the figure title or trailing whitespace below the caption.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.7 — Concurrency budget — one 8×H100 host, 640 GB pool
issue.issue: The displayed equation inside the figure uses '+' where the arithmetic requires division: it reads '≈ 436 GB + 24.9 GB = 17.5 → ~17 requests'. As printed this is false (436 + 24.9 = 460.9, not 17.5). The line immediately above it ('in-flight = KV budget ÷ KV per request') and the caption ('KV budget ÷ per-request KV price sets concurrency') both use division, so the figure contradicts its own prose and caption.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 129 (PDF 149): equation line reads '≈ 436 GB + 24.9 GB = 17.5 → ~17 requests'; the preceding line reads 'in-flight = KV budget ÷ KV per request'; caption reads 'KV budget ÷ per-request KV price sets concurrency — at 24.9 GB/request max-fit is KV'. Independent recomputation: 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB/request = 17.51 → ~17 requests (matches the printed result 17.5); 436 + 24.9 = 460.9 GB, which cannot equal 17.5. The glyph is a plus sign with a visible vertical stroke, not a division sign with dots above/below.
issue.acceptance_test: In the built PDF at 300 dpi the operator between '436 GB' and '24.9 GB' must be '÷' (division sign), and the line must read '≈ 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB = 17.5 → ~17 requests'. Verify by OCR/visual inspection at 300 dpi, not at 150 dpi.

issue.figure: FIGURE 8.2 — Per-GPU roofline: dense FP16, one H100 vs one H200
issue.issue: The prefill operating point is labelled with an arithmetic intensity of '9.2K FLOP/byte', which is ~1000× too large, and the marker appears to be plotted near x ≈ 10^4 rather than between 10^0 and 10^1. The label conflates the token count (9.2K tokens) with the intensity value. The caption gives an intensity for the decode-batch-8 point (8 FLOP/byte) but none for prefill, so the caption does not repair the figure.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 145 (PDF 165): orange annotation reads 'prefill 9.2K / intensity = 9.2K / FLOP/byte'; the orange marker sits on the compute plateau at an x-position near the right edge of the plot (≈10^4), to the right of both ridge lines (206 and 295). Independent recomputation from the book's own canonical inputs: prefill FLOPs = 2 × 70e9 params × 9200 tokens = 1.288e15 FLOP; bytes ≈ 140 GB weights + 24.9 GB KV ≈ 165 GB → 7.8 FLOP/byte; weight-only (the basis the figure uses for decode, where intensity = B) → 1.288e15 / 140e9 = 9.2 FLOP/byte. The correct value is therefore ≈9.2 FLOP/byte, not 9.2K. The figure's own decode labels ('decode batch B=8 (intensity = B FLOP/byte)') confirm the weight-only convention, under which prefill intensity = 9.2.
issue.acceptance_test: The prefill annotation must read 'prefill 9.2K tokens: intensity ≈ 9.2 FLOP/byte (weight-only)' and the marker must be plotted at x = 9.2 (between the 10^0 and 10^1 ticks, i.e. left of both ridge lines) on the compute plateau. The caption must state the prefill intensity explicitly (≈9.2 FLOP/byte) so the figure and caption agree.

issue.figure: FIGURE 8.2 — Per-GPU roofline: dense FP16, one H100 vs one H200
issue.issue: The x-axis tick sequence skips a decade: it reads 10^-1, 10^0, 10^1, 10^2, 10^4. A reader cannot locate the 10^3 decade, which is exactly where the ridge lines (206, 295) and the prefill marker region fall, and the last tick is inconsistent with the plotted data range.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 145 (PDF 165): x-axis tick labels are '10^-1', '10^0', '10^1', '10^2', '10^4'. The ridge annotations 'H100 ridge = 295' and 'H200 ridge = 206' both lie between 10^2 and 10^4, i.e. in the decade that has no tick.
issue.acceptance_test: The x-axis must show a complete decade sequence (10^-1, 10^0, 10^1, 10^2, 10^3, and 10^4 only if the range requires it), with 10^3 present so that the 206/295 ridge lines and the prefill marker can be located unambiguously.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.6 — Memory floor: inference vs fine-tuning (canonical 70B, FP16 unless noted)
issue.issue: The dash pattern of the three horizontal reference rules does not match the legend entries. The legend assigns dashed to '2×H100 (160 GB)', dash-dot to '8×H100 (640 GB)' and dotted to '1×H100 (80 GB)', but the rule drawn at ~640 GB renders as a plain long-dash line and the rule at ~160 GB renders dotted. A reader matching styles to levels would conclude that the 640 GB line is the 2×H100 line and the 160 GB line is the 1×H100 line — the opposite of the truth, and the 160/640 distinction is the whole point of the figure (the red annotation 'Full fine-tune exceeds an 8×H100 host' depends on it).
issue.evidence: Rendered page 128 (PDF 148): legend rows read '— — 2×H100 (160 GB)', '— · — 8×H100 (640 GB)', '· · · 1×H100 (80 GB)'. In the plot area the long-dash rule sits at y ≈ 640 GB and the dotted rule at y ≈ 160 GB (just under the ~165 GB inference bar top). The 640 GB rule is the one the red annotation refers to as the 8×H100 host size.
issue.acceptance_test: In the vector source, each rule's dash pattern must equal its legend sample: the 640 GB rule dash-dot, the 160 GB rule dashed, the 80 GB rule dotted. Verify by rendering the figure alone at 300 dpi and comparing rule style to legend sample side by side.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.8 — Memory Tetris: how the 8×H100 host (640 GB) fills with context
issue.issue: The caption twice refers to 'the 80 GB rank-boundary lines' as a feature of the figure, but the figure draws no per-rank boundaries — it draws a single dash-dot rule at 640 GB labelled '640 GB = 8× 80 GB ranks'. The caption therefore describes a visual element that does not exist, and the reader is invited to check a claim against a figure that cannot support it.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 131 (PDF 151): the only horizontal rule in the plot is the red dash-dot line at 640 GB with the label '640 GB = 8× 80 GB ranks'. Caption text: 'The FP16 KV cache (orange) is the only block that grows, consuming the fixed ~436 GB KV budget (dashed 80 GB rank boundaries)' and 'the 80 GB rank-boundary lines are a visualization guide; sharding, KV partitioning, fragmentation, and interconnect must be validated per rank.' No 80 GB gridlines are present.
issue.acceptance_test: Either draw the eight 80 GB rank boundaries as vertical gridlines (which would materially strengthen the 'aggregate residency ≠ per-rank feasibility' point the caption is making), or reword both caption sentences to refer to the single 640 GB aggregate rule that is actually drawn.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.8 — Memory Tetris: how the 8×H100 host (640 GB) fills with context
issue.issue: The figure note 'Bar heights are not to scale (GB)' contradicts the drawing: the three bars are rendered approximately in proportion to their labelled totals (229 / 288 / 539 GB), so a reader who trusts the note will misread the visual as schematic when it is in fact quantitative — and a reader who trusts the drawing will be misled by the note into distrusting a correct proportionality.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 131 (PDF 131): bar labels '9.5K context = 229 GB used', '32K context = 288 GB used', '128K context = 539 GB used'. Measured bar heights in the 150 dpi render are approximately 55 px, 80 px and 155 px from a common baseline, i.e. ratios 0.35 / 0.52 / 1.00 against the labelled ratios 0.425 / 0.534 / 1.00 — proportional to within roughly 8%, not schematic. The note directly below the legend reads 'Bar heights are not to scale (GB).'
issue.acceptance_test: Choose one and make it true: (a) keep the proportional bars and replace the note with 'No y-axis scale is shown; all values are labelled in GB', or (b) keep the note and redraw the bars so the proportionality is visibly broken. The chosen wording must not assert a property the drawing contradicts.

issue.issue: The two conditioning boxes ('Prompt embeddings' and 'I2V condition') sit flush against the top edge of the denoiser box, so the conditioning arrows that the figure's own legend declares as a distinct visual class ('Dashed: denoiser conditioning') are effectively invisible. The distinction between the T2V path and the optional I2V branch — which the caption makes a point of — is carried by arrowheads that cannot be seen.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 150 (PDF 170): the 'Prompt embeddings' and 'I2V condition' boxes have their bottom edges at approximately y = 237 px and the 'Wan2.2 dense T2V-5B + scheduler' box top edge at approximately y = 240 px in the 150 dpi render, leaving ≈3 px (≈0.02 in at print size) for an arrow shaft and arrowhead. By contrast the 'Latent' box has a clearly visible arrow into the denoiser box. The legend states 'Dashed: denoiser conditioning'.
issue.acceptance_test: Increase the vertical clearance between the two conditioning boxes and the denoiser box to at least 0.15 in (≈22 px at 150 dpi) so that each conditioning arrow has a visible shaft and arrowhead, and confirm at print size that the reader can trace Prompt → UMT5-XXL → Prompt embeddings → denoiser and reference image → VAE encode → I2V condition → denoiser without ambiguity.

issue.issue: The patch notation 'Patch (1, 2, N): N = 27,280 video tokens' uses N both as a patch dimension and as the token count, so the tuple reads as a patch size of (1, 2, 27280). The intended patch size is (1, 2, 2), which is what produces 27,280 tokens.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 150 (PDF 170), denoiser box: 'Patch (1, 2, N): N = 27,280 video tokens'. Independent check: 31 × (44/2) × (80/2) = 31 × 22 × 40 = 27,280 tokens, consistent with a (1, 2, 2) patch over the 31×44×80 latent. The caption confirms the latent geometry (T_L = (F-1)/4+1 = 31, H_L = 44, W_L = 80) but does not state the patch tuple.
issue.acceptance_test: The denoiser box must read 'Patch (1, 2, 2) → N = 27,280 video tokens', with N used only for the token count.

issue.issue: The self-loop arrow on the right edge of the denoiser box is unlabeled and its arrowhead direction is not clearly readable at print size, while the box interior already carries the text 'Loop: denoising / scheduler iteration'. The reader is asked to decode an unlabeled connector whose meaning is stated elsewhere in the same box.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 170 (PDF 170): a thin line leaves the right edge of the 'Wan2.2 dense T2V-5B + scheduler' box, runs down outside it, and re-enters with a small arrowhead near the lower-right corner; no text annotates it. The box's third line reads 'Loop: denoising / scheduler iteration'.
issue.acceptance_test: Either label the loop arrow (e.g. 'x_{t-1} → x_t, 50 steps') and remove the redundant box line, or remove the arrow and keep the box text. The arrowhead must be unambiguous at print size.

issue.figure: FIGURE 8.1 — Where inference computation and data movement actually live
issue.issue: The red gradient arrow that carries the figure's central claim ('capacity grows / speed drops / distance grows') spans only the registers→HBM portion of the stack. The 'other GPUs / remote — farthest' tier, where distance is in fact largest and where the 'far' annotation sits, lies below the arrow's lower end, so the distance claim is not visually carried to the tier it is most needed for.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 157 (PDF 157): the red double-headed arrow runs from approximately y = 155 px (level of 'small · fast · close') to approximately y = 305 px (level of 'large · slow' at HBM). The 'GPU interconnect' block (≈y 340–375) and 'other GPUs / remote — farthest' block (≈y 380–415) with its 'far' annotation (≈y 390) are below the arrow. The caption asserts 'the vertical ordering is a relative speed/capacity/distance ranking'.
issue.acceptance_test: Extend the gradient arrow to the bottom of the stack so that it spans all seven tiers, or add a separate distance marker covering the interconnect and remote tiers, so that the 'distance grows' claim is visually supported at the tier where it is asserted.

issue.figure: FIGURE 8.1 — Where inference computation and data movement actually live
issue.issue: The figure's semantic classes are carried by colour alone in the legend ('blue = compute, orange = memory, green = interconnect'), and the caption repeats this as a 'Color key'. Blue and green are close in luminance in grayscale, so the compute tier (tensor cores / ALU) and the two interconnect tiers (GPU interconnect, other GPUs / remote) risk merging in a grayscale print or for a reader with colour-vision deficiency. The caption's own warning that 'compute, memory and interconnect are separate architectural constraints' is exactly the distinction that must survive grayscale.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 157 (PDF 137): legend swatches are blue (compute), orange (memory), green (interconnect); the caption reads 'Color key: blue = compute, orange = memory (registers to HBM), green = interconnect'. The blocks do carry some texture, but the texture is not stated in the legend as the redundant encoding, and the legend gives no pattern key.
issue.acceptance_test: Confirm by converting the figure to grayscale at print size that the compute block and the two interconnect blocks remain distinguishable; if not, add a distinct hatch to the green blocks and state the hatch in the legend ('blue = compute, orange = memory, green = interconnect; green blocks are cross-hatched') so the encoding does not depend on hue.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.6 — Memory floor: inference vs fine-tuning (canonical 70B, FP16 unless noted)
issue.issue: The '1×H100 (80 GB)' legend entry has no visible referent: the 80 GB rule is drawn beneath the inference bar (which spans 0–165 GB) and is not visible in the rendered figure, so a reader cannot locate the single-GPU reference the legend promises.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 128 (PDF 148): the visible horizontal rules are one at ~640 GB and one at ~160 GB; no rule is discernible at 80 GB, which lies inside the footprint of the ~165 GB inference bar. The legend nevertheless lists '1×H100 (80 GB)' with a dotted sample.
issue.acceptance_test: Draw the 80 GB rule on top of the bars (or extend it beyond the bar edges) so all three legend entries have a visible referent, and confirm at print size that the 80 GB rule is discernible against the blue hatched inference bar.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.8 — Memory Tetris: how the 8×H100 host (640 GB) fills with context
issue.issue: The figure title 'how the 8×H100 host (640 GB) fills with context' overstates what the figure shows: even at 128K context the host is only 539/640 GB used, i.e. it never fills. The title invites the reader to look for a saturation event that the figure does not contain, and it slightly pre-empts the caption's own point that the KV budget is the binding constraint.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 151 (PDF 151): title 'Memory Tetris: how the 8×H100 host (640 GB) fills with context'; bar labels '9.5K context = 229 GB used', '32K context = 288 GB used', '128K context = 539 GB used'; the 640 GB rule is drawn above all three bars with visible headroom in every case.
issue.acceptance_test: Retitle to something the figure supports, e.g. 'Memory Tetris: how the 8×H100 host (640 GB) fills with context — and where it stops filling', or 'Memory Tetris: KV growth inside the 8×H100 host (640 GB)', and ensure the title does not assert saturation.

issue.figure: FIGURE 8.2 — Per-GPU roofline: dense FP16, one H100 vs one H200
issue.issue: The caption's parenthetical listing the operating points is malformed and incomplete: 'The prefill (9.2K input, decode (batch=1) and decode (batch=8, intensity = 8 FLOP/byte) points are illustrative operating points' has an unbalanced parenthesis and supplies an intensity for only one of the three points. The reader is left without a caption-side value to check the prefill point against — which is how the FIG-8.2-01 error survives.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 145 (PDF 165), caption: 'The prefill (9.2K input, decode (batch=1) and decode (batch=8, intensity = 8 FLOP/byte) points are illustrative operating points, and a kernel's position on the roofline depends on fusion and kernel efficiency.'
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite as 'The prefill (9.2K tokens, intensity ≈ 9.2 FLOP/byte), decode (batch=1, intensity ≈ 1 FLOP/byte) and decode (batch=8, intensity ≈ 8 FLOP/byte) points are illustrative operating points', with balanced parentheses and an intensity given for every point.

issue.figure: FIGURE 8.2 — Per-GPU roofline: dense FP16, one H100 vs one H200
issue.issue: A single annotation, 'memory-bound slope (= intensity × BW)', is attached to two lines with different bandwidths (3.35 and 4.8 TB/s). The annotation reads as if one slope exists, which undercuts the figure's central comparison — that the H200's memory-bound line is steeper and its ridge is at lower intensity.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 145 (PDF 165): the orange annotation 'memory-bound slope (= intensity × BW)' sits at lower-left with a single leader, while two distinct memory-bound lines are drawn (blue for H100 at 3.35 TB/s, red for H200 at 4.8 TB/s). The caption separately notes 'the memory-bound slope are per-GPU'.
issue.acceptance_test: Label the two memory-bound lines individually (e.g. 'H100: 3.35 TB/s' and 'H200: 4.8 TB/s') and either delete the single-slope annotation or reword it as 'memory-bound slope = intensity × BW (one slope per GPU)'.

issue.issue: The caption's operating point is mislabeled and contradicts the book's own prose. The caption states 'At 140 GB the ideal times are about 0.55 s, 6.1 s and 98 s', but the plotted model is T = 1.75 x (logical tensor) / BW, so the values 544 ms / 6,125 ms / 98,000 ms correspond to 245 GB SENT (1.75 x 140 GB), not to a 140 GB transfer. The prose on PDF p.177 / printed p.157 gives the correct 140 GB one-way times (0.31 s NVLink, 5.6 s HDR, 56 s Ethernet). A reader who checks the caption against p.157 sees two different '140 GB' answers differing by exactly the 1.75x ring factor and cannot tell which is right.
issue.evidence: Figure subtitle (p.178): '140 GB tensor (245 GB sent at 1.75x); NVLink 544 ms | HDR 6,125 ms | RoCE 98,000 ms'. Recomputation: 1.75 x 140 GB / 450 GB/s = 0.544 s; 1.75 x 140 / 40 = 6.125 s; 1.75 x 140 / 2.5 = 98 s. At 140 GB logical the times are 140/450 = 0.311 s, 140/40 = 3.5 s (or 5.6 s at the 25 GB/s single-port nominal used on p.157), 140/2.5 = 56 s. Caption text: 'At 140 GB the ideal times are about 0.55 s, 6.1 s and 98 s.'
issue.acceptance_test: Caption must read 'At 245 GB sent (1.75 x the 140 GB logical tensor) the ideal times are about 0.55 s, 6.1 s and 98 s', and must add one clause stating that the 1.75x ring factor is why these exceed the one-way 140 GB times quoted on p.157 (0.31 s / 5.6 s / 56 s). A reader must be able to reconcile Fig 9.1 with the p.157 paragraph without arithmetic guesswork.

issue.issue: The RoCE bandwidth assumption is not realizable as labeled and disagrees with the caption. The legend reads '2x5GBE RoCE: assumed effective 2.5 GB/s'. Two 5 GbE ports carry 10 Gb/s = 1.25 GB/s in aggregate, so an 'effective 2.5 GB/s' exceeds the physical link by 2x. The caption instead describes 'an assumed effective 25GbE RoCE path' (25 Gb/s = 3.125 GB/s nominal, 2.5 GB/s effective = 80% efficiency, which is plausible). The legend and caption therefore specify two different fabrics for the same curve, and one of them is impossible. The related prose on PDF p.183 / printed p.163 compounds this with a unit error: '35 Gb/s = 3.125 GB/s unidirectional' is false (35 Gb/s = 4.375 GB/s; 3.125 GB/s = 25 Gb/s), and 35 Gb/s is not a standard Ethernet rate.
issue.evidence: Legend (p.178): '2x5GBE RoCE: assumed effective 2.5 GB/s'. Caption (p.178): '2.5 GB/s for an assumed effective 25GbE RoCE path'. Prose (p.183): 'Option C - 35 Gb/s Ethernet (RoCEv2) across 8 nodes. 35 Gb/s = 3.125 GB/s unidirectional'. Recomputation: 2 x 5 Gb/s = 10 Gb/s = 1.25 GB/s < 2.5 GB/s; 35 Gb/s / 8 = 4.375 GB/s; 25 Gb/s / 8 = 3.125 GB/s.
issue.acceptance_test: Legend, caption and p.183 prose must name ONE fabric with a consistent nominal rate, consistent unit conversion, and an effective value <= nominal. E.g. legend 'RoCE: 25 GbE nominal (3.125 GB/s), assumed effective 2.5 GB/s', caption matching, and p.183 corrected to '25 Gb/s = 3.125 GB/s' (or '35 Gb/s = 4.375 GB/s' with the effective value restated). A reviewer must be able to confirm effective <= nominal for every curve in the legend.

issue.figure: Figure 9.1 (cross-reference: equations intended to reproduce the Fig 9.1 HDR and RoCE points)
issue.issue: Both ring-time equations on this page fail to reproduce the values they are evidently derived from, and one of them contradicts the Fig 9.1 legend. (a) 'T_ring ~ 2*140 GB / 8*2.5 GB/s ~ 98 s' evaluates to 280/20 = 14 s, not 98 s; 98 s requires the numerator 2*(N-1)/N*140 GB = 245 GB over the per-node 2.5 GB/s, i.e. the '8' and the '2*140' are both wrong as printed. (b) 'T_ring ~ 2*(N-1)/N * M/B_eff ~ 7.140 GB / 6.1 s ~ 80 GB/s' yields 245/6.1 = 40 GB/s, not 80 GB/s, and 40 GB/s is exactly the value the Fig 9.1 legend assigns to the two-rail HDR path ('Two-rail HDR: assumed effective 40 GB/s'). The printed 80 GB/s therefore contradicts the figure it is meant to explain. The numerator as rendered ('7.140 GB') is also not a recognizable quantity.
issue.evidence: p.183: 'T_ring ~ 2*(N-1)/N * M/B_eff ~ 7.140 GB / 6.1 s ~ 80 GB/s' and 'T_ring ~ 2*140 GB / 8*2.5 GB/s ~ 98 s'. Fig 9.1 legend: 'Two-rail HDR: assumed effective 40 GB/s'; Fig 9.1 subtitle: 'HDR 6,125 ms'. Recomputation: 245 GB / 6.1 s = 40.2 GB/s; 245 GB / 2.5 GB/s = 98 s; 280 GB / 20 GB/s = 14 s. The page's own downstream claims ('about 180x', '54 s, 610 s or 9,800 s') are consistent with 0.544/6.125/98 s, confirming 98 s is the intended value and the printed formula is the defect.
issue.acceptance_test: Both equations must be rewritten so that substituting the stated inputs reproduces the printed result exactly, and the derived bandwidth must equal the Fig 9.1 legend value (40 GB/s for HDR). Specifically: T_ring ~ 2*(N-1)/N * 140 GB / 40 GB/s ~ 245 GB / 6.1 s ~ 40 GB/s, and T_ring ~ 2*(N-1)/N * 140 GB / 2.5 GB/s ~ 245 GB / 2.5 GB/s ~ 98 s. The '180x' and '54/610/9,800 s' claims must then still hold.

issue.issue: The caption's statement 'In round 1, rank i sends chunk (i-1) mod N in both phases' is correct for the reduce-scatter phase but wrong for the all-gather phase. In a ring all-gather, round 1 has rank i send its own chunk i to rank i+1; only in round 2 does it forward chunk (i-1) mod N. As written, the caption teaches the wrong chunk index for one of the two phases it is describing, and the figure's own 'Balanced ring neighbor order (both phases)' panel cannot disambiguate it because it shows only the neighbor order, not the chunk indices.
issue.evidence: Caption (p.179): 'In round 1, rank i sends chunk (i-1) mod N in both phases, so rank r ends the reduce-scatter holding reduced chunk r.' Independent derivation: reduce-scatter round 1 sends chunk (i-1) mod N (rank i's chunk i-1 is the one it received last round); all-gather round 1 sends chunk i (own), round 2 sends chunk (i+1) mod N, round 3 sends chunk (i+2) mod N. The figure's per-phase byte counts (6 B sent + 6 B received per rank per phase = 3 rounds x 2 B) are consistent with either indexing, so the caption is the only place the error can live.
issue.acceptance_test: Caption must state the chunk index per phase correctly, e.g. 'In reduce-scatter round 1, rank i sends chunk (i-1) mod N to rank i+1; in all-gather round 1, rank i sends its own chunk i to rank i+1'. Optionally add the chunk index to the ring panel so the figure carries the information rather than the caption alone.

issue.figure: Figure 9.2 (SUM first: replication second) - caption byte accounting
issue.issue: The caption's byte accounting does not reconcile with the figure's own annotations. As rendered, the caption reads 'Each rank sends 2 B and receives 12 B in both phases', while the figure states '6 B sent + 6 B received/rank' for each phase and 'Per rank: 12 B sent + 12 B received = 24 B endpoint total'. The caption's 'receives 12 B' is inconsistent with the figure's 6 B received per phase (12 B received total across both phases) and with the 24 B endpoint total. If the source actually reads 'sends 2 B and receives 2 B per round in both phases', the figure and caption agree but the caption omits the word 'per round', which is exactly the distinction a reader needs (per-round 2 B vs per-phase 6 B vs per-rank 12 B). Either way the caption as printed is ambiguous or wrong on the single most quantitative claim of the figure.
issue.evidence: Figure annotations (p.179): '3 neighbor rounds / 6 B sent + 6 B received/rank' (reduce-scatter), '3 neighbor rounds / 6 B sent + 6 B received/rank' (all-gather), 'Per rank: 12 B sent + 12 B received = 24 B endpoint total'. Caption (p.179): 'Each rank sends 2 B and receives 12 B in both phases.' Recomputation: 3 rounds x 2 B chunk = 6 B sent per phase; 2 phases x 6 B = 12 B sent per rank; 12 B sent + 12 B received = 24 B endpoint total, matching the figure.
issue.acceptance_test: Caption must state all three accounting levels unambiguously and consistently with the figure: 'per round, each rank sends one 2 B chunk and receives one 2 B chunk; over the 3 rounds of each phase that is 6 B sent and 6 B received per rank; across both phases, 12 B sent and 12 B received per rank (24 B endpoint total)'. Verify against the source text, not the 150 dpi render, before editing.

issue.issue: The figure title 'Ring traffic and directional bandwidth' does not describe what is plotted. The axes are ideal ring completion TIME (ms) versus logical input tensor per rank (GB); bandwidth appears only as the parameter of three curves. A reader scanning the page gets no hint that the figure is a time-versus-size tradeoff, which is the figure's actual intellectual content (how ring time scales with tensor size at three bandwidths).
issue.evidence: Figure title (p.178): 'Ring traffic and directional bandwidth'. Axes: y = 'Ideal ring completion time (ms)', x = 'Logical input tensor per rank (GB)'. Legend encodes three bandwidths.
issue.acceptance_test: Retitle to something like 'Ideal ring all-reduce time vs per-rank tensor size at three directional bandwidths', so the title states the dependent and independent variables and the parameter.

issue.issue: The RoCE curve (red, dotted, small markers) is the faintest element in the plot and is the curve the reader most needs to read (it is the extreme case and the one whose value the caption quotes). At print size the dotted stroke and its markers are thin relative to the solid blue curve, and the red is the lightest of the three inks, so in grayscale the RoCE curve is the least legible of the three. Dash pattern and marker shape do provide grayscale separation, so this is a polish item, not a failure of the grayscale strategy.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 178: red dotted line with small filled markers, orange dashed with triangles, blue solid with circles. The red curve spans the full plot height (0.039 ms to 98,000 ms) and its markers are visibly smaller/thinner than the blue curve's.
issue.acceptance_test: Increase the RoCE curve's line weight and marker size to match the blue curve's visual weight, and confirm on a grayscale proof that all three curves remain distinguishable by dash pattern plus marker shape alone.

issue.issue: Phase is encoded by color alone in the box borders and the two phase labels ('Reduce-scatter' in orange, 'All-gather' in blue). In grayscale the orange border and the blue border are close in value, so a grayscale reader must rely on the adjacent text labels to know which phase a row belongs to. The figure is otherwise well structured (rows are labeled, the ring panel is separate), so this is a robustness improvement rather than a defect.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 179: input row boxes have blue borders; reduce-scatter output row boxes have orange borders; all-gather output row boxes have blue borders; the words 'Reduce-scatter' and 'All-gather' are the only non-positional cue distinguishing the two phases.
issue.acceptance_test: Add a redundant non-color cue to the phase rows (e.g. a phase tag chip or distinct border pattern/dash) so that a grayscale print still distinguishes the reduce-scatter row from the all-gather row without relying on hue.

issue.figure: Figure 9.3 (The payload path is not the bootstrap path)
issue.issue: The caption's gloss of the NCCL box conflates two distinct things. The figure's box reads 'Ring / tree / NVLS or ColNet offload'; the caption says this 'names NCCL's NVLink SHARP and ColNet in-network reduction paths'. NVLS is the NVLink SHARP transport, not the in-network reduction itself, and 'offload' is doing unstated work: the reader is left unsure whether the box means 'algorithms that offload reduction to the fabric' or 'transports that carry offloaded reduction'. The figure's own layer-3/4 boxes already separate transport from device execution, so the ambiguity is avoidable.
issue.evidence: Figure (p.181), NCCL box: 'Ring / tree / NVLS or ColNet offload'. Caption (p.181): "The NCCL box's 'NVLS or ColNet offload' names NCCL's NVLink SHARP and ColNet in-network reduction paths, used only where the fabric and build support them (NCCL NVLS transport, pinned to v2.32.3-1; NCCL ColNet tuning, pinned to v2.32.3-1)."
issue.acceptance_test: Caption must distinguish the reduction mechanism (NVLink SHARP, ColNet) from the transport (NVLS) and state explicitly that these entries are conditional on fabric and build support, matching the pinned versions already cited.

issue.issue: The red dashed control path is drawn as a long routed line down the left margin to the ProcessGroupNCCL box and down the right margin to the ProcessGroupXCCL box. On the left, the dashed line runs very close to (and appears to touch) the left border of the ProcessGroupNCCL box and passes immediately beside the '1 Framework backend' heading, which weakens the visual separation between 'control/setup' and 'payload/execution' that the figure exists to establish. The right-hand dashed run also visually suggests a continuation into layers 2-4 that the figure does not actually draw.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 181: red dashed line descends along the left edge of the figure and terminates at the left border of the ProcessGroupNCCL box; the '1 Framework backend' label sits between the dashed line and the box column.
issue.acceptance_test: On a print proof, confirm the dashed control path does not touch or abut the ProcessGroupNCCL box border or the '1 Framework backend' heading; add clearance (or route the dashed path above the layer-1 row) so that control and payload paths are unambiguously separate. Also confirm the dashed path terminates at the layer-1 boxes only.

issue.issue: The prose paragraph that introduces the ring model quotes one-way 140 GB times (0.31 s NVLink, 5.6 s HDR, 56 s Ethernet) without stating the 1.75x ring factor that Fig 9.1 applies, so the reader meets two different sets of times for '140 GB' before reaching the figure. The figure's caption then compounds this (see FIG-9.1-CAP-01). The prose itself is correct; the missing signpost is the defect.
issue.evidence: p.177: 'A one-way 140 GB transfer on the directional peak takes about 0.31 s [1P][DERIVED]' and 'the nominal 25 GB/s of one HDR port gives a best-case 5.6 s; an assumed practical-effective 2.5 GB/s Ethernet path gives 56 s'. Fig 9.1 (p.178) plots 544 ms / 6,125 ms / 98,000 ms at the same 140 GB logical tensor because it charges 1.75x the tensor per rank.
issue.acceptance_test: The p.157 paragraph must add one sentence stating that a ring all-reduce moves 2*(N-1)/N = 1.75x the tensor per rank at N = 8, so Fig 9.1's times are 1.75x the one-way times quoted here, and must point forward to Fig 9.1 by name.

issue.figure: Figure 22.1 (cited on this page as support for the attention-term share of prefill FLOPs)
issue.issue: The bullet 'Attention / memory constrained (within prefill)' cites Fig 22.1 and gives the attention term as '4*n_layers*L*4', which as rendered is not a recognizable attention-FLOP expression (the standard form is 4*n_layers*L^2*d_model). The accompanying claim 'at 32K it is already ~60%' is workload- and model-dependent and must be checked against the canonical model's layer count and hidden size: with n_layers = 80 and d_model = 8192, attention FLOPs at 32K are 4*80*32768^2*8192 = 2.68 PFLOP against 4.48 PFLOP of linear work, i.e. ~37%, not ~60% (60% is reached near ~80K). The claim may still be correct if the canonical model differs, but as printed it is unsupported by the formula shown and by the cited figure.
issue.evidence: p.172: 'at 128K contexts this term dominates prefill cost (at 32K it is already ~60% - the 4*n_layers*L*4 term, Fig 22.1)'. Recomputation with the canonical 70B reference (n_layers = 80, d_model = 8192): attention = 4*80*L^2*8192; at L = 32,000 -> 2.68 PFLOP; linear = 2*70e9*32,000 = 4.48 PFLOP; share = 37.5%. Share reaches 60% at L ~ 80,000.
issue.acceptance_test: Verify the canonical model's n_layers and d_model, then restate the attention FLOP expression in a self-consistent form (4*n_layers*L^2*d_model) and recompute the 32K share; if it is not ~60%, correct the number or restate it as 'at 32K it is already ~X%'. Confirm that Fig 22.1 plots the same quantity at the same operating point, and that the page's own footnote arithmetic (2*70B*L -> 0.28 PFLOP at 2K, ~4.5 PFLOP at 32K, ~1.29 PFLOP at 9.2K) is reproduced in Fig 22.1.

issue.figure: none - prose only (no figure on this page)
issue.issue: Quantitative claim is wrong by a factor of ten. The bullet prints 'extreme sparsity (16/86 ~ 1.8% expert activation)'. 16/86 = 0.18605 = 18.6%, not 1.8%. The printed fraction and the printed percentage are mutually exclusive, and the percentage is load-bearing: the sentence uses it to argue that the memory-bound EP decision is made against total rather than active parameters, and the bullet's closing claim about an 'activated-vs-total residency crossover' rests on the sparsity magnitude.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 181, bullet 2 ('How should EP sizing and all-to-all communication be budgeted for frontier MoE models at extreme sparsity?'). Recomputation: 16 / 86 = 0.1860465; x100 = 18.60%. To yield ~1.8% the denominator must be ~889 (16/896 = 1.786%), which contradicts the '512 experts' printed two clauses earlier. The same bullet prints 'routes 1e1 of 512 experts' - '1e1' is not a well-formed count (10 in scientific notation, or a mangled '16'/'10') - so neither the numerator nor the denominator of the sparsity fraction can be recovered from the page. 'Kimi 10qB' is likewise a malformed parameter count. Note the operator is '~', so the defect is not a rounding quibble: 18.6% vs 1.8% is a factor of 10, far outside any rounding bound.
issue.acceptance_test: Recover the active-expert count, total-expert count and activated/total parameter split from the cited primary sources ([1P] arXiv 2606.24653 / 2607.24653 and the HF model card). Print one self-consistent triple (active / total = percentage) with correct rounding. Delete '1e1' and '10qB' or replace them with well-formed numerals. Then re-derive the sentence: if the corrected sparsity is ~18.6%, the 'extreme sparsity' framing and the 'activated-vs-total residency crossover' argument must be re-argued, not merely re-digitised.

issue.issue: An evidence fragment is duplicated verbatim inside a single bullet, and the two copies disagree with each other on the arXiv identifier and on the model name. The bullet contains '[1P]: arXiv 2606.24653; Qwen3-8-Flash-Next routes 1e1 of 512 experts (128B total / 6B active) [1P]: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.' twice - once at the head of the bullet and again immediately after '...increasingly central to serving large MoE fleets'.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 181, bullet 2. First copy: 'arXiv 2606.24653 ... Qwen3-8-Flash-Next ... HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next'. Second copy: 'arXiv 2607.24653 ... Qwen3-8-Flash-Next ... HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next'. The copies differ in the arXiv month component (2606 vs 2607) and in the model name spelling ('Qwen3-8-Flash-Next' vs 'Qwen3.8-Flash-Next'), so this is not a clean copy-paste of one string - it is two independently edited variants of the same citation, at least one of which is wrong. The duplication also breaks the sentence: '...large MoE fleets [1P]: arXiv ... . The architecture this changes the serving calculus:' leaves a citation stranded between the clause it was supposed to support and the clause that follows.
issue.acceptance_test: Delete the duplicated citation block and retain exactly one. Verify against the primary source that (a) the arXiv identifier is correct (2606.24653 or 2607.24653, not both), (b) the model name is spelled identically in the citation and in the prose, and (c) the [1P] label binds the clause it supports rather than being repeated. Confirm the bullet reads as one continuous argument with no citation between 'fleets' and 'The architecture'.

issue.issue: The figure has no numbered caption on the page where it appears. The figure is followed only by a 'Figure note (grayscale): ...' line, which is a note about the color key, not a caption. The body text on the same page refers to 'Fig. 10.1', and p. 181 refers to 'Fig 10.1', so the figure is referenced by a number that the reader cannot find anywhere on the figure's own page.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, rendered page: the framed figure occupies the upper ~55% of the page; immediately below it is the legend row (weights/GPU/data/comms) and then the italic line 'Figure note (grayscale): each box's text label carries its role, so the in-figure color key (blue = weights . orange = GPU . green = data . red = comms) is redundant, not load-bearing.' No 'Figure 10.1' string and no descriptive title appear above, inside, or below the frame. Either the caption is absent, or it sits on printed p. 172, separated from its figure by a page break - both are defects.
issue.acceptance_test: The figure must carry a numbered caption ('Figure 10.1 - <title>') on the same printed page as the figure, and the caption must state what the reader should learn (e.g. that each panel shows what is split, what is replicated, and what is communicated). Verify by searching the built PDF for 'Figure 10.1' and confirming the page index equals the page index of the figure.

issue.issue: Panel B asserts a pipeline bubble but never draws one. The annotation under the GPU row reads 'idle (bubble) at fill/drain - pipeline-wide', and the body prose on the same page says 'an idle bubble appears as the pipeline fills and drains'. Nothing in the diagram shows an idle stage, an unfilled time slot, or any time axis, so the one property that distinguishes PP from TP and DP in the prose is invisible in the figure.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, panel B: three GPU boxes in a row with two arrows between them and the annotation 'idle (bubble) at fill/drain - pipeline-wide' beneath. There is no bubble glyph, no dashed 'idle' segment, and no fill/drain timeline. A reader who has never seen a pipeline diagram cannot tell what the annotation refers to; a reader who has can only take it on trust.
issue.acceptance_test: Panel B must depict the bubble - for example a small fill/drain timeline inset beneath the GPU row showing stage occupancy over time with the idle interval hatched and labeled, or an explicitly drawn idle segment inside one stage box - and the annotation must point at what it names. Alternatively, remove the annotation and the corresponding prose clause. Acceptance: a reader who has never seen a pipeline diagram can point to the idle region and say which stage is idle during fill and which during drain.

issue.issue: Panel B does not depict the thing it claims to split. Panels A and C each show the split object explicitly - a weight matrix W in A, batch shards A/B in C - but panel B, titled 'splits the layer stack', shows only three generic boxes labeled 'GPU 0', 'GPU 1', 'GPU 2'. The layer stack, the stage boundaries, and the mapping of layers to stages are all absent, so the panel's title is not supported by anything the eye can see.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, panel B: three orange dashed boxes labeled GPU 0 / GPU 1 / GPU 2, two arrows, the label 'activations -> P2P at stage boundaries', and the note 'idle (bubble) at fill/drain - pipeline-wide'. No layer-stack bar, no layer ranges, no stage partition. Compare panel A, which draws 'one layer's weight matrix W' as a bar, and panel C, which draws 'batch shard A' / 'batch shard B' as bars. The asymmetry is the defect: the figure's comparative job is to show what each strategy partitions, and panel B is the only one that does not.
issue.acceptance_test: Panel B must draw the layer stack as a partitioned object - e.g. a vertical bar divided into three contiguous segments labeled with the layer ranges they carry (layers 0-22 / 23-45 / 46-69 for the canonical 70B model, or a generic 'layers 0-n1 / n1-n2 / n2-N') - with each segment visually mapped to its GPU and the stage boundaries aligned with the P2P arrows. Acceptance: the reader can state which layers each GPU holds without reading prose.

issue.issue: The inter-GPU communication arrows in panel B are drawn in the GPU color (orange dashed), not the communication color (red) that the figure's own legend assigns to 'comms'. Panels A and C both use red for their communication (the all-reduce box in A, the 'gradients -> all-reduce' text in C), so the figure contradicts its key in exactly one panel - and the panel where the arrows are the only carrier of the meaning.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173: legend row reads 'weights (blue) | GPU (orange) | data (green) | comms (red)'. Panel B's two stage-boundary arrows are orange dashed, visually identical in style to the GPU box borders they connect. In grayscale the arrows and the boxes are both dashed outlines of similar tone, so the direction and the role of the connectors are hard to separate.
issue.acceptance_test: All inter-GPU communication arrows in all three panels use the comms style (red dashed), or the legend is removed and every arrow carries an explicit text label. Acceptance: a grayscale proof shows the arrows distinguishable from the boxes they connect, and no reader can mistake an orange arrow for a GPU.

issue.confidence: medium (fill state must be confirmed at full resolution)
issue.issue: The three GPU boxes in panel B do not appear to share the same fill. 'GPU 1' and 'GPU 2' carry the orange cross-hatch used for GPUs everywhere else in the figure, while 'GPU 0' appears to have an unfilled (white) interior with only the orange dashed border. If this is a rendering defect, the figure misrepresents one of three identical objects; if it is intentional, it encodes a distinction (an idle stage?) that nothing in the figure or prose explains.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, panel B, rendered at 150 dpi: the leftmost box labeled 'GPU 0' reads as white interior / orange dashed border; the middle and right boxes read as orange cross-hatch. The legend defines 'GPU (orange)' as a filled swatch, so an unfilled GPU box is inconsistent with the key.
issue.acceptance_test: Confirm the fill state of the 'GPU 0' box in the source at full resolution. All three GPU boxes must carry identical orange cross-hatch fill, unless the empty box is deliberately the drawn bubble - in which case it must be labeled as such (see FIG-10.1-02) and the legend must accommodate it. Acceptance: a grayscale proof shows three visually equivalent GPU boxes.

issue.issue: Panel A draws the weight matrix as a single undivided bar with two arrows leaving it, which reads as the same matrix being handed to both GPUs (replication) rather than being partitioned across them (sharding). The panel title says 'splits one layer's weights' and the caption says 'Tensor parallel shards one layer's weight matrix across GPUs', but the drawn object is never divided.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, panel A: one blue hatched bar labeled 'one layer's weight matrix W' spanning both GPUs, with two blue arrows descending to 'GPU 0' and 'GPU 1'. The arrows leave from different x positions, which weakly hints at a partition, but no boundary, no shard labels, and no 'W[:, :d/2]' / 'W[:, d/2:]]' annotation is present. The figure therefore does not distinguish TP from naive weight replication - the single most consequential distinction in the panel.
issue.acceptance_test: The bar must be visibly partitioned into two labeled shards (e.g. 'W[:, 0:d/2]' and 'W[:, d/2:d]'), each routed to exactly one GPU, with the partition boundary drawn. Acceptance: a reader can answer 'is the weight matrix copied or divided?' from the figure alone, and the answer is unambiguous.

issue.issue: The body prose identifies replicated activations as a defining property of TP ('activations are replicated'), but the figure shows no activations at all. The only blue element is the weight bar, so the figure depicts TP as a scheme in which only weights move. A reader could reasonably infer that TP's communication is weight traffic rather than activation traffic, which inverts the actual cost structure.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, panel A and the paragraph immediately below the figure: 'Tensor parallel shards one layer's weight matrix across GPUs - activations are replicated, and each GPU's partial sums are all-reduced...'. Panel A contains no activation element; the red box is labeled 'all-reduce partial sums -> full output', which is the output side, not the input side.
issue.acceptance_test: Panel A must show the replicated input activation (a neutral-filled bar labeled 'input activation x (replicated to every GPU)') feeding both GPUs, visually distinct from the weight shards and from the red comms element. Acceptance: the figure shows both the replicated input and the reduced output, so the reader can see that TP's per-layer traffic is activation traffic.

issue.issue: Panel C shows no weights, so the property that distinguishes DP from TP - that every GPU holds a full copy of the model - is not visible. The figure's own framing (p. 181) promises that reading across a row gives 'what it splits, what it replicates, what it communicates'; panel C shows only what is split (the batch) and what is communicated (gradients), leaving 'what it replicates' blank.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, panel C: two green hatched boxes 'batch shard A' / 'batch shard B' above two orange GPU boxes, with the red text 'gradients -> all-reduce (training only)' and the notes 'inference: independent replicas, no sync' and 'throughput scales linearly until a shared resource binds'. The word 'replicas' appears only in prose; no blue weight element appears anywhere in the panel, so a reader comparing panels A and C sees weights in A and nothing in C.
issue.acceptance_test: Panel C must show a full copy of the weight matrix inside each GPU box (a small blue hatched bar labeled 'full copy of W' per GPU), making the replication axis visible and directly comparable with panel A's sharded bar. Acceptance: the reader can state that DP replicates weights and TP shards them by looking at the two panels side by side.

issue.issue: The red annotation 'gradients -> all-reduce (training only)' is superimposed on the lower portion of the orange cross-hatched GPU boxes. Red text over an orange cross-hatch fill is the lowest-contrast combination in the figure, and in grayscale it becomes mid-gray text over a busy texture - the annotation is the one element that carries the training-vs-inference distinction.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, panel C: the red text baseline sits inside the vertical span of the 'GPU 0' and 'GPU 1' boxes, crossing their cross-hatch fill and their lower borders. The same problem does not occur in panel A, where the red comms box sits below the GPU boxes.
issue.acceptance_test: Move the annotation clear of the GPU boxes with at least 2 pt of clearance, or place it in a white callout band below the panel. Acceptance: the annotation is fully legible in a grayscale proof at 100% print size, with no glyph overlapping a hatch stroke or a box border.

issue.confidence: medium (hatch direction must be confirmed at full resolution)
issue.issue: The figure separates 'weights' (blue) from 'data' (green) primarily by hue. Both fills appear to use a single-direction diagonal hatch, so in grayscale the weight bar in panel A and the batch-shard boxes in panel C differ only in fill density, not in pattern. The GPU fill (cross-hatch) is the only pattern that survives grayscale unambiguously.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173: legend swatches for 'weights (blue)' and 'data (green)' are both single-direction hatched rectangles; 'GPU (orange)' is cross-hatched. The figure's own caption note claims the color key is 'redundant, not load-bearing' because 'each box's text label carries its role' - but that claim only holds for the boxes, and it is precisely the hue that carries the weights-vs-data distinction in the legend itself.
issue.acceptance_test: Assign three distinguishable fill patterns (e.g. weights = 45-degree hatch, data = 135-degree hatch, GPU = cross-hatch) so that all three fills remain separable in grayscale, and confirm on an actual grayscale proof that the panel A weight bar cannot be confused with the panel C batch-shard boxes. Acceptance: a reader can classify each filled element correctly from a grayscale print.

issue.issue: The caption note makes a claim the figure contradicts: 'each box's text label carries its role, so the in-figure color key ... is redundant, not load-bearing'. The inter-GPU arrows in panel B carry no text label at all, so for the one element whose role is not self-evident the key is the only decoder - and it decodes them wrongly (see FIG-10.1-04). Declaring a key redundant while retaining it, in a note whose stated justification is false, is an internal inconsistency in the figure's own documentation.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, caption note vs panel B. Boxes in A, B and C all carry role-bearing text ('one layer's weight matrix W', 'GPU 0', 'batch shard A', 'all-reduce partial sums -> full output', 'gradients -> all-reduce (training only)'); the two panel B arrows carry none.
issue.acceptance_test: Either (a) label every arrow with its role and delete the legend and the 'redundant, not load-bearing' clause, or (b) keep the legend, fix the arrow colors per FIG-10.1-04, and rewrite the note to state what the key is for (e.g. 'the key is required for the arrows, which carry no text label'). Acceptance: the note's claim is true of every element in the figure.

issue.issue: The prose describing panel A is garbled and does not match the figure's own label. The page reads 'each GPU's partial sums are all-reduced at layer-level dependencies in the illustrated layout', which is not a coherent statement, and 'at layer-level dependencies' conflicts with the figure's annotation 'communication: all-reduce every layer'. The reader is left unsure whether the all-reduce happens once per layer, once per stage, or at some other granularity - which is exactly the distinction that determines TP's communication volume.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, paragraph below the figure vs panel A annotation 'communication: all-reduce every layer -> on-node the canonical config (NVLink)' and the red box 'all-reduce partial sums -> full output'.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite as a single unambiguous sentence, e.g. 'each GPU's partial sums are all-reduced at every layer boundary, so the collective runs once per layer'. Acceptance: the prose and the figure annotation state the same granularity, and the phrase 'layer-level dependencies' no longer appears.

issue.issue: The three panels are presented as one figure but are split across two separate rounded frames with a visible seam: panels A and B share one frame (with an internal rule between them), and panel C sits alone in a second frame below. The prose on both p. 173 and p. 181 describes the figure as 'the three canonical patterns ... in three stacked panels', so the framing contradicts the description and weakens the figure's comparative job - the reader must work out that the lower frame belongs to the same figure.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173: an upper rounded rectangle containing panel A and panel B, a gap of white space, then a second rounded rectangle containing panel C, then the legend row outside both frames.
issue.acceptance_test: Place all three panels inside a single frame with consistent internal rules, or drop the frames entirely and use whitespace plus rules to separate panels. Acceptance: the figure reads as one object at a glance, and the legend is either inside the frame or restyled as part of the caption.

issue.issue: The panel A annotation 'communication: all-reduce every layer -> on-node the canonical config (NVLink)' is grammatically broken ('on-node the canonical config' has no verb) and compresses two distinct facts - collective frequency and interconnect medium - into one line.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, panel A, line below the GPU row.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite as 'communication: all-reduce at every layer boundary -> on-node in the canonical configuration (NVLink)', or split into two lines. Acceptance: the sentence parses and the collective frequency and the interconnect are separately readable.

issue.issue: The red dashed comms box in panel A sits immediately below the GPU boxes with very little clearance, and its left edge extends under 'GPU 0' while its right edge extends under 'GPU 1'. At 150 dpi the clearance between the dashed box's top edge and the GPU box bottoms is on the order of 1-2 pt, which risks visual collision at print size and in grayscale.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, panel A: the red dashed rectangle containing 'all-reduce partial sums -> full output' begins immediately below the bottom borders of the two GPU boxes.
issue.acceptance_test: Increase clearance to at least 2 pt between the comms annotation box and the GPU box borders, and confirm no dashed stroke touches or crosses a box border in a grayscale proof.

issue.issue: The label 'activations -> P2P at stage boundaries' floats above the GPU row, centered over 'GPU 1', rather than being attached to the arrows it describes. A reader scanning the panel sees an unconnected caption and two unlabeled arrows.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, panel B: the text sits on its own line above the three GPU boxes; the two arrows between the boxes carry no text.
issue.acceptance_test: Place the label on or immediately above the arrow pair it describes, or label each arrow individually. Acceptance: the label is unambiguously associated with the arrows.

issue.issue: The legend row sits outside the figure's frame, below the second rounded rectangle, so the key that decodes the figure's fills is visually detached from the figure it decodes and reads as a separate strip of body text.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173: the legend row ('weights (blue) | GPU (orange) | data (green) | comms (red)') appears below the panel C frame, between the frame and the caption note.
issue.acceptance_test: Move the legend inside the figure frame (bottom of the single frame per FIG-10.1-13) or set it as a caption line immediately under the figure with matching styling. Acceptance: the key is visually bound to the figure.

issue.issue: Inconsistent abbreviation punctuation for the same figure reference: printed p. 173 writes 'Fig. 10.1 shows the three canonical patterns', printed p. 181 writes 'Fig 10.1 illustrates the three canonical patterns' (no period after 'Fig').
issue.evidence: Printed p. 173, first body line below the figure; printed p. 181, second paragraph of the page.
issue.acceptance_test: Use one form throughout ('Fig. 10.1'). Acceptance: a global search for 'Fig ' and 'Fig.' returns a single convention.

issue.issue: Broken sentence in the same bullet: 'The architecture this changes the serving calculus: a frontier MoE's activated footprint ...'. The clause 'The architecture this changes the serving calculus' has no main verb and no object.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 181, bullet 2, sentence beginning 'The architecture this changes the serving calculus:'.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite as 'This changes the serving calculus: ...' or 'The architecture this changes is the serving calculus: ...'. Acceptance: the sentence parses.

issue.figure: FIGURE 11.2 — 'Serving = four separate concerns, not a stack' (2×2 box grid: 1 Request scheduling / 2 State management / 3 Reuse / 4 Resource specialization)
issue.issue: The figure's border-style encoding contradicts the caption's own legend. The caption states: 'the canonical baseline uses the first three, resource specialization joins when the workload outgrows a node (dashed border) — not in the canonical baseline'. That makes dashed border = 'not in the canonical baseline'. But in the rendered figure, boxes 2 (State management) and 3 (Reuse) are ALSO drawn with dashed borders, while box 1 (Request scheduling) is the only solid-bordered box. Under the caption's stated convention, the figure therefore asserts that state management and reuse are excluded from the canonical baseline — the exact opposite of the caption's sentence and of the surrounding chapter (Ch. 11 repeatedly treats PagedAttention and prefix caching as part of the canonical baseline). There is no legend anywhere on the page to disambiguate the border styles, so the reader has no way to resolve the conflict.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 212 (printed 192): box 1 border = solid purple; box 2 = dashed red; box 3 = dashed green; box 4 = dashed orange. Caption text on the same page: 'the canonical baseline uses the first three, resource specialization joins when the workload outgrows a node (dashed border) — not in the canonical baseline'. Only one of the three dashed boxes is explained by the caption; the other two are unexplained and semantically wrong under the caption's rule. Cross-check with printed page 191 (PDF 211), which describes PagedAttention/prefix caching as active mechanisms of the canonical 640 GB node baseline.
issue.root_cause: The figure was authored with 'dashed = distinct/independent concern' (a stylistic device) while the caption repurposed 'dashed' as 'dashed = excluded from canonical baseline'. Two incompatible meanings were assigned to one visual channel.
issue.correction: Pick one meaning for border style and make the figure and caption agree. Preferred: solid border for the three concerns present in the canonical baseline (1, 2, 3) and dashed for 4 only, plus a one-line legend inside the figure ('dashed = not in the canonical baseline; see § 11.3'). If the intended distinction was instead 'solid = scheduling, dashed = the other three', then rewrite the caption clause to say so explicitly and remove the '(dashed border)' parenthetical from the canonical-baseline sentence.
issue.acceptance_test: Render the page and confirm: (a) exactly one box carries the 'not in canonical baseline' border style, and it is box 4; (b) a legend or caption clause states the border-style meaning unambiguously; (c) no reader can reach the conclusion 'PagedAttention and prefix caching are not in the canonical baseline' from the figure alone.

issue.issue: The caption's central claim is that the four concerns 'interact — batching pressure feeds KV residency', and it gives a concrete coupling example ('prefix caching under aggressive continuous batching: cached prefixes and the live batch's pages draw on the same 640 GB KV pool, so reuse needs headroom'). The figure, however, draws four fully disconnected boxes with no arrows, no shared resource, and no coupling annotation. A reader who takes the diagram at face value learns 'four independent, non-interacting components' — which is the opposite of the caption's first clause and is the more consequential misconception, because the coupling (shared KV pool) is exactly what determines whether the four dials can be set independently in practice.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 212: no connectors of any kind between boxes 1–4; the only shared object mentioned in the caption (the 640 GB KV pool) appears nowhere in the drawing. Title 'Serving = four separate concerns, not a stack' reinforces the 'independent' reading.
issue.root_cause: The figure was designed to make the 'not a stack' point (no vertical ordering) and over-corrected into 'no relations at all', losing the interaction the caption asserts.
issue.correction: Add a minimal interaction cue without implying a stack: e.g. a single dashed, non-directional connector or a shared '640 GB KV pool' band beneath boxes 2 and 3 labelled 'shared KV pool → reuse needs headroom', plus a small annotation on the 1→2 edge ('batching pressure → KV residency'). Keep the boxes unordered (no arrows forming a chain). Alternatively, retitle to 'Serving = four concerns, not a stack — but they interact' and let the caption carry the coupling.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader shown only the figure (caption hidden) can state both (a) that the four concerns are not ordered as a stack and (b) that at least one pair shares a constrained resource and therefore cannot be tuned fully independently.

issue.issue: Grayscale distinguishability is weak. The four boxes use hue alone to differentiate the concerns: purple (1), red (2), green (3), orange (4). In grayscale, red and orange collapse to nearly the same mid-gray, and green to a similar mid-gray; the only non-color differentiator is border style, which — per FIG-11.2-01 — is itself ambiguous and identical for boxes 2, 3 and 4. The italic 'e.g.' sub-labels are drawn in light tints of the same hues (light red, light green, light orange), which lose further contrast in grayscale and at the small size used. The book must remain interpretable in grayscale and for color-vision-deficient readers.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 212 at 150 dpi: boxes 2/3/4 are visually near-identical in stroke weight and dash pattern, differing only by hue; the sub-label text is noticeably lower-contrast than the box titles.
issue.root_cause: Color was used as the primary categorical channel with no redundant (shape/pattern/label) encoding, and the one redundant channel available (border style) was overloaded with a conflicting meaning.
issue.correction: Add a redundant non-color channel: distinct border patterns per concern (solid / long-dash / dotted / double-line) or a small numeral badge plus a short axis label, and darken the 'e.g.' sub-labels to the same hue as their box titles (or to a neutral dark gray). Keep hue as a tertiary cue only.
issue.acceptance_test: Convert the page to grayscale and confirm all four boxes remain individually identifiable by a non-color cue, and that every 'e.g.' sub-label remains legible at 100% print size.

issue.issue: Two small semantic/pedagogical points. (a) The boxes are numbered 1–4 in reading order, which implies a sequence or precedence even though the title and caption insist the concerns are 'not a stack' and are addressed 'in any order'; the numbering is the only element in the drawing that suggests ordering. (b) The caption's closing italic paragraph states the actual intellectual payload — 'request scheduling exchanges latency for utilization, state management exchanges memory capacity for concurrency, reuse avoids re-prefill FLOPs, and resource specialization splits two compute/memory regimes into two pools' — but none of these trade-offs is encoded in the figure, so the figure carries the least informative content of the pair.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 212: numerals '1 ·', '2 ·', '3 ·', '4 ·' precede the box titles; no trade-off text appears inside any box.
issue.root_cause: Numbering was used for reference convenience; the trade-off dimension was left entirely to the caption.
issue.correction: Either drop the numerals (or replace them with non-ordinal tags such as 'SCHED'/'STATE'/'REUSE'/'SPEC') so no ordering is implied, or add a one-line trade-off under each 'e.g.' label (e.g. 'latency ↔ utilization'). If the trade-offs are added, the figure becomes the primary carrier of the caption's key insight and the caption can be shortened.
issue.acceptance_test: Figure alone conveys, for each of the four concerns, the mechanism and the resource it trades; no visual element implies an ordering among the four.

issue.issue: Page composition: the figure plus its long caption (roughly 20 lines, including a separate italic paragraph) ends about three-quarters of the way down the page, leaving a large empty band at the bottom of a page that is otherwise a single figure-and-caption unit. The caption is also unusually long relative to the figure it annotates — the figure is four boxes with short labels, while the caption carries the mechanism choices, the interaction example, the canonical-baseline rule, the cross-reference to § 11.3, and a separate trade-off paragraph.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 212: bottom ~25% of the text block is blank; caption occupies more vertical space than the diagram.
issue.root_cause: Caption was written to stand alone as a mini-essay, and the figure was not sized to carry more of that content.
issue.correction: Move the trade-off content into the figure (see FIG-11.2-04) and compress the caption to: what the figure shows, the canonical-baseline rule, and the § 11.3 pointer. This both shortens the caption and lets the figure be enlarged to fill the page, improving label legibility.
issue.acceptance_test: Caption reduced to ≤ 12 lines; figure enlarged so that the smallest label is ≥ 8 pt at final print size; no page in the chapter ends with more than ~20% trailing whitespace.

issue.figure: FIGURE 11.3 — P/D disaggregation: two cases, two different KV links
issue.issue: Case A's KV volume is internally inconsistent: the byte/time annotation reads '~35 GB ≈ 0.08 s (on-node, undirectional)' but the workload annotation directly beneath it reads 'illustrative 1.3K-token, FP16 full-MHA'. At the book's canonical FP16 full-MHA KV rate (~2.62 MB/token), 1.3K tokens is ~3.4 GB, not 35 GB; 35 GB corresponds to ~13.3K tokens, which is exactly what case B states. Either case A's token count is wrong (should be 13.3K-token), or case A's byte/time figures are wrong (should be ~3.5 GB ≈ 0.008 s). As drawn, the figure's central comparison ('0.08 s vs 0.9 s') is either wrong or confounded by a 10× difference in workload, which contradicts the figure's own subtitle ('the P/D split is the same; the transfer link — and its cost — is not').
issue.evidence: Figure text: A = '~35 GB ≈ 0.08 s (on-node, undirectional)' / 'illustrative 1.3K-token, FP16 full-MHA'; B = '~35 GB ≈ 0.9 s (cross-host)' / 'illustrative 13.3K-token, FP16 full-MHA'. Figure note: 'A: 0.08 s ≈ whole 35 GB over one unsharded 450 GB/s link (conservative; shard = 0.02 s).' Arithmetic: 35 GB ÷ 2.62 MB/token = 13,359 tokens ≈ 13.3K (matches B); 1.3K × 2.62 MB = 3.4 GB (does not match A's 35 GB). Time check: 35 GB ÷ 450 GB/s = 0.0778 s ≈ 0.08 s (so the 35 GB / 0.08 s pair is self-consistent and the token count is the outlier).
issue.acceptance_test: At 100% zoom, read the case-A workload annotation. If it reads '1.3K-token', change it to '13.3K-token' (or change A's byte/time pair to '~3.5 GB ≈ 0.008 s' and re-derive the note). Acceptance: the identity 'bytes ÷ 2.62 MB/token = stated token count' holds for BOTH cases, and the two cases carry the same KV volume so that the only variable is the link.

issue.figure: FIGURE 11.3 caption (prose claims) vs figure annotations
issue.issue: The caption's numeric chain cannot be reconciled under a single prompt length and a single time base. The caption states 'per-request 1→19 PFLOPs over the ~1.08 s prefix budget vs 0.89 peak single-H100; on the canonical 8-H100 host the same prefix takes ~0.47 s at 35% MFU, Ch 12'. Two problems: (a) the FLOPs string is either '1.29 PFLOPs' (a low-resolution '1.29' can read as '1→19') or a literal range '1→19 PFLOPs' — if it is the latter it is wrong by ~15× for the canonical prefix; (b) '0.89 peak single-H100' equals 989 TFLOPS × 0.9 s, i.e. it is computed over 0.9 s while the comparison is stated against a '~1.08 s prefix budget' (peak over 1.08 s would be 1.07 PFLOPs). The two time bases are mixed in the same comparison. Separately, 'the same prefix takes ~0.47 s' is only consistent with ~1.29 PFLOPs (≈9.2K tokens), NOT with the figure's illustrative 13.3K-token prompt (≈1.86 PFLOPs → ≈0.67 s at 35% MFU on 8×H100), so 'the same prefix' is ambiguous between the canonical prefix and the figure's prompt.
issue.evidence: Caption text as printed. Recomputation: 2·N_params·N_tokens for 70B at 9,200 tokens = 1.29 PFLOPs; 8 × 989 TFLOPS × 0.35 = 2.769 PFLOPS effective → 1.29 / 2.769 = 0.466 s ≈ 0.47 s (consistent). For 13.3K tokens: 1.86 PFLOPs → 0.672 s (not 0.47 s). 989 TFLOPS × 0.9 s = 0.89 PFLOPs; 989 TFLOPS × 1.08 s = 1.07 PFLOPs. Figure annotation: 'illustrative 13.3K-token'.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite the caption so that (i) the prompt length is stated in tokens, (ii) the FLOPs figure is written unambiguously (e.g. '≈1.29 PFLOPs = 2·N·T for 9.2K tokens'), and (iii) the time base for '0.89 PFLOPs' is stated (e.g. '989 TFLOPS × 0.9 s of the 1.08 s budget'). Acceptance: a reader can reproduce 1.29 PFLOPs, 0.89 PFLOPs, and 0.47 s from the stated inputs, and the caption says explicitly whether 'the same prefix' is the canonical 9.2K-token prefix or the figure's 13.3K-token illustrative prompt.

issue.issue: The bottom annotation row is semantically incoherent and contradicts the figure's stated thesis. Case A's prefill stage is fed by a label 'prompt' (up-arrow), while case B's prefill stage is fed by 'generated tokens → prompt' (up-arrow) — the two cases therefore show different inputs for the same stage, even though the subtitle asserts 'the P/D split is the same'. The label 'generated tokens → prompt' also mixes two arrow directions (a right-pointing '→' inside a label attached to an up-pointing arrow) and is not explained anywhere on the page: it is either an unexplained second-turn/feedback flow (which is not drawn as a distinct path) or a mislabeled arrow. The reader cannot tell which.
issue.evidence: Figure bottom row, left to right: 'prompt' (up-arrow into case-A PREFILL); 'generated tokens →' (down-arrow from case-A DECODE); 'generated tokens → prompt' (up-arrow into case-B PREFILL); 'generated tokens →' (down-arrow from case-B DECODE). Subtitle: 'the P/D split is the same; the transfer link — and its cost — is not'. No prose on the page explains the 'generated tokens → prompt' label.
issue.acceptance_test: Either (a) make both cases' prefill input 'prompt' and delete 'generated tokens → prompt', or (b) if a multi-turn feedback flow is intended, draw it as a visually distinct dashed path from the decode output back to the prefill input and add one clause of prose naming it. Acceptance: every arrow in the figure has exactly one label, and the two cases differ only in the link (and host boundary), never in the request flow.

issue.figure: FIGURE 11.3 — headline transfer times vs figure note
issue.issue: The headline per-case transfer times are the non-physical variant, while the physically realizable variant appears only in the smallest type in the note. The headline says '≈ 0.08 s (on-node, undirectional)' for 35 GB over one 450 GB/s link; the note says 'conservative; shard = 0.02 s'. With a 4-GPU tensor-parallel prefill stage, no single GPU holds the whole KV, so the unsharded 35 GB hop cannot occur — the realizable figure is 8.75 GB per GPU at 450 GB/s = 0.019 s. The figure therefore headlines an upper bound that is 4× the realizable value, and the reader is never told which number governs the decision the caption claims the figure informs ('the KV-transfer cost decides'). The on-node-vs-fabric ratio is either 11× (headline) or 45× (realizable) — a 4× difference in the figure's headline conclusion.
issue.evidence: Figure headline: '~35 GB ≈ 0.08 s (on-node, undirectional)'. Figure note: 'A: 0.08 s ≈ whole 35 GB over one unsharded 450 GB/s link (conservative; shard = 0.02 s).' Recomputation: 35/4 = 8.75 GB; 8.75/450 = 0.0194 s ≈ 0.02 s; 0.875/0.0194 = 45× vs 0.875/0.0778 = 11×.
issue.acceptance_test: Either headline the sharded (realizable) time and put the unsharded value in the note as an upper bound, or label the headline explicitly 'upper bound (unsharded)'. Acceptance: the figure states which number is used for the on-node-vs-fabric comparison, and the ratio quoted in the caption/prose matches that number.

issue.figure: FIGURE 11.3 — host-boundary encoding, case A vs case B
issue.issue: The visual device that encodes 'host' is inconsistent between the two cases, which undercuts the figure's central contrast (one NVLink domain vs across hosts). Case A's two stage boxes sit inside a single light-gray enclosure labelled '8× H100 host' at the top, so the reader sees that both stages share one host. Case B has no equivalent enclosure: '8× H100 host' appears as a line of text inside each colored stage box, so the reader must infer the host boundary from text. The second line of each stage box also carries different semantics in the two cases ('4 GPUs' in A, '8× H100 host' in B), so the same slot means 'GPU count' on the left and 'host descriptor' on the right.
issue.evidence: Case A: light-gray rounded enclosure spanning both PREFILL and DECODE boxes with '8× H100 host' centred above them; inner boxes labelled 'PREFILL / 4 GPUs' and 'DECODE / 4 GPUs'. Case B: no enclosure; boxes labelled 'PREFILL / 8× H100 host' and 'DECODE / 8× H100 host'. Header: 'A. Within one NVLink domain (8 GPUs: 4+4). B. Across hosts (fabric)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Apply the same host-boundary device in both cases (e.g. a light-gray enclosure around each host, with the fabric link drawn crossing between two enclosures), and make the second line of every stage box mean the same thing (GPU count). Acceptance: a reader can state, from the geometry alone, that case A's stages share one host and case B's do not.

issue.issue: The two KV links — the entire subject of the figure — are drawn identically: both are solid red right-pointing arrows with a red 'KV' label above and a red bandwidth label below. Nothing in the drawing distinguishes an on-node NVLink hop from a cross-host fabric hop except the position of the boxes and the text of the bandwidth label. In grayscale (and for a color-vision-deficient reader) the two links are indistinguishable, so the figure's title claim ('two different KV links') is carried entirely by words rather than by the visual encoding. A line-style or fill distinction (solid = NVLink, dashed = fabric) would carry the distinction in grayscale and would also make the 'sharded vs unsharded' distinction in the note visible.
issue.evidence: Case A: solid red arrow, 'KV' above, '450 GB/s per GPU per direction' below. Case B: solid red arrow, 'KV' above, '40 GB/s per host NIC' below. Both arrows are the same color, weight, and style.
issue.acceptance_test: Differentiate the two links by line style (and, if useful, by arrowhead or a small link glyph) in addition to color, and confirm the distinction survives a grayscale conversion. Acceptance: a grayscale rendering of the page still lets the reader tell which hop is on-node and which is cross-host without reading the bandwidth labels.

issue.issue: The smallest in-figure annotations appear to be set below the 8 pt floor used for figure annotations and body prose: the two 'illustrative …, FP16 full-MHA' lines, the '450 GB/s per GPU per direction' and '40 GB/s per host NIC' labels, the 'square = one GPU (hatched = prefill)' legend, and the four-line note block ('Caveat — aggregate KV migration at peak…'). By relative glyph height against the caption body text, these sit at roughly 65–75% of body size (≈6.5–7.5 pt). This is compounded by information design: the decisive caveats (the 'shard = 0.02 s' alternative and the '1.4 TB/s exceeds any single link' conclusion) live only in the smallest type at the bottom of the figure. The figure currently occupies about 85% of the text-block width and less than half of the available vertical space, so there is room to enlarge it by roughly 15–20% without collision.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 213: the note block's line 'A: 0.08 s ≈ whole 35 GB over one unsharded 450 GB/s link (conservative; shard = 0.02 s).' is visibly much smaller than the caption body text directly below the figure; the same holds for the 'illustrative …' lines and the legend. The figure's bounding box ends roughly 30 px above the caption, leaving unused vertical space.
