Acceptance: no in-figure annotation is below 8 pt, and the note block is legible at 100% on a printed proof without magnification.

issue.issue: Red carries two unrelated meanings in this figure: it outlines the PREFILL stage box (stage identity) and it draws the KV transfer arrow plus the KV bandwidth labels (data-path identity). In grayscale, red and orange (the prefill GPU tiles) also converge in luminance, so the prefill box outline, the prefill tiles, and the KV path all fall into a similar tone band. Shape carries most of the load, so the figure is still readable, but the visual language is not doing the work it appears to do.
issue.evidence: Case A/B: PREFILL box outline red; KV arrow red; 'KV', '450 GB/s per GPU per direction', '40 GB/s per host NIC' red; prefill GPU tiles orange with diagonal hatch; decode box outline and tiles blue. Grayscale luminance of red and orange are close.
issue.acceptance_test: Reserve one hue for stage identity (orange = prefill, blue = decode) and render the KV path in a neutral/dark tone with a distinct line style. Acceptance: in grayscale, no two semantically different elements share both hue and shape.

issue.issue: The figure is labeled '[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]' as a whole, but it mixes three provenance classes: the 450 GB/s per-GPU-per-direction NVLink figure is a first-party hardware specification, the 40 GB/s per-host NIC figure is an assumption about the fabric, and the 13.3K-token prompt is an illustrative workload. A single trailing label on the figure under-covers the hardware and assumption spans, so a reader cannot tell which numbers are measured hardware facts and which are chosen for the illustration.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'FIGURE 11.3: P/D disaggregation has two cases, two KV links; the KV-transfer cost decides — see Note 1.3-1. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]'. Figure contents: '450 GB/s per GPU per direction' (H100 NVLink spec), '40 GB/s per host NIC' (assumed fabric), 'illustrative 13.3K-token' (illustrative workload).
issue.acceptance_test: Split the label span so that the hardware-specification and assumption numbers carry their own markers (e.g. [1P] on the 450 GB/s label, [ASSUMPTION] on the 40 GB/s label), or state the provenance of each in the caption. Acceptance: every number in the figure can be assigned to exactly one provenance class by the reader.

issue.issue: The caveat's aggregate figure uses '40 req/s' — a canonical-workload rate — with no attribution inside the figure, so the reader cannot tell whether it is the book's canonical request rate or an illustrative peak. This matters because the caveat's whole point is a peak-aggregate argument: if 40 req/s is canonical, the 1.4 TB/s figure is a canonical-workload result and should be labeled as such; if it is illustrative, the caveat should say so.
issue.evidence: Figure note: 'Caveat — aggregate KV migration at peak: 35 GB/request × 40 req/s = 1.4 TB/s of payload.' The caption points to 'Note 1.3-1' for the canonical numbers but the figure itself carries no pointer.
issue.acceptance_test: Add '(canonical)' or '(illustrative)' to the 40 req/s figure, or add an in-figure pointer to Note 1.3-1. Acceptance: the reader can determine the provenance of 40 req/s from the figure alone.

issue.issue: Two small layout issues. (a) The two case headers are run together on a single line as one sentence — 'A. Within one NVLink domain (8 GPUs: 4+4). B. Across hosts (fabric)' — so the reader's eye must split one line into two headers, and the period after '(8 GPUs: 4+4)' reads as sentence punctuation rather than as a header boundary. (b) The legend 'square = one GPU (hatched = prefill)' is placed inside the case-A panel, where it can be read as applying only to case A, although it governs the GPU tiles in both cases.

Acceptance: each header is visually bound to one case, and the legend's scope is unambiguous.

issue.issue: The note's parenthetical '(per-GPU in a per-host NIC in B)' is grammatically and semantically ambiguous: it can be read as 'per-GPU [link] in A, per-host NIC in B' or as 'per-GPU [traffic] carried over a per-host NIC in B'. The two readings imply different link-sharing assumptions, and the second reading would change the 35 GB ÷ 40 GB/s = 0.875 s figure.

issue.issue: The caption names the first column 'Intel CPU' while the figure's own column header reads 'Intel GPU' and that column's Hardware box reads 'Discrete GPU or integrated GPU'. Caption and drawing disagree on what the first path is.

The caption drops the 'qualification' semantics on which the red gate box depends, so a reader who takes the caption as the legend reads the dashed lines as mere grouping and misses that the dashed path is what the gate qualifies.

Caption: 'Solid arrows denote dependencies; dashed column outlines group each column (dashed = complete path, not interchangeable APIs).' The gate box below the columns is the only place the qualification meaning is realized.

issue.issue: Three cells print a false arithmetic equation: the operator between the requirement and the per-unit rate is '+' where the derivation requires division. As printed, '368K + 19.8K = 18.6', '92,000 + 24,725 = 3.72', and '368,000 + 24,725 = 14.88' are all numerically false. The derived conclusions (19 hosts, 4 cards, 15 cards) are correct under division, so the defect is the operator, not the result.
issue.evidence: Cell (a) peak: '~19 hosts (368K + 19.8K = 18.6, cell 19 before headroom)' — 368,000/19,800 = 18.59 -> 19. Cell (c) avg: '~4 H100 cards (92,000 + 24,725 = 3.72)' — 92,000/24,725 = 3.72. Cell (c) peak: '~15 H100 cards (368,000 + 24,725 = 14.88), before headroom' — 368,000/24,725 = 14.88. The requirement values 92,000 and 368,000 tok/s are independently confirmed by Fig 12.1 (10 avg / 40 peak rps x 9,200 in-tokens).
issue.acceptance_test: All three parentheticals print a true equation using a division operator ('368K / 19.8K = 18.6', '92,000 / 24,725 = 3.72', '368,000 / 24,725 = 14.88'), and a re-derivation of each cell from the stated requirement and rate reproduces the printed host/card count.

issue.issue: The lead-in paragraph labels the rates as 'per-host' and then states '~24,700 tok/s for the 8-GPU node', but column (c) consumes 24,725 tok/s per H100 card, and the same parenthetical computes the node aggregate as 8 x 24,725 = 197,800. The unit of the rate is therefore stated inconsistently (per-host vs per-card) and the node figure is given two different values (24,700 vs 197,800). A reader who takes 'per-host' literally computes 92,000/197,800 = 0.47 hosts for (a) and 92,000/24,725 = 3.72 cards for (c) — i.e. a fleet count off by roughly an order of magnitude in column (a).
issue.evidence: Lead-in: 'Host counts are an illustrative capacity screen from the fixed per-host prefill rates (~19,800 tok/s for the 70B candidates; ~24,700 tok/s for the 8-GPU node; the 8-GPU node, 8 x 24,725 = 197,800, not this layout)'. Column (c) cells divide the requirement by 24,725 and report 'cards', not hosts; column (a) divides by 19,800 and reports 'hosts'.
issue.acceptance_test: The lead-in states the unit of each rate unambiguously (e.g. '~19,800 tok/s per 70B host; ~24,725 tok/s per H100 card, so an 8-GPU node offers ~197,800 tok/s aggregate — not the layout used here'), and every table cell's divisor is labelled with the same unit as the cell's output (hosts vs cards).

issue.issue: The two prefill-capacity row labels contain an undefined token: 'avg r2K tok/s' and 'peak r2K tok/s'. 'r2K' is not defined anywhere on the page and cannot denote a value, since the two rows carry different requirements (92,000 and 368,000 tok/s). If the source string is 'req', the built PDF has a rendering/encoding artifact; if the source literally reads 'r2K', it is an unexplained abbreviation in a row header.
issue.evidence: Row labels as rendered: 'Prefill capacity (hosts or cards), avg r2K tok/s' and 'Prefill capacity (hosts or cards), peak r2K tok/s'. Cell derivations use 92,000 tok/s (avg) and 368,000 tok/s (peak), consistent with Fig 12.1's '10 avg / 40 peak rps' and '9.2K-in'.
issue.acceptance_test: Row labels read 'required tok/s' (or state the requirement explicitly, e.g. 'avg req 92K tok/s' / 'peak req 368K tok/s'); the string 'r2K' does not appear in the built PDF; the label is unambiguous without reference to the cell contents.

issue.issue: The figure uses 'SLO' for two different things in adjacent boxes: the REQUIREMENTS box ends 'SLO = quality', while the CONSTRAINTS box begins 'SLO: throughput at target load'. The caption resolves the intent (throughput gate for a and b, quality gate for c), so the figure's own box 1 contradicts both box 2 and the caption. A reader who takes 'SLO = quality' as the canonical workload's SLO will misread the whole gate structure.
issue.evidence: Box 1: 'canonical workload ~2,000 users, 10 avg / 40 peak rps, 9.2K-in/300-out, SLO = quality'. Box 2: 'SLO: throughput at target load (10 avg / 40 peak rps, 9.2K-in/300-out)'. Caption: 'each must measure its gate (throughput for a,b; quality for c) at the target load (Chs. 14-17)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Box 1 states the workload's SLO in the same terms as box 2 (e.g. 'SLO: TTFT/TPOT at target load'), and the word 'quality' appears in the figure only where the quality gate (candidate c) is introduced; caption and boxes agree on which gate applies to which candidate.

issue.issue: The OUTCOME box reports a single host count for both throughput-gate candidates: '~5 avg / ~19 peak hosts'. Table 12-3 shows those numbers are the prefill pool only for candidate (b), which additionally requires a separate decode pool ('decode pool sized to 3K tok/s agg / 12K tok/s peak'). Read as applying to (a) and (b) alike, the figure understates (b)'s host requirement by the entire decode pool.
issue.evidence: Fig 12.1 outcome box: 'CAPACITY SCREEN: (a) - (b) pass / validation open until Chs. 14-17 / ~5 avg / ~19 peak hosts, headroom not demonstrated'. Table 12-3 (PDF 237 / printed 217): (a) '~5 hosts' avg, '~19 hosts' peak, 'Decode pool sizing: none - decode shares the host'; (b) 'prefill pool ~5 hosts' avg, 'prefill pool ~19 hosts, before headroom', 'decode pool sized to 3K tok/s agg / 12K tok/s peak'.
issue.acceptance_test: The outcome box either reports per-candidate host counts ('(a) ~5 avg / ~19 peak hosts; (b) ~5 prefill hosts avg / ~19 peak + decode pool') or explicitly labels the single number as the prefill-pool screen only, with a pointer to Table 12-3 for the decode pool.

issue.issue: The CONSTRAINTS box's second line, 'memory fit per host - quality gate', conflates a capacity constraint with a gate type. Memory fit is a capacity constraint (it is what the throughput/capacity screen checks), while the quality gate applies only to candidate (c) per the caption and the figure's own '? QUALITY GATE (c)' box. As written, the constraint list implies that memory fit is validated by a quality gate.
issue.evidence: Box 2: 'SLO: throughput at target load (10 avg / 40 peak rps, 9.2K-in/300-out) / memory fit per host - quality gate'. Box 4: 'OUTCOME - THROUGHPUT GATE ... ? QUALITY GATE (c): pending quality validation'.
issue.acceptance_test: Box 2 lists 'memory fit per host' as a capacity constraint without attaching 'quality gate' to it, and the quality gate appears in the figure only in the candidate-(c) outcome box; a reader can state which constraint each gate tests.

issue.issue: The 'DE-ESCALATE: privacy - sovereignty - cost' label is placed at the top of the figure, immediately to the right of the upward red escalation arrowhead, while de-escalation is represented by the separate downward blue dashed arrow on the far right. The label is therefore visually attached to the escalation arrow it does not describe, and a reader scanning the top of the figure can plausibly conclude that the top of the ladder is 'de-escalate' or that the red arrow is the de-escalation path.

Caption: 'Escalation (red) fires when demand, KV residency, or goodput outgrows a tier; de-escalation (blue) fires on privacy, sovereignty, and cost'.

issue.figure: FIGURE 15.2, panel (a) 'Caching removes prefill work' — in-plot note f(r)=(1-S+P)/S
issue.issue: The formula printed inside panel (a) does not reproduce the curve drawn in that panel, and the caption repeats the same formula. As rendered, the note reads f(r)=(1-S+P)/S with P=40% and S=60%. Substitution gives f(1) = (1-0.60+0.40)/0.60 = 0.80/0.60 = 1.333, i.e. 133 GFLOPs at r=1, whereas the drawn green curve starts at exactly 100 (the no-cache value) at r=1 and ends near 60-64 at r=10. The drawn series is reproduced by f(r) = S + P/r = 0.60 + 0.40/r (f(1)=1.00, f(2)=0.80, f(5)=0.68, f(10)=0.64), which is the only formula family consistent with the caption's own definitions ('P = 40% - the reusable prefix share of the prompt - and S = 60% - the unique suffix'). As printed, the note is wrong at every plotted point, and the caption's gloss 'the in-plot note's f(r)=(1-S+P)/S' propagates the error into the prose. (The exact glyphs must be confirmed against the figure source: if the source string contains an '/r' term, the same defect persists, because (1-S+P/r)/S = 1.333 at r=1.)
issue.evidence: Recomputation from the page's own stated inputs: P=0.40, S=0.60. Printed formula: f(1) = (1-0.6+0.4)/0.6 = 1.333 -> 133 GFLOPs; f(10) = (1-0.6+0.4)/0.6 = 1.333 (no r dependence at all as read). Drawn curve: f(1) = 1.00 (100 GFLOPs, coincident with the flat 'no cache' series), f(10) ~= 0.60-0.64. Candidate correct form S + P/r: f(1)=1.00, f(2)=0.80, f(3)=0.733, f(5)=0.68, f(8)=0.65, f(10)=0.64 - matching the drawn curve's steep initial drop and its flattening toward ~0.62. The caption's own definition of reuse ('mean number of requests served from each cached prefix block, so 1 = no sharing and hence no prefix reduction') also requires f(1)=1, which the printed formula violates.
issue.acceptance_test: Extract the exact note string from the figure source; recompute f(1), f(2), f(5), f(10) with P=0.40, S=0.60; confirm the plotted series equals the printed formula at all four points. If not, replace the note with f(r) = S + P/r (or (S*r + P)/r), update the caption gloss accordingly, and re-verify that the caption's '1 = no sharing and hence no prefix reduction' statement holds at r=1.

issue.figure: FIGURE 15.2, panel (a) y-axis label 'Prefill FLOPs / req (G)'
issue.issue: The left panel's y-axis is labeled in absolute units ('Prefill FLOPs / req (G)', 0-100) while the caption describes the same panel as 'prefill work vs average prefix reuse, as a percent of no-cache prefill work'. The two cannot both be true. As an absolute value the axis is also implausible: 100 GFLOPs of prefill per request corresponds to roughly 7 prompt tokens on a 7B model (2*N*T = 1.4e10*T) and to 0.7 tokens on a 70B model, so no realistic model/prompt pair yields a 100 GFLOPs prefill baseline. The plotted quantity is therefore a normalized ratio, and the axis label misrepresents it as an absolute cost. A reader who trusts the axis could conclude that prefill is trivially cheap and therefore never compute-bound - the exact misconception the surrounding chapter is trying to prevent.
issue.evidence: Caption text on the page: 'left: prefill work vs average prefix reuse, as a percent of no-cache prefill work, lower is better'. Axis text: 'Prefill FLOPs / req (G)' with the 'no cache' series flat at 100. Prefill FLOPs check: 2 * 7e9 * T = 100e9 -> T ~= 7.1 tokens; 2 * 70e9 * T = 100e9 -> T ~= 0.71 tokens. Both are far below any realistic prompt length, confirming the axis is normalized, not absolute. The '(G)' suffix is also ambiguous between 'giga' and 'GFLOP'.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel the axis 'Prefill work per request (% of no-cache)' (dropping '(G)'), or state the absolute baseline in the caption (e.g. 'no-cache prefill = X GFLOPs for the canonical model and prompt') and verify X against the book's canonical workload. Confirm the caption and axis then describe the same quantity.

issue.figure: FIGURE 15.2, caption clause 'caching raises decode goodput (right: decode goodput vs batch size, ...)'
issue.issue: The caption attributes the right-hand panel to caching, while the panel's own x-axis is 'Decode batch size' and the body text on the same page attributes it to batching: 'batching raises decode goodput (right plot) until bandwidth saturates, while prefix caching lowers the prefill work per repeated prompt (left plot)'. If the caption string is 'caching', the caption contradicts its own parenthetical, contradicts the prose, and teaches the reader that prefix caching raises decode goodput - a claim the figure cannot support and that the book's own lever separation (left = prefill phase, right = decode phase) is designed to prevent. The figure title ('Prefill caching vs batching: two independent effects') and the panel titles are consistent with the prose, so the caption is the odd element out.
issue.evidence: Caption: '...; caching raises decode goodput (right: decode goodput vs batch size, arbitrary goodput units, rising with diminishing gains as HBM bandwidth approaches saturation ...)'. Body text, same page: 'batching raises decode goodput (right plot) until bandwidth saturates, while prefix caching lowers the prefill work per repeated prompt (left plot)'. Panel (b) x-axis: 'Decode batch size'. No caching variable appears on the right panel's axes.
issue.acceptance_test: Grep the caption source for 'raises decode goodput' and confirm the grammatical subject is 'batching'. If it is 'caching', change it to 'batching' and re-verify that the caption's two-lever mapping (left = prefix caching, right = batching) matches both panel titles and the prose paragraph.

issue.figure: FIGURE 15.2, panel (a) title 'Caching removes prefill work'
issue.issue: The panel title asserts elimination, but the drawn curve has a nonzero floor: the green series asymptotes at roughly 60-64 GFLOPs, i.e. 36-40% of the no-cache prefill work survives even at r=10, because the unique suffix (S=60%) is never cached. The caption's own wording ('prefix caching cuts prefill work per repeated prompt') is the accurate one; the panel title overstates it.
issue.evidence: Drawn green series: f(10) ~= 0.60-0.64 of the no-cache value, consistent with the floor S = 0.60 imposed by the uncacheable suffix. Panel title: 'Caching removes prefill work'.
issue.acceptance_test: Retitle panel (a) to 'Prefix caching cuts prefill work' (or 'Caching removes the shared prefix's prefill work'); confirm the title asserts reduction, not elimination, and that it agrees with the caption's verb.

issue.figure: FIGURE 15.2, panel (b) y-axis label 'Relative decode goodput (a.u.)'
issue.issue: 'Relative' has no stated base and neither plausible base matches the drawn curve. If the series were normalized to batch size 1, the b=1 point would read 100; it reads about 5. If it were normalized to the peak, the b=10 point would read 100; it reads about 90. The caption supplies only 'arbitrary goodput units', so the axis mixes two conventions ('relative' and 'arbitrary') without defining either.
issue.evidence: Drawn series: b=1 -> ~5, b=10 -> ~90. Caption: 'arbitrary goodput units'. Axis: 'Relative decode goodput (a.u.)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Either drop 'Relative' ('Decode goodput (arbitrary units)') or state the base explicitly ('normalized to the b=10 point'); confirm the stated base reproduces the drawn endpoint values.

issue.figure: FIGURE 15.2, figure title 'Prefill caching vs batching: two independent effects'
issue.issue: The figure title introduces 'prefill caching', a third caching term, on a page whose caption and prose use 'prefix caching'. The book elsewhere treats prefix caching, prompt caching, and KV caching as distinct concepts with distinct scopes; adding 'prefill caching' in a prominent heading risks the reader treating it as a fourth mechanism or as a synonym for one of the existing three.
issue.evidence: Figure title: 'Prefill caching vs batching: two independent effects'. Caption on the same page: 'prefix caching cuts prefill work per repeated prompt'. Body text: 'prefix caching lowers the prefill work per repeated prompt (left plot)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Rename the figure title to 'Prefix caching vs batching: ...' (or 'Caching the prefill phase vs batching the decode phase'); grep the manuscript for remaining 'prefill caching' occurrences and confirm each is either defined or replaced.

issue.figure: FIGURE 15.2, panel (b) red annotation block and x-axis ticks
issue.issue: The red annotation ('diminishing gains / past ~b=6 (no hard / plateau); goodput units / still rise; tail / latency keeps rising') is the smallest glyph set in the figure, is set inside the plot area immediately to the left of the dashed b~6 line, and its lower lines sit at the same vertical band as the rising curve near b=5-7, so the reader must decode a six-line parenthetical in the tightest region of the panel. The x-axis carries only the labels 1 and 10, so the referenced b=6 cannot be located from ticks alone; the reader must infer it from the dashed line's position.
issue.evidence: Panel (b) x-axis labels: '1' and '10' only; annotation references '~b=6'; dashed vertical line drawn at approximately b=5-6 with no label; annotation's lower lines ('still rise; tail', 'latency keeps rising') occupy the y-band that the curve traverses between b=4 and b=7.
issue.acceptance_test: At 100% print size, confirm the annotation is at least 8 pt and does not touch the dashed line or the curve; add x-axis ticks at 2/4/6/8 or label the dashed line 'b=6'; consider moving the parenthetical into the caption, where the same content already appears.

issue.figure: FIGURE 15.2, figure title ('two independent effects') and the body paragraph immediately below the caption
issue.issue: The independence claim is stronger than the page's own reasoning supports. The figure title says 'two independent effects' and the body text says 'They are not competing on the same axis: the decode bottleneck is unaffected by caching.' But the same paragraph states that caching leaves 'more prefill-recompute headroom ... under the same host'. Under continuous batching, freed prefill headroom changes how many sequences can be resident, which changes the decode batch size - precisely the quantity on the right panel's x-axis. The levers act on different phases (which is the correct framing), but they are not independent and the decode bottleneck is indirectly affected.
issue.evidence: Body text on the page: 'batching raises decode goodput (right plot) until bandwidth saturates, while prefix caching lowers the prefill work per repeated prompt (left plot) so more prefill-recompute headroom remains under the same host. They are not competing on the same axis: the decode bottleneck is unaffected by caching.' Figure title: 'Prefill caching vs batching: two independent effects'.
issue.acceptance_test: Reword to something like 'the two levers act on different phases: caching changes prefill-phase cost and, indirectly, the concurrency available to the decode phase; batching changes the decode-phase batch size directly'; remove 'independent' from the figure title and confirm the revised claim is consistent with the continuous-batching discussion elsewhere in the chapter.

issue.figure: TCO break-even figure (referenced in prose as "the figure"; figure itself NOT on this page or p. 291 — see FIG-291-04)
issue.issue: The break-even arithmetic that defines the figure's break-even band is typeset with the wrong operator. As rendered, the clause reads "6,232,677.2 = 155,816.93 × 0.025" and "10,387,795.33 = 155,816.93 × 0.015". Multiplication gives 3,895.42 and 2,337.25, not the printed results. The printed results are exactly the QUOTIENTS (155,816.93 ÷ 0.025 = 6,232,677.2; 155,816.93 ÷ 0.015 = 10,387,795.33), i.e. break-even requests/month = monthly cost ÷ cost per request. The same operator appears in the 22-host clause ("6,510,426.6 = 162,760.59 × 0.025") and in the 70%×95% clause ("232,197.23 × 0.0208 = … 11.2M req/mo"). If the source glyph is actually "÷" and only the 150 dpi render is ambiguous, this is a false positive — but if the source says "×", the entire break-even derivation (the 6.2–10.4M band and the 7.5M canonical point that the figure plots) is arithmetically wrong as printed.
issue.evidence: Recomputed from the page's own inputs: 155,816.93 ÷ 0.025 = 6,232,677.2 (printed value matches to 7 s.f.); 155,816.93 ÷ 0.015 = 10,387,795.33 (matches); 155,816.93 ÷ 0.0208 = 7,491,198.56 (matches the printed canonical point); 162,760.59 ÷ 0.025 = 6,510,423.6 vs printed 6,510,426.6 (Δ = 3.0, i.e. 5e-5 relative — rounding of the unrounded monthly cost, not a finding); 162,760.59 ÷ 0.0208 = 7,825,028.4 (matches printed 7,825,028); 232,197.23 ÷ 0.0208 = 11,163,328 ≈ 11.2M (matches printed). Every printed RESULT is a quotient; no printed result is a product. Multiplication by the same factors yields values off by 1,600× and 4,444× respectively.
issue.acceptance_test: Open the source for printed p. 270 and confirm the glyph. If it is "×", replace with "÷" in all four instances (21-host low end, 21-host high end, 22-host low end, 70%×95% case) and re-verify that each printed result still equals cost ÷ price-per-request. Then confirm the figure's break-even band endpoints (6.2M and 10.4M) and its canonical-price marker (7.5M at $0.0208) are unchanged and still consistent with the corrected equations.

issue.issue: Two clauses in the same paragraph appear to have lost an operand at the 150 dpi render, leaving dangling fragments that make the derivation unreadable: (a) the 22-host clause renders as "6,510,426.6 = 162,760.59 × 0.025 = 0.015, canonical-price point 7,825,028 = 7.8M …" — the high-end product for the $0.015/request price is missing, so the reader sees "= 0.015" with nothing on its left; (b) the 70%×95% clause renders as "gives 232,197.23 × 0.0208 = 0.0208 = 11.2M req/mo", which contains a duplicated "= 0.0208" fragment. Either the source has dropped terms (a real defect) or the render has dropped them (a false positive). Either way the sentence as it currently reads cannot be followed.
issue.evidence: Expected values if the intended chain is complete: 22-host high end = 162,760.59 ÷ 0.015 = 10,850,706 (a plausible missing term); 70%×95% case = 232,197.23 ÷ 0.0208 = 11,163,328 = 11.2M (a plausible missing term). The printed "= 11.2M req/mo" is consistent with the quotient, not the product.
issue.acceptance_test: Read the source lines for printed p. 270 and confirm whether the terms 10,850,706 and 11,163,328 are present. If absent, restore them so that each clause reads as a complete chain (cost ÷ price = volume = rounded value). Re-render at 300 dpi and confirm no clause ends with a bare "= 0.015" or repeats "= 0.0208".

issue.figure: TCO feasible served-volume figure (the figure that "shades and labels" the infeasible region; not present on this page)
issue.issue: The feasible served-volume bound — the quantity that determines where the figure shades the infeasible region — is stated with a broken numeric chain, and the printed value is 1,000× too small. The sentence reads: "the fixed 21-host fleet is sized for the 40 rps peak over the canonical active window of 62,000 active seconds/month (6,240,000 requests × 10 rps), so the most it can serve is 40 × 62,000 = 2,560,000 = 24,960 requests/month. Everything to the right of 24,960 on the x-axis — the plot runs to 10^8 — is infeasible …". Three separate errors: (i) the active window is 62,000 s but the same page later calls it "the canonical 624,000-active-seconds … duty cycle", and 6,240,000 requests at 10 rps is 624,000 s, not 62,000 s; (ii) 40 × 62,000 = 2,480,000, not 2,560,000 — the printed chain does not even multiply out; (iii) the correct bound is 40 × 624,000 = 24,960,000 = 24.96M requests/month, so "24,960 requests/month" and "to the right of 24,960 on the x-axis" are both wrong by 10³. The parenthetical "(6,240,000 requests × 10 rps)" also has the wrong operator: requests ÷ rate = seconds. The paragraph's own logic confirms 24.96M is intended: it asserts the 6.2–10.4M break-even band and the canonical 6.24M both lie INSIDE the feasible region, which is only true if the bound is 2.496×10^7 (a bound of 2.496×10^4 or 2.56×10^6 would put the canonical volume outside the feasible region and contradict the paragraph).
issue.evidence: Recomputed: 6,240,000 ÷ 10 = 624,000 s (matches the page's own later "624,000-active-seconds"); 40 × 624,000 = 24,960,000 req/mo = 24.96M; 40 × 62,000 = 2,480,000 ≠ 2,560,000 (printed); 24,960,000 < 10^8 (plot range) and > 10.4M (break-even high end) — consistent with the shaded region starting at 2.496×10^7. Cross-check of the "24× shape" sentence: 40 rps × 2,592,000 s (30 days) = 103,680,000 ≈ 103.7M, which is the same construction with a full-month window, corroborating that the canonical window is 624,000 s and the bound is 24.96M.
issue.acceptance_test: Correct the chain to "40 × 624,000 = 24,960,000 = 24.96M requests/month" and change "to the right of 24,960 on the x-axis" to "to the right of 24.96M (2.5×10^7)"; change "(6,240,000 requests × 10 rps)" to "(6,240,000 requests ÷ 10 rps = 624,000 s)". Then open the figure and verify its shaded/labeled infeasible region begins at 2.496×10^7 on the x-axis, that the 6.2M–10.4M band and the 6.24M canonical marker fall to the LEFT of that boundary, and that the 10^8 axis limit is unchanged. If the figure was drawn from the printed (wrong) bound, redraw it — this is the single most consequential figure/prose mismatch in this batch.

issue.figure: TCO break-even / feasible-volume figure (referenced three times as "the figure")
issue.issue: The figure that carries the chapter's central visual argument is referenced only as "the figure" — three times across two pages — with no figure number, while the book's own convention elsewhere on the same page is numbered ("reported with Fig 16.1"). The reader on printed p. 270 is told "the figure marks the [ILLUSTRATIVE] price band" and "the figure shades and labels that region" before any figure is reachable, and neither p. 290 nor p. 291 contains a figure at all (both pages are text-only, including the §16.4 'Measurement' list). The references therefore point forward by at least one page to a figure the reader cannot locate by number.
issue.evidence: Rendered inspection of PDF pp. 290 and 291 at 150 dpi: no figure, no table, no graphic of any kind on either page; the only figure references present are the unnumbered "the figure" (printed p. 270, twice; printed p. 271, once) and "Fig 16.1" (printed pp. 270 and 271). The figure's own location was not verified in this batch.
issue.acceptance_test: Number the figure (e.g. Fig 17.x) and replace all three instances of "the figure" with that number. Confirm the figure falls on the same page as its first reference or immediately after it, and that the caption states what the reader should learn (break-even band as a region; feasible-volume ceiling; shaded infeasible region) rather than merely naming the diagram.

issue.issue: The range is printed as "(here −6.2–10.4M req/mo)" with a leading dash glyph that reads as a minus sign, i.e. as a negative lower bound. The same range is written correctly elsewhere on the page as "the same 6.2–10.4M band". A reader scanning the figure's axis labels (which presumably show 6.2M and 10.4M) could reasonably mis-read the prose as describing a negative volume.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 270: "the honest output is a range (here −6.2–10.4M req/mo) rather than a single 'the break-even is 7.5M' claim"; three lines later: "the same 6.2–10.4M band reported with Fig 16.1". The two forms are inconsistent within one paragraph.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite as "(here 6.2–10.4M req/mo)" or "(here 6.2M to 10.4M req/mo)" so no glyph precedes the lower bound; confirm the figure's axis labels use the same 6.2M/10.4M endpoints.

issue.figure: TCO feasible served-volume figure (the figure that shades the infeasible region)
issue.issue: The 24×-shape envelope is printed as "40 rps × 2,592,000 s × 103/M req/mo", which chains two multiplications and then a malformed unit ("103/M"). The third operator should be "=" and the value should be 103.7M (or 103M), not "103/M". This is the sentence that tells the reader where the figure's x-axis limit comes from, so its garbling is visible against the plotted 10^8 axis.
issue.evidence: Recomputed: 40 × 2,592,000 = 103,680,000 = 103.68M ≈ 103.7M; 2,592,000 s = 30 days × 86,400 s (the full-month window implied by "24× shape", i.e. 24 h/day vs the canonical 624,000 s duty cycle). The printed "103/M" is not a valid unit.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite as "40 rps × 2,592,000 s = 103.7M req/mo" and confirm the figure's x-axis maximum (10^8) and any annotation of the 24× envelope agree with 103.7M.

issue.figure: n/a — §16.4 'Measurement' list (prose adjacent to the TCO figure discussion)
issue.issue: Item 2 of the Measurement list renders as a run-on with a missing clause: "Raw utilization = served ÷ provisioned; effective utilization = SLO-meeting goodput ÷ theoretical capacity = cost per useful request uses the effective definition." The "=" before "cost per useful request" is not a valid operator and the sentence appears to have lost a sentence break (and possibly the word "Cost"). This is the definition of the metric that the figure's y-axis/break-even logic depends on, so a garbled definition here undermines the figure's caption.
issue.evidence: Rendered text on printed p. 271, §16.4, numbered item 2. The intended reading is almost certainly two sentences: "Raw utilization = served ÷ provisioned; effective utilization = SLO-meeting goodput ÷ theoretical capacity. Cost per useful request uses the effective definition." The 150 dpi render may have dropped a period and a capital, so this must be checked in the source before editing.
issue.acceptance_test: Read the source for §16.4 item 2 and confirm the sentence break and the leading "Cost" are present; re-render and confirm the item reads as two well-formed sentences with no stray "=".

issue.figure: TCO feasible served-volume figure (the figure that shades the infeasible region)
issue.issue: The phrase "the canonical 624,000-active-seconds/simo duty cycle" contains what appears to be a typo ("simo" for "same"). This is the same quantity that FIG-291-03 shows to be mis-stated as 62,000 s two paragraphs earlier, so the two occurrences of the duty-cycle figure must be made identical and correctly spelled; a reader comparing them will otherwise be unsure whether the book intends two different duty cycles.
issue.evidence: Printed p. 271: "the canonical 624,000-active-seconds/simo duty cycle"; printed p. 271 three lines earlier: "the canonical active window of 62,000 active seconds/month". The two values differ by 10× and the second is the one contradicted by the arithmetic (see FIG-291-03).
issue.acceptance_test: Correct "simo" to "same" (or to the book's defined term, if one exists) and confirm that every occurrence of the canonical active window on pp. 270–271 reads 624,000 s.

issue.issue: The figure caption's parenthetical for the managed-API cost at the canonical volume is numerically inconsistent with the figure's own price and geometry. The caption states "$20.80 per 1,000 requests (~$5,816.93/mo at 6.24M req/mo)". At $20.80 per 1,000 requests, 6.24M requests/month = 6,240 x $20.80 = $129,792/mo, not $5,816.93/mo (a factor of ~22.3). The figure's own geometry requires managed(6.24M) = $129.8K, because the caption's own takeaway ("at 6.24M req/mo self-host sits above the API") and the plotted crossing (self-host $155.8K horizontal line crossed by the managed line at 7.5M) both require managed(6.24M) = 155,800/7.49M x 6.24M = $129.8K. The $5,816.93 figure appears to be a stale value from an earlier price/volume basis.
issue.evidence: Recomputed: 6,240 units x $20.80 = $129,792. Cross-check via the plotted break-even: $155,800 / $0.0208 per request = 7,490,385 requests/mo = 7.5M (matches the figure's 'break-even = 7.5M' annotation), and $0.0208 x 6.24M = $129,792 (matches the blue-line crossing geometry). $5,816.93 corresponds to $0.9322 per 1,000 requests, i.e. a price 22.3x lower than the stated $20.80; it reconciles with no other series in the figure (self-host $155.8K, cloud $87.6K).
issue.acceptance_test: Replace the parenthetical with the derived value (~$129,792/mo, or '~$129.8K/mo') and confirm by recomputation that 6,240 x $20.80 = $129,792; confirm no other occurrence of '5,816.93' remains in Ch. 16 or its notes; confirm the caption's 'self-host sits above the API' claim still holds (155.8K > 129.8K).

issue.issue: The x-axis label "Requests/month (log) - duration varied at FIXED 40 rps peak, FIXED 21-host fleet" is not reconcilable with the two annotated x-values without an unstated assumption, and the two available readings give materially different meanings to the same axis. Reading A (axis label): x = 40 rps x duration, so the canonical point 6.24M req/mo is a 156,000-second (43-hour) burst at peak, and 'feasible max 24.96M' is 624,000 s of sustained peak. Reading B (Note 16.1.1, which calls 624,000 s the 'canonical active s'): the canonical month has 624,000 active seconds and the canonical load is 6.24M/624,000 = 10 rps average (25% of the 40 rps peak), with 24.96M = 40 rps sustained over the whole active window. The figure asserts Reading A in the axis label while its annotations and the note only make sense under Reading B. A reader cannot tell whether the canonical point is a sustained 10-rps load or a 43-hour peak burst, which changes what the break-even and the feasible-max boundary mean.
issue.evidence: 6,240,000 / 624,000 s = 10.0 rps exactly; 40 x 624,000 = 24,960,000 = the 'feasible max 24.96M' annotation; 6,240,000 / 40 rps = 156,000 s. Note 16.1.1 (PDF p. 294) reads '40 rps x 624,000 canonical active s x 24.96M req/mo', i.e. it treats 624,000 s as the canonical active window, which is Reading B.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite the x-axis label to state the basis explicitly, e.g. 'Requests per canonical month (624,000 active s/mo); canonical load 10 rps avg; fleet peak 40 rps', and add the canonical average rate (10 rps) to the 'canonical 6.24M req/mo' annotation. Verify that the label, the canonical annotation, the feasible-max annotation, and Note 16.1.1 all express the same reading.

issue.issue: Two legend entries describe features that are not drawn. 'break-even = 7.5M' and 'sensitivity = 6.2-10.4M (a region, not a point)' are given line-style swatches (red dashed) that are visually identical to the 'managed $20.80/1K' swatch, but the plot contains no marker at the 7.5M crossing and no shaded vertical band spanning 6.2M-10.4M. The legend therefore promises a region and a point that the reader cannot locate, and the annotation text 'sensitivity = 6.2-10.4M (a region, not a point)' explicitly asserts a region that does not appear in the figure. This is the figure's central sensitivity result (the break-even is a range, not a point) and it is the element most in need of visual encoding.
issue.evidence: Rendered page inspection: the only red dashed line in the plot area is the managed-API centerline inside the hatched price band; no vertical band is visible between 6.2M and 10.4M; no cross or dot is visible at the blue/red crossing near 7.5M. Legend swatches for entries 4, 5 and 6 are all red dashed segments, so entries 5 and 6 are indistinguishable from entry 4 even in color.
issue.acceptance_test: Draw the 6.2M-10.4M sensitivity interval as a distinct vertical band (or hatched column) on the x-axis with its own legend swatch, and mark the 7.5M break-even with a distinct marker on the crossing. Confirm that each legend swatch maps to exactly one visible plotted element and that no two legend entries share an identical swatch.

issue.issue: The infeasible region is shaded across the full plot width to the right of 24.96M, including the region occupied by the managed-API line, and is labelled only 'INFEASIBLE (> 24.96M)'. The 24.96M bound is a property of the self-host fleet's own capacity (40 rps x 624,000 s), not of the managed API, which has no such bound in this analysis. A reader can reasonably infer that the managed API is also infeasible beyond 24.96M req/mo, or that the managed line is invalid there. The caption does not qualify the shading.
issue.evidence: Note 16.1.1 (PDF p. 294) derives the bound from the self-host fleet: 'The feasible served-volume bound (40 rps x 624,000 canonical active s ...) and the shaded infeasible region right of it are derived in the Feasible served-volume bound paragraph'. The managed API is described in the same note as a zero-intercept linear function of served volume with no capacity ceiling.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel the region to name the binding constraint, e.g. 'self-host fleet infeasible beyond 24.96M req/mo (40 rps peak)', and/or restrict the shading to the self-host series' domain. Confirm the caption or note states that the bound applies to the self-host fleet only.

issue.issue: The caption is overloaded and partly ungrammatical. It runs to roughly 230 words and simultaneously carries (a) the takeaway, (b) the cloud-marker caveat, (c) a 'Geometry/source' provenance clause, (d) a derivation pointer, and (e) a two-sentence availability/scope caveat that belongs in Note 16.1.1. The availability clause also contains a broken sentence: 'the canonical workload is own 99.97% multi-region active-active SLA (Ch 4) is UNTESTED and NOT PROVED here' (two copulas, missing possessive). A reader who reads only the caption gets a dense, partly unparsable block; a reader who reads only the figure gets none of the caveats.
issue.evidence: Rendered page inspection of the caption block under Figure 16.1; the sentence 'every line is a single-region cost - the canonical workload is own 99.97% multi-region active-active SLA (Ch 4) is UNTESTED and NOT PROVED here; failover is N-1 single-host only with no region-failure test, and the three modes are not compared on matched availability/SLO/warm-capacity assumptions (Table 16-1, Sec 16.3).'
issue.acceptance_test: Reduce the caption to at most three sentences (takeaway + one scope qualifier + pointer to Note 16.1.1), move the availability/scope caveat into Note 16.1.1, and repair the broken clause to 'the canonical workload's own 99.97% multi-region active-active SLA (Ch 4) is UNTESTED and NOT PROVED here'. Confirm the caption still contains the 'not apples-to-apples' warning and the pointer to the note.

issue.figure: Figure 16.1 (legend text and in-plot annotation boxes)
issue.issue: The legend text and the four in-plot annotation boxes appear to be set below the 8 pt print floor for figure in-text annotations. At the 150 dpi rendering the legend glyphs are roughly half the height of the body text on the same page, which corresponds to approximately 6-7 pt at US Letter. The legend carries the figure's key numeric results ($155.8K/mo, $87.6K/mo, $20.80/1K, 7.5M, 6.2-10.4M) and the annotation boxes carry the caveats, so legibility is load-bearing here, not decorative.
issue.evidence: Rendered page inspection at 150 dpi: legend text height is visibly ~55-60% of the 10.5 pt body text height on the same page; the same ratio holds for the 'break-even = 7.5M', 'sensitivity = 6.2-10.4M', 'canonical 6.24M req/mo' and 'cloud $87.6K/mo' boxes. This is an estimate from the rendering, not a measurement of the source font size.

Re-render at 150 dpi and confirm the legend is readable at 100% print size without magnification.

issue.issue: Grayscale distinguishability is weak in two places. (a) The managed-API centerline ($20.80/1K) is a red dashed line drawn inside the red hatched price band; in grayscale both collapse to similar mid-gray and the centerline is difficult to separate from the band texture. The legend also uses red for three different entries (price band, managed line, break-even, sensitivity), so color alone is currently carrying distinctions that texture should carry.
issue.evidence: Rendered page inspection; the figure's own caption states 'Geometry/source: log-cost/month vs requests/month' and the legend distinguishes series primarily by hue (red/blue/green).
issue.acceptance_test: Convert the figure to grayscale and confirm that (i) the managed centerline is distinguishable from the price band, (ii) the infeasible region is distinguishable from the price band, and (iii) every legend entry maps to a uniquely identifiable plotted element. If not, differentiate by texture/dash pattern/line weight rather than hue.

issue.issue: The x-axis spans 1e4 to 1e8 requests/month, but the entire decision-relevant region (canonical 6.24M, sensitivity 6.2-10.4M, break-even 7.5M, feasible max 24.96M) occupies roughly the rightmost 20% of the axis, while the two leftmost decades are empty of any annotation or comparison. The reader must scan a mostly empty plot to find the crossing, and the 6.2M-10.4M sensitivity interval (a factor of 1.7) is compressed into a sliver.

issue.acceptance_test: Tighten the x-limits (e.g. 3e6 to 1e8) or add an inset/zoom panel over 5M-30M, and confirm that the canonical point, the sensitivity band, the break-even marker and the feasible-max line are all visually separated and legible.

issue.issue: The four annotation boxes are clustered in the upper-left of the plot, far from the features they describe, and none has a leader line. 'break-even = 7.5M' sits roughly three decades to the left of the actual crossing it names; 'canonical 6.24M req/mo' and 'cloud $87.6K/mo (occupancy input) priced at 6.24M req/mo only' sit above and left of the green diamond. The reader must map text to features by value-matching rather than by spatial proximity, which is the slowest and least reliable reading mode for a diagram.
issue.evidence: Rendered page inspection: the annotation block occupies the region x ~ 1e4-1e6, y ~ 1e5-1e6, while the crossing is at x ~ 7.5M and the diamond at x = 6.24M, y = 8.76e4.
issue.acceptance_test: Reposition each annotation adjacent to its feature (or add leader lines), and confirm that each annotation can be associated with its target without reading the numeric values.

issue.issue: The 'feasible max 24.96M' label states a result without its derivation, and the derivation (40 rps x 624,000 active s/mo) appears nowhere on the figure. The reader cannot check the bound from the figure, and the number's relation to the x-axis label ('duration varied at FIXED 40 rps peak') is exactly the ambiguity flagged in FIG-16.1-02. The 'canonical 6.24M req/mo' annotation likewise omits the corresponding 10 rps average rate.

issue.acceptance_test: Add the derivation to the label or the annotation, e.g. 'feasible max 24.96M req/mo (40 rps x 624,000 active s/mo)', and 'canonical 6.24M req/mo (10 rps avg)'. Confirm the arithmetic 40 x 624,000 = 24,960,000 and 6,240,000/624,000 = 10 rps.

issue.issue: The legend entry 'price band $15-25/1K' does not say whose price band it is. In a figure that also contains a self-host cost line, a cloud cost marker, and a managed-API line, an unqualified 'price band' is ambiguous: it is the managed-API price band (the sensitivity range 6.2M-10.4M derives from it), not a band of self-host cost. The reader could plausibly read it as a band of self-host TCO.
issue.evidence: Rendered page inspection of the legend; the caption and Note 16.1.1 both attribute the $15-25/1K range to the managed API price sensitivity ('Sensitivity: a $15-25/1K price band moves the break-even to ~6.2-10.4M req/mo').
issue.acceptance_test: Rename the legend entry to 'managed API price band $15-25/1K' and confirm no other series in the figure is described as a price band.

issue.figure: Note 16.1.1 (the note that defines Figure 16.1's series and bounds)
issue.issue: Note 16.1.1 contains two garbled constructions that directly define Figure 16.1 and would mislead a reader auditing the figure. (a) 'The feasible served-volume bound (40 rps x 624,000 canonical active s x 24.96M req/mo)' uses a multiplication sign where an equality is meant; read literally it asserts that the bound is the product of 40 rps, 624,000 s and 24.96M requests, which is off by a factor of 24.96M. (b) 'the case (0) /KV-screen line = the case (i) 12-host line, $162,760.59/mo, is priced in Sec 16.3 but not plotted' asserts an identity between case (0) (the plotted $155.8K/mo 21-host line) and case (i) (a 12-host line at $162,760.59/mo that is explicitly not plotted); the two cannot both be true, and the sentence's scope is ambiguous as to which line is flat and which is unplotted. A third fragment, 'for the 21-host peak KV-screen fleet = zero spare', leaves '= zero spare' dangling.
issue.evidence: Rendered page inspection of Note 16.1.1 on PDF p. 294; the figure's own legend and caption identify the plotted self-host series as '$155.8K/mo (21 hosts)' and the caption calls it 'case 0', while the note assigns $162,760.59/mo to case (i) and says it is not plotted.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite (a) as '40 rps x 624,000 canonical active s = 24.96M req/mo' and (b) as 'the case (0) /KV-screen line (plotted, $155.8K/mo) - the case (i) 12-host line, $162,760.59/mo, is priced in Sec 16.3 but not plotted - is flat because the fleet is paid regardless of volume'. Confirm that exactly one self-host series is plotted and that its value ($155.8K/mo) matches the legend and caption.

issue.issue: Case labels drift between the caption and the note: the caption writes 'case 0' (arabic, no parentheses) while the note writes 'case (0)' and 'case (i)' (roman numeral in parentheses). The reader cannot tell whether 'case 0' and 'case (i)' are the same enumeration scheme, and the caption's parenthetical '($155.8K/mo, case 0) /KV-screen sensitivity line' uses a slash as an undeclared separator in a way that reads as a typo.
issue.evidence: Rendered page inspection: caption on PDF p. 298 reads 'case 0'; Note 16.1.1 on PDF p. 294 reads 'case (0)' and 'case (i)'. The slash separator appears in both places ('case (0) /KV-screen line').
issue.acceptance_test: Adopt one enumeration convention (e.g. 'case 0', 'case 1') and use it in the caption, the note, Table 16-1 and Sec 16.3; replace the slash separator with a dash or parentheses. Confirm no remaining 'case (i)' / 'case (0)' forms.

issue.figure: FIGURE 19.1 — The agent loop: a four-state machine

Worked Example', same truncated sentence ending '...§4's illustrative distribution'. The figure therefore carries the number FIGURE 19.1 twice in the book, three printed pages apart.

Caveat: real systems add guardrails, compaction and fallbacks not shown here; the 9,200-token prompt at 2.62 MB/token KV (FP16) and the counterfactual completion semantics are quantified in Fig 19.2.' issue.issue: The lead-in sentence promises five metrics; the table as rendered shows four. 'To validate fleet-level optimization claims, five core metrics should be measured at regular intervals:' is followed by a table with exactly four rows (Aggregate rps; Scheduler-added p99 latency; Scheduler-added median latency; Scheduling overhead). The page ends with substantial white space below the last row, which is consistent with the table terminating here rather than continuing.

Verify by rendering printed pages 350-351 together and counting rows.

issue.issue: The in-figure operator contradicts the caption. The green bar is labelled '>=24.9 GB' (a lower bound) while the caption states compaction 'bounds the footprint across turns at roughly the single-shot level — about 24.9 GB, 27% below the append-only case'. If the value is only known to be >=24.9 GB, it could equal 34.0 GB and the '27% below the append-only case' claim is not established. The bar is also drawn with its right edge exactly at 24.9, so the encoding presents 24.9 as the value while the label presents it as a minimum. The reader cannot tell whether the bar length is the quantity or its floor.
issue.evidence: Figure label: '>=24.9 GB' (green, right of the bar end). Caption: 'compaction (summarize or truncate the accumulated history each turn) bounds the footprint across turns at roughly the single-shot level — about 24.9 GB, 27% below the append-only case'. Independently: 24.9/34.0 = 0.732, i.e. 26.8% below, so the 27% figure is only valid if compaction is approximately 24.9 GB, not merely at least 24.9 GB.
issue.acceptance_test: Make the operator and the encoding agree. Preferred: label the bar '~24.9 GB (bound)' and change the caption to 'bounds the footprint at roughly the single-shot level — about 24.9 GB, i.e. at most ~27% below the append-only case'. If the intent is genuinely a lower bound, label the bar '>=24.9 GB' AND draw it as an open-ended bound (arrow or hatched extension) AND rewrite the caption to remove the '27% below' claim. Verify that no reader can derive '27% below' from a value the figure only bounds from below.

issue.issue: The figure's title promises 'three different things' but the encoding shows one quantity three times, twice identically. All three bars are plotted on a single magnitude axis ('FP16 KV per request (GB)'), and the prefix-cache-eviction bar is drawn to exactly the same length as the append-only bar (34.0 GB). The three things the policies actually move are different quantities — request KV, cached-prefix footprint, and re-prefill cost — and only the first is on the axis. A reader who glances at the chart (or reads only the bar labels) will conclude 'prefix-cache eviction does nothing', which is the opposite of the caption's point that it 'freed cached prefix memory and cost[ing] a re-prefill'.
issue.evidence: Bars: Append-only 34.0 GB (red, dotted); Compaction >=24.9 GB (green, diagonal); Prefix-cache eviction '34.0 GB unchanged' (blue, cross-hatch). Caption: 'prefix-cache eviction leaves the request's own context and KV unchanged (still 34.0 GB) while freeing cached prefix memory and costing a re-prefill.' The in-figure annotation 'evicts the reusable prefix — moves cache/re-prefill' carries the real message in 7-8 pt gray text, below the visual weight of the bars.
issue.acceptance_test: Restructure so the encoding carries the claim: either (a) replace the single-axis bar chart with a small 3-row x 3-column matrix (policy x {request KV, cached-prefix KV, re-prefill tokens}) in which the prefix-cache row differs visibly, or (b) keep the bars but add a second, visually distinct element for the prefix-cache policy showing the re-prefill cost (e.g. a hatched 're-prefill' segment or a callout with the re-prefilled token count), and change the title to match what is plotted. Acceptance: a reader who sees only the figure (no caption) should be able to state that the three policies differ in three different ways.

issue.page: PDF 354 / printed 334 (also PDF 357 / printed 337); legend counterpart on PDF 356 / printed 336
issue.figure: FIGURE 19.3 formula block and FIGURE 19.2 legend — symbol for the 800-token retrieved count
issue.issue: The symbol used for the retrieved-token count is not legible and may be a digit. The formula reads 'append-only total = I0 + T*6 + T*Y + O_final' with the gloss '(I0 = 9.2K input, 6 = 800 retrieved, Y = 65 generated, O_final = 300 output (once))'; the FIGURE 19.2 legend uses the same token, 'retrieved (6=800)'. At 150 dpi the glyph reads as the digit 6. If a reader takes it literally as the number six, the term becomes T*6 = 24 instead of T*800 = 3,200 — a 133x error in the very quantity the figure exists to quantify. If the intended symbol is a letter (R, Q, S, B), it must be legible at print size.
issue.evidence: Rendered formula block: 'append-only total = I0 + T*6 + T*Y + O_final, T = 4 turns @ 2.62 MB/token (I0 = 9.2K input, 6 = 800 retrieved, Y = 65 generated, O_final = 300 output (once))'. FIGURE 19.2 legend: 'retrieved (6=800)'. Note the sibling symbols I0, Y, O are unambiguous, so the ambiguity is specific to this one glyph.
issue.acceptance_test: Inspect the source glyph at 400% zoom in the final PDF and confirm it is a letter, not the digit 6. If it is a digit, replace it with a letter (e.g. R for retrieved) consistently in the FIGURE 19.2 legend, the FIGURE 19.3 formula block, and the FIGURE 19.3 caption/notes, and re-verify that I0 + T*R + T*Y + O_final = 9,200 + 3,200 + 260 + 300 = 12,960 tokens = 34.0 GB. Acceptance: no reader can read the term as the integer six.

issue.issue: Several in-figure text elements appear to fall below the 8 pt print floor for figure annotations: the subtitle ('canonical 2.62 MB/token; append-only and single-shot values are derived, the compaction and prefix-cache policy bars are illustrative'), the three per-bar annotations ('[DERIVED] bounding case — nothing evicted; bounds system tolerance', '[ILLUSTRATIVE] summarize/truncate each turn — moves the footprint', '[ILLUSTRATIVE] evicts the reusable prefix — moves cache/re-prefill'), the note block ('counterfactual: each bar = a separate completed request after 4 turns...'), and the formula block. These carry the figure's evidence labels ([DERIVED] / [ILLUSTRATIVE]) and its arithmetic, so they are load-bearing, not decorative.
issue.evidence: At 150 dpi the annotation lines are visibly smaller than the caption body text immediately below the figure and are rendered in light gray, further reducing effective contrast. The [DERIVED]/[ILLUSTRATIVE] labels are the book's own evidence-label vocabulary (Ch 4 / Appendix A) and must be readable to do their job.
issue.acceptance_test: Measure the rendered cap-height of the smallest in-figure annotation in the final PDF at 100% zoom; confirm >= 8 pt (and >= 4.5:1 contrast against the plot background). If below, raise the annotation font size and/or darken the gray to near-black, and re-check that the widened annotations still fit inside the plot frame without colliding with the bars or the axis.

issue.figure: FIGURE 19.2 — five-line note block below the panels

If it must remain small, promote the two most load-bearing caveats (counterfactual-not-trajectory; retained-vs-processed tokens) into the figure subtitle or the caption, where they are set at body size.

issue.figure: FIGURE 19.1 — key line and box sub-labels
issue.issue: The key line ('fill key: pale blue = continuing states (top row); amber = terminal outcomes (bottom row)') and the italic role tags inside the state boxes ('model', 'action', 'state', 'check') are set small and light. issue.figure: FIGURE 19.2 — title and x-axis invite the wrong reading
issue.issue: The figure title ('Token growth vs resulting KV growth across agent turns') and the panel (a) x-axis ('Agent turns' with categories '(single-shot)', 1, 2, 3, 4) read as the trajectory of one live agent over four turns. The figure's actual semantics are four separate counterfactual requests, each completed after N turns. The counterfactual framing appears only in the caption ('each column is a counterfactual completion') and in the small note ('not successive states of one live agent'), i.e. below the visual weight of the axis label. The x-axis also mixes a baseline category ('(single-shot)') with a numeric variable (turn count) on one scale.

issue.acceptance_test: Rename the x-axis to something like 'counterfactual request completed after N turns' (with the '(single-shot)' baseline relabelled '0 turns (single-shot)'), and/or add '(counterfactual)' to the figure title. Acceptance: the axis label alone, without the caption, must not permit the reading 'one agent's KV grew from 24.9 to 34.0 GB'.

The subject is singular ('a production stack') but the verb is plural ('pay for themselves'), and the three-way list ('a production stack that can hold this flat', 'prefix-caching', 'FP8 KV') mixes a noun phrase with two gerunds.
issue.evidence: Rendered caption on PDF 356: 'Caveat: a production stack that can hold this flat, prefix-caching, or FP8 KV pay for themselves on agentic workloads.'
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite as, e.g., 'Caveat: on agentic workloads, a production stack that can hold the footprint flat, prefix caching, or FP8 KV pays for itself.' Acceptance: subject and verb agree and each list item is a noun phrase.

issue.figure: FIGURE 19.2 — caption mixes units within one sentence

The token endpoints (9,500 and 12,960) are the quantities panel (a) actually plots and are never stated, so the reader cannot check panel (a) against the caption, and the sentence's subject list ('tokens and FP16 KV cache') is followed by a single pair of GB values.

issue.issue: The note line 'tokens per submitted request grow ~2.5x under no prefix reuse (inv. 68/25/52%, Table 19-1: 2.52x)' contains an unexplained shorthand ('inv.') and three unexplained percentages. Nothing on this page lets a reader decode them, and the 2.52x figure is not derivable from anything plotted here (the bars show retained context growing 12,960/9,500 = 1.36x). The note correctly distinguishes retained from processed tokens, but the number it introduces cannot be checked by the reader.

issue.figure: FIGURE 19.2 panel (a) — floating annotation 'generated Y = 65/token output O = 300'
issue.issue: An orange annotation floats in the upper-left of panel (a) with no leader line and no anchor to any bar segment. It reads like a data label for the tallest bar rather than a legend restatement, and the slash in '65/token' can be misread as '65 per token'. It also duplicates information already in the legend ('generated (Y=65)', 'output (O=300)').
issue.evidence: Rendered panel (a): orange text 'generated Y = 65/token output O = 300' positioned above the bars, left of centre, with no connector; the legend below already carries 'generated (Y=65)' and 'output (O=300)'.

issue.figure: FIGURE 19.1 — 'Decide' state conflates model judgment with the budget check
issue.issue: The caption's central correction is 'a turn/token budget check — not the model's judgment — ends the loop at the limit', but the figure encodes the opposite emphasis: the 'Decide' box carries the italic role tag 'check' (styled identically to the model-driven 'model' tag) and the prompt 'resolved?', and the exit to 'Stopped' is a plain arrow labelled 'limit hit' leaving that same box. The figure therefore shows the limit check as an outcome of the model's decision state. The key line ('no resolution within the turn limit -> stopped') does encode the budget check, but at the smallest type on the page.
issue.evidence: Figure: 'Decide / check / resolved?' with a downward arrow labelled 'limit hit' to 'Stopped / limit / terminal'. Caption: 'a turn/token budget check — not the model's judgment — ends the loop at the limit.'
issue.acceptance_test: Make the budget check a distinct element: either add a separate 'Budget check' node on the exit path (with the 'limit hit' arrow originating there), or relabel the exit arrow 'turn/token budget exhausted (scheduler-side, not model judgment)'. Acceptance: the figure alone must not imply that the model chooses to stop at the limit.

issue.figure: FIGURE 19.2 vs FIGURE 19.3 — cross-figure colour/hatch semantics
issue.issue: The colour+hatch vocabulary is not consistent across two figures two pages apart. In FIGURE 19.2 panel (a): blue diagonal = 'initial context (I0 = 9,200)', green dotted = 'retrieved (6=800)', orange hatch = 'generated (Y=65)', dark green solid = 'output (O=300)'. In FIGURE 19.3: red dotted = 'Append-only', green diagonal = 'Compaction', blue cross-hatch = 'Prefix-cache eviction'. So blue denotes 'initial context' in one figure and 'prefix-cache eviction' in the other, and green denotes 'retrieved' in one and 'compaction' in the other. Red dotted means 'KV/request quantity' in FIGURE 19.2(b) and 'append-only policy' in FIGURE 19.3. The figures are individually defensible (each is directly labelled, and hatch patterns survive grayscale), but the book does not hold one visual language for 'policy' versus 'quantity'.
issue.evidence: FIGURE 19.2 legend swatches: blue diagonal, green dotted, orange hatched, dark green solid. FIGURE 19.3 bars: red dotted, green diagonal, blue cross-hatch. No legend or note in either figure states that the two figures share a colour vocabulary.
issue.acceptance_test: Establish and apply one rule across Ch 19 figures — e.g. reserve a single hue family for policies (FIGURE 19.3) and a different family for token categories (FIGURE 19.2) — or add a one-line note that colours are local to each figure. Acceptance: no colour+hatch pair denotes different concepts in two figures of the same chapter.

issue.issue: The figure subtitle uses the book's evidence vocabulary ('the compaction and prefix-cache policy bars are illustrative') while the caption uses a different word for the same status ('the other two bars are qualitative'). 'Qualitative' is not one of the book's defined label sets ([CANONICAL] [DERIVED] [ILLUSTRATIVE] [ASSUMPTION] [1P] [HYPOTHESIS], plus the Ch 4 three-axis taxonomy), so the same two bars carry two different status words in the same figure.
issue.evidence: Subtitle: 'canonical 2.62 MB/token; append-only and single-shot values are derived, the compaction and prefix-cache policy bars are illustrative'. Caption: 'Caveat: only the append-only case is priced in this book — the other two bars are qualitative.'
issue.acceptance_test: Use 'illustrative' in both places (or 'qualitative' in both), matching the defined vocabulary in Ch 4 / Appendix A. Acceptance: one status word per bar set across subtitle, in-figure annotations, and caption.

issue.issue: The blue bar's value label '34.0 GB unchanged' is the longest label in the figure and is placed immediately to the right of a bar that ends at 34.0 on an axis whose last tick is 40. The remaining axis space is small relative to the label width, so the label runs to the right edge of the plot frame and risks crowding or colliding with the figure margin in the final trim.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 354: the blue label extends to approximately the horizontal position of the '40' tick label, with essentially no clearance to the plot frame's right edge; the red '34.0 GB' label on the identical bar end has ample clearance because it is shorter.
issue.acceptance_test: Inspect the final PDF at 100% zoom for margin clearance and for any overlap with the plot frame or the '40' tick label. If clearance is under ~2 mm, shorten to '34.0 GB (unchanged)' on two lines, move the label inside the bar, or extend the axis to 45 GB.

issue.figure: Table 20-1 — 'Aggregate rps' target and undefined 'per-query time'
issue.issue: Two definitional weaknesses. (a) 'Aggregate rps' is defined as an observed quantity ('Total queries processed per second across all hosts') but its Target is a provisioning requirement ('>= 2x peak rps for comfort margin'), so the row mixes a measurement with a capacity decision; a reader could read it as a measured condition that the fleet must satisfy. (b) 'Scheduling overhead' is defined as 'Fraction of per-query time spent in dispatcher, not compute' with target '< 5%', but 'per-query time' is undefined (end-to-end? service time? queueing-inclusive?), and the two scheduler rows bind very differently: at the canonical 8.6 s service time, 5% is ~430 ms, far looser than the '< 100 ms' p99 row, so the table does not tell the reader which constraint governs.
issue.evidence: Rendered table rows: 'Aggregate rps | Total queries processed per second across all hosts | >= 2x peak rps for comfort margin (stress/soak target — see note)'; 'Scheduling overhead | Fraction of per-query time spent in dispatcher, not compute | < 5%'; 'Scheduler-added p99 latency | 99th-percentile time a request waits in the fleet dispatcher (NOT end-to-end — model execution is multi-second here) | < 100 ms'.
issue.acceptance_test: Rename the first row to make the metric a capacity figure (e.g. 'Provisioned aggregate rps' with definition 'aggregate capacity across all hosts') or restate the target as a threshold on the measured value; define 'per-query time' explicitly (e.g. 'end-to-end request latency'); and add a note stating which of the scheduler rows binds first at the canonical service time. Also verify that the 'see note' referenced in the first Target cell exists and is reachable from this page (NOT VERIFIED here — the note is not on this page).

issue.issue: The table's first definition uses 'queries' ('Total queries processed per second across all hosts') while the same table's second row uses 'requests' ('time a request waits in the fleet dispatcher'), and the surrounding book consistently uses 'request' for the unit of work (e.g. 'per-request tokens', 'requests/second'). 'Query' is used elsewhere in the book for the agentic user input ('Take a user query routed to an agentic RQA pipeline'), so the two terms are not interchangeable in this book's own usage.
issue.evidence: Rendered table: row 1 'Total queries processed per second across all hosts'; row 2 '99th-percentile time a request waits in the fleet dispatcher'; row 4 'Fraction of per-query time spent in dispatcher, not compute'.
issue.acceptance_test: Use 'request' consistently in Table 20-1 (and 'per-request time' in row 4), or, if 'query' is deliberately distinguished from 'request' in this chapter, define the distinction in the table's note. Acceptance: no row in the table mixes the two nouns for the same object.

issue.figure: FIGURE 20.1 — Fleet capacity vs host count (canonical workload)
issue.issue: The figure's caption and its own Note assign different host counts to the same derate name. Caption: 'the throughput-efficiency derate flattens the canonical 40 rps peak once 22 hosts are provisioned — 21 ideal / 22 at 95% efficiency on the KV screen — 23 with the p95 derate on the case (ii) prefill screen (§3)'. Note: 'this figure models the KV-residency/throughput screen only (21 hosts ideal, 22 at p95; the prefill screen in §3 binds higher — 23 hosts (case (ii) with the p derate)...)'. The in-figure annotation agrees with the caption ('21 hosts (ideal / 22 at 95%)'), so the Note is the outlier: it labels the 0.95 throughput-efficiency factor as 'p95' while the caption reserves 'p95 derate' for a different, larger derate that yields 23 hosts.
